en: First Chapter, First Pāda. (In this Pāda, there is an investigation of passages containing clear marks of Brahman. 1. The Section on the Desire to Know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1.
This is the first aphorism of the Vedānta-mīmāṃsā-śāstra, which is intended to be explained:
*athāto brahmajijñāsā* (Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman).
Therein, the word *atha* (now) is understood in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), not in the sense of formal commencement (*adhikāra*).
Because the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is not something for which one lacks qualification,
and because an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) has no syntactic connection within the meaning of the sentence;
it serves as an auspicious purpose only when employed for another primary purpose by virtue of its mere sound.
Furthermore, since dependence on what was previously mentioned is, in effect, not different from immediate succession (*ānantarya*),

and given that it has the sense of immediate succession, just as the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) necessarily depends upon the prior occurrence of Vedic study, so too must that which the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) necessarily depends upon be stated;
however, the immediate succession following one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāyānantarya*) is common to both.
[Objection: But surely there is a distinction here for the purpose of understanding ritual action (karma). [Reply: No;
because even prior to the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā), the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) is possible for one who has studied the Vedānta.
And just as there is a rule of immediate succession regarding the cutting out of the heart and other organs, [so too is there a rule regarding the sequence of study].
Because a sequence was intended [in the previous case], no such sequence is intended here;

for there is no evidence for a relationship of subordinate and principal, or for a qualification based on prior entitlement, and because the objects of the inquiry into Dharma and the inquiry into Brahman differ in their respective fruits.
Knowledge of dharma has prosperity as its fruit, and that depends upon performance;
however, the realization of Brahman has the supreme good as its fruit and does not depend upon any other performance.
Furthermore, dharma is something to be accomplished and does not exist at the time of its cognition.
Because [the object of knowledge] there is dependent upon human activity;
here, however, the existent Brahman is the object of inquiry, and because it is eternal, it is not dependent upon human activity.
Furthermore, there is a difference in the operation of the injunction.
For an injunction that is the defining characteristic of dharma informs a person only by enjoining him toward its own object;
however, an injunction regarding Brahman merely informs the person.
Since the realization [of Brahman] is produced by the injunction itself, the person is not enjoined toward that realization.
Just as there is the comprehension of an object through the contact of the sense organ with that object, so it is here.
Therefore, something must be stated immediately prior to which the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) is taught.
It is said: [it is] the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities (*nityānityavastuviveka*).
Dispassion toward the enjoyment of objects for the sake of this world or the next,
perfection in the means such as tranquility and self-restraint, and the desire for liberation.
For when these [means] exist, it is possible to desire to know and to know Brahman both before and after the desire to know Dharma (dharmajijñāsā), but not in their absence.
Therefore, by the word *atha*, the immediate succession following the attainment of the aforementioned means is taught.
The word *ataḥ* signifies "because of this" (the reason).

For the Veda itself demonstrates that the means to the highest good, such as the Agnihotra and other rites, yield impermanent results, in passages such as: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).
Likewise, it demonstrates that the supreme human goal is attained through the knowledge of Brahman, in passages such as: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
Therefore, immediately after the attainment of the aforementioned means of accomplishment, the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā) must be undertaken.
"Inquiry into Brahman" (brahmajijñāsā) means the desire to know Brahman.
And Brahman has the definition that will be stated later: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]."
For this very reason, one should not suspect that the word *brahman* has any other meaning such as "genus" (*jāti*) and so forth;
furthermore, the genitive case in *brahmaṇaḥ* denotes the object (*karman*), not a residual relation (*śeṣa*),
because the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) requires an object.
And because no other object of inquiry is specified.

Now, it may be argued that even if the genitive case is taken in the sense of a residual relation (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), the fact that Brahman is the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not contradicted, since a general relation necessarily implies a specific one.
Even so, for one who abandons the directly perceived objecthood of Brahman and instead postulates an indirect objecthood by way of a commonality, the effort would be futile.
If it is argued that it is not futile because it serves the purpose of promising an investigation into everything resting upon Brahman, we say no.
Because when the primary subject is embraced, those things required by it are implied by the sense [of the text].
For Brahman is the primary subject because it is that which is most desired to be attained through knowledge.

Once that primary subject—the object of the desire to know—is embraced, those other matters without which the desire to know Brahman would not be complete are already implied by the sense; therefore, they need not be formulated as separate sūtras.
Just as when it is said, "The king is going," the going of the king together with his retinue is understood, so it is here;
and because it conforms to the Vedic scripture:
"From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).
Such scriptural passages as these,
including "Seek to know that; that is Brahman," demonstrate directly that Brahman is the object of the desire to know.
And that [usage] is supported by the sūtra if the genitive case is understood as the objective (karmaṇi-ṣaṣṭhī);
therefore, "of Brahman" (brahmaṇaḥ) is the genitive in the sense of the object.
The desire to know is *jijñāsā*.
Knowledge culminating in realization is the object of the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*),
because desire has as its object the fruit of an action.
For Brahman is intended to be understood by means of the instrument of knowledge (pramāṇa) that is cognition; indeed,
the realization of Brahman is the supreme human goal, because it eradicates the evils such as ignorance— the seed of the entire cycle of transmigration.
Therefore, Brahman is to be sought after with the desire to know.
Furthermore, that Brahman must be either well-known or unknown.
If it is well-known, it need not be an object of inquiry;
if, on the other hand, it is unknown, it cannot possibly be an object of inquiry.
It is said: there indeed exists Brahman, whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated; it is omniscient and endowed with all powers.
For when the word *brahman* is etymologically analyzed, meanings such as eternal purity and so forth are understood,
because they follow from the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* (to grow or expand).
Furthermore, the existence of Brahman is well-established because it is the Self of all.
For everyone believes in the existence of a self;
no one thinks, "I am not.
If the establishment of the existence of a self did not occur, the entire world would perceive, "I am not."
And the Self is Brahman.

If, then, Brahman is already well-known in the world as being the Self, it follows once again that it is already known and thus not an object of inquiry. No; because there are conflicting views regarding its specific nature.
Ordinary people and the Lokāyatikas maintain that the self is merely the body characterized by consciousness;
others hold that the senses themselves are conscious and constitute the self;
still others say it is the mind.
Some maintain that consciousness alone is momentary;
others hold it to be empty; and yet others assert that there exists a transmigrating agent distinct from the body and so forth.
Others say he is the enjoyer;
some say he is merely the enjoyer and not the agent;
and some say there exists a Lord distinct from him, who is omniscient and the creator of all.
Others maintain that the self is the enjoyer;
thus, many are in disagreement, relying upon various arguments and statements, as well as fallacious arguments and fallacious statements.
In this regard, one who accepts something without investigation may be thwarted from the supreme good and incur misfortune.

Therefore, under the guise of introducing the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) of the Vedānta texts—aided by reasoning that does not contradict them and having liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) as its purpose—is now commenced.

[Sūtra 1] [Note: An *adhikaraṇa* (topic) is to be understood as having five components: the subject matter (*viṣaya*), doubt (*saṃdeha*), connection (*saṃgati*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Thus, when there is effort arising from the desire to act produced by knowledge, the dharma of sacrifice and so forth comes into being.]

Some maintain that because Brahman is free from all veils, it possesses the nature of the fruit [of knowledge], and therefore a fourth-case compound (*caturthī-samāsa*) must be accepted here on the grounds of its utility for knowing that [Brahman], according to the rule "the fourth case is used when one thing exists for the sake of another" (*caturthī tadarthe*), and so forth. Furthermore:
"Because it attains, because it takes up, because it eats the objects here, and because its existence is continuous, it is called the Self (*ātman*)."
An enumeration of those who hold erroneous views: the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) among the Mādhyamikas; the proponents of momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇikajñānavāda*) among the Yogācāras;
and the proponents of momentary external objects inferred from the forms of cognition (*jñānākārānumeyakṣaṇikabāhyārthavāda*) among the Sautrāntikas.
The doctrine of momentary external objects belongs to the Vaibhāṣikas; the doctrine of the body as the [only] object belongs to the Cārvākas;
and the doctrine of the transformation of the body distinct from the body belongs to the Digambaras—such [doctrines] are to be inferred accordingly.
Section 2: On the Origin and Other Attributes. Sūtra 2.
It has been stated that Brahman is to be investigated.
But what are the characteristics of that Brahman? To this, the venerable author of the Sūtras replies:
"From which [Brahman] proceed the origin and so forth of this [world].
(BS 1.1.2) The term "origin and so forth" (*janmādi*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities are included in the meaning (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).
The meaning of the compound is the origin, subsistence, and dissolution (*janmasthitibhaṅga*) [of the world].
The status of birth as the beginning [of the cosmic process] depends both on scriptural indication and on the nature of reality.
First, regarding scriptural indication: in the passage, "From which indeed these beings are born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), one observes the sequence of birth, maintenance, and dissolution.
It is also the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*),
because it is possible for a substratum (*dharmin*) that has acquired its existence through birth to undergo the effort of remaining [in that state].
The word "this" (*asya*) is a designation by means of the pronoun *idam* for the substratum brought to mind by perception and other means of knowledge.
The genitive case [in "of this"] is used in the sense of relating the attributes such as birth and so forth.

The word "from which" (yataḥ) is an indication of the cause. [It refers to] the birth, subsistence, and dissolution of this world—which is differentiated by name and form, joined with many agents and enjoyers, the locus of actions, times, causes, and fruits determined for each [being], and whose structure is inconceivable even by the mind.
The ellipsis of the sentence is: "That from which [the world] arises—being an omniscient and omnipotent cause—is Brahman.
Although other modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*) are included within these three, only birth, subsistence, and destruction are mentioned here;

for if one were to adopt the sequence of "is born," "exists," and so forth as recited by Yāska, those states would only be possible during the period of the world's subsistence, and thus the origin, subsistence, and destruction of the world from its primal cause would not be grasped.
"Do not fear that"; for whatever is the origin of Brahman, in that very same [Brahman] its persistence and dissolution are also grasped.

It is not possible to conceive of the origin and so forth of the world— characterized as described above— from anything other than the Lord who possesses the aforementioned characteristics; that is, not from the Pradhāna (primordial matter), nor from insentient atoms, nor from non-existence, nor from a transmigrating soul, nor from inherent nature (svabhāva),
because specific places, times, and causes are here accepted as the material basis.
The proponents of God as the cause (Īśvarakāraṇins) consider this very same inference to be the proof for the existence of a Lord distinct from transmigrating beings and so forth.
[Objection: But has not that very same thing been presented here in the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādi-sūtra)? [Reply:
No, because the purpose of the Sūtras is to string together the flowers of the Vedānta passages.
For it is the Vedānta passages that are cited by the Sūtras and subjected to inquiry. This inquiry culminates in the ascertainment of the meaning of those passages.

However, since there exist Vedānta passages that declare the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, inference—provided it does not contradict the Vedānta passages—is not precluded from being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for strengthening the grasp of their meaning.
Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*) is accepted as an auxiliary to scripture (*śruti*).

For instance, the scripture states: "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.5), and: "Just as a learned and intelligent man, having been led by a guide, would reach Gandhāra itself, even so here a person who has a teacher knows [the Truth]" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.14.2).
And thus [the Sūtra] indicates that the Self requires the assistance of human intellect.

It is not the case that, as in the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, as well as experience (*anubhava*) and so forth, are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) here according to their respective applicability; for the knowledge of Brahman culminates in experience and has an already existent entity (*bhūtavastu*) as its object. For in the case of a subject matter that is to be accomplished (*kartavya*), there is no dependence on experience, and thus scripture and the like alone would possess authority, since what is to be accomplished derives its existence from the person [who performs it].
Worldly and Vedic action can be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise;
for example, one travels by horse, or otherwise, on foot.
Or it does not go;
likewise: "One takes the ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra, one does not take the ṣoḍaśin cup at the Atirātra."
Furthermore, injunctions and prohibitions such as "one offers after sunrise" and "one offers before sunrise," as well as options, general rules, and exceptions, would be meaningful in this context.
But the object itself is not conceptualized as "it exists thus," "it does not exist thus," or "it does not exist";
rather, conceptualizations depend upon human intellect.
Knowledge of the true nature of the object does not depend upon human intellect.
What then? That [cognition] depends solely on the actual state of things (*vastutantra*).
For, regarding a single post, the cognition "it is either a post or a person or something else" is not a cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*);
therein, the thought "it is a person or something else" is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
The knowledge that "it is indeed a post" is a cognition of reality (tattvajñāna),
because it is dependent upon the object itself. Likewise, the validity of cognitions concerning real entities is dependent upon the object itself.
This being the case, even the knowledge of Brahman depends solely upon the thing itself (*vastutantra*), because its object is an existent reality (*bhūtavastu*).

[Objection: If Brahman is an existent reality, it must necessarily be an object of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); thus, the investigation of Vedāntic passages would result in being purposeless. [Reply: No.
Because there is no apprehension of a connection due to [Brahman] not being an object of the senses;
by their very nature, the senses have [empirical] objects as their domain, not Brahman as their domain.
For if Brahman were indeed an object of the senses,
this effect would be apprehended as being connected with Brahman;
however, when only the effect is apprehended, it is impossible to determine whether it is connected with Brahman or connected with some other entity whatsoever.
Therefore, the *Janmādi-sūtra* is not intended for the presentation of an inference; rather, it is for the purpose of pointing out a Vedānta passage.
But what is that Vedānta passage which the Sūtra seeks here to indicate?
"Bhṛgu Vāruṇi indeed approached his father Varuṇa, saying:
'Teach me, O Blessed One, the Brahman.'"
Having begun thus: "That from which these beings are born; that by which, once born, they live; that into which they enter when they pass away."
"Seek to understand that;
that is Brahman. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1)
And its definitive statement is: "Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born; by bliss, once born, they live; into bliss they enter at their passing."

Other similar passages of this kind, which have as their subject matter the Cause whose nature is eternally pure, conscious, and free, and who is omniscient, are also to be cited. // 2 // [This concludes] the section on the Scripture being the Source [of knowledge of Brahman].
Having introduced the idea that Brahman is omniscient by demonstrating its status as the cause of the world, the author confirms that very point, saying:
"Because it is the source of the scripture" (Śāstrayonitvāt).

Brahman is the source—that is, the cause—of the great scripture consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth, which is augmented by numerous branches of knowledge, which illuminates all objects like a lamp, and which is almost omniscient.
The possibility of a treatise such as this— the Veda and so forth— which possesses the qualities of omniscience, arising from anyone other than an omniscient being, does not exist.
For whatever extensive treatise originates from a particular person—
even one whose subject matter covers only a single portion of what is knowable, such as grammar and the like— it is well known in the world that he possesses knowledge far exceeding that [treatise].

What more need be said? From that Great Being, the Source, there arose— without effort and as if in mere play, like a person’s natural breath— the collection known as the Rigveda and so forth, which is divided into numerous branches and recensions, which is the cause of the distinctions among gods, animals, humans, castes, and stages of life, and which is a mine of all knowledge.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The Ṛgveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.10),
and so forth; [it follows that] that great Being possesses unsurpassed omniscience and omnipotence.

Alternatively, the aforementioned scripture, such as the Ṛgveda and others, is the *yoni*—that is, the cause or the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—for the realization of the true nature of this Brahman.
The intended meaning is that Brahman, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world, is understood solely through the authority of scripture.
The scripture was cited in the previous sūtra: "From which indeed these beings are born," and so on.
For what purpose, then, is this sūtra, since by citing such a treatise in the previous sūtra itself, the fact that Brahman has scripture as its source (śāstrayonitva) was already demonstrated?

It is said in reply: Since it might be suspected that in that [previous] case, because scripture was not explicitly mentioned by the words of the sūtra, only inference based on "birth and so forth" was presented, this sūtra is intended to remove that suspicion.
"It proceeded [from Him], because He is the source of the scriptures" (Sūtra 1.1.3).
Regarding this, there are four Vedas to be supplemented (*upabṛṃhaṇīya*).

Among them, the *Purāṇas* primarily supplement those passages that set forth creation and so forth, as well as the *arthavādas* consisting of accounts of the deeds of others and ancient legends; incidentally, they also supplement the portion concerning non-duality and the portion concerning ritual action.

The Nyāya-śāstra, however, supplements [the Veda] by analyzing and making known the categories of existence through the definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the objects of cognition (prameya).
The Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsās, for their part, are employed by way of determining the intended meaning (tātparya).
The Dharma-śāstra supplements the scriptural portion consisting of injunctions (vidhi), whether it be the Śruti or the Smṛti.

The *Śikṣā* reinforces the meaning of the injunction that "one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied" by means of defining the places of articulation, the organs of pronunciation, and so forth.
The *Kalpas*, however, are employed for the purpose of defining ritual applications.
As for *Vyākaraṇa*, it analyzes the meanings of words, determining that "in this particular sense, this word is correct."

Nirukta demonstrates the etymological meaning within various words; Chandaḥśāstra elucidates the meters found in the Vedas, such as Gāyatrī and others, by means of their defining characteristics; and Jyotiṣa establishes the specific times prescribed in such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the Full Moon [offering] on the full moon day" and "one should sacrifice with the New Moon [offering] on the new moon day."
And thus, the greatness of that [text] is evident, since many great sages who composed treatises such as the Purāṇas were engaged in providing explanations for its various regions.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose subject matter (artha) is dharma in an extensive form"; the meaning is "extensive" (vistṛta).
4. The Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 4: But how can it be said that Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, when—
"Since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their purpose are useless" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1).
Thus, it was demonstrated that the scripture is subordinate to action;
consequently, the Vedāntas would be useless.
Because they do not have action as their purpose;
or else, they are subordinate to injunctions for ritual action by virtue of revealing the agent, the deity, and so forth,
or they serve the purpose of enjoining other actions such as meditative worship (*upāsanā*).
For it is not possible to teach an established entity,
because an established entity is the object of perception and other means of valid cognition;
and in teaching such a thing, there would be no human purpose, as it is devoid of anything to be abandoned or acquired.

For this very reason, so that passages such as "He wept" (*sa arodīt*) would not be rendered meaningless, it was stated [in the Jaimini Sūtras] that "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, they exist for the purpose of praising the injunction" (Jai.Sū. 1.2.7); thus, their meaningfulness is established by way of being eulogistic. Furthermore, regarding mantras such as "For food, thee" (*iṣe tvā*), their relevance to ritual action has been stated by virtue of their denoting the action and its means.
Nowhere is the meaningfulness of Vedic statements seen or established as possible without contact with an injunction;
nor is an injunction possible regarding the nature of an already established entity,
because an injunction has action as its object.

Therefore, since the Vedāntas reveal the nature of the agent, the deity, and so forth required for ritual action, they are subordinate to injunctions regarding action (*kriyāvidhi*). Alternatively, if this is not accepted for fear of contradicting the context (*prakaraṇa*), then at least they must be concerned with rituals such as meditation (*upāsanā*) mentioned within their own sentences. Thus, it follows that Brahman does not have the scripture as its source (*śāstrayonitva*). To this, it is replied: [The opponent’s position: Therefore, since the Vedāntas reveal the nature of the agent, the deity, and so forth required for ritual action, they are subordinate to injunctions regarding action. Alternatively, if this is not accepted for fear of contradicting the context, then at least they must be concerned with rituals such as meditation mentioned within their own sentences. Consequently, Brahman does not have the scripture as its source. To this, it is replied: [The Siddhāntin’s position]... [follows].
Note: "Of the sacred tradition" (*āmnāyasya*) refers to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Its meaning is as follows: since the Veda, which is the sacred tradition, is intent upon enjoining action (*kriyāpratipādanaparatvāt*), those passages that do not have that purpose—namely, those that do not concern action, such as the sentence "He wept" (*sa roroda*) and so forth—are purposeless.
Therefore, it is said that the authority of the Vedas is non-eternal and indefinite.
The established conclusion is that "there is a syntactic connection of words denoting existing entities with words denoting action.

This means that within those Vedic sentences, there is a connection of words denoting existing entities (*bhūta*)— that is, sentences conveying accomplished facts— with words denoting action (*kriyārtha*), such as "one should not give silver on the sacrificial grass" (*barhiṣi rajataṃ na deyam*) or "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*).

And thus, when the connection is established by supplying meanings such as "condemnation," its status as a means of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is proven through the establishment of its focus on action;
the meaning is that this is because no fruit arises from the knowledge of an already-established entity.
But that [status] is due to *samanvaya* (coherence). (BBs 1.1.4)
The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside the prima facie view.
That Brahman—the omniscient, omnipotent cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world—is understood from the Vedānta scriptures alone.
How so? Because of the harmony (samanvaya) [of the texts].
For in all the Vedāntas, the sentences are consistently followed as demonstrating this very meaning with full intent:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1); "One only, without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
"In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).
"This is that Brahman—without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
"This very Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19) "Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front," (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11), and so forth.
And once the coherent connection (*samanvaya*) of the words contained therein is understood with respect to the nature of Brahman, it is not appropriate to assume any other meaning.
Because this would entail the abandonment of what is heard in scripture and the postulation of what is not heard;

furthermore, it is not understood that those [passages] are intent upon establishing the nature of a creator, as seen in the text: "By what means, then, could one perceive whom? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13).
Thus, from such scriptural passages as those which investigate action, its factors, and its results,
it follows that Brahman does not fall within the domain of perception and other means of knowledge, even though it possesses the nature of an established reality,
as stated in "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Thus, because the nature of Brahman-Atman cannot be understood without the scripture;
as for the objection that instruction would be purposeless because [Brahman] is devoid of anything to be abandoned or acquired,
this is not a fault.

Since the fulfillment of the human goal is achieved solely through the realization of the identity of Brahman—which is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted—thereby effecting the abandonment of all afflictions;
there is no contradiction whatsoever even if the presentation of deities and so forth serves the purpose of meditation (upāsanā) contained within its own specific scriptural context.
However, it is not possible for Brahman to be subordinate to an injunction for meditation in that manner.
Because, in the case of oneness, since it is devoid of anything to be abandoned or acquired, there arises the sublation of the dualistic cognition of action, agent, and so forth;
for once dualistic cognition has been uprooted by the cognition of oneness, its recurrence is impossible,
whereby Brahman could be understood as being subordinate to injunctions for meditative worship.
Although elsewhere the validity of Vedic statements has not been observed without contact with an injunction (*vidhi*),
nevertheless, because the knowledge of the Self culminates in its own fruit, the authority of the scripture concerning that subject cannot be denied.
Nor is the authority of the scripture something to be established through inference.
Therefore, it would have to depend upon an illustration seen elsewhere;
thus, it is established that Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition (*śāstrapramāṇaka*).

Here, others raise an objection: even if Brahman has scripture as its means of valid cognition, nevertheless, Brahman is presented by the scripture solely as the object of an injunction for realization (*pratipattividhi*).
Just as sacrificial posts, the Āhavanīya fire, and so forth, though they are not worldly (alaukika), are presented by the scripture as subordinate elements of injunctions, so it is here.
Why is this so?
Because the purpose of scripture consists in [prescribing] engagement and cessation.

For thus say those who know the purport of the treatise: "Its purpose is indeed seen to be the comprehension of ritual action" (*dṛṣṭo hi tasyārthaḥ karmāvabodhanam*); "An injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one toward action" (*codaneti kriyāyāḥ pravartakaṃ vacanam*);
"The knowledge of that [Dharma] is instruction" (*tasya jñānamupadeśaḥ*)—(Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.5).
"Of those [words] that have attained their [final] form, there is a recitation for the sake of action" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.25),
and "Because the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.1).
Therefore, the scripture is purposeful insofar as it impels a person toward a particular object and withdraws him from another particular object;
and other [scriptural portions] are useful as being subordinate to that.
By analogy with that, the Vedāntas should likewise possess purposefulness.

And since [the Vedas] have injunction as their primary purport, it is logical that just as the Agnihotra and other rites are enjoined for one who desires heaven and so forth, so too is the knowledge of Brahman enjoined for one who desires immortality.

But has it not been stated here that there is a difference in the objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*)—that in the Karma-kāṇḍa the object of inquiry is Dharma, which is yet to be brought into being (*bhavya*), whereas here the object of inquiry is Brahman, which is already existent (*bhūta*) and eternally accomplished?
In that case, the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman ought to be distinct from the fruit of the knowledge of Dharma, which depends upon performance.
It cannot be so;
for Brahman is presented precisely as that which is to be realized by one who is engaged in the performance of duties, as in the passage:
"The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
"That Self which is free from evil—that is to be sought, that is to be desired to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1);
"One should meditate on it as the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7); "Meditate on the Self alone as the world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15).

In light of injunctions such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9), when the inquiry arises as to what this Self is and what that Brahman is, all the Vedānta texts are employed to provide the definition of their essential nature: [the Self is] eternal, omniscient, omnipresent, eternally satisfied, and by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free.
"Consciousness is bliss, Brahman"—such passages as these [are examples].
And from the meditation upon that [Brahman], liberation, though seen in the scriptures, will become the fruit;
for when there is the mere statement of a reality not entered into by an injunction of action, the possibility of relinquishing or acquiring [it] exists.
The Vedānta statements would be as purposeless as sentences such as "the earth consists of seven islands" or "this king is going.
[Objection: But even when stating a mere fact, there is purposefulness—as in "this is a rope, this is not a snake"—because it removes the fear produced by delusion.
Likewise here too, there would be purposefulness through the teaching of the reality of the Self as non-transmigrating, which removes the delusion of being a transmigrator.
This might be so,
provided that the delusion of a snake [is removed] just like upon hearing the true nature of the rope.
The delusion of being a transmigrating being would cease through the mere hearing of the nature of Brahman;
yet it does not cease,
because even for one who has heard of Brahman, the characteristics of a transmigrating being— such as pleasure and pain— are observed just as before.

And because we see the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) following hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the passage, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5),
Brahman must therefore be accepted as having the scripture as its authority only by virtue of being the object of an injunction regarding its realization.
To this it is replied: No;
because of the difference between the fruits of ritual action (*karman*) and the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*).
Ritual action—whether physical, vocal, or mental—is established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* and is designated as *dharma*.

That which is the object of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*)— enunciated in the aphorism "Now, therefore, the desire to know dharma" (*atha ato dharmajijñāsā*, Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.1)— is indeed dharma; for even *adharma*, such as violence (*hiṃsā*) and the like, must be desired to be known because it is characterized by prohibitive injunctions, so that it may be avoided.

Regarding the two—dharma and adharma—which are characterized by injunctions and which consist of benefit and harm, their fruits, pleasure and pain, are directly perceived as being experienced through the body, speech, and mind alone; they are produced by the contact of the senses with their objects and are well known among all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary plants.
Furthermore, a gradation of pleasure is traditionally taught among embodied beings, beginning from the human state up to the end of the realm of Brahmā.
And from that, a gradation of the dharma which is its cause is understood;
from the gradation of the dharma follows a gradation of eligibility.
And a gradation of eligibility based on factors such as desire and capability is well known.
And thus, it is only for those who perform sacrifices and other rites that there is travel by the northern path due to the excellence of their knowledge and meditative concentration;
whereas for those who possess only the means of sacrifice, public works, and charity, there is travel by the southern path through the sequence of smoke and so forth.

Even in that case, there is a gradation of pleasure and a gradation of its means, as established by the scripture: "Having dwelt there as long as their [meritorious] works last" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5).

From this it is understood that, likewise, among humans and others down to the denizens of hell and the immobile beings, even a mere fragment of pleasure is to be accomplished solely through dharma characterized by injunctions; this is understood as existing in varying degrees of intensity.

Similarly, because suffering exists in varying degrees among embodied beings in higher and lower realms, its cause—adharma—is understood to exist in varying degrees, as is the case for those who perform it, regarding the adharma characterized by the prohibition of injunctions.

Thus, for those possessed of defects such as ignorance, the form of *saṃsāra*—which is preceded by the assumption of a body caused by the varying degrees of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and which consists in the varying degrees of pleasure and pain—is well-established through *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and reasoning.
Accordingly, the *Smṛti* reiterates the nature of *saṃsāra* as described: "For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.1).
And: "The pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who is indeed bodiless. (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.12.1)

Thus, by the prohibition of contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant, it is understood that the state of bodilessness called liberation is denied to be an effect of dharma characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
For if it were an effect of dharma, the prohibition of contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant would not be tenable.
If it is argued that bodilessness itself is the effect of dharma, [the answer is: no.
Because that [Self] is of the nature of its own being:
"The wise man does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self— bodiless, yet dwelling within bodies that are transient" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.21).
For [it is known] from such scriptural passages as: "Indeed, it is without breath, without mind, pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2), and "For this Person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15).

Therefore, it is established that the state of bodilessness called liberation— which is distinct from the fruits of actions to be performed— is eternal. In this regard, some things are "transformative eternal" (*pariṇāminitya*), such as for those who maintain the eternity of the world consisting of earth and so forth, wherein even while undergoing modification, the cognition "this is that very same thing" is not sublated.
And just as the qualities (guṇas) belong to the Sāṃkhyas,
this [reality], however, is ultimate,
immutably eternal.
Pervading all like space,
devoid of all modification,
eternally satisfied.
It is partless,
its very nature being self-luminous;
wherein neither merit nor demerit, along with their effects and the three periods of time, ever recur.
That state of being bodiless is called liberation:
"Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this [world] of what is done and what is not done, other than what has been and what is yet to be" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.14).
From such scriptural passages as these,
it follows that if Brahman— the subject of this inquiry now commenced— were taught as something to be accomplished through action, [it would contradict the nature of Brahman].
If liberation were accepted as something to be accomplished by that which is to be performed,
it would necessarily be impermanent.
This being the case, it would follow that liberation is merely some excellence among those aforementioned fruits of action, which exist in varying degrees and are themselves impermanent.
Furthermore, liberation is accepted as eternal by all proponents of liberation;
therefore, it is not logical to teach Brahman as something subordinate to an action to be performed.
Moreover, [it is said]: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
"And his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8);
"Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing at all" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9).
"Truly, O Janaka, you have attained fearlessness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4);
"Then he knew himself alone, saying, 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all" (Vājasaneyi Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad 1.4.10).

In this regard, scriptural passages such as, "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7), by demonstrating that liberation follows immediately after the knowledge of Brahman, preclude any other intervening activity. Likewise, [the scripture says]: "Seeing this very [truth], the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and I was the Sun'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Thus, this [statement] should be cited to exclude any other activity between the vision of Brahman and the state of being the Self of all;
just as in the expression "he sings while standing," it is understood that there is no other action performed by that agent between the acts of standing and singing. As it is said:
"For you are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore of ignorance" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.8).

"Indeed, I have heard from those like your reverence that the knower of the Self overcomes sorrow; therefore, O Venerable One, I am in sorrow. May you, O Venerable One, carry me across to the further shore of this sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3);
and "To him whose impurities had been wiped away, the Venerable Sanatkumāra showed the further shore of darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
Such scriptural passages as these demonstrate that the fruit of the knowledge of the Self is solely the cessation of the obstacles to liberation.

And likewise, there is the aphorism composed by the Teacher, which is reinforced by reasoning: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of each preceding one, resulting in liberation" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.2).
And the removal of false knowledge occurs through the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self.
Furthermore, this knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of a metaphorical identification (*saṃpad*), as in the passage:
"The mind is indeed infinite; the Viśvedevas are infinite; by that [identification], he conquers an infinite world" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).
Nor is it of the nature of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Just as in the passages "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1) and "The sun is Brahman, thus says Āruṇi" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1), there is the superimposition of the vision of Brahman upon the mind, the sun, and so forth.
Nor is it based on the connection with a specific ritual action, as in the cases: "Air, indeed, is the absorber" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.3.1) or "Breath, indeed, is the absorber";
nor does it take the form of a purificatory rite that is a subsidiary part of a ritual action, like the act of looking at the clarified butter (*ājya*).

For if the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self were accepted as being of the nature of a metaphorical identification (*saṃpad*) and so forth, [then the statement] "That thou art" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.7) [would be undermined].

The syntactical coherence of such statements as "I am Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10) and "This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), which are intent upon establishing the reality of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, would be undermined.

Furthermore, scriptural passages such as "The knot of the heart is rent asunder; all doubts are cut away" (Muṇḍaka 2.2.8), which declare that the fruit [of knowledge] is the cessation of ignorance, would be contradicted [if this were not the case].
Also: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka 3.2.9).
Statements such as these, which speak of attaining that state of being, would not be logically consistent with the view that [the knowledge] consists of identification (*saṃpad*) and the like.
Therefore, the realization of the oneness of Brahman and the Self is not of the nature of identification and so forth;
consequently, the knowledge of Brahman is not dependent upon human effort.
Rather, it is dependent upon the object, like the knowledge of a thing that is the object of means of valid cognition such as perception.
It is impossible by any reasoning to conceive of such a Brahman and its knowledge as entering into the sphere of action (kārya).
Nor can Brahman enter into the sphere of action by being the object of the act of knowing.

Because of the negation of its being the object of the act of knowing, as in "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown" (Kena Upaniṣad 1.3), and also because of [the statement]:
"By what should one know Him by whom one knows all this? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13).

Likewise, there is also a negation of Brahman being the object of the act of worship: having introduced the fact that Brahman is not an object of cognition with the words, "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed," [the text continues], "Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.4).
If it be argued that since Brahman is not an object of cognition, its being the source of the scriptures (śāstrayonitva) is untenable, we say: no.
Because the scripture has as its purpose the cessation of the distinctions imagined by ignorance,
it does not seek to teach Brahman as an object characterized by "this-ness.
Rather, by teaching [Brahman] as the inner self— which is not an object— it removes the distinctions of the known, the knower, and the act of knowing that are imagined by ignorance.
And so says the scripture: "He for whom it is not thought has understood it; he who thinks he knows it does not know it.
It is unknown to those who understand it, and known to those who do not understand it" (Kena Upaniṣad 2.3).
And so forth, as in: "One should not see the seer of seeing," and "One should not know the knower of knowing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2).

Therefore, since liberation consists in the presentation of the nature of the eternally liberated Self by means of the cessation of the state of being a transmigrator imagined through ignorance, it does not suffer from the defect of impermanence.
However, for one for whom liberation is something to be produced, it would be either mental, vocal, or...
Or it is logical that [liberation] depends upon some bodily action;
likewise, if those two positions maintain that liberation is something to be modified (*vikārya*), then liberation would necessarily be impermanent.
For curds and the like, being modifications, [are not eternal].
Or, something produced, such as a jar and so forth, is seen in the world to be eternal;
nor is there a dependence on an effect even by way of being attained.
Because it is not to be attained when it is one's own essential nature;
and even if Brahman were distinct from one's essential nature, it would still not be something to be attained,
because Brahman is omnipresent and thus its nature is eternally attained by everyone.
Nor is liberation something to be produced by conditioning, such that it would depend upon an activity, like space.
For what is called "conditioning" (saṃskāra) must occur either by the imparting of qualities to that which is to be conditioned or by the removal of defects.
It cannot occur through the imparting of qualities, because liberation is the very nature of Brahman, to which no excellence can be added.
Nor is it by the removal of defects, since liberation consists in the eternally pure nature of Brahman; rather,
liberation— which is an inherent attribute of one's own self— becomes firmly established and is manifested when the self is being purified through ritual action.
If it is argued that luminosity is a quality [produced] when a mirror is refined by the act of polishing, we say no;
for it is impossible for the self to be the locus of an action. An action cannot even come into being unless it effects a modification in its own locus.
If the self were to undergo modification through action, the consequence would be the impermanence of the self;
furthermore, statements such as "this is said to be unchangeable" would be contradicted,
and that is undesirable.
Therefore, action residing in itself is not possible for the Self;
nor is it refined by action residing in something else, because such action does not have the Self as its object.
[Objection: But surely the embodied one is seen to be refined by actions residing in the body, such as bathing, sipping water, and wearing the sacrificial thread? [Reply: No.
Because it is precisely the Self, as grasped by ignorance and associated with the body and so forth, that undergoes purification;
for it is directly perceived that bathing, sipping water, and other such acts inhere in the body.

Therefore, it is logical that by means of those [acts] which have the body as their locus, that certain entity which is grasped by ignorance as the Self—being indeed conjoined with the body—is purified.

Just as through the equilibrium of the bodily constituents (dhātu-sāmya) resulting from medical treatment applied to the body, there arises for that which is conjoined with it and identifies with it the fruit of health—
the cognition "I am healthy"—
so too, by means of bathing, sipping water, the sacred thread, and so forth, that in which the cognition "I am pure, I am consecrated" arises is what is being refined.
And that [agent] is indeed conjoined with the body;
for by that very agent— the subject of the notion of "I" who is the object of the ego-consciousness— all actions are accomplished,
and he alone enjoys their fruit.
This is evident from the wording of the mantra: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and also from:
"The wise say that the Self, when joined with the body, the senses, and the mind, is the enjoyer" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.4).
And so it is said: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
the overseer of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious, alone and devoid of qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
He has pervaded [all], being pure, bodiless, unbreathing, without veins, clean, and untouched by evil.
And thus [it is said in] the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad* (8):
these two mantras demonstrate that Brahman is incapable of having any excellence added to it and is eternally pure;
and liberation is the state of being Brahman.
Therefore, liberation is not something to be produced by action (*saṃskārya*).
Consequently, no one can point out any other means for the entry of action toward liberation.
Thus, apart from knowledge alone, even the slightest trace of action cannot logically find a place here.
Is it not the case that what is called "knowledge" (jñāna) is a mental action? No;
because of its distinct nature.
For an action is that which is enjoined independently of the actual nature of the thing itself.
And it is dependent upon the mental activity of the person, as in:
"To whichever deity the oblation has been taken, one should meditate upon that deity in the mind when about to utter *vaṣaṭ*";
and "One should meditate upon the twilight in the mind" (AiB 3.8.1).
And in such passages as these,
although meditation (*dhyāna*) is reflection (*cintana*) and thus mental, it can nevertheless be performed, not performed, or performed otherwise by a person,
because it is dependent upon the person.
Knowledge, however, is produced by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And since a valid means of cognition has as its object a thing as it truly is, knowledge cannot be made, unmade, or otherwise made;
it is dependent solely upon the thing itself.
Nor is it dependent on scriptural injunction.
Nor is it dependent on the person;
therefore, even though cognition is mental, there is a great distinction [between it and perception].
And as it is said: "The person, O Gautama, is indeed the fire."
In the passage, "Woman indeed, O Gautama, is the fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.7.1), the mental conception of woman and man as fire occurs;
because it is produced solely by an injunction, that [conception] is indeed an action and dependent upon the person.

However, the cognition of fire that arises toward a well-known fire is neither dependent on an injunction nor dependent on a person; rather, it is dependent solely on the perceptible object. Thus, this is indeed knowledge, not an action.
This should be understood to apply to all objects that are the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This being the case, even the knowledge whose object is the *ātman* as Brahman, which is in accordance with reality (*yathābhūta*), is not dependent upon scriptural injunction (*codanā*).

Even when verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth are heard in reference to that [Brahman], they become blunt because their object is one that cannot be enjoined, like the sharpness of a razor applied to a stone.
Because its object is a reality that is neither to be abandoned nor to be adopted, one might ask:
for what purpose, then, are those statements that have the appearance of injunctions, such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen, to be heard"?
We reply: they are for the purpose of turning one away from the objects of natural inclination.
For a person who proceeds with his face turned outward, thinking "may what is desired be mine" and "may what is undesired not be mine," does not attain the ultimate human goal therein;

therefore, for one who desires that ultimate human goal, [the scriptures] turn him away from the sphere of activity of the natural aggregate of body and organs and set him in motion toward the inward current of the inner self, [saying]: "The Self, indeed, is to be seen."
Such passages as these teach the true nature of the Self— which is neither to be rejected nor accepted— to one who has set out in search of that Self:
"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).

"Where, however, for him everything has become the Self alone—then by what and whom should one see? By what and whom should one know? O, by what should one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15);
and "This Self is Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19), and so forth.
As for the claim that knowledge of the Self, being primarily concerned with what is not to be done, serves neither for rejection nor for acquisition—that is indeed accepted as it stands.
For this is our very ornament: that when the realization of Brahman as the Self occurs, all duties come to an end and one has accomplished all that was to be done.
And thus says the Śruti: "If a person were to know the Self, realizing 'This exists,' desiring what, or for the sake of what longing, would he suffer along with the body?"
"Becoming wise and having accomplished all that was to be done by knowing this, O Bhārata" (Bhagavad Gītā 15.20);
such is the Smṛti.
Therefore, Brahman is not presented as an object of an injunction for practice.

As for what some say— that "there is no portion of the Veda which speaks of a mere entity apart from injunctions regarding engagement or withdrawal, or that which is subordinate to them"— that is not so,
because the Person of the Upaniṣads is not subordinate to anything else.

That Person who is understood through the Upaniṣads alone— the non-transmigrating Brahman, distinct from the four kinds of substances such as those that are produced and so forth, situated within its own context, non-dual, and without parts—
it cannot be said that "He does not exist" or "He is not apprehended," for it is said: "This Self is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
This follows from the word "it" (iti),
because the self is impossible to deny, for whoever is the denier is himself the self.
[Objection: But surely it is untenable to say that the Self is known only from the Upaniṣads, since it is the object of the notion of "I. [Reply:
No, because it has been refuted by being established as the witness thereof.

Indeed, apart from the agent who is the object of the notion of "I," no person—who is the witness thereof, residing in all beings, equal, one, immutably eternal, and stable—has ever been apprehended in the section on ritual injunctions or in the systems of logic.
Therefore, it cannot be rejected by anyone, nor can it be reduced to being a mere subordinate element of ritual injunction (*vidhiśeṣatva*).
Precisely because it is the Self (*ātman*) of all, it is neither to be abandoned nor to be acquired.
For every collection of perishing modifications perishes only up to the limit of the Puruṣa.
The person (puruṣa) is indestructible because of the absence of any cause for destruction,
and because of the absence of any cause for modification, it is eternally immutable.
Therefore, its nature is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated.

Hence it is said: "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal" (Katha Upaniṣad 1.3.11), and "I ask you about that Puruṣa who is known through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26).
Thus, the qualification "belonging to the Upaniṣads" (aupaniṣada) is appropriate for the Person (puruṣa), as he is revealed as the primary subject within the Upaniṣads.
Therefore, the statement that there is no portion of the Veda concerned with an already existing reality (bhūtavastu) is mere temerity.
As for the citation from those who know the purport of the scriptures: "For its purpose is seen to be the comprehension of ritual action," and so forth.
Because that [Brahman] is the object of the desire to know dharma, this should be understood as having the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions in mind.

Furthermore, for those who accept with absolute certainty the principle that "since the Veda has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that [action] as their meaning are useless," there follows the undesirable consequence that teachings concerning existing entities (*bhūta*) would be useless.

This is because, apart from injunctions regarding engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and what is subordinate to them, if the scripture teaches an existing entity, it must do so for the sake of something to be accomplished (*bhavya*).
What is the reason for saying that [the Veda] does not teach an eternally immutable reality (*bhūta*)?
For a reality being taught does not become an action (*kriyā*).
If it is argued that even though a reality is non-action, the teaching of reality is solely for the sake of action because it serves as a means (*sādhana*) to action; [we reply: ...
This is not a fault; for even though it has action as its purpose, the reality that possesses the power to transcend action is indeed taught.
Its purpose, however, is simply to serve the function of action.
And the reality is not left untaught by this much alone.
Even if it were taught, what would that avail you?
It is said in reply: the teaching of the reality of the self, which has not yet been understood, ought to be exactly like that.

By the realization of that [Self], the cessation of false knowledge—which is the cause of transmigratory existence—is accomplished as the purpose; thus, its purposefulness remains established through the teaching of things that are means to action.
Furthermore, abstention is taught in such injunctions as "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," and that [abstention] is not an action.
Nor is it a means for action.

If it were argued that the teaching of things that do not have action as their purpose is useless, then it would follow that the teachings on abstention—such as "A Brahmin is not to be killed"—are useless;
and that is undesirable.

Nor can it be maintained that the negative particle (*nañ*)—through its association with the meaning of "killing" as established by its own nature—is capable of being construed as having the sense of a non-occurring action, apart from the state of indifference consisting in the cessation of the act of killing;
for this is the very nature of the negative particle: that it makes known the absence of that which is connected to itself.
And the cognition of non-existence is the cause of indifference;
that [cognition], like a fire whose fuel is consumed, subsides by itself.

Therefore, we consider that in prohibitions such as "A Brahmin must not be killed," the meaning of the prohibition is simply indifference resulting from the cessation of the action that had been prompted.
This is the case except for those [passages] such as the *Prajāpati-trāta* and others.

Therefore, it should be understood that the statement regarding "uselessness" refers to those *arthavādas* which consist of mere descriptions of facts (*bhūtārtha*) that do not serve a human purpose (*puruṣārtha*).

As for what was also said—that a mere fact stated without entering into an injunction of what is to be done would be useless, like the statement "the earth consists of seven continents"—[that too is refuted].
That has already been answered:
because a purpose is observed even in the mere statement of a fact, such as "This is a rope, this is not a snake.

But it was argued that since one who has heard of Brahman continues to be a transmigrating being just as before, [the knowledge of Brahman] lacks purpose, just like the statement regarding the nature of the rope.

To this it is replied: It is not possible to show that one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self continues to be a transmigrating being as before, because that would contradict the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self produced by the authority of the Vedas.

For although it is observed that those who identify the body and so forth with the Self possess suffering, fear, and the like, it cannot be imagined that the very same person—once the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self has arisen from the authority of the Vedas and that identification has ceased—would still possess that same state of suffering, fear, and the like caused by false knowledge.

For it is not observed that a wealthy householder who possesses pride in his wealth experiences suffering caused by the loss of that wealth simply because he was previously wealthy; likewise, that same person, once having renounced the world and being free from pride in wealth, does not experience that same suffering caused by the loss of wealth. Nor is it observed that one wearing earrings experiences happiness caused by the pride of wearing earrings simply because he was previously so adorned; likewise, that same person, once separated from the earrings, does not experience that same happiness caused by the pride of wearing earrings.
This has been stated by the Śruti: "Verily, while one is embodied, pleasure and pain do not touch" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1).
If it is argued that the state of being bodiless occurs only when the body has fallen away and not while one is living, we say no.
Because having a body is caused by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*);
for, apart from false knowledge characterized by the conceit of identifying the Self with the body, it is impossible to conceive of the Self's state of having a body through any other cause.
We have already stated that its eternal bodilessness is due to its not being caused by karma.
If it is argued that having a body is caused by dharma and adharma produced by that [self], we say no;
for the connection with a body is unestablished, and thus it is unestablished that dharma and adharma are produced by the self.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) between the connection with a body, dharma and adharma, and their being produced by that [connection]; thus, this postulation of beginninglessness is merely a succession of the blind.
Furthermore, because there is no inherence of action [in it], agency is logically impossible for the internal self.
If it is argued that agency is observed in the case of kings and others by virtue of mere proximity, we say no;
for their agency is established through their connection with servants acquired by means of granting wealth and other such means.
However, it is not possible to conceive of any basis for the relationship between the self and its own master through the body and so forth, in the same way that one gives wealth and the like;
rather, false identification (*mithyābhimāna*) is the perceptible cause of that relationship.
By this, the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamānatva*) of the self is also explained.

To this they say: "The conceit of 'mine' regarding one's own body and so forth, on the part of a self that is distinct from the body and such, is figurative and not false. If this is argued, we say no;
for the distinction between the figurative and the primary is well-established only for one who has a well-known difference between entities.
For it is only for him whose distinction between entities is well-known [that such a distinction applies].

Just as a specific form possessing a mane and so forth is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the primary referent of the word and cognition "lion," and another person is established as being endowed with lion-like qualities such as cruelty and valor— thereby becoming a secondary referent for the word and cognition "lion" in relation to that person— it is not the case that these apply to one for whom no distinct entity is established.
In that case, however, the word and the cognition regarding something else are based solely on error and are not figurative.
For example, when a post is not perceived in its specific details due to dim darkness, the word and cognition "this is a person" have the post as their object;
or, for example, when there is a sudden, certain word and cognition of "silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl.

In the same way, how can the word and the cognition "I" arising with respect to the aggregate of the body and so forth—without any figurative application (*nirupacāra*)—be said to be secondary (*gauṇa*), given the failure to distinguish between the Self and the non-Self?
Even for learned men who do distinguish between the Self and the non-Self, the word and the cognition remain undiscriminated, just as they do for shepherds.
Therefore, for those who maintain the existence of a Self distinct from the body and so forth, the notion of "I" with respect to the body and such is purely false; it is not secondary.
Therefore, since embodiedness has its cause in false cognition, it is established that even for the wise person while living, there is bodilessness.
And thus, with reference to the knower of Brahman, there is this scriptural text: "Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie."
"Then this bodiless, immortal life-breath is indeed Brahman, it is indeed light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7);

and also: "Having eyes, as if without eyes; having ears, as if without ears; having speech, as if without speech; having a mind, as if without a mind; having a life-breath, as if without a life-breath. And the Smṛti also says: "What is the description of one whose wisdom is steady? (Bhagavad Gītā 2.54).
Thus, by describing the characteristics of one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajña) in these and other ways, [the scripture] demonstrates that the knower has no connection with any worldly activity.
Therefore, for one who has realized the identity of Brahman and the Self, there is no state of transmigratory existence as before.
Conversely, he in whom the state of transmigratory existence persists as before has not realized the identity of Brahman and the Self; thus, the position is faultless.

As for the further argument that, because reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are seen to follow hearing (*śravaṇa*), Brahman is subordinate to an injunction and does not culminate in its own nature—this is not so;
for reflection and meditative absorption have as their purpose realization (*avagati*).
For if Brahman, once realized, were employed elsewhere, then it would indeed be subordinate to an injunction.
But that is not the case, because reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), like hearing (*śravaṇa*), also have comprehension as their purpose.

Therefore, it is not possible for Brahman to be established by the authority of scripture through being the object of an injunction for realization; hence, Brahman is an independent object of scriptural authority, on account of the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts.
Success! This being the case, it is logical that a separate treatise concerning that [Brahman] is commenced with the words, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*).

For if the work were intended solely as an injunction for spiritual realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*), a separate treatise would not have been commenced, since it would already have been begun with the words, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*).

And if it were to be commenced in that manner, it would have begun thus: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into the remaining duties" (*atha ataḥ pariśiṣṭa-dharma-jijñāsā*), or "Now, therefore, the inquiry into what serves the purpose of the sacrifice and what serves the purpose of the person" (*atha ataḥ kratvartha-puruṣārthayoḥ jijñāsā*), as in [Jaimini Sūtra] 4.1.1.

However, since the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self has not been previously promised, the commencement of the scripture for that purpose is appropriate: "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*atha ato brahma-jijñāsā*).
Therefore, all objects of knowledge and all other means of valid cognition culminate solely in the realization: "I am Brahman."

For once there is the realization of the non-dual Self, which is neither to be rejected nor accepted, it is impossible for the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) to exist, as they would then be devoid of objects and devoid of a cognizer.

Moreover, they say: "When the secondary self and the false self no longer exist due to the sublation of [identifications with] the son, the body, and so forth, how could any duty (kārya) remain when there is the awakening: 'I am the existent Brahman, the Self'?"
Prior to the realization of the Self that is to be sought, the Self possesses the status of a knower;
once sought, it is the knower itself that becomes free from evil, defects, and the like.
"Just as the notion of the body being the self is accepted as a valid means of knowledge [in common parlance],
so too is this worldly means of knowledge valid until the certainty of the Self is attained.

Thus ends the group of four aphorisms. [Note: The intention is that this serves to refute the opponent's claim that Brahman is taught as being subordinate to ritual action. Anticipating the objection that—just as the *juhū* ladle is subordinate to the sacrifice by virtue of its completeness—the Self might likewise be subordinate to ritual action by virtue of knowledge, and therefore the Vedāntas would be subordinate to those injunctions, the author says: "By what means? (tat kena)].

The act of subsequent performance (*pratipattikarma*) is a subsidiary member (*aṅga*) that follows the principal act (*pradhānakarma*). For example, it is like the offering to Sviṣṭakṛt, the giving of oblations (*balidāna*), and so forth, performed with the same substance after the principal oblation of cooked grain (*caruhoma*); or as in the *śrāddha* rite, the casting of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) into the current of the Gaṅgā or another river after the offering of the cakes and worship.

"Non-entry" means the absence of connection. "The injunction of performance" refers to the mandate (*niyoga*); the meaning is that it is the object [of the mandate] by way of delimiting the performance which constitutes its domain. A sacrifice (*yāga*) is the offering of a substance, such as a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), directed toward a deity, such as Agni.
It is bodiless and without a physical frame; it is beyond the pleasant and the unpleasant, happiness and suffering, and what is done and what is left undone.
From the effect that has been made and from the cause that has not been made— he,
that Brahman, knew (avait), having known it.

To him for whom the impurity of passion and the like— which colors the mind like tree bark and such— has been rubbed away, washed off, and destroyed by the alkaline water of the practice of knowledge and dispassion;
[to him] who possesses *adhyāsa*, which is the cognition of something as being that which it is not according to the scriptures,
and *ādeśa*, which is instruction.
At the time of dissolution, the wind envelops and withdraws fire and the other elements; thus it is the "enveloper" (saṃvarga).
During the state of sleep, the vital breath (prāṇa) withdraws speech and the other senses; thus, by virtue of its association with the act of withdrawal, it is the "enveloper.
That which is "other than" (anya) this known object of knowledge is distinct from it.
Moreover, there is something other than even the unknown— that which is the object of ignorance— namely,
that Brahman which is not uttered or manifested by speech, i.e., by sound,
and by which that very speech is uttered and manifested.
Because it is the object of cessation (*nivṛtti-viṣayatvāt*).

Although [the self] does not serve as the substratum for its own attributes (*dharma*), the word "attribute" (*dharma*) is used with the intention that there will be an eternal attribute called liberation; or else, it refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The individual soul is one;
it is the pippala, the fruit of karma;
it shines forth, that is, it manifests.
He is the supervisor of karma and the bestower of the fruits of karma.
By the term "pure" (*śukram*), the absence of external impurity is expressed.

Although the negation of bodily defects is already established by the phrases "without wounds" and "without sinews," their repeated negation is for the purpose of demonstrating that even the assumption of forms such as a boar through divine play (*līlā*) is not unreal.
And thus it is said: "O Nārada, this is indeed an illusion created by me that you see me as endowed with the qualities of all beings; you ought not to view me in this way.
He is called "pure" because he is devoid of the ignorance (avidyā) that serves as the material cause of the body.
The term "unstruck by evil" (*apāpaviddham*) is used for the sake of being free from the causes [of rebirth] associated with that [evil].
Here, "entry" (*anupraveśa*) means a relationship;
for one becomes a "person to be enjoined" (*niyojya*) only when they possess the realization: "This is to be done by me."
Furthermore, that which is the object of an injunction (*vidhi*) must be achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhya*).
Since knowledge is not achievable through effort, the sense is that the knowledge of the Self cannot be both [an end and an object of an injunction].
Those things characterized by the "shadow of an injunction" (*vidhicchāyā*) are similar to well-known injunctions regarding sacrifices and the like.
The stream within the inner self is the flow of mental modifications.
One is satisfied with the thought: "What was to be done has been done; what was to be attained has been attained" (Pañcaśikha).
*Anusaṃjvaret* means one should grieve along with the body as it is being tormented.

The word "pratipatti" (cognition) has as its object only the intellect in its forms of valid cognition (*pramā*) and invalid cognition (*apramā*). As it is said: "Because he attains (*āpnoti*), because he takes up (*ādatte*), because he eats (*atti*) objects here, and because his existence (*bhāva*) is continuous (*saṃtata*), he is therefore called the Self (*ātman*). (Ātmapurāṇa).
"The person taught in the Upaniṣads is the object of the notion of 'I';
[he is] distinct from that individual self (jīvātman) which is the agent and the object of the notion of 'I', being conditioned by the aggregate of the body and the senses"—
such are the words beginning with "ityevamādyā" (Bhāṣya Pāda).
The "vow of the student" (baṭorvrata), beginning with "One should not look at the rising sun," refers to the Prajāpati-vrata.
"Inclusion in an injunction" means connection with an injunction.
The meaning is that because an immutable entity cannot be joined with action, it lacks agency.
The meaning is: "the word" and "verbal comprehension.
"Without figurative usage" means without the knowledge of [its] qualities (*guṇa*);
that is to say, for the learned who possess mere proficiency in hearing and reflection, but for whom direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) has not yet arisen.

The slough of a snake (*ahinirlvayanī*)—the skin of a serpent cast off and discarded from an anthill or similar place—is dead, having been abandoned by the snake and devoid of its sense of identity; it simply remains as it is. This and other such points are to be inferred. Because its purpose is the realization (*avagati*) of Brahman through direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*), even the offering to Brahman is [included] as a subordinate element (*vidhiśeṣatva*) of that injunction.

Now, regarding the phrase "athātaḥ" (now, therefore): since the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*) has been established in the third [book] by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other criteria, an inquiry was initiated at the beginning of the fourth [book] as to which [element] is prompted for the sake of the sacrifice and which for the sake of the person, given that the prompting of the subordinate occurs only through the principal. Therefore, because knowledge does not sublate the object of cognition (*prameya*) or the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).
"Gaumeti" [is explained as follows]:

The conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) with respect to one's son, wife, and so forth, is secondary (*gauṇa*), because in those cases there is an experience of difference.
