However, with respect to the body, sense organs, and so forth, it is not secondary because there is an experience of non-difference; rather, it is false (*mithyā*).

If both of these selves were non-existent— namely, if the secondary self (*gauṇātman*) were non-existent, there would be the sublation of son, wife, and so forth; and if the illusory self (*mithyātman*) were non-existent, there would be the sublation of the body, senses, and so forth—
then how could the maintenance of worldly life, the realization that "I am the existent Brahman," and the direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) of non-duality (*advaita*) come to be?

Because the Self must be sought through the knowledge of the Self— according to the teaching, "That Self which is free from evil is to be sought"— prior to that knowledge, the selfhood of the self and the distinction between the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing exist. Therefore,
the meaning is that in the absence of those [distinctions], the effect [of liberation] does not arise.
"From the certainty regarding the Self" means from the direct realization of the nature of Brahman. (Section 5:

Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa, Sūtras 5–11) Thus, it has been shown that the Vedānta passages—which have the comprehension of Brahman as the Self as their purpose and are unified in their intent toward Brahman as the Self—do so even without entering into the sphere of ritual action.
It has been stated that the ultimate culmination is in Brahman;
and it has been stated that Brahman is omniscient, omnipotent, and the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world.

However, the Sāṃkhyas and others, believing that an established entity can only be known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), infer other causes such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and interpret the Vedānta passages as being directed toward those very causes.
In all Vedānta passages concerning creation, it is by means of inference from the effect that the cause is intended to be characterized.
The Sāṃkhyas maintain that the conjunctions of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa* are eternally inferable;
the followers of Kaṇāda, however, infer from these very same passages that God is the efficient cause and atoms are the material cause.
In this way, other logicians as well, relying on fallacious statements and fallacious arguments, arise here as proponents of prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣavādins*).

In that regard, the Teacher—who is proficient in words, sentences, and the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—sets forth and refutes these misconceptions based on fallacious statements and fallacious arguments, in order to demonstrate that the Vedānta texts have as their ultimate purport the realization of Brahman.
Among them, the Sāṃkhyas, maintaining that the Pradhāna—which consists of the three *guṇas* and is insentient—is the cause of the world, say: "Those which..."
You have stated that the Vedānta passages demonstrate that Brahman, who is omniscient and omnipotent, is the cause of the world;
however, those same passages can also be interpreted according to the view that the Pradhāna is the cause.
To begin with, the quality of omnipotence is applicable to the Pradhāna as well, insofar as it relates to its own transformations.
In this way, even omniscience is logically established.
How so?
That which you consider to be knowledge is a property of sentient beings.
This is according to the Smṛti passage: "From *sattva* knowledge is born" (Gītā 14.17).
And by means of that knowledge, which is an attribute of *sattva*, persons who possess the cause and effect [of knowledge] are well known as omniscient yogins;
for omniscience is well known to occur when *sattva* reaches its unsurpassed excellence.
It is not possible to conceive of omniscience or even limited knowledge for the solitary *puruṣa*, who is neither an agent nor an object of action and consists of mere consciousness.

However, because the *pradhāna* is composed of the three *guṇas*, the *sattva* quality—which serves as the cause of all knowledge—exists even in the state of *pradhāna*; thus, omniscience is figuratively attributed to the *pradhāna*, which is in fact insentient.
Furthermore, even by you, who necessarily accept an omniscient Brahman, omniscience must be admitted only in the sense of possessing the capacity for all knowledge.
For Brahman does not exist only while performing the act of knowing all objects;
for if that knowledge were eternal, Brahman’s independence with respect to the act of knowing would be lost.
Alternatively, if that knowledge were non-eternal, Brahman would also cease from the act of knowing.
In that case, omniscience would necessarily follow simply from possessing the power of all knowledge.
Furthermore, you maintain that Brahman is devoid of all causal instruments prior to its manifestation;
yet, in the absence of the body, senses, and other such means of knowledge, the arising of knowledge for anyone is logically untenable.
Furthermore, since a transformation is impossible for the *pradhāna*—which is composed of multiple constituents—it is logical that it can be the cause, just like clay and other such materials;
however, this is not the case for Brahman, which is uncomposite and of a single nature. Such being the position reached, this Sūtra is commenced:
[The effect is] inferable even without a connection to the causal substance.

That which is a reflection in the intellect is preceded by a corresponding original object (*bimba*), because it is a reflection, like the appearance of a face in a mirror; this is the inference. Grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya are the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding words and sentences.
Those who possess misconceptions regarding fallacious statements and fallacious arguments [are as follows]:
with respect to the activity of knowing— that is, with respect to the meaning of the verbal root *jñā*—
independence is agency (*kartṛtva*).
By the word "etcetera," the objects of knowledge, the knower, and so forth are included.
He refutes the causality of *pradhāna* and other such principles through arguments in the *Tarkapāda*;
the causality of Brahman is established in the *Smṛtipāda*.
"On account of seeing, [the cause] is not that which is not based on scripture.
(BBs 1.1.5) It is not possible to rely upon the non-conscious *pradhāna* imagined by the Sāṃkhyas as the cause of the world in the Vedānta texts;
for that is "not based on scripture" (*aśabda*).
How is it that [the cause] is not denoted by the word [Brahman]?
Because of "seeing"—that is, because the cause is heard of as being a seer.
How so?
For it is heard thus: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1);
and having begun thus, it continues, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,' and It emitted heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

In this passage, having determined that the world—which is denoted by the word "this" and is differentiated by name and form—existed in the essence of Being prior to its origination, [the text] describes the emission of heat and the other elements from that very subject denoted by the word "Being," preceded by Its deliberation.
It demonstrates the state of being a creator. Likewise, elsewhere it says: "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking."
"He thought, 'Shall I now create the worlds?
He created these worlds" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1);
thus, [the scripture] declares that creation is preceded by reflection alone.
And in another place, having introduced the Puruṣa as consisting of sixteen parts, it says: "He reflected;
He created Prāṇa" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.3).
Here, by the word "īkṣateḥ," the intended meaning is the indication of the root's sense (dhātvartha).
It is not a specification of a verbal root, as in the case of the word *yajati*.
Therefore: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving; whose austerity consists of knowledge..."

Therefore, other passages such as "From that, this [world]— consisting of name, form, and food— is not born" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.9), which have the omniscient Lord as their cause, should also be cited. As for what was said— that the Pradhāna might be omniscient through knowledge as an attribute of its constituent quality (sattva)— [that is refuted].
That is not tenable;
for in the state of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), because the qualities (*guṇa*) are in equilibrium, knowledge—which is a property of *sattva*—is not possible.
But was it not said that it will be omniscient by virtue of possessing the capacity for all knowledge?
That too is not tenable. If,

while the qualities are in equilibrium, the Pradhāna is called "all-knowing" by relying on the power of knowledge dependent upon Sattva, then it might as well be called "limited in knowledge" by relying on the power that obstructs knowledge and dependent upon Rajas and Tamas.
Furthermore, the activity of a sentient being that is not witnessed by a seer (sākṣin) is not denoted by the verb "to know" (√jñā).
And the non-conscious primordial matter (pradhāna) lacks the status of a seer. Therefore, the omniscience of the primordial matter is untenable.
However, since yogins possess consciousness, their omniscience is established on the basis of the excellence of their being; thus, [the case of the iron ball] is not a valid illustration.
Furthermore, if it were to be postulated that their status as observers is caused by a witness (sākṣin), just as the burning power of an iron ball and the like is caused by fire.

That being the case, it is logical that the very cause by virtue of which the Pradhāna possesses the quality of being a seer is the omniscient, primary Brahman, the cause of the world. As for what was further stated— that even for Brahman, primary omniscience is not tenable because, if its cognitive activity were eternal, independence with respect to that cognitive activity would be impossible— [that objection is refuted as follows].
To this it is replied: First, you must be asked this: how can there be a loss of omniscience if there is the activity of eternal knowledge?
For it is a contradiction to say that one who possesses eternal knowledge capable of illuminating all objects is not omniscient.
For if knowledge were impermanent, one would sometimes know and sometimes not know, which would result in non-omniscience.
This fault does not exist if knowledge is eternal. If it is argued that when knowledge is eternal, the designation of independence regarding its objects is untenable, we say no;
for even though the sun possesses pervasive heat and light, we observe the designation of independence in such expressions as "it burns" and "it illuminates."
[Objection: Surely, when there is a conjunction of the sun with that which is to be burned and that which illuminates, there may be the designation "it burns" and "it illuminates";
however, since Brahman has no conjunction with knowledge and action prior to creation, the illustration is dissimilar. [Reply: No;
for even in the absence of an object, we observe the designation of agency in the expression "the sun shines."

Thus, even in the absence of karma, the designation of Brahman as the agent in the passage "It thought" (tadaikṣata) is logically consistent; therefore, there is no inequality [in the creation]. Moreover, if there were a dependence on karma, the scriptural texts concerning Brahman's status as the seer would be all the more justified.
But what, then, is that karma?
As for that which becomes the object of the Lord’s knowledge prior to creation,
we say it is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which are unmanifest yet intended to be manifested, and which are indefinable as being either identical to or different from [Brahman].
For it is by the grace of this [name-and-form] that the experts in the Yoga-śāstra maintain that even yogins possess direct perceptual knowledge whose objects are the past and the future.
What need is there to say that the eternally perfected Lord possesses eternal knowledge regarding the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world]?
As for the objection raised— that prior to creation, it is impossible for Brahman to be a perceiver without a connection to a body and the like— that criticism does not apply.
Since Brahman’s nature as knowledge is eternal—just like the light of the sun—it is illogical for it to require the means of knowledge.

Furthermore, the arising of knowledge in a transmigrating being who possesses ignorance and other defects may depend upon the body and so forth; however, this is not the case for the Lord, who is devoid of any cause that could obstruct His knowledge.

These two mantras demonstrate the Lord's independence from the body and His unobstructed knowledge: "For Him there exists neither effect nor instrument, and neither one equal to Him nor one superior to Him is seen."
"His power is heard to be indeed manifold, and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8); and also:
"Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes, he hears without ears;
he knows what is to be known, yet there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the Great Person" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19).

But surely there is no transmigrating being other than Īśvara who possesses causes that obstruct knowledge, according to the Śruti: "There is no other seer; there is no other knower than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
In that case, why is it said that the arising of knowledge for a transmigrating being depends upon a body and so forth, whereas for Īśvara it does not?
To this it is replied: True, there is no transmigrating being other than the Lord;
nevertheless, it is precisely because of the connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the aggregate of the body and so forth [that the distinction appears].
It is like the relation of space with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as a jar, a water-pot, or a mountain cave;

and the worldly usage of words and concepts based on that—such as "the hole in a jar" or "the hole in a water-pot"—is observed even though there is no actual difference from space. Furthermore, a false notion of distinction within space, such as "the space within a jar," is seen to be produced by those adjuncts despite the non-difference [of all such spaces] from space.

Likewise here too, a false notion of distinction between the Lord and the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī), produced by the non-discrimination of the connection with the limiting adjuncts of the aggregate of the body and so forth, [arises].

Moreover, it is observed that even while the Self alone exists, there is an adherence to the notion of "Self" with respect to the non-Self—the aggregate of the body and so forth—due solely to a prior false cognition.

This being the case, the state of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*) is established, and for such a transmigrator, the status of being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*) in dependence upon the body and other factors is logically consistent.

As for what was also said—that because the *pradhāna* consists of multiple elements, its causality is possible (as in the case of clay and the like), whereas it is not possible for Brahman, which is not an aggregate—that argument is refuted.
That [position] which holds Pradhāna to be primary has already been refuted by the very fact that it is not based on the Word (Śabda).

Furthermore, he will elaborate later—starting with the sūtra "Not so, because of its being of a different nature" (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.4)—how it is possible to establish Brahman alone as the cause even through reasoning, whereas this is impossible for Pradhāna and the others. // 5 //

To this, he says: What was stated—that the non-conscious *pradhāna* is not the cause of the world because it possesses the quality of "seeing" (*īkṣitṛtva*)—is otherwise possible as well, since we observe metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) regarding non-conscious things as if they were conscious.

For example, observing that the bank of a river is about to collapse due to its proximity to falling water, one says, "the bank wishes to fall"; thus, metaphorical usage as if the non-conscious bank were conscious is observed.

In the same way, although the Pradhāna is insentient, it will be figuratively described as if it were sentient with respect to the imminent creation, as in the phrase "It thought. Just as in the world a certain sentient being, having bathed and eaten, resolves in the afternoon, "I shall go to the village by chariot," and subsequently proceeds accordingly according to that very rule,
so too does the Pradhāna proceed according to a fixed rule in the form of the Mahat and the other evolutes.
Therefore, it is treated as if it were endowed with consciousness.
But for what reason, setting aside the primary sense of "seeing," is a figurative sense imagined, as in:
"That fire saw"?
And because we observe the metaphorical attribution of consciousness to water and fire— which are themselves insentient— in the passage, "Those waters thought" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3–4),
it is understood that even this act of seeing, though performed by a creator, is merely figurative.
"Because [the term] is used in a figurative sense.
This being the position reached, the following sūtra is commenced:
[The Omniscient One is so called] because he knows everything in a general way.
"Omniscient" (sarvavit) means one who knows everything by way of presenting each specific attribute, such as a jar and so forth.
This Brahma, being born, is the effect known as Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having set forth the Sāṃkhya's own position as a solution to their view, [the author] refutes it with the words: "As for what was said..."
The meaning of the word "that" (tat) is the lack of cognition in that which is insentient.
He states the Sāṃkhya view that includes a Lord (seśvara-sāṃkhya): "Now," etc.
The word *pratatā* means "continuous" (*saṃtatā*).
"Even when it is absent," meaning even when it is not intended to be expressed;
"sutarām" (all the more) is said because there is no sublation of the meaning of the suffix, just as there is none of the meaning of the base.
"Kārya" means the body.
The instruments are the collection of sense faculties;
"clinging" is false conceit.
If it is argued that [the term "self"] is used figuratively, we say no, because of the word "self. (BBs 1.1.6)

As for the claim that the word "seeing" (īkṣati) is used figuratively with respect to the Pradhāna—which is insentient and denoted by the word "Sat"—just as it is with water and fire, that is incorrect.
Why? Because of the word "Self" (ātman).

Having begun with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), and having stated the creation of fire, water, and food with "It thought; it created that fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3), [the text identifies] that very Being under discussion as the seer,
and those very things as fire, water, and food.

Referring to it by the word "deity," the text says: "That deity thought: 'Come, let me enter these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman) and differentiate names and forms'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).

In that context, if the non-intelligent Pradhāna were postulated as the seer through a figurative sense (guṇavṛtti), then it alone—being the subject under discussion—would be referred to as "that deity. It would not, however, designate itself by the term "living self."
For the so-called *jīva* is conscious, the presiding overseer of the body, and the sustainer of the vital breaths,
according to its well-known etymology;
how then could it be the self of the unconscious *pradhāna*?
For "self" (ātman) indeed means one's own nature.
It is not possible for the conscious individual soul (jīva) to be the nature of the non-conscious primordial matter (pradhāna).
However, if the conscious Brahman is accepted as the primary observer, then the application of the word "self" with reference to the individual soul becomes logical.

Likewise, in the passage, "That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth; that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.3), having taught that the previously mentioned subtle essence (*aṇiman*), which is Being (*sat*), is the Self by using the word "Self," he teaches it as the Self of the conscious Śvetaketu with the words "That art thou, Śvetaketu. Water and fire, however, are non-conscious because they are objects [of perception].
Furthermore, because [the terms] "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) and so forth are indicated as being merely that which is employed [by another],

and because there is no reason for them to have primary significance— unlike the word "Self" (ātman)— it is logical that their status as "seers" (īkṣitṛtva) is figurative, like the word "bank" (kūla). Moreover, even in those two cases, the status of being a seer depends precisely upon being presided over by the Existent (sat).
However, it has been stated that for the Existent (Sat), the status of being the seer is not figurative because of its own word [ātman]. // 6 //
Now, it might be argued that the word "self" (ātman) is applied even to the insentient *pradhāna* because it performs all purposes for the self,
just as the word "self" is used for a servant who carries out all the king's purposes, as in the expression, "Bhadrasena is my self."
For the *pradhāna*, by effecting the experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) of the person (*puruṣa*), who is the self (*ātman*), renders assistance to him,
just as a servant engaged in peace, war, and other matters assists a king. Alternatively, the single word "self" (*ātman*) may refer to both the conscious and the unconscious.

Since we observe the usage of the term *ātman* in the senses of "the self consisting of the elements" (*bhūtātman*) and "the self consisting of the senses" (*indriyātman*), just as the single word *jyotis* (light) can refer both to a sacrifice and to a flame— how then is it established that the word *ātman* in the context of the verb *īkṣate* (he sees) is not used in a secondary sense? To this, he recites the following reply:

The meaning is this: by means of this Self—which is of the nature of Being (*sat*), which was experienced during the previous creation, and which is the cause for sustaining the vital breaths—the Supreme Deity, having entered the aforementioned deities after the act of creation, thought, "I shall clearly and completely fashion name and form. The sense is that the capacity to see in water and fire is figurative, based on their qualities, just as the desire to fall is attributed to the bank [of a river].
Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that [Being].
The non-intelligent *pradhāna* cannot be the referent of the word "Self," because,
taking up the previously mentioned *sat* (Being) as "That is the Self," the text says, "That art thou, Śvetaketu," [addressing] the conscious Śvetaketu, who is to be liberated.

For it is taught that one who is devoted to That [the Self] attains liberation, as stated: "The man who has a teacher knows; for him there is delay only so long as he is not released, then he shall be merged" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2).

For if the non-conscious *pradhāna* were denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*), and [the scripture] were to cause the seeker of liberation—who is conscious—to grasp that "you are That," meaning "you are non-conscious," then the scripture would be a teacher of the contrary and would lead to the person's harm; thus it would not be an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
However, it is not proper to consider the faultless scripture as lacking authority.

Furthermore, if the authoritative scripture were to teach that the non-conscious, non-self is the Self to one who is ignorant but desirous of liberation, he— out of faith— would not abandon that view of the Self, following the maxim of the blind man and the cow's tail,
nor would he realize the Self as distinct from it; and if that were the case, he would be deprived of the goal of human existence and would encounter misfortune.

Therefore, just as one teaches the means such as the *agnihotra* exactly as they are to one who desires heaven and the like, so too it is logical that for one who desires liberation, the Self is taught exactly as it is in the words, "That is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu. This being the case, the teaching of liberation for one whose resolve is true (*satyābhisandha*) is justified by the analogy of grasping and releasing the heated axe.

For otherwise, if the instruction regarding the reality of the Self as Being were not primary, this would be a mere meditative identification (*saṃpad*) with an impermanent fruit—just like [the passage], "One should know: 'I am the hymn'";
in that case, the instruction on liberation would be untenable.
Therefore, the word "self" (ātman) is not used figuratively with respect to the atom (aṇiman).
However, in the case of a servant, because the distinction between master and servant is directly perceived, the figurative use of the word "self"—as in "Bhadrasena is my self"—is appropriate.

Furthermore, just because a word is seen to be used figuratively in some instances, it is not on that account proper to assume a figurative meaning for an object established by the authority of scripture (śabda-pramāṇaka).
Because it would follow that there could be no confidence in anything at all.
As for the claim that the word "self" (ātman) is common to both the conscious and the unconscious— just as the word "light" (jyotis) applies to both a sacrifice and a flame—
that is not so.

Because it is improper for a word to have multiple primary meanings, the term *ātman* is primarily applied only to sentient beings; however, it is used in reference to the elements and so forth through the metaphorical attribution of sentience, as in "the self of the elements" (*bhūtātman*) and "the self of the senses" (*indriyātman*).
Even though the word *ātman* is common to both, its application to one or the other cannot be determined without some determining factor, such as the context or an accompanying word.
Furthermore, there is no reason whatsoever here for something insentient to be the determiner;
rather, that which is under discussion is the Seer, and the sentient Śvetaketu is present. For we have already stated that it is impossible for the sentient Śvetaketu to have an insentient self.
Therefore, it is determined that the word "Self" (ātman) here refers to the conscious [Brahman].

As for the word "light" (jyotis), although it is conventionally established in common usage to mean fire alone, it is applied to the sacrifice only through a similarity to fire imagined by an explanatory passage (arthavāda); thus, it does not serve as a valid example.

Alternatively, one may explain the word "Self" in the preceding sūtra itself by way of having dispelled all doubts regarding its secondary or common [meanings], and thereafter explain it as an independent reason for refuting the Pradhāna as the cause.
"Because liberation is taught for one who is devoted to That.
Therefore, the non-intelligent *pradhāna* is not that which is denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*). (Note:
In this context, the use of the first-person pronoun (*uttama-puruṣa*) where the third person (*prathama-puruṣa*) would be expected is a Vedic archaism.)

The construction is as follows: at that time, the scripture—which says "you are insentient" to one who is actually sentient and desirous of liberation—would become a non-authority because it speaks erroneously and thus leads to the person's misfortune.
Here, "contradiction" (vihati) means the absence of being a recipient of liberation.
As it is said: "Just as one who is truthful does not burn when grasping a heated axe, he is then released."
The *uktha* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
This knowledge arising from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) is what is being described here.
Furthermore, why is it that the *pradhāna*, which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being), is not [the referent]?
"And because there is no mention of its being something to be discarded.

(BBs 1.1.8) If the non-Self, namely Pradhāna, which is denoted by the word "Being," were taught here as "That is the Self; you are That," then, lest one who has heard that teaching should become intent upon it through ignorance of the Self, the Teacher—desiring to teach the primary Self—would have stated that [Pradhāna] is to be discarded.

Just as one who wishes to show the star Arundhatī first causes [the pupil] to grasp a large, non-primary star situated near it, saying "This is Arundhatī," and having set that aside, subsequently causes him to grasp Arundhatī herself—
so too [the teacher] would say, "This is not the Self.
But he did not speak in this manner.
For it is observed that the conclusion of the sixth chapter indeed culminates in the realization of the Self as pure Being alone;
the word "and" (ca) is used because [otherwise] there would be a contradiction with the initial proposition.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the contradiction with the original thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) and its further implications.
Even though there is the statement that [everything] is to be abandoned, a contradiction with the thesis would follow;
for it was previously asserted that "by knowing the cause, everything is known."
"Furthermore, did you ask for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?

How, O Venerable One, does that instruction come about? "Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, everything made of clay would be known—the modification being a mere verbal handle, a name, while the reality is simply 'clay'—so it is."
This is because it is heard at the beginning of the passage: "Thus, my dear, is that instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1, 3).

Furthermore, when the Pradhāna—which is denoted by the word *sat* and is the cause of the class of objects of enjoyment—is known, whether as something to be abandoned or as something not to be abandoned, the class of enjoyers does not thereby become known.
Because the class of enjoyers is not a modification of the Pradhāna, the Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "Sat" (Being). // 8 //
And for what further reason is the Pradhāna not denoted by the word "Sat"?

O Śvetaketu, you have asked your teacher about that which is called an *ādeśa*— that is, that reality which is to be pointed out (*ādiśyate*) and is accessible through the teachings of the scriptures and the instructions of the teacher.

The name itself, when commenced and uttered by speech, is the modification; however, there is no modification over and above the names such as "jar" or "bowl" that exists in reality from the perspective of ultimate truth. For clay alone is real, because of its absorption [into itself]. With reference to that very cause denoted by the word "Being," it is heard in scripture: "When a person here sleeps—[then he is] with Being... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1).
"O gentle one, then he has become united; he has gone to his own (svam apītaḥ). Therefore, they say of him 'he sleeps' (svapiti), for he has gone to his own.
This scripture explains the etymology of the word "sleeps," which is a name well-known in the world for a person.
By the word *sva* (self) here, the Self is meant; that which was introduced as denoted by the word *sat*. "He becomes merged" (*apīto bhavati*) means he has gone into it (*apigato bhavati*).
It is well known that the root *i*, preceded by the prefix *api*, has the sense of merging.
Because the terms "origin" (*prabhava*) and "dissolution" (*apyaya*) are seen used for birth and destruction respectively,

the individual soul (*jīva*)— having assumed those specific qualities by its connection with particular limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the movements of the mind— wakes while perceiving the objects of the senses.
Distinctly characterized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those experiences, it becomes designated by the word "mind" (*manas*) while seeing dreams.

When those two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cease, as in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because of the absence of distinctions created by the adjuncts, he is as if dissolved in his own self; thus it is said, "He has indeed gone to his own" (*svaṃ hyapīto bhavati*).

This is shown by the etymological explanation of the word *hṛdaya* as heard in scripture: "This very Self is in the heart; this is its etymological derivation: 'he is in the heart' (*hṛdi ayam*); therefore it is called the heart" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.3.3).

Or again, the scripture shows the root cause for the application of the words *aśanāyā* (hunger) and *udanyā* (thirst): "The waters lead away that which is eaten," and "the fire leads away that which is drunk" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.3, 5).
Thus, by means of the etymological derivation of the name "svapiti" (he sleeps), [the text] demonstrates this meaning: that he has gone into his own self, which is denoted by the word "sat" (Being).
Furthermore, a conscious Self could not take an unconscious Pradhāna as its own essential nature.
If, on the other hand, the Pradhāna itself were denoted by the word "sva" (own) because it belongs to the Self, [then the following would apply].

Even so, it would entail a contradiction to say that "the conscious goes into the unconscious"; moreover, another scriptural passage— “Embraced by the conscious Self, he knows nothing that is external, nor anything internal” (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21)—
shows this merging into the conscious even during the state of deep sleep.

Therefore, that in which all conscious beings merge—that which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being)—is the conscious cause of the world, and not the *pradhāna*. [Furthermore, why is it not the *pradhāna* that is the cause of the world? In deep sleep, when a person has the name "he sleeps," the construction is as follows: the person has become united with "Sat," having attained oneness with It.
For what other reason is the *pradhāna* not the cause of the world?
Because of the commonality of their destination (gati).

If, as in the systems of the logicians, there were a divergence in the understanding of the cause within the Vedāntas—such that in some places conscious Brahman would be the cause of the world, while in others something else entirely would be so—then, at times, one might even have interpreted the scriptural mentions of "seeing" (*īkṣati*) and so forth in accordance with the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause. However, [this is not the case].
This is not so;
for in all the Vedāntas, there is indeed a uniform understanding of a conscious cause.

"Just as when a fire blazes, sparks fly out in all directions, even so from this Self all the vital breaths (prāṇas) go forth each to its own abode, from the vital breaths the gods, and from the gods... [the worlds].
"The worlds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3);
"From this very Self, indeed, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1);
"All this, verily, is from the Self alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.1).
Furthermore, all the Vedāntas demonstrate that the Self is the cause, as in the passage: "From the Self this vital breath is born" (Praśna Upaniṣad 3.3).
And we have already stated that the word "Self" (ātman) denotes a conscious being.

And this is a great ground for authority: that the Vedānta texts have a uniform purport (*samānagati*) regarding an intelligent cause, just as the eyes and other senses have a uniform purport regarding form and other objects.
Therefore, due to this uniformity of purport, Brahman, who is omniscient, is the cause of the world. 10.
FN: *Gati* means comprehension (*avagati*).
"They would stand opposed" means that all ten directions would be spread out as having diverse modes of movement.
Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in making known what was previously unknown.
And for what further reason is the omniscient Brahman the cause of the world?
Because it is so stated in scripture (śrutatvāt).
Indeed, by its own specific word, the Lord who is omniscient is heard in scripture to be the cause of the world in the *Mantropaniṣad* of the Śvetāśvataras.
With reference to the omniscient Lord, [the scripture] states: "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the organs; of him there is no progenitor and no lord" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9).
Therefore, it is established that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, and not the non-intelligent Pradhāna or anything else. // 11 //
The presiding deities are the vital breaths (jīva), and their presiding deity is [the Self].
Knowledge would depend on reality (vastu), while worship depends on action (karman).
"More extensively" means more clearly manifest.
6. The Section on that Consisting of Bliss (Ānandamayādhikaraṇa), Sūtras 12–19:

By means of the sūtras beginning with "From which [proceeds] the origin, etc., of this" and ending with "And because it is so heard," those Vedāntic passages cited [in the commentary] establish the meaning that the omniscient and omnipotent Lord is the cause of the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world.
This has been established through reasoning.
Furthermore, by introducing the commonality of their conclusions, it has been explained that all Vedāntas maintain that the cause is conscious.
Therefore, what is the purpose of the subsequent portion of the work?

It is said: for Brahman is understood to be of two forms— qualified by the distinctions of the modifications of name and form as limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and its opposite, which is devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
"For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa). Verily, the Infinite is immortal, and that which is finite is mortal. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
"The wise one, having fashioned all forms and assigned names, remains calling them forth" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7);
"Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, stainless—
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
"Neither so, nor so" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6),
"neither gross nor subtle" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8),

and "one state is deficient, the other is complete"— in this way, thousands of scriptural passages demonstrate the dual nature of Brahman by distinguishing between the spheres of knowledge and ignorance.
In that state of ignorance, all worldly transactions regarding Brahman— such as the relationship between the object of worship and the worshiper—
take place. Among these, some meditations on Brahman are for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), while others are for the sake of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*).
Some [meditations] are for the purpose of the successful accomplishment of actions;
their distinction arises from the differentiation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of specific qualities.

Although the Supreme Self, the Lord, is indeed one and the same, yet He is to be meditated upon as distinguished by this or that specific quality; nevertheless, the fruits differ precisely according to the meditation on those qualities.

According to the Vedic scripture: "In whatever way one worships it, that very thing one becomes," and also: "As a person's resolve is in this world, so does he become after departing from here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
And from the Smṛti: "Whatever state of being one remembers when one leaves the body at the end..."
"O son of Kuntī, one who is constantly permeated by that [state] goes to that very state" (Gītā 8.6).

Although the single Self is hidden within all beings, both moving and stationary, nevertheless, due to the gradations of the specific limiting adjuncts of the mind (*cittopādhiviśeṣatāratamya*), there is a gradation in the manifestation of the Self— which, though eternally unchanging and uniform— by means of specific powers of lordship (*aiśvaryaśaktiviśeṣaiḥ*).
It is heard in the scripture: "He who knows his Self as most fully manifest" (Ai. Ā. 2.3.2.1).
It is also stated in the Smṛti: "Whatever exists that is possessed of glory, beauty, or power, know that to have arisen from a mere fraction of my splendor" (Gītā 10.41).
Wherever there is an excellence such as majesty and so forth, that very thing is enjoined as the Lord for purposes of meditation.
Likewise, here too, the Teacher will state that the golden person within the solar orb is indeed the Supreme Self, because of the indicative mark of the rising above all evil.
Thus [it is said]: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its indicative marks" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.22).
This is to be seen in such passages as these.

Likewise, even the knowledge of the Self, which is the cause of immediate liberation, though taught by way of specific limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), must be determined— after reflecting on the course of the statements— by means of the inquiry into the purport of the sentences, since it is subject to doubt as to whether it refers to the higher or the lower [Brahman] due to its unintended connection with specific adjuncts.

Just as here [in the Sūtra] it was stated, "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition," so too this subsequent section of the text is commenced to demonstrate that even the single Brahman is taught in the Vedāntas both as an object of meditation and as an object of knowledge, according to its connection with required limiting adjuncts (upādhi) or its freedom from the connection with limiting adjuncts.

Furthermore, that refutation of non-intelligent causes which was stated on the grounds of "the commonality of movement" (*agatisāmānyāt*) is now further elaborated by one who explains other passages concerning Brahman through the negation of causes contrary to Brahman:
"The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman], because of repetition" (*ānandamayo 'bhyāsāt*). In the *Taittirīyaka*, [it says] "consisting of food" (*annamaya*),...
consisting of vital breath, consisting of mind,
and consisting of consciousness.
And it is handed down in succession: "Different from this self consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).

Regarding this, a doubt arises: Is the Supreme Brahman itself—the one previously introduced as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)—referred to here by the term "consisting of bliss"?

Thus, is there a different entity from the Brahman consisting of food and so forth, namely the one consisting of bliss? What, then, is the initial position? That the one consisting of bliss is a non-primary self, distinct from Brahman.
Why?
Because it falls within the series of selves beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, even if it were argued that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the primary self because it is the innermost of all,
this would not be so, because of its connection with limbs such as "dear" (*priya*) and because scripture declares it to be a body.
If the Self consisting of bliss were the primary [Self], there would be no contact with "dear" (priya) and so forth;
however, here it is heard in scripture: "His very dearness is the head," and so on.
Furthermore, its being embodied is heard: "This is indeed its embodied self."
Regarding the phrase "of the former":
the meaning is that this very one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of that former one, which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).
Furthermore, for one who possesses a body, contact with the pleasant and the unpleasant cannot be averted.
Therefore, when it has been reached that the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the transmigrating soul, this is said: "The one consisting of bliss [is Brahman] because of repetition.
The supreme Self alone must be the one consisting of bliss.

Because of repetition;

Having introduced the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), its nature as essence (rasa) is stated in the words, "He is indeed essence," and it is further said, "For only by attaining this essence does one become blissful."
"For who indeed could breathe, and who could live, if this bliss were not present in the ether? For it is he alone who causes bliss."

And [it is said], "Ānanda is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6);

Thus, because the word "bliss" (ānanda) is repeatedly applied to Brahman, it is understood that the self consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman.

Because that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the innermost of all; for the scripture, desiring to teach the primary Self itself, follows the common understanding of the world and,

having referred to the body consisting of food (*annamaya*)— which is not the Self but is well-known as the Self even among the utterly deluded— as being like a statue cast from molten copper poured into a mold, [proceeds] from that...

It is more consistent [to hold] that, by first making one grasp what is not the Self as the Self— progressively from "that which is next" to "that which is next"— starting with each preceding one as being similar to each succeeding one, [the text] taught the Blissful (ānandamaya) as the primary Self, which is the innermost of all, out of consideration for the ease of comprehension.
Just as in the illustration of Arundhatī, when many stars that are not actually Arundhatī have been shown, the one finally pointed out is indeed the primary Arundhatī.
In the same way, here too, because the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the innermost of all, it possesses the status of the primary Self (*ātman*).
As for what you say—
that the attribution of having the head and so forth to the primary Self is untenable with respect to the elements such as pleasure (*priya*)— that is not so.
There is no fault, for that [bliss] is produced by an immediately preceding limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and is not inherent.
Furthermore, the fact that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is "embodied" (*śārīra*) is shown through a succession of bodies beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*),

"And because of the designation of that as its cause.

For it is well known in the world that whoever causes others to be blissful is himself possessed of abundant bliss; just as in common experience, one who brings about wealth for others is understood to be a person of great wealth, so it is here.
Therefore, since the suffix *mayaṭ* can also signify abundance, the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the supreme Self.
And it is proclaimed as being based on the wording of the mantra.
For this reason also, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the supreme Self alone;
because, having begun with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," [the text continues] "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
In this mantra, that Brahman which was under discussion is determined by the qualifiers "Being," "Knowledge," and "Infinity"—
from which, through the sequence beginning with space, all beings, both stationary and moving,
were born; and which, having created the beings, entered into them and abides in the cave of the heart.

The "innermost of all," for the cognition of which it was introduced with the words, "Another inner Self, another inner Self," is that very Brahman described in the mantra-text which is celebrated here as "Another inner Self, consisting of bliss" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
Furthermore, it is logical that the Mantra and the Brāhmaṇa have a single meaning, as there is no contradiction;
otherwise, there would be the abandonment of the subject at hand and the introduction of something irrelevant.
Moreover, unlike the cases of the "consisting of food" (annamaya) and so forth, no other inner self is designated beyond the one "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
And this very [knowledge] culminates in that, as stated in the passage: "This is that knowledge of Bhārgava and Vāruṇi" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.6).
Therefore, the one consisting of bliss is indeed the supreme Self. (Note:
The word *yasmāt* is connected with the remote word *tasmāt*.)
The construction is that "only that which has been determined [in the previous section] is sung here.
The meaning is: because, while there is identity of purpose (*ekārthatva*), there exists the relationship of means and end (*upāyopeyatva*). "Not the other, because it is untenable" (BBs 1.1.16).
For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss is the supreme Self alone, not the other;
"the other" means the transmigrating individual soul (jīva) who is distinct from the Lord.
The individual soul (jīva) is not denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
Why?
Because it is logically untenable.
For, with reference to that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is heard in scripture: "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate.
He performed austerity."
"Having performed austerity,
he created all this, whatever exists here" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

In this regard, prior to the production of the body and so forth, the act of meditative contemplation, the non-difference of the created modifications from the creator, and the creation of all modifications do not occur apart from the supreme Self. (16)
"And because of the designation of difference.
(BBs 1.1.17) For this reason as well, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not the transmigrating being;
because, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss, it says: "He is indeed essence (*rasa*)."
"Having obtained the essence (rasa), he indeed becomes blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7); thus, it designates the individual soul (jīva) and the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) as distinct.
For that which has already been obtained cannot itself be the object to be obtained.

How then are the Śruti and Smṛti statements "the Self is to be sought" and "there is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self" to be understood, given that it has been stated that what is already attained cannot be something yet to be attained?
"Certainly.

Nevertheless, even while remaining as one whose self-luminosity has never departed from itself, the worldly conviction that non-selves such as the body are the self is observed to arise due to the non-comprehension of reality.

Consequently, although the Self is already present within the body and so forth, there occur various designations of distinction, such as: 'the Self has not been sought, it is to be sought; it has not been obtained, it is to be obtained; it has not been heard, it is to be heard; it has not been thought, it is to be thought; it has not been known, it is to be known.'"

This is indeed established; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), any seer or hearer other than the omniscient Supreme Lord is strictly denied by such passages as, "There is no other seer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
The Supreme Lord, moreover, is distinct from the body—which is constructed by ignorance and designated as the "intellectual self" (*vijñānātman*) that is both agent and enjoyer.

Just as from a magician holding a shield and sword who ascends into the sky by means of a thread, that very magician—who is the ultimate reality—is distinct [from the illusion] and remains on the ground;
or just as from the space within a jar, which is delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the space that is without limiting adjuncts and undelimited is distinct;
and it is with reference to such a distinction between the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) that [the Sūtra states]: "Not the other, because it is not possible."
And it has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "Also because of the designation of difference" (1.1.17).
[The commentary explains: "Adhikāra" means context;
that [Self] is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the essence, the sap.
Of that which is of an indivisible single essence:
"Laukika" means not departing from the world, i.e., lacking authoritative means of knowledge;
and because it is [already] established by desire, there is no dependence upon inference. (BBs 1.1.18)

Furthermore, in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because there is the designation of a desiring subject in the passage, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), the non-intelligent *pradhāna* postulated by the Sāṃkhya school—whether as the one consisting of bliss or as the cause—cannot be accepted even on the basis of inference. This is because of the Sūtra: "On account of [Brahman's] seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not the cause]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5).

Thus, although the Pradhāna has already been refuted, it is refuted once again here by way of incidental discussion, relying on the scriptural passage concerning its being a "desirer" cited in the preceding sūtra, for the purpose of elaborating upon the uniformity of the goal (gati-sāmānya). 18.
And in this [passage], it teaches his union with that:
"For this reason also, the word 'consisting of bliss' (ānandamaya) does not refer to the Pradhāna or to the individual soul (jīva);
because, in this very Self consisting of bliss under discussion, it teaches the union of this awakened individual soul with that [Self]."
Union with that [Self] is *tadyoga*, which is the attainment of its state;
the meaning is liberation (*mukti*).

The scripture teaches that yoga is as follows: "For when he finds fearless support in this which is invisible, incorporeal, indefinable, and without abode, then he becomes one who has attained fearlessness.
But when he perceives even the slightest difference in this, [then fear arises]."
"Then fear comes to him" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
This means that when one perceives even a slight interval in this [Self] consisting of bliss— an interval characterized by a lack of identity— then one does not turn back from the fear of saṃsāra.
But when one becomes established in this [self] consisting of bliss through uninterrupted identity, then one turns away from the fear of saṃsāra;
and that is possible only if the supreme Self is accepted, not if the pradhāna or the individual soul (jīva) is accepted.

Therefore, it is established that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is the Supreme Self. However, this must be addressed here: "Now, this person consists of the essence of food (annarasamaya)," and "From that very one, who consists of the essence of food... [and so forth].

Since there is a continuous series of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the sense of a modification— beginning with "another inner self consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*), followed by "another inner self consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), and then "another inner self consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*)— how can it be that, all of a sudden, in the case of the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) alone, the suffix *mayaṭ* is taken to mean "abundance" and to have Brahman as its referent, according to the logic of the "half-old woman"?
If it is argued that this is because of the context of Brahman established by the words of the mantra, we say no.
In that case, it would follow that even those consisting of food (*annamaya*) and the rest are Brahman.

To this he replies: It is appropriate that those consisting of food and the rest are not Brahman, because after each of them, another inner self (*ātman*) is described; however, after the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), no other inner self is mentioned.
"Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something not under discussion.

To this it is replied: even though it is not heard that there is another inner self distinct from the one consisting of bliss—as was the case with those beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*)—nevertheless, the one consisting of bliss is not Brahman.
For, concerning that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), it is heard in scripture: "Joy (*priya*) is its head; delight (*moda*) is its right wing;
extreme delight (*pramoda*) is its left wing."
"Ānanda is the Self; Brahman is the tail, the support" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5).
In this context, that which is introduced as Brahman in the wording of the mantra—namely, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—is [the subject].
Therefore, in this context, it is said, "Brahman is the tail, the support.

It is precisely with the desire to make that known that the five sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), are postulated.
In that case, how can there be the consequence of abandoning the subject under discussion and introducing something not under discussion?
But surely, Brahman is mentioned as a limb of the one consisting of bliss in the passage, "Brahman is the tail,

the support," just as in the cases of those consisting of food and so forth, where it says, "This is the tail, the support," and so on. In that case, how can it be understood that Brahman is the primary subject itself?
We reply: because it is the subject under discussion.

But surely, even if Brahman is understood as a constituent part of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), its status as the subject under discussion is not lost, since the one consisting of bliss is itself Brahman.

To this it is replied: if that were the case, there would be an inconsistency, namely that the very same Brahman which is the whole (the *ātman* consisting of bliss) would also be its part, the tail which is the support.

However, if one must choose between the two, it is more reasonable to accept the reference to Brahman in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," because of its connection with the word "Brahman."
[The opponent argues: "Because in the passage concerning the *ānandamaya*, there is no connection with the word *brahman*.
Furthermore, after it has been stated, "Brahman is the tail, the support," this verse is spoken: "Regarding that, there is also this verse:
'He becomes non-existent indeed...'"
"If one knows 'Brahman is non-existent,' or if one knows 'Brahman exists'— therefore they know him as truly existing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

And in this verse, since the merits and defects of perceiving the existence or non-existence of Brahman itself are stated— without specifically drawing in the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya)— it is understood that in the statement "Brahman is the tail, the support," Brahman alone is the primary subject. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to suspect the existence or non-existence of the self consisting of bliss.
Since that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), characterized by distinctions such as "dear" and "delight," is well known to all the world,
how then is Brahman— which is itself the primary subject— indicated as a mere tail of the one consisting of bliss, in the statement: "Brahman is the tail, the support"?

This is not a fault; for by "tail" (puccha) is meant that which is like a tail—namely, that the bliss of Brahman is the support, the ultimate resort, and the single nest of all worldly varieties of bliss; this is what is intended to be expressed here.
Nor is it a part [of Brahman], because of another scriptural passage: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).
Furthermore, if that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) were Brahman, Brahman would have to be admitted as possessing attributes by virtue of having "pleasure" and so forth as its limbs;
however, Brahman without attributes is heard of in the remainder of the passage, because it is described as being beyond the reach of speech and mind: "From whence words turn back."
"Having known the bliss of Brahman, together with the mind, even before reaching it, one does not fear anything from anywhere. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.9)

Furthermore, when it is said "abounding in bliss" (*ānandapracura*), the existence of suffering is also implied, because in common worldly usage, abundance depends upon the relative scarcity of its opposite.
This being the case, [the scripture states]:
"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (*bhūmā*)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Thus, the scriptural statement regarding the non-existence of anything distinct from Brahman would be contradicted if [the ānandamaya] were [merely] the manifold Brahman;
furthermore, because there is a distinction of "dear" and so forth for each body, the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) would also be diverse,
whereas Brahman does not differ with respect to each body.
"Truth, knowledge, infinite is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1),
according to this scriptural testimony of infinity;
and "The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11).
And this is because of another scriptural passage;
furthermore, no repetition of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) is heard.
For in every instance, it is only the meaning of the nominal stem itself that is repeated: "He is indeed the essence (rasa)."
"Verily, having obtained this essence, one becomes blissful;
for who indeed could inhale, and who could exhale, if this bliss did not exist in the ether?"
"This is the inquiry into bliss":
"He who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.8–9),
and "He understood that bliss is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 6.6).

And if it were certain that the word "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) has Brahman as its referent, then the repetition of "bliss" (ānanda) alone in the subsequent passages could be construed as a repetition of the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya).
However, the "consisting of bliss" is not Brahman.
We have already stated that this is due to reasons such as "having bliss as its head" (*priyaśiras-tva*).

Therefore, since we observe the use of the nominal stem *ānanda* for Brahman in another scriptural passage— namely, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)— it follows accordingly.

It should be understood that such applications concerning Brahman as "If this bliss did not exist in the ether" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 7.22.1) and so forth do not constitute a repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

As for the repetition of the word "bliss" itself ending in the suffix *-maya*, namely, "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.8), that does not have Brahman as its object.
This is because the non-self entities such as the *annamaya* (consisting of food) and so forth—which are subject to transformation—are enumerated in the series of those to be transcended.

[Objection: But if the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss), which is likewise to be transcended like the *annamaya* and others, were Brahman, then the fruit of the attainment of Brahman would not have been indicated for the knower.
[Response: This is not a fault.
Because the fruit, which is the attainment of Brahman— the tail and support— has already been indicated by the very instruction on approaching that which consists of bliss;
and because this is further elaborated upon by the verse beginning with, "From whence words turn back," and so forth.
As for the scriptural passage cited— "He, consisting of bliss, desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—

since it is connected with the Brahman that is more proximately situated in the phrase "Brahman is the tail, the support," it does not establish that the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is Brahman.

Furthermore, because the subsequent text beginning with "He is indeed the essence" (raso vai saḥ) is dependent upon that [preceding section], it does not have the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) as its subject matter.
Now, an objection may be raised: "The masculine designation in the phrase 'He desired' (so 'kāmayata) is not appropriate for Brahman.
This is not a fault.
Because in the passage, "From that very Self, indeed, space was produced," Brahman is the subject under discussion by means of the word *ātman* even though it is in the masculine gender;

whereas in the Bhārgavi-Vāruṇī knowledge— "Bliss is Brahman, so he understood"— since the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard there, and since qualities such as having "pleasure as its head" are not mentioned, it is appropriate that bliss itself is Brahman.
Therefore, without relying on even the slightest distinction, the status of Brahman as having "the head as dear" and so forth cannot be established by itself alone;
nor is it intended here to teach a qualified (saviśeṣa) Brahman, because of the scriptural testimony that it transcends the sphere of speech and mind.

Therefore, just as in the case of the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others, the suffix *-maya* in the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) must be understood in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), not in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*).

The Sūtras, however, are to be explained as follows: Regarding the passage "Brahman is the tail, the support," is Brahman intended here as a limb of the *ānandamaya*, or as something primary in its own right? Since the word "tail" suggests it is a limb, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached; in response, it is said: "The *ānandamaya* [is Brahman] because of repetition. In the statement "the Self consists of bliss," Brahman is taught as being primary in its own right by the words "Brahman is the tail, the support."
Because of repetition;
for in the concluding verse, "He becomes [that] alone," it is Brahman alone that is being repeated.
If it be argued that it is not so because of the word denoting a modification, we say no, because of its abundance.

By the word "modification" (vikāra), the word "member" (avayava) is intended. Regarding what was stated— that because "tail" is a word denoting a member, Brahman does not possess self-subsistence— that objection must now be refuted.
To this it is replied: this is not a fault, because a word for a part can be justified even by way of abundance (*prācurya*). Abundance means being prevalent (*prāyāpatti*).
The meaning is that it is a statement occurring in a context primarily concerned with parts. For,

although the limbs beginning with the head and ending with the tail have been mentioned for those [sheaths] consisting of food and so forth, even in the case of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), after mentioning other limbs such as the head, the statement "Brahman is the tail, the support" is not intended to denote a literal part, because it occurs in a context where the mention of parts has reached its conclusion.
For the reason that it is "due to practice," the primacy of Brahman has been established.
And because of the designation of it as the cause:
Brahman is designated as the cause of the entire collection of effects, including that which consists of the *ānandamaya*—it created all this.
Namely, "Whatever there is" (Tai. 2.6).
Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for Brahman, which is the cause, to be a constituent part (*avayava*) of its own modification, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), in a primary sense.
Other sūtras as well should be understood as establishing that very Brahman which is designated by the statement concerning the "tail," according to their respective contexts. // 19 //

[The Self] is non-self (anātmya), being devoid of identity with the group of sense organs superimposed as its correlates, which are the effects of the fivefold-formed elements; it is indefinable (anirukta), being free from non-difference from the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma)—so called because they are "extracted" (nirucyante) [from the gross]; and it is the void of the abode (nilayana), where Māyā, the locus of total dissolution, resides.

"Udaram" means "ut api," that is, even a slight interval or distinction. The meaning is that while the state of being within Brahman is not heard [in the text] with respect to the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), its being the "tail" is indeed heard. By the word "puccha" (tail), mere support is meant; by "pratiṣṭhā" (foundation), it is meant as a firm basis.
It is the single nest and the foundation for the world together with its grasping (sopādāna),
from which words turn back without having manifested it through the operation of their expressive power;
its nature depends upon that which is its counterpart and its opposite.
Just as in the expression "a village consisting of Brahmins," there is a scarcity of Śūdras;
"commencement" (upakramaṇa) refers to sublation (bādha),
which consists in the exclusion of those things to be abandoned through discrimination among those things to be approached.
Prāyāpatti is the attainment within the intellect of the sequence of parts [of a word].
This is the section on the internal [word] (antaradhikaraṇa). 20–21:
"Because its properties are taught as being internal" (BBs 1.1.20).

This is recorded in scripture: "Now, this golden person who is seen within the sun, with golden beard and golden hair, entirely golden down to his fingernails; as a lotus flower is reddish-yellow like a monkey's buttocks, so are his eyes; his name is 'Ut,' for he has risen above all evils. Indeed, he who knows this rises above all evils."
"Thus with reference to the deities" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7–8);
"Now with reference to the self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.1); "Now, this person who is seen within the eye" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.5), and so forth.

In this regard, a doubt arises: Is some transmigrating being who has attained excellence through the power of superior knowledge and action that is taught as the object of meditation in the solar orb and in the eye, or is it the eternally established Supreme Lord?
Thus [it is asked]: what, then, is the initial position? That he is a transmigrating being (saṃsārī).
Why? Because of the scriptural mention of his possessing form (rūpavattva).

In the case of the person in the sun, a form beginning with "golden-bearded" has been cited; in the case of the person in the eye as well, that very same form is obtained by extension through the statement: "The form of this one is the same as the form of that one.
And yet, it is not appropriate for the Supreme Lord to possess a physical form.

This is because of the scriptural text, "It is without sound, touch, form, and imperishable" (Kā. 1.3.15), and also because of the mention of a support in the passages, "He who is within the sun," and "He who is within the eye."
For no support could be taught for the Supreme Lord, who is without support, established in His own majesty, and all-pervading;
as the two scriptural passages state: "In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1), and "He is omnipresent and eternal like space."
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the limitation of his sovereignty:
"He is the lord of those worlds that are beyond this one, and of the desires of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.8); thus, there is a limitation to the sovereignty of the Person in the Sun.
"He is the one who rules over those worlds that are below this one, and over the desires of men"—this refers to the Person in the eye.
Furthermore, it is not fitting for the Supreme Lord to possess a sovereignty that is limited by boundaries, as it is said:
"He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

Because of this scriptural statement without qualification, the prima facie view is that the Supreme Lord is not the one within the eye or the sun; to this we reply: "The one within [is the Supreme Lord], because of the teaching of His attributes.
The Person who is heard of in the texts, "He who is within the sun" and "He who is within the eye," is indeed the Supreme Lord, not a transmigrating soul.
Why? Because of the teaching of his attributes.
For the attributes of that Supreme Lord are taught here.
For example, having announced the name of this person in the sun as "Ud" (He has risen), it etymologically explains that name by the departure of all evil: "He has risen above all evils."
And that very etymological explanation is extended to the person in the eye as well by the statement, "Whatever is its name, that is its name.
Furthermore, the departure of all evil is heard in scripture to belong to the Supreme Self alone, in such passages as, "The Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

Likewise, with regard to the person in the eye, [the text] determines his identity with the Ṛgveda, Sāman, Uktha, Yajus, and Brahman, stating, "He is indeed the Ṛk, he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha, he is the Yajus, he is the Brahman."
And that [creation] is possible for the Supreme Lord, because He is the cause of all and because it is logically consistent that He is the self of all;
furthermore, with respect to the divine sphere (*adhidaivata*), the *Ṛk* and *Sāman* consist of earth, fire, and so forth.

Having proceeded through the internal (adhyātma) perspective consisting of speech, breath, and so forth, [the text] says: "The Ṛk and the Sāman are its two joints (geṣṇau)," with reference to the divine (adhidaivata).
Likewise, with reference to the internal as well: "Whatever are its two joints, those are its joints.
And that is possible only for the Self of all.

And by the passage, "Now, those who sing here on the lute, they sing of this; therefore they are winners of wealth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.7.6), [the text] shows that even in worldly songs it is this very one who is being sung of. And that is consistent with the acceptance of the Supreme Lord.
"Whatever being possesses grandeur, beauty, or power,
know that to be born from but a fragment of my splendor"—
thus it is seen in the *Bhagavadgītā* (10.41).
The fact that He is heard to possess unobstructed lordship over the desires of the world also leads one to understand Him as the Supreme Lord.

As for what was said—that the hearing of His form, such as having a golden beard and so forth, is not possible in the case of the Supreme Lord—to this we reply: by the power of His will, the Supreme Lord may also assume a form composed of *māyā* for the sake of favoring His practitioners.
For it is remembered [in scripture]: "O Nārada, this which you see me as is indeed an illusion created by me; endowed with the qualities of all beings, you ought not to know me in such a way.
Furthermore, where the supreme form of the Lord is taught as one in which all distinctions have been discarded, [it is understood as the ultimate reality].
Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying," and so forth.

However, because He is the cause of all, the Supreme Lord is also designated as the object of worship as being distinguished by certain qualities of transformation, such as: "He who possesses all works, all desires, all odors, and all tastes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2), and so on.
Likewise, the description of having golden hair and beard and so forth will also be possible.

As for the argument that it cannot be the Supreme Lord because of the mention of a substratum, it is said in reply: even for one who is established in his own majesty, the instruction regarding a specific substratum will be for the purpose of meditation.

Because Brahman is all-pervading like space, its existence as the inner self of all is logically established. Even the scriptural mention of limitations on its sovereignty is intended solely for the purpose of meditation, depending on the distinction between the internal (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata).
Therefore, it is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught as being within the eye and the sun. 20. @----------------------

He alone must be the person here within the sun,
because of the identity of the scriptural statement;
