8. The Section on Space (Ākāśādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 22:
"Space [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark. (BBs 1.1.22) They recite this: "What is the goal of this world? "Space," he said. "For indeed, all these beings arise from space alone..."
"They arise from space and dissolve back into space; for space is indeed greater than these, space is their final resort" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the Supreme Brahman denoted by the word "space," or is it the elemental space (bhūtākāśa)?
Why does this doubt arise?
Because its usage is observed in both senses:
first, the word *ākāśa* is well-established in common worldly usage and in the Veda as referring to a particular element;
second, it is also seen being employed in certain instances with reference to Brahman.
Where Brahman is determined by the force of a supplementary statement or by the hearing of something unique, as for example:
"If this bliss did not exist in this space" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), and "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form; that which is within them is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
And so it is in such passages as these.
Therefore, a doubt arises:
what, then, is appropriate here?
"It is the elemental ether.
Why? Because that [elemental ether] quickly enters the intellect through its more well-known usage.
Furthermore, it is not possible to understand this word "ether" as being common to both [the elemental ether and the supreme Brahman].
Because it would entail the fallacy of multiple meanings [for a single word].
Therefore, the word "ether" (ākāśa) must be used in a figurative sense with respect to Brahman;
for Brahman is similar to ether in many respects, such as omnipresence and other qualities.
And when the primary meaning is possible, a secondary meaning ought not to be accepted;
moreover, here the acceptance of the primary ether itself is possible.
[Objection: But if the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) were accepted, the remainder of the passage would not be consistent—namely, "All these beings, indeed, arise from the ether alone," and so forth.

This is not a fault, because it is logically possible for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) also to serve as a cause through the sequence beginning with air; for it is known from scripture: "From this very Self, indeed, the ether was produced."
"From space comes air;
from air, fire" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), and so forth.
Even the qualities of being "greater" and "the ultimate resort" are applicable to the elemental ether when compared with other elements.

Therefore, when it is argued that by the word "ether" (ākāśa) the elemental ether is meant, we reply: "The ether [is Brahman], because of its characteristic mark. It is appropriate to understand Brahman by the word "ether.
Why? Because of its characteristic mark.
For this is a characteristic mark of the supreme Brahman: "All these beings, indeed, arise from the ether alone."
For it is the established rule in the Vedāntas that the origin of all beings is from the Supreme Brahman.
But has it not been shown that the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) also possesses causality through the sequence beginning with air?
True, it has been shown.

Nevertheless, because the fundamental cause, Brahman, is not accepted [in that interpretation], the restriction "from ether alone" (ākāśādeva) and the qualification of the elements as "all" (sarvāṇi) would not be consistent.

Likewise, the characteristic mark of Brahman found in the phrase "they merge into ether," as well as the qualities of being "greater" and "the ultimate resort" in the passages "for ether is indeed greater than these" and "ether is the ultimate resort," would be inconsistent.

For superiority (*jyāyastva*) is indeed taught as non-relative only with respect to the Supreme Self alone: "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space, greater than heaven, greater than these worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.3).
Likewise, the quality of being the ultimate resort (*parāyaṇatva*) is also more appropriately established in the Supreme Self alone because He is the supreme cause.
And there is a scriptural text: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss; [He is] the ultimate resort of the giver who bestows [all things]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28).

Furthermore, having censured Śālāvatya’s position on account of the defect of its being finite, Jaivali, desiring to state something infinite, adopted *ākāśa* (space); and having identified that *ākāśa* with the *udgītha*, he concludes: "This is that *udgītha* which is higher than the high; this is that which is infinite" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.2).
And that infinity is a characteristic mark of Brahman.

As for what was further stated—that the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) is understood more immediately by the force of common usage—to this we reply: although it may be understood more immediately, it is not accepted [as the referent] upon seeing the attributes of Brahman found in the remainder of the passage.
Furthermore, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is shown to refer even to Brahman in such passages as: "Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.14.1).
Likewise, the application of synonyms for ether to Brahman is also observed: "In the imperishable, the supreme ether, all the gods are seated upon the *ṛc*s" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.164.39);
and "This very knowledge of Bhṛgu and Varuṇa is established in the supreme ether" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 3.6).
"Oṃ, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5), and "Kha is the ancient one" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.1), and so forth.
Even though the word "ether" (ākāśa) occurs at the beginning of the sentence, its determination as having Brahman as its object is justified by the force of the remainder of the passage.
For indeed, the word "fire" (agni), even when occurring at the beginning of the sentence in the expression "Agni studies the Anuvāka," is seen to refer to a young boy.
Therefore, it is established that the word "ether" denotes Brahman. // 22 //
FN: "Of the knower"—that is, of the cognizer, the self consisting of consciousness as conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
With the word "of this," the Brahmin Śālāvata asks Jaivali, the king.
The "carrier" (*nirvahitṛ*) is the cause of origination and subsistence;

that which exists between those two *nāma-rūpa*—that is, other than them or in their midst—is Brahman untouched by *nāma-rūpa*. Thus, by the force of the statement, the meaning here is that "space" (*ākāśa*) is Brahman.
[The term] "giver" (*rāti*) refers to the giver of wealth, namely the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
Infinity with respect to space is "otherness" (paratva);
with respect to qualities, it is "excellence" (utkṛṣṭatva) or "superiority" (varīyastva);

"Parovarīyastva" means being superior to others, such as the *svara* (the syllable Om) and so forth;
"vyoman" means in the sky, that is, in the supreme and most excellent [ether].
In that immutable syllable, Brahman, all the Vedas— consisting of the Ṛg verses— are the indicators;
in which syllable all the gods are seated, established upon it.
9. The Section on Prāṇa. Sūtra 23:
"For this very reason, [the word] prāṇa [refers to Brahman].
Regarding the Udgītha, after beginning with, "O Prastotṛ, that deity which is connected with the Prastāva," it is heard in scripture: "Which one is that?"
"Which deity? "The vital breath (prāṇa)," he said; "for indeed all these beings enter into the vital breath alone and emerge from the vital breath alone.
This is that deity which is connected with the Prastāva" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.4–5).
In this regard, the doubt and its resolution are to be understood as before.

In such passages as "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2) and "The breath of breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18), the word *prāṇa* is seen to have Brahman as its referent.

However, since [the term] is more commonly established in both worldly usage and the Vedas as a modification of air (vāyu), a doubt arises here as to which one is appropriately taken up by the word "prāṇa.
What, then, is appropriate in this case?
It is appropriate to take the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is a modification of air, as the material cause;
for we have already stated that the word "breath" is more commonly established in that sense there.
But is it not the case that, as before, it is more appropriate here too to understand Brahman alone on account of its characteristic marks?
Here too, in the supplementary passage, the entering and emerging of beings is understood as an action belonging to the Supreme Lord. No;
for even in the case of the principal vital breath (prāṇa), the entering and emerging of beings is observed.

For it is thus recorded in scripture: "When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, and the mind into the vital breath; when he awakes, they are born again from the vital breath alone."

(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.3.3.6). This is also directly perceived: during the time of sleep, while the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains unimpaired, the functions of the senses (*indriya*) cease; and at the time of awakening, they reappear.

Furthermore, because the elements (*bhūta*) have the senses as their essence, the subsequent statement regarding the dissolution and emergence of the elements into the primary vital breath (*mukhya prāṇa*) is not contradictory.

Furthermore, the Sun and Food are designated as the deities of the *udgītha* and *pratihāra*, while the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is designated as the deity of the *prastāva*. Since those two [the Sun and Food] do not possess the nature of Brahman, it might follow by analogy that the vital breath also does not possess the nature of Brahman. To this objection, the author of the Sūtras replies: "For this very reason, the vital breath [is Brahman]."
The phrase "from its characteristic mark" was indicated in the preceding sūtra.
For this very reason, on account of that characteristic mark, even the word *prāṇa* must be the Supreme Brahman.

Indeed, the connection of *prāṇa* with the characteristic marks of Brahman is heard in scripture: "All these beings, verily, enter into *prāṇa* alone, and from *prāṇa* they emerge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.11.5).

The origination and dissolution of all beings, which are stated to have the vital breath (prāṇa) as their cause, lead to the understanding that the vital breath is Brahman. Now, it was argued that even if the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is accepted, the observation of entering into and emerging from [the body] is not contradictory,
since this is seen during sleep and waking.

To this it is replied: In the cases of sleep and waking, it is observed that only the sense organs themselves undergo the process of entering into and emerging from their support, which is the vital breath (prāṇa), and not all elemental beings (bhūtas).
But here [in the case of death], it refers to elemental beings together with their sense organs, together with their bodies, and permeated by the individual soul (jīva).
This is because of the scriptural text: "Indeed, all these beings...

Even when the scriptural mention of "beings" (bhūta) is understood as referring to the great elements (mahābhūta), there is still no contradiction in its being a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Brahman.
Now, it may be argued that even together with their objects, the sense organs undergo dissolution into the vital breath (prāṇa) during sleep and emerge from the vital breath during waking.
We hear: "When one who is asleep sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this very breath; then speech enters into him along with all names" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
Even there, on account of that indicative mark, the word "breath" (prāṇa) refers to Brahman alone.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the vital breath (prāṇa) is not Brahman because of its proximity to food and the sun, that is incorrect;
for when the word "prāṇa" is understood through the force of the remainder of the passage to have Brahman as its referent, mere proximity is of no consequence.
Furthermore, as for the fact that the word "prāṇa" is more commonly known to refer to the fivefold vital breath, that must be refuted in the same manner as was done for the word "ākāśa.
Therefore, it is established that the prāṇa, who is the deity of the Prastāva, is Brahman.
In this regard, some cite the passages "the breath of breath" and "for the mind, my dear, is fastened to breath.
That is incorrect.
Because of the difference in words and the context, doubt is untenable.

Just as in the expression "the father of the father," it is understood that the father indicated by the genitive case is one, while the father indicated by the nominative case in "the father of the father" is another; likewise, because of the difference in words in the phrase "the breath of breath," it is determined that the "breath of breath" is other than the well-known vital breath (prāṇa).
For that very thing cannot be designated as "belonging to itself," since such a designation requires a distinction [between possessor and possessed].
Furthermore, when something is mentioned within a particular context—even by another name—it is understood that it is that very same subject of the context being mentioned.
For example, in the section concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the word *jyotis* in the phrase "One should sacrifice with the Jyotis every spring" refers to the Jyotiṣṭoma.

Likewise, in the context of the Supreme Brahman, how could the word "prāṇa" heard in the scripture, "For the mind, my dear, is bound by prāṇa," be understood as referring merely to a modification of air?
Therefore, because it is a subject of doubt, this [latter] example is not appropriate.
However, regarding the deity of the Prastāva, the doubt, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), and the final conclusion have already been established. // 23 //

[What is its] entering and emerging—its dissolution and arising?"
In that state,
speech is indicative of the unmentioned organs of action,
while sight and hearing are indicative of the corresponding organs of perception.
The intellect (*buddhi*) is also characterized by the mind (*manas*).

Among the elements, the senses are the "essence" because of their subtlety and their proximity to the enjoyer; therefore, by the statement regarding their dissolution and emergence, the others are also established—this is the meaning of the "completion of the remainder.
The meaning is that proximity [of the senses] to the sentence is difficult to obtain.
The analysis of the compound is as follows: *prāṇa* (the vital breath) is that whose binding support and essential nature (*svarūpa*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
This concerns the section on "Light" (*jyotis*), Sūtras 24–27:
"It is Light, because of the mention of its feet" (BBs 1.1.24).

Regarding this, they recite: "Now, that light which shines beyond this, on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme—this indeed is that light which is within this person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7).
In this regard, a doubt arises: is the word "light" here used to denote the light of the sun and so forth, or is it the Supreme Self?
It has been stated that even a word whose primary referent is another object may have Brahman as its referent because it possesses the characteristic marks (liṅga) of that [Brahman].
Here, however, it is investigated whether those very characteristic marks exist or do not exist.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
The word "light" (jyotis) refers exclusively to the sun and so forth.
Why? Because of its well-known usage.
For these two words, "darkness" (tamas) and "light," are well known to have mutually opposed domains.
Darkness, such as that of night, is said to be the obstructer of the functioning of the eye;
light, such as the sun, is its benefactor.
Likewise, this scriptural expression "it shines" is well known to have the sun and so forth as its subject.
For it is not possible that Brahman, which is devoid of form and other qualities, should "shine" in a primary sense;
moreover, because of the scriptural statement regarding its having heaven as its boundary.
Indeed, it is not logical for heaven to be the boundary of Brahman, the seed of the moving and the unmoving, who is the Self of all.
But for the light that is an effect and is limited, heaven would be the boundary;
for there is a Brāhmaṇa text stating, "The light beyond heaven.
Now, it may be objected that even for the light that is an effect, it is inconsistent to have heaven as its boundary, since such light is perceived everywhere.
"Let it be, then, that the first-born light is that which has not yet undergone triplication. No;
for there is no purpose for light that has not undergone triplication.
"If you say that its very purpose is to be an object of meditation, we say no."
For it is observed that even the sun and other such objects are objects of meditation only when they are employed for some other purpose;
furthermore, there is the general scriptural statement: "Of these, I shall make each one threefold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.3).
Furthermore, it is not well-known that even non-tripartite fire has heaven as its limit.
Let it be, then, that only tripartite fire is denoted by the word "light" (jyotis).
But was it not stated that light such as fire and so forth is perceived even below heaven?
This is not a fault;

for even in all cases, the specification of a particular location such as "beyond heaven" for the light that is being understood is not contradictory, as it serves the purpose of meditation. However, the postulation of a specific location for Brahman, which is without parts, is not tenable.
Furthermore, the scriptural mention of a plurality of substrates in the passage, "In all the worlds that are on the back, unsurpassed and supreme," is far more appropriate for the light as an effect.
Moreover, in the passage, "This indeed is that light which is within a person here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7), the supreme light is seen being superimposed upon the gastric light.
Furthermore, superimpositions arise based on similarity, as for example:
"Of that [breath], *bhūḥ* is the head; this is the single syllable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3).
However, it is well known that the light within the belly is not Brahman.
For it is heard [in scripture] that "this is its sight" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7) and "this is its hearing," thereby indicating its being characterized by heat and sound;
and because of the scriptural statement: "One should meditate upon this as both seen and heard."
Furthermore, because a small fruit is heard [in the scripture], "He who knows this becomes pleasing to the sight and famous" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.8), it is not Brahman;
for the meditation on Brahman is intended for a great fruit.
Furthermore, there is no other mark of Brahman in its own sentence regarding light, such as the marks [found] in the case of the vital breath (prāṇa) and space (ākāśa).
Nor is Brahman indicated in the preceding sentence either, because of the mention of a meter [therein]: "The Gāyatrī, indeed, is all this that has become."
Moreover, even if Brahman were somehow indicated in the preceding sentence, there is still no recognition of it here;
for in that passage, heaven is heard of as its locus in the words, "Three quarters of it are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).

Furthermore, in this context, because the phrase "the light beyond heaven" (paro divo jyotiḥ) specifies heaven as a boundary, it follows that the ordinary light is what should be understood here; such being the position, we reply: the light here must be understood as Brahman.
Why? Because of the mention of its "conduct" (caraṇa).
The meaning is "because of the mention of feet.

For in the preceding passage, Brahman was indicated as having four quarters: "Such is His greatness; yet the Puruṣa is greater than that. All beings constitute one quarter of Him; His three quarters are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
By this mantra,
that which was previously indicated as the four-footed Brahman’s immortal three-footed form connected with heaven is recognized here as well because of its connection with heaven.

For one who abandons that and imagines an ordinary light, the faults of abandoning the subject at hand (*prakṛtahāna*) and introducing what is not the subject at hand (*aprakṛtaprakriyā*) would follow.
Brahman does not merely continue from the preceding passage into the passage concerning light;
rather, Brahman will also continue into the subsequent Śāṇḍilya-vidyā.
Therefore, it must be understood that "light" here refers to Brahman.
As for what was said— that these two words, "the light shines" and so forth, are well-known to refer to the light as an effect—
this is not a fault;
because when Brahman is understood through the context, these two words possess no distinguishing [contrary] power.
For it is possible to apply [the term *brahman*] even to Brahman as characterized by the light of the manifesting effect,
according to the Vedic mantra: "By that splendor kindled, the sun shines" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.7).

Alternatively, this word "light" (*jyotis*) does not refer exclusively to the luminous energy that assists the function of the eye, because it is seen to be used in other contexts as well; for example:
"By speech alone as his light, he sits" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.5).
And as it is said, "May the mind, which is light, enjoy [the offering]" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.3.3), therefore whatever illuminates anything is designated by the word "light" (*jyotis*).
This being so, the term "light" is appropriately applied to Brahman as well, since its nature is consciousness and it is the cause of the illumination of the entire universe.

And from such scriptural passages as: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.5.15), and "The gods worship that Light of lights as life, as immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).
As for what was said—that it is not possible for the all-pervading Brahman to have a celestial limit—it is replied here:
even for the all-pervading Brahman, the appropriation of a specific location for the purpose of meditation is not contradictory.
Now, it may be objected that since Brahman is without parts (*niṣpradeśa*), the conceptualization of a specific location is not tenable.
This is not a fault;

for even though Brahman is without spatial parts (*niṣpradeśa*), it is logical to conceive of specific locations based on its connection with particular limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). To illustrate: the sun...
Meditations on Brahman connected with specific locations, such as "in the eye" and "in the heart," are heard in the scriptures.
By this, the multiplicity of supports expressed in the phrase "on all sides, behind" has been established. As for what was also said—
that because the light is superimposed upon the effect (the gastric fire) inferred from heat and sound, the light beyond the sky must also be an effect— it is as follows:
That too is incorrect;
for it is possible that even the Supreme Brahman may serve as a symbol (pratīka) for the name and so forth, just as it serves as a symbol for the light within the stomach.
Furthermore, in the passage "One should meditate on it as seen and heard," the state of being "seen" and "heard" will occur by way of the symbol.
As for the claim that Brahman is not to be resorted to because it is heard to yield only small fruits,
that too is untenable;
for Brahman is not to be resorted to for the sake of some [limited] fruit.
There is no restrictive cause for [the result] being "this much" and not more;
for where the supreme Brahman, from which all specific distinctions have been removed, is taught as one's own self,
there it is understood that the fruit is exclusively of a single nature, namely liberation.
But where Brahman is taught in connection with specific qualities or specific meditative forms (*pratīka*),

there only various fruits pertaining to the sphere of transmigratory existence are seen, as in such scriptural passages as: "He who knows this becomes an eater of food, a giver of wealth, and finds wealth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.24).
Although there is no mark of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) for "light" (*jyotis*) within its own sentence, nevertheless, that which is seen in the preceding sentence must be accepted.

This was stated by the author of the Sūtras: "Light [is Brahman], because of the mention of the feet. But how can the scriptural mention of "light" be displaced from its own object by the proximity of Brahman found in another sentence?
This is not a fault.

Since the word "that" (*yat*), which is a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) and is read earlier in the phrase "that light which is beyond this," refers by its own inherent power to Brahman—which is indicated in the preceding passage and recognized through its connection with heaven—the application of the word "light" (*jyotis*) to Brahman as its object is also established by implication.
Therefore, in this context, "light" should be understood as Brahman. // 24 //
Note: The word "atha" (now) is intended to introduce another form of meditation following the meditation on Brahman as conditioned by the *gāyatrī*.
Therefore, that light which shines beyond and further than the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) is superimposed upon the gastric fire (*jāṭhara-jyotis*), identifying it with "this [light] here.
The meaning of "beyond" (*pṛṣṭheṣu*) is "above" all classes of living beings and all worlds, beginning with the earth (*bhūr*).
"No" means that [the shining] belongs only to that which possesses form and parts, due to its connection with light;
that which is not mixed with fire, water, and earth is said here to be "made of three.
Another purpose is the destruction of darkness and so forth.

Having divided each of those three—fire, water, and food—into two parts, and having further divided one part of each into two and placed it into the other parts, the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is accomplished.
This is logical because they are participants [in the process].

Just as the vision of Prajāpati’s head was taught in the syllable *bhūḥ* due to their identity, so too must a similarity be stated here; otherwise, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) would not be established.
This is "sight" (dṛṣṭi) when one perceives this heat through touch;
this is "hearing" (śruti), as is understood from the remainder of the text, when one hears a roar-like sound after covering the ears.
He is "lovely to behold" (cakṣuṣya), meaning beautiful to look upon.
"Śruta" means "widely heard.
"Prākṛta" means born from *prakṛti*, that is to say, an effect.

The capacity to bestow radiance by being separated from Brahman is "differentiation" (*viśeṣakatva*); the absence of that is "non-differentiation" (*aviśeṣakatva*), meaning the state of not distinguishing [itself] from Brahman. Its possession of limits is due to its being for the purpose of valid cognition (*pramiti*) or for the purpose of meditative worship (*upāsti*).
The syntactical connection is "even beyond the sky.

For the gastric light is a modification of the Supreme Self that has entered into the body in the form of the individual soul (jīva); it arises from the flaccidity of the body when the soul is absent, and from the heat of one who is living.
Therefore, worship through a symbol (pratīkopāsana) is justified.
He is called *annāda* because he eats food in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), or because he is the giver of food on all sides.
He is called *vasudāna* because he bestows wealth—that is, gold and the fruits of action; thus, these are designations based on his specific attributes.

The construction is as follows: by the power of its own capacity—that is, the capacity of the pronoun (*sarvanāman*) consisting in its denotation of what is proximate—when [the object] is referred to by that force, [the objection does not hold].

If it is argued that [Brahman is not denoted] because of the mention of "meter" (*chandas*), we say no; for there is a teaching of the fixing of the mind (*ceto'rpaṇa*) in that manner, and such is the scriptural vision.
Now, as for what was stated previously—that even in the preceding sentence Brahman was not denoted—[that is refuted here].

As for the objection that this refers to the meter named Gāyatrī— on account of the statement, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this being, whatever exists here" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.1)— that must be refuted.
But how can it be said that Brahman is not denoted because of the mention of the meters,
when in this very Ṛgvedic verse, "Such is its greatness," Brahman is shown to have four quarters?
This is not so.

Having commenced with the Gāyatrī in the passage, "The Gāyatrī indeed is all this," and having explained that very Gāyatrī through its various forms as the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the means of knowledge, the mantra—"This is that four-footed, sixfold Gāyatrī; of this [Brahman] the greatness is as much as has been declared by the Ṛk"—is cited in reference to that very Gāyatrī whose nature has already been explained.
How, then, could it suddenly denote Brahman as being four-footed?

Even the word "Brahman" that occurs there in the passage, "That which is indeed this Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.5, 6), refers only to the Vedic metre because the metre is the subject under discussion; for in the passage, "He who knows this secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of Brahman thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.3), they explain it as "the secret doctrine of the Veda" (vedopaniṣadam).
If it be argued that Brahman is not the subject under discussion because of the mention of the *chandas* (metre),

this is no fault. For, "because of the emphasis on fixing the mind in that manner" (*tathā cetorpaṇanigrahāt*), by means of the metre called *gāyatrī*, the fixing of the mind— the concentration of consciousness— upon Brahman, which is inherent in that [metre], is declared by this scriptural statement concerning Brahman.
"Indeed, the Gāyatrī is all this.
For it is not possible for the Gāyatrī, which is merely a particular arrangement of syllables, to possess the nature of being the Self of all.
Therefore, that which is the cause of the world—Brahman—which is inherent in the modification called Gāyatrī, is here said to be "all this."

As in the passage, "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). Furthermore, we shall explain that the effect is non-different from its cause in the sūtra: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] [is established] on account of such terms as 'originating' and so forth" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.14).

Likewise, elsewhere too, meditation upon Brahman through the medium of its modifications is observed: "For the Bahvṛcas meditate upon Him in the Great Hymn; the Adhvaryus [meditate upon Him] in the Fire; the Chandogas [meditate upon Him] in the Mahāvrata."

Thus, even though the meters are mentioned, Brahman with four quarters is indeed indicated in the preceding passage. That very same Brahman is referred to in the passage concerning light (*jyotir-vākya*) for the purpose of enjoining another form of meditation.
Another says: Brahman is denoted directly by the word *gāyatrī* because of a commonality of number;
for just as the *gāyatrī* has four feet consisting of six syllables each, so too does Brahman have four quarters.
Likewise, elsewhere also, a word denoting a *chandas* is seen to be employed in another sense due to a commonality of number;
for example, having begun with, "Those five and these other five, being ten, constitute the *kṛta*," it says, "This is that *virāj*, the eater of food" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 4.3.8).
In this view, Brahman alone is what is expressed, so there is no denotation of a *chandas*.
In every respect, Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage.
[FN: The meaning is that for one who knows this *brahmopaniṣad*—the secret of the Veda consisting of the Madhu-vidyā—there occurs the attainment of Brahman, which is devoid of rising and setting.
Those versed in the Ṛgveda worship this [Brahman] during the recitation of the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*).]
The Adhvaryus, who are followers of the Yajurveda, [recite] at the Kratu sacrifice; the Chandogas, who are followers of the Sāmaveda, [recite] at the Mahāvrata sacrifice.
In the Saṃvarga-vidyā, with respect to the divine (adhidaiva), fire, sun, moon, and water dissolve into air;
with respect to the self (adhyātma), speech, sight, hearing, and mind dissolve into breath.
These five others are related to the divine (ādhidaivika), and the other five are related to the self (ādhyātmika); these, being ten when combined, are called "the completed" (kṛta).
"The completed" refers to the game of dice.

"And because the designation of the quarters beginning with 'the existent' (bhūta) is appropriate only in this way; for this reason also, it must be accepted that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage. (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.26) Thus, Brahman is the topic of the previous statement.
For [the text] designates the elements and so forth as its feet;
indeed, having pointed out the elements, earth, body, and heart, it says: "This is that Gāyatrī, which has four feet and sixfold divisions.
For the elements and so forth cannot logically be the feet of mere meter (chandas) without resorting to Brahman.
Furthermore, if Brahman were not the basis [of this teaching], this verse—"Tāvān asya"—could not be understood.
For by its own inherent force, this Ṛk denotes Brahman alone:
"All beings are one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6).
Thus, because it is established that [Brahman] is the self of all;
moreover, this verse is recited in the *Puruṣasūkta* precisely as referring to Brahman.
And Smṛti shows that Brahman alone possesses such a nature: "Pervading this entire universe, I stand with but a single portion" (Bhagavad Gītā 10.42).
And in this case, the designation "That which is indeed Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.7) is justified in its primary sense;
likewise, [the reference to] "the five persons of Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.6).
And thus, the scriptural mention of the "persons of Brahman" (*brahmapuruṣa*) within the apertures of the heart is possible only if their connection with Brahman is intended.
Therefore, it is established that Brahman is the subject under discussion in the preceding passage;
that very same Brahman is referred to in the passage concerning light (*jyotis*), being recognized through its connection with the heavenly world (*dyusambandha*). // 26 //

FN: Six aspects of Brahman, known as Gāyatrī, are heard in scripture: the elements, the earth, the body, the heart, speech, and the vital breath. "If it be argued that [the two meditations] are not identical because of the difference in instruction, we say no, because there is no contradiction in either case. (BBs 1.1.27)
Furthermore, as for what was stated previously— that in the passage "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven," the sky (*dyau*) is taught as a substratum by means of the locative case,
whereas in the subsequent passage "Now, that which is beyond the sky," it is taught as a limit by means of the ablative case—
it follows from this difference in teaching that there is no recognition of that same entity here.
That must be refuted.
To this it is said: this is not a fault, because there is no contradiction in either case.
In both cases—whether the instruction is in the locative case or the ablative case—there is no contradiction with recognition.
Just as in common worldly usage, a hawk, even though it is connected to the top of a tree, is seen to be described in two ways:
"the hawk is on the treetop" and "the hawk is beyond the treetop."
Thus, the eternally existent Brahman, though actually in heaven itself, is taught as being "beyond heaven.

Another says: Just as in the world a hawk, even when not actually connected with the top of a tree, is seen to be described in two ways—as "the hawk on the treetop" and "the hawk ahead of the treetop."
And thus, although Brahman, which exists beyond heaven, is taught as being "in heaven," there is therefore a recognition here of the Brahman previously specified.
Consequently, it is established that the Supreme Brahman alone is denoted by the word "light. // 27 //
The Section on Pratardana (Pratardanādhikaraṇam). Sūtras 28–31:
"The Vital Breath [is Brahman], because of the same conclusion [reached in other passages].

(BBs 1.1.28) In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad, there is the narrative of Indra and Pratardana: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra through both battle and manliness."

In that [text] it is heard: "He said: 'I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātman); meditate upon me as life and immortality. Likewise, later on: "Now, indeed, it is Prāṇa alone, the conscious self, who, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.1, 2, 3). Similarly: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and so forth.
And previously [it was stated]: "This very vital breath (prāṇa) is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8), and so forth.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the mere wind denoted here by the word *prāṇa*, or is it the self of a deity, or the individual soul (jīva), or else the supreme Brahman?
But has it not already been explained in the section "Therefore, the Prāṇa" that the word *prāṇa* refers to Brahman?
And here too, there are marks of Brahman, such as "blissful, undecaying, immortal," and so forth.
How, then, can a doubt arise here once again?
We say it is because multiple indicative marks are observed;
for here not only the indicative marks of Brahman are found, but there are indeed other indicative marks as well.
"Know Me alone" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1)—
this statement of Indra is a characteristic mark of the deity-self;
"having taken hold of this body, it causes it to rise"— this is a characteristic mark of the vital breath (prāṇa).
"One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," and so forth—these are marks of the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, a doubt arises.
On this point, since it is well-known that the vital breath (prāṇa) is air (vāyu), that conclusion is reached; however, it is stated in reply: the Brahman is to be understood by the word "prāṇa."

Why? Because it is understood in that way. For, when the sentence is examined in its proper sequence from beginning to end, the coherence of the word-meanings is found to be intent upon the exposition of Brahman.
To begin with, at the outset:
When Indra said to Pratardana, "Choose a boon," Pratardana offered as his choice the supreme human goal, saying, "You yourself choose for me that which you consider most beneficial for a human being.
How could the vital breath (prāṇa), which is being taught to him as the most beneficial, not be the Supreme Self?
For there is no attainment of the most beneficial state anywhere other than through the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
This is because of such scriptural passages as: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8), and likewise:
"He who knows Me—verily, his world is not destroyed by any action, neither by theft nor by the killing of an embryo" (Kaushītaki Upaniṣad 3.1).
And such passages as these are consistent with the acceptance of Brahman;

for the destruction of all karma through the knowledge of Brahman is well-established in such scriptural texts as: "His actions perish when He, the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8).
Furthermore, the state of being the self of wisdom (*prajñātmatva*) is possible only in the case of Brahman;
for it is not possible for the insentient wind to be the self of wisdom.
Likewise, in the concluding passage as well, qualities such as bliss—expressed in the words "blissful, undecaying, immortal"—are not properly possible in anything other than Brahman.

"He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action; for it is he who causes him whom he wishes to lead up from these worlds to perform good action, and it is he who causes him whom he wishes to lead down from these worlds to perform evil action"—and also: "He is the lord of the world, He is the master of the world" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.8).
All of this can be consistently understood if the Supreme Brahman is relied upon as the referent, but not if the primary vital breath (mukhya prāṇa) is taken as such.
Therefore, the "breath" (prāṇa) is Brahman. [28] *Note:
This means that the sequence of words is observed to be connected solely with the purpose of establishing Brahman.*
By the words "He said, no," and so forth, everything has been stated: his being untouched by dharma and the like, his being the cause of that [creation], and his lordship over it.

"If it be argued that [the Self] is not [meant here] because of the instruction regarding the speaker's self, [we reply: for there is an abundance of internal connection in this [text]. (BBs 1.1.29) As for what was previously stated—that "Prāṇa is Brahman"—[it is not so].
That is refuted:
the word "prāṇa" does not refer to the Supreme Brahman.
Why? Because there is an instruction regarding the Self of the speaker.

For the speaker, a certain specific deity named Indra who possesses a body, declared himself to Pratardana, beginning with "Know me alone," and continuing with the statement of egoity, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self.

How could this Prāṇa, being taught as the very self of the speaker, be Brahman? For the capacity for speech is not possible for Brahman, as it is said: "Without speech, without mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad).
This is established by such scriptural passages as these.

Likewise, he praised himself by means of attributes connected with a physical body—which are impossible in Brahman—through statements such as: "I slew the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ; I delivered the Arunmukha Atis to the jackals.
And so forth.
And the state of being Prāṇa is appropriate for Indra because of his possession of strength;
for it is known from scripture that "Prāṇa is indeed strength," and Indra is well-known as the deity of strength.
For they say that whatever constitutes the exercise of power is indeed the work of Indra.
Furthermore, the nature of the self as wisdom is possible for the divine self because its knowledge is unimpeded;
for they say that the gods possess unimpeded knowledge.

Since the instruction regarding the Self as the deity is thus determined, statements such as "being most beneficial" and so forth must be applied to that very subject as far as possible. Therefore, having raised the objection that Prāṇa is not Brahman because Indra is the one teaching the Self, it is answered: "For in this [chapter], there is an abundance of internal connection. An "internal connection" (adhyātma-sambandha) means an abundance or multiplicity of connection with the inner Self (pratyagātman), which is perceived in this chapter.

The statement, "As long as the vital breath (prāṇa) dwells in this body, so long is there life," shows that the power of sustaining and withdrawing life belongs solely to the vital breath— which is the conscious self (prajñātman) existing as the innermost subject— and not to any particular external deity. Likewise, the passage "In the existence of the vital breaths lies the highest good" indicates that the vital breath is to be understood as residing within the self, having the senses as its support.

Likewise, [the texts state]: "Prāṇa alone, whose self is intelligence (prajñātman), having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3); and beginning with, "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," it continues: "Just as the felloe of a chariot wheel is fixed on the spokes and the spokes are fixed on the nave, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed on the elements of intelligence (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the elements of intelligence [are fixed on Prāṇa]."

"Resting in the vital breath— this very vital breath is the conscious self (prajñātman), blissful, undecaying, and immortal"— thus [the text] concludes by referring to the inner self alone, which is not overwhelmed by the activities of the objects and the senses.
Furthermore, the concluding statement, "One should know that as my Self," is appropriate for the acceptance of the inner self, but not for the acceptance of something external.
And another scriptural passage states: "This Self is Brahman, which has become all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19).
Therefore, because of the abundance of references to the inner self (adhyātma), this is indeed an instruction on Brahman and not an instruction on the nature of a deity. // 29 //

How, then, is there a teaching regarding the self by the speaker? [The answer is: Having slain the Brahmin Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he gave over the Arunmukhas—those whose mouths (*mukha*) contain the *ruta*, meaning the Vedāntic utterances that "speak" (*ru*) according to reality—to the *sālāvṛkas*, the wild dogs of the forest, who are ascetics (*yatīn*) turned away from the Vedāntas.
I have given [this explanation].

Just as in a wheel, where the rim (*nemi*) is fixed upon the spokes (*ara*), and the spokes are fixed upon the nave (*nābhi*)—the central hub of the wheel—so too are the five elements, beginning with earth, measured out; thus, the five objects of experience, sound and so forth, are the "measures" (*mātrā*). These ten are the "elements and measures" (*bhūtamātrā*).
But according to the perspective of the scriptures, the instruction is like that of Vāmadeva.

Indra, the deity, seeing his own self as the Supreme Self through the vision of a seer (*ārṣa-darśana*)—in accordance with the scriptures, perceiving "I am indeed the Supreme Brahman"—taught: "Know me alone."
It is just as when the seer Vāmadeva, seeing this, realized: "I was Manu and I was the Sun.
This is in accordance with the Śruti: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
As for what was further stated—that after saying "Know me alone," Indra praised himself by means of his corporeal attributes such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son—[that too is explained].
That must be refuted.

To this it is said: The mention of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son and so forth is not intended for the purpose of praising Indra as an object of knowledge by way of saying, "Since I am one who has performed such deeds, therefore know me.
How, then, is it?
It is for the purpose of praising consciousness (*vijñāna*).
For this reason, having introduced acts of daring such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, the text subsequently connects them with the praise of consciousness:
"In that regard, my greed was not diminished; he who knows me—verily, for him there is no [obstruction] by any action whatsoever."
By the words "the world is measured," etc.,
this is what is meant:
since even such cruel deeds as these have been committed by me, who has become Brahman, not even a single hair of mine is harmed.
"Whoever else knows me, his world is not harmed by any action whatsoever.
But that which is to be known is Brahman itself, as will be stated later: "I am the breath, the conscious self.
Therefore, this is a statement concerning Brahman.

If it be argued that [the passage does not refer to Brahman] because of the indicative marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), we say no; because there is a threefoldness of meditation, and because [these marks] are here connected with that [Brahman].

Although, due to the observation of an abundance of internal connections, this is not an instruction regarding the supreme Self as a deity, nevertheless, the passage cannot be a statement about Brahman.
Why? Because of the indicative marks of the individual soul and the indicative marks of the chief vital breath.
First, in this passage, a clear indicative mark (liṅga) of the individual soul (jīva) is perceived: "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker," and so forth.

For here, the status of being the object of knowledge is predicated of the individual soul, who is the presiding overseer of the body and the organs and is active through the instruments such as speech.

Likewise, there is also an indicative mark of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa): "Now, indeed, it is the vital breath alone, the conscious self (prajñātman), which, having taken hold of this body, causes it to rise."
Furthermore, the maintenance of the body is the specific function of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa);

for in the dialogue of the vital breaths, concerning speech and the other organs, it is said: "The most excellent among them, the vital breath, said: 'Do not fall into delusion; it is I who, having divided myself fivefold and having firmly supported this vital breath, maintain it.
(Praśna Upaniṣad 2.3)
Because of such scriptural hearing.

As for those who read, "having taken hold of this body," their [text] is to be explained as meaning that [the Self], having taken hold of this living soul (*jīva*) or the aggregate of the senses, causes the body to rise up.
Furthermore, the state of being the conscious self (*prajñātmatva*) is appropriate for the living soul (*jīva*) because it possesses sentience.

Even in the case of the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*), this is indeed appropriate because it depends upon other vital breaths which are the instruments of cognition (*prajñā*). Furthermore, if both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the principal vital breath are accepted [as the referents], then both modes of description are justified: the description of non-difference through their co-existence, and the description of difference through their distinct natures—as in: "That which is the vital breath is cognition; that which is cognition... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.2.1).

"That breath (prāṇa) dwells together with this [other] in this body; together they depart. But if Brahman were intended, what would be distinguished from what? Therefore, if it is argued that here both the individual soul (jīva) and the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) are understood as distinct, and not Brahman—then [we reply]:
This is not so;
for here [the text speaks of] "veneration by the knowers of the three Vedas" (*traividyopāsā*).

If this were the case, it would follow that there are three kinds of veneration: veneration of the individual self (*jīva*), veneration of the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), and veneration of Brahman.
And it is not proper to accept this [duality] within a single sentence;
for the unity of the sentence is understood from its opening and its conclusion.

Having begun with "Know me alone," and having stated, "I am Prāṇa, the conscious self (prajñātman); meditate upon me as life and immortality," it concludes at the end: "This very Prāṇa is the conscious self, bliss, undecaying, and immortal."
Thus, the opening and the conclusion are seen to be of a single form;
in that case, it is proper to rely on the unity of meaning.
Furthermore, the characteristic marks of Brahman cannot be interpreted as being directed toward anything else.
Because it is impossible to consign the ten elements (*bhūtamātrā*) and the ten cognitions (*prajñāmātrā*) to anything other than Brahman;
and because, even in other contexts, the word "prāṇa" refers to Brahman due to its dependence on it and the presence of Brahman's characteristic marks;

and because here too, this is understood to be an instruction regarding Brahman due to the connection with Brahman's characteristic marks, such as the presentation of [Brahman] as the most beneficial.
As for the indication of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) that was shown—namely, "having taken hold of this body, it causes it to rise"—that is incorrect;
because the activity of the vital breaths is dependent upon the Supreme Self, it can be figuratively attributed to the Supreme Self.
"No mortal lives by the out-breath (*prāṇa*) or the in-breath (*apāna*)."
For there is the scriptural text: "But by the other [the Self] they live, on which these two depend" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.5.5).

Furthermore, as for the characteristics of the individual soul (jīva) shown in such passages as "One should not seek to know speech, but should know the speaker," that too does not preclude the position that it is Brahman;
for the so-called individual soul is not absolutely different from Brahman.
This is known from such scriptural passages as "That thou art" and "I am Brahman.
However, by resorting to the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect, Brahman itself is called the individual soul (jīva), the agent, and the enjoyer.

In order to show that its true nature is Brahman by setting aside the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the instruction beginning with "One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker" is not contradictory, as it serves to direct [the mind] toward the inner Self (pratyagātman). "That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed..."
Know that very Brahman to be yourself; it is not this which people here worship.

Furthermore, another scriptural passage such as *Kevalya Upaniṣad* 1.4 shows that the very Self, while engaged in activities such as speaking and so forth, possesses the nature of Brahman. As for what was said— that the perception of a distinction between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the conscious self (*prajñātman*), expressed in the statement "for these two dwell together in this body and depart together from it," is not tenable within the doctrine of Brahman—
that is not a fault.

Since it is logical to designate as non-different the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which are the two substrates of the powers of knowledge and action and serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), there is no contradiction in identifying them as "the vital breath itself is the conscious self" (*prāṇa eva prajñātmā*), because the inner self, though conditioned by these two adjuncts, is non-different in its essential nature. Alternatively, the meaning of the sūtra *na upāsātraividhyād āśritatvād iha tadyogāt* is this: even in a passage concerning Brahman, the presence of characteristics belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) is not contradictory.
How so? Because of the threefold nature of meditation (*upāsā*).

Here, in this meditation on Brahman, a threefold aspect is intended: by means of the attributes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), by means of the attributes of wisdom (*prajñā*), and by means of its own inherent attributes.
Among these, [it is said]: "Meditate on life as the immortal; life is the vital breath."
"This body, having grasped it, causes it to rise," and "Therefore, one should venerate this very thing as the Uktha"— these are attributes of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Having begun with, "Now we shall explain how all beings become unified within this consciousness (prajñā)," [the text continues].
"Speech alone was one limb that she milked out; beyond it, the constituent of being (bhūtamātrā) is established as its name.

Having mounted speech by means of discernment (prajñā), one obtains all names through speech. Such is the attribute of discernment. Indeed, these ten constituents of being are with respect to discernment, and the ten constituents of discernment are with respect to being.
For if there were only the elements and not the cognitions, they would not be cognitions;
and if there were only the cognitions and not the elements, they would not be elements.
Indeed, no form whatsoever could be established internally.

"This is not a plurality. Just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon the spokes and the spokes are fixed upon the hub, even so these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are fixed upon the elements of intelligence (prajñāmātrāḥ), and the elements of intelligence are fixed upon the vital breath (prāṇa). This very vital breath is the self consisting of intelligence"—such is the attribute of Brahman.
Therefore, this single meditation upon Brahman itself is intended to be threefold, by way of the attributes of the two limiting adjuncts and its own inherent attribute.
Elsewhere as well— in passages such as "consisting of mind, having breath for a body" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2)— meditation on Brahman is based upon the attributes of its limiting adjuncts.

Here too, that [interpretation] is appropriate, because the unity of meaning of the passage is understood from its opening and conclusion, and because the marks of prāṇa, prajñā, and Brahman are perceived.
Therefore, it is established that this is a statement concerning Brahman. // 31 //
Thus ends the first quarter of the first chapter in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda. [Note:
The meaning is that, as appropriate, some passages here concern the individual soul (*jīva*), some concern the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), and some concern Brahman.

In the dialogue of the vital breaths, speech and all the other senses, each considering itself to be superior, approached Prajāpati with the desire to determine which among them was truly preeminent.]
He said to them, "He, upon whose departure the body becomes most wretched, he is the best among you.
Then, as speech and the other organs departed one by one, the body remained healthy.
But when the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) was about to depart, there was great agitation among them all.

The preeminent Prāṇa said: "I alone, having divided myself fivefold into the states of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, support—that is, take recourse in—the *bāṇa*, which is this unstable body; for it shines (*bhāti*) and moves (*vāna*), thus it is *bāṇa*.
There are ten elemental constituents (*bhūtamātrā*): the five objects such as sound and the five elements such as earth.
There are ten cognitive constituents (*prajñāmātrā*): the five sense organs and the five cognitions."
This is the case elsewhere, such as in the passage beginning with "Therefore, [it is] Prāṇa.

That consciousness by which speech is raised up—that is, impelled and rendered capable of speaking—is that very Brahman which is inaccessible to speech and the other senses. Regarding the word "one should meditate," there would be a syntactical split (vākyabheda) if one were to meditate on the three [entities] independently.
The meaning is that it does not belong to Brahman alone by virtue of its own nature;
rather, life is its "longevity" because living depends upon it.
And "it causes one to rise," thus it is called *uktha*; this is a characteristic of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates the subject matter (*jīvadharma*). First Chapter, Second Section.
[In this section, there is an investigation of passages containing indistinct marks of Brahman that have as their object Brahman as the object of meditation.]
1. The Section on Being Established Everywhere (Sarvatra-prasiddhi-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 1.1.8.

In the first quarter (pāda), it was stated [in Sūtra 1.1.2] that "Brahman is the cause of the origin and so forth of this [world]," meaning that Brahman is the cause of the origin, etc., of the entire world, including ether and the rest.
Of that Brahman, who is the cause of the entire world, there is omnipresence (vyāpitva).
eternal nature, omniscience, and omnipotence.
Attributes of this kind, such as "being the self of all," have indeed already been mentioned.

Furthermore, by demonstrating the reasons why certain words— well-known in other senses— have Brahman as their object, several passages containing clear marks of Brahman (*spaṣṭabrahmaliṅga*), which were previously doubtful, have been determined to be devoted to Brahman.
Furthermore, other passages containing indistinct marks of Brahman are subject to doubt: do they set forth the supreme Brahman, or do they refer to some other entity?
To resolve this, the second and third sections (pādas) are commenced.
"Because of the teaching of that which is well-known everywhere" (BBs 1.2.1).

The following is recorded in scripture: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, as it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; one should meditate upon it with a calm mind. Now, a person consists of volition; as is his volition in this world, so does he become after departing from here.
Let him form a volition: 'Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body, and having light for its form'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1, 2), and so forth.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is the embodied self (śārīra ātman) taught here as the object of meditation by means of these attributes such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya), or is it the supreme Brahman? What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is the embodied self.
Why? Because the connection with the mind and other organs is well known for that [individual self], which is the lord of the body and the instruments of action, but not for the supreme Brahman,
according to such scriptural passages as, "For He is without breath, without mind, pure" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).

Objection: Since Brahman has already been presented by its own word in the statement "All this, indeed, is Brahman," how can it be suspected here that the embodied self (śārīra ātman) is the object of meditation?
Response: This is not a fault.

This sentence is not intended to enjoin the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon Brahman; rather, it is intended to enjoin tranquility (*śama*). For this reason, it says: "All this, indeed, is Brahman, for it originates from, dissolves into, and breathes within That; therefore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind.
What is meant by this is as follows: since this entire collection of modifications is nothing but Brahman, [one should remain tranquil].
Because it arises from that, because it consists of that, and because it does not differ from that;
and since passion and the like are impossible if everything were of a single nature, one should therefore meditate upon it as peaceful.
Moreover, if the passage were intended solely for the injunction of tranquility (śama), it would not be possible to enjoin the meditation on Brahman by means of this sentence;
rather, meditation is enjoined by the statement, "He should form a resolve" (sa kratuṃ kurvīta).
Here, "resolve" (kratu) means intention or meditative concentration (dhyāna).

Furthermore, its being the object [of the meditation] is not heard; rather, "consisting of mind, having prāṇa as its body" is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of the individual soul (jīva). Therefore, we say that this meditation has the individual soul as its object.
Even such attributes as "possessing all actions, possessing all desires," though heard in the text, are compatible with the individual soul when taken in a figurative sense.

"‘This is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice or a grain of barley’—this [scriptural statement] regarding the heart as the abode and the minuteness of the individual soul (jīva), which is the size of the tip of an awl, is appropriate for the jīva, but not for the unlimited Brahman.
Now, one might object: "But the statement ‘greater than the earth,’ and so forth, would likewise not be appropriate for something limited.
To this we reply: First of all, both minuteness and greatness cannot be attributed to a single entity simultaneously, because they are contradictory.
And when one of the two must be adopted, it is proper to adopt "minuteness" because it is mentioned first; as for "greatness," that will apply with reference to the state of being Brahman.

Furthermore, since it has been determined that the subject matter concerns the individual soul (jīva), the mention of Brahman at the end—namely, "This is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4)—[is merely a concluding reference].
Thus, since that [passage] also serves to refer back to the subject under discussion, it concerns the individual soul (jīva) alone.
Therefore, [the Self] is to be meditated upon by means of attributes such as consisting of mind (manomaya) and so forth.
Why? Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere.

It is logical that what is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the referent of the word "Brahman"— the cause of the world— is precisely that which is taught here as qualified by attributes such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya), since it is heard at the beginning of the passage in the statement, "All this, indeed, is Brahman. In this way, there will be neither the abandonment of the subject under discussion nor the introduction of something not so discussed.
But was it not stated that at the beginning of the passage, Brahman was mentioned with the intention of enjoining tranquility (*śama*), and not with its own intended meaning?

To this it is replied: although Brahman was mentioned with the intention of enjoining tranquility, nevertheless, when qualities such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth are being taught, that very same Brahman remains proximate.
The individual soul (*jīva*), however, is neither proximate nor is it denoted by its own specific term; thus there is a distinction. // 1 //
FN: That in which something is born is *tajja*;
that in which it exists is *talla*;
and that in which it moves—that is, acts—is *tadana*. Thus, being *tajja*, *talla*, and *tadana*, it is *tajjalān*.
By the maxim of "the vegetable-king" (*śākapārthiva*), there is an elision of the middle term *tat*.
While it should have been stated as *tajjalānam*, the elision of a constituent part is a Vedic (archaic) usage.

Due to the transposition of case endings, the meaning is that one should meditate upon that which consists of mind (*manomaya*), whose body is breath (*prāṇaśarīra*), and whose form is light (*bhārūpa*).
Since it says this, the meaning is that [the self] is intent upon the method of tranquility (*śama-vidhi*).
"The size of the tip of an iron rod pierced by a needle" is the meaning.

For one who, by means of the pronoun within the compound *prāṇaḥ śarīram asya* ("of whom the vital breath is the body"), abandons the relevant Brahman—the proximate referent—and instead desires the individual soul (*jīva*), which is not the subject under discussion, the fault follows that there is an abandonment of the relevant subject and the introduction of an irrelevant one.
The ellipsis is "the disparity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
And because the qualities intended to be expressed are appropriate [in Brahman]. "Intended" (vivakṣita) means those desired to be spoken.

Although in the impersonal Veda, because there is no speaker, the intended meaning (*vivakṣita*) cannot exist, it is nevertheless figuratively designated by means of its result, which is adoption (*upādāna*). For in the world, that which is expressed by words and is to be adopted is said to be "intended," while that which is not to be adopted is said to be "not intended."
Therefore, even in the Veda, that which is stated as something to be adopted is intended [by the author], while the other is unintended;
moreover, what is to be adopted and what is not to be adopted is understood from the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedic sentences.

Therefore, those qualities intended here for meditation—which are taught as attributes to be adopted, such as "having true resolve" (*satyasaṃkalpa*) and so forth—are appropriate in the case of the Supreme Brahman.
For the quality of having true resolve is possible only for the Supreme Self, because its power is unimpeded in the creation, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world].
And as a quality of the Supreme Self, it is stated: "The Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
In this context, it is heard in the scripture: "He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true.
By the phrase "whose self is space" (ākāśātmā) and so forth, the meaning is that his self is like space.
Brahman’s similarity to space is possible through attributes such as omnipresence and the like.
This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Greater than the earth.
Even when it is explained as "that of which space is the self," that too is possible, since Brahman— the cause of the entire universe and the Self of all— possesses space as its nature.
For this very reason, [the text says] "possessing all works" and so forth;
thus, the qualities intended here as objects of meditation are appropriate for Brahman.

As for what was said—that the marks of the individual soul (jīva) found in the passage "consisting of mind, having vital breath as its body" are not appropriate for Brahman—[that objection is addressed as follows:]
We reply that even this is possible in the case of Brahman.
For, because Brahman is the Self of all, qualities such as "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth, which belong to the individual soul (jīva), become related to Brahman.
And thus there are Śruti and Smṛti passages concerning Brahman: "Thou art woman; thou art youth, or even maiden."
"You are the aged one who moves with a staff; you are the newborn one whose face is turned in every direction" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3), and also:
"With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all" (Bhagavad Gītā 13.13).
The scriptural text, "For it is without breath, without mind, pure," has the pure Brahman as its subject matter;
however, the distinction here is that the text, "Consisting of mind, having the vital breath for its body," has the qualified Brahman as its subject matter.
Therefore, because the intended qualities are logically consistent, it is understood that the Supreme Brahman alone is taught here as the object of meditation. // 2 //
Note: "Taking up" (*upādāna*) and "not taking up" (*anupādāna*) refer to acceptance and rejection.
"Purposefulness" (*tātparya*) is a property of words (*śabdadharmah*), defined as the suitability for the comprehension of a meaningful result.
The meaning is that these two [acceptance and rejection] are understood through the cognition of [the speaker's] intention and other such factors.
He who, having become aged and decrepit, moves about supported by a staff—he too is you; likewise, he who is born as a child is also you.
But because [the self] does not arise [as a new entity], it is not the body.
By the preceding sūtra, the possibility of those qualities intended [to belong] to Brahman was stated;
by this one, however, their impossibility in the embodied soul (śārīra) is stated.
The word "tu" (however) serves the purpose of restriction.
By the reasoning already stated, it is Brahman alone that possesses the qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*), and not the embodied individual soul (*jīva*).
For this reason, [it is said to be] "one whose resolve is true" (*satyasaṃkalpa*).
He whose self is space,
who is speechless,
and who is without regard.
Furthermore, qualities of this kind, such as "greater than the earth," are not appropriately applicable to the embodied soul (śārīra) in their literal sense.
The term "embodied soul" (śārīra) means that which exists in the body.
But surely the Lord (Īśvara) also exists in the body?
True;
it exists within the body, but it does not exist *only* in the body,
for [the scripture says], "Greater than the earth, greater than the intermediate space."
And because its all-pervasiveness is heard in the scriptural statement, "It is omnipresent and eternal like space," whereas the individual soul (jīva) exists only within the body,
since it has no functioning outside the body, which is the locus of its experience. // 3 //

FN: He is "vākī" because he possesses speech (*vāk*); one who does not possess speech is "avākī," meaning devoid of all sense organs such as speech and the rest. Because his desires are fulfilled, he has no concern for anything, and thus he is "anādaraḥ" (without regard).
And [this is known] from the designation of action and agent. (BBs 1.2.4)
For this reason as well, the embodied soul does not possess qualities such as being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*):
because there is a designation of object and agent in the passage, "Having departed from here, I shall attain him" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.4).
By the word "him" (*etam*), the text designates the Self under discussion—possessing qualities such as being "consisting of mind"—as the object and the goal to be attained.
"I shall fully realize" refers to the lay follower (upāsaka) as the agent and the one who attains;
"I shall fully realize" means "I shall attain."
Moreover, when a distinction exists, it is not logical to designate one and the same entity as both the object of an action and its agent.
Likewise, the relationship between the object of meditation (upāsya) and the meditator (upāsaka) is necessarily based upon a difference.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the embodied self (śārīra) cannot be the one characterized by "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and so forth. // 4 //
FN: The connection is that [the text] designates "this" as the means of attainment.
Because of the specific wording of the scripture (BBs 1.2.5), for this reason as well, the one characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind is other than the embodied self.

Because there is a difference in words within the same context in another scriptural passage: "Just as rice, or barley, or śyāmāka grain, or the kernel of a śyāmāka grain—so is this golden person within the inner self" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.3.2).

Since the word denoting the embodied soul is the locative form "antarātman," it is distinct from the other, nominative form "puruṣaḥ," which denotes the Self characterized by consisting of mind and so forth.
Therefore, the difference between those two is understood. (5) [Note:
"Belonging to the same context" means having the same subject matter of knowledge.
In the phrase *antarātman*, there is a Vedic elision of the case ending.]
The meaning is "within the inner self.
And because of the Smṛti:
the Smṛti also demonstrates the distinction between the embodied self and the Supreme Self: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings."
"Causing all beings, mounted on a machine, to revolve by means of Māyā" (Gītā 18.61), and so forth.
Here [the opponent] asks: "Who, moreover, is this so-called embodied self (śārīra) that is distinct from the Supreme Self?"
That [self] which is negated by such passages as "But because of impossibility, not the embodied one" (B.S. 1.2.3) and so forth;
for scripture—such as "There is no other seer but He, no other hearer but He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23)—excludes any self other than the Supreme Self.
Likewise, Smṛti also states: "And know Me, O Bhārata, as the Knower of the Field in all fields" (Gītā 13.2), and other passages of this kind.
To this, it is replied: This is true.
The very Self, though delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, is figuratively designated as the "embodied one" (śārīra) by the ignorant.
Just as space, although unlimited, appears to be limited due to the influence of limiting adjuncts such as jars or water-pots, so it is with this case.

And with respect to that [conditioned state], the conventional distinction between action and agent is not contradicted prior to the instruction of the oneness of the Self through the teaching, "That thou art."

But once the oneness of the Self is grasped, there would indeed be the complete cessation of all worldly transactions such as bondage and liberation. "If it be argued that [the Self is not omnipresent] because of its being designated as small and because of its being described as such, we say no; for it is to be perceived as such, and it is like space. (Brahmasūtra 1.2.7)
It is "small" because its abode is narrow— its nest being defined as "this is my Self within the heart"—
and because it is designated as minute by the word itself in the passage, "It is smaller than a grain of rice or a grain of barley."
What was stated—that it is the embodied soul (*jīva*), merely the size of the tip of an awl, that is taught here, and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing in the agent—must now be refuted.
To this, it is replied: this is not a fault.
First of all, the designation of that which has a delimited location as being omnipresent is not possible in any way.

However, for that which is omnipresent—because it exists in all locations—even the designation of a delimited location is possible through some particular perspective. For example, although he is the lord of the entire earth, he is nevertheless designated as the "lord of Ayodhyā. But by what perspective is the omnipresent Lord (Īśvara), while existing in all places, designated as having the size of a thumb-joint and as being minute?
Thus we say: "Because it is to be perceived in this way.

In this manner, the Lord, endowed with a multitude of qualities such as extreme subtlety and so forth, is taught there in the lotus of the heart as the one to be perceived—that is, the one to be seen.
Just as Hari resides in the Śālagrāma stone, so too his cognitive awareness perceives Him there; although the Lord is omnipresent, He becomes gracious when worshipped in that specific place.
And this should be viewed as being like space:
just as space, although all-pervading, is designated as "smaller than the eye of a needle" in relation to such things as the eye of a needle,
so too is Brahman.
Thus, since it is dependent upon being perceived [in that way], the fact that Brahman has the heart as its abode and is minute in size is not ultimate.

In this regard, it might be suspected that because Brahman has the heart as its abode, and because those whose abode is the heart differ from body to body, and because defects such as plurality, possession of parts, and non-eternality are observed in the case of parrots and other beings who have different abodes, these defects would also apply to Brahman.
The objection that this [same] consequence would also apply to that [other case] is likewise refuted. // 7 // [FN:
The term "small" (*alpa*) is stated as a synonym for the word "child" (*arbhaka*) in order to negate its application to a mere infant.]

Even if it is somehow intended with respect to the state of Brahman, [the objection] that "there would be the attainment of enjoyment because [Brahman] is to be perceived and seen" is not valid, because of the difference in nature. (BBs 1.2.8)
Since the all-pervading Brahman is connected to the hearts of all living beings,
and since it is not distinct from the embodied soul by virtue of its nature as consciousness,
it would follow that the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is likewise non-distinct [for Brahman].
And because of oneness:
for there exists no transmigrating self other than the supreme Self,
as it is said, "There is no knower other than this" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23).
Based on such scriptural passages as these,
if it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) attains the experience of transmigratory existence just like the Supreme Self, we reply:
no, because of the distinction [between them].
