First of all, it does not follow that Brahman experiences enjoyment (saṃbhoga) in the same way as the embodied soul (śārīra) simply because of its connection with the hearts of all living beings, owing to their difference (vaiśeṣya).
For there is indeed a distinction between the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara):
the one is the agent, the enjoyer, the means for merit and demerit, and possesses pleasure, pain, and so forth.
The other is the opposite, possessing qualities such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva).
Due to this distinction between these two, enjoyment belongs to one and not to the other.
Furthermore, if a connection with an effect were admitted based on mere proximity without relying on the inherent power of the object, [it would lead to absurdities].
There would also be the undesirable consequence of space and so forth being subject to burning and the like.
These same objections and refutations apply equally to those who maintain that the self is all-pervading and manifold.

Furthermore, as for the argument that because Brahman is one and there is no other self, it follows that Brahman must experience the experiences of the body—this too is addressed by the same response.
To this we say: first of all, this "Beloved of the Gods" (the fool) must be asked:
how have you determined that there is no self in the intermediate state?
If you say, "From such scriptural authorities as 'That thou art,' 'I am Brahman,' and 'There is no other knower than this,'" [we reply:]...
Therefore, the scriptural meaning must be understood according to the scriptures; one cannot apply the "half-old woman" principle (*ardhajaratīya*) here.

Furthermore, the scripture—in the passage "That thou art"—teaches that Brahman, characterized by such attributes as being free from sin, is the Self of the embodied soul (*śārīra*). This very teaching precludes the status of being an experiencer for the embodied soul itself.
How, then, could there be the consequence of Brahman experiencing through the experience of that [soul]?
Now, if the oneness of the embodied soul with Brahman is not grasped, then the experience of the embodied soul is caused by false knowledge;
it does not, however, affect Brahman in its ultimate reality.
For when the sky is imagined by the ignorant to possess a surface or impurity and so forth, the sky does not thereby actually become characterized by a surface, impurity, or the like in reality.
To this he says: "Not so, because of the distinction" (*na vaiśeṣyāt*).
Even though there is oneness, it does not follow that Brahman undergoes experience through the experience of the embodied soul, because of the distinction.
For there is indeed a distinction between false knowledge and right knowledge.
Experience is constructed by false knowledge,
whereas unity is perceived by right knowledge;
and the reality perceived by right knowledge is not touched by experience constructed by false knowledge.
Therefore, not even a trace of enjoyment can be attributed to the Lord. [Note:
The meaning is that being the locus of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
This very distinction is what constitutes "particularity" (*vaiśeṣya*).]

The suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*), or it signifies a specific excellence (*viśeṣa*). The meaning of the sūtra is that "excellence" refers to the fact that dharma and so forth serve as causes for their own substratum's fruit; [the suffix is added] because of that.
For those who maintain that there are many selves, [the term] "half" refers to this:
one desires only half—the face—of an aged woman, not her limbs; this is the maxim of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīnyāya*).

The meaning is that even though the Lord, characterized by being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and so forth, is designated as being within the heart for the purpose of meditation, because He is free from defects, the statement "In Him all this [is contained]" and so forth is consistently applicable to Him alone; this is the conclusion of the *Śāṇḍilyavidyā* section.
**Section 2: The Eater (Adhikaraṇa)** BBs_1.2.9:
"The Eater [is Brahman], because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving."
In the Kaṭhavallīs it is recited: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who knows where He is? (1.2.24).
Here, a consumer is perceived, indicated by the mention of food and condiment.
In this regard, there arises the doubt: is fire the eater, or the individual soul (jīva), or rather the supreme self (paramātman)?
Because no specific distinction is determined,
and because in this text questions and explanations regarding three— namely fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the supreme self (paramātman)—
are found; what, then, is the prima facie conclusion?
"Agni eats.
Why? Because of the Vedic revelation and common renown that "Agni is the eater of food" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6).
Or it may be the individual soul (jīva), because of the scriptural observation: "One of them eats the sweet fruit";
it cannot be the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Since it is seen in the text, "Another, not eating, looks on" (Muṇḍaka 3.1.1), this being the position reached, we reply: the Eater here must be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the mention of both the moving and the non-moving.
For the world of moving and non-moving things—the stationary and the living—is perceived here as food, with death as its condiment;
and for such food, no one other than the Supreme Self can be its consumer in its entirety.
However, it is logically consistent that the Supreme Self, while withdrawing the entire collection of modifications, consumes everything.
But surely, the mention of "the moving and the unmoving" is not found here; how then can the mention of "the moving and the unmoving" be employed as a reason as if it were already established?
This is not a fault.
Because death is perceived as the sprinkling [of water] upon the entire multitude of living beings,
and because it is logical that the mention of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas serves the purpose of illustration due to their preeminence;
as for the argument that even the Supreme Self cannot possibly be the "eater," [it is not so].
"Because of the scriptural vision: 'Another, not eating, looks on.
To this it is replied: This vision is a prohibition against the enjoyment of the fruits of karma, because that [enjoyment] is what is proximately present."
It is not a negation of the withdrawal of modifications, because Brahman is well-known in all the Vedāntas as the cause of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone must be the "eater" (attā) here. // 9 //

FN: That Supreme Self, for whom both the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya castes are like two well-known dishes of boiled rice, and for whom Death—being the destroyer of all—stands as the condiment, like clarified butter mixed with the rice;
there, that Eater, the causal Self, resides.

The meaning is that one who possesses the means taught in the mantra, "Not from one who has not desisted from evil conduct," knows that Self which is without distinction; whereas another, devoid of those means, does not know It in this way. This [mention of] "brahmin and kṣatriya" is merely illustrative (upalakṣaṇa); nor are only these two castes intended here.
Because by means of death as a condiment, all living beings are established [as food], and because it is appropriate to mention the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya as the foremost among living beings;
and also because of the context. (BBs 1.2.10)

For this reason as well, the Supreme Self alone must be the "Eater" here, because this context pertains to the Supreme Self, as seen in the passage: "The wise one is neither born nor does He die" (Katha Upanishad 1.2.18).
Thus, it is logical to understand the term "this" as referring to the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, the statement, "Who indeed knows where he is? indicates that being difficult to discern is a characteristic mark of the Supreme Self. // 10 //
3. The Section Concerning Those Entered into the Cave. Sūtras 11–12.
"For two selves have entered the cave, because that is seen [in scripture].
(BBs 1.2.11) It is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Drinking the Truth, having entered the cave in this world, in the highest upper realm..."
"The knowers of Brahman speak of shadow and light, as do those who maintain the five fires and have thrice performed the Nāciketa sacrifice" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.1).
In this regard, a doubt arises:
are the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva) indicated here, or rather the individual soul and the Supreme Self (paramātman)?
If they are the intellect and the living self (jīva), then it follows that the living self is established as distinct from the aggregate of causes and effects dominated by the intellect;
and this, too, must be established here.
"Regarding this doubt concerning a person after death—some say he exists, others say he does not exist—may I be instructed by you in this; this is the third of the boons. (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.1.20).
Since [Naciketas] asked thus, [Yama replied: "I will tell you... and so forth.
Now, the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) are [discussed], whereby the supreme self is established as distinct from the individual soul.
That too must be established here: "Other than dharma, other than adharma, other than this which is done and not done..."
"Tell me that which you see as other than what has been and what is to be" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.14);
since this was asked, the objector here says: "Neither of these two positions is possible."

Why? Because "drinking the *ṛta*" means the enjoyment of the fruits of action; and by the use of the dual number in the phrase "in the world of the well-done," the Śruti shows that the drinking belongs to two.

Therefore, the position that [the two] are the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is not possible; for this very reason, the position that they are the knower of the field and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is also not possible,
because even in the case of the conscious supreme self, the drinking of the *ṛta* is impossible.
"Another, not eating, looks on," according to the wording of this mantra.

To this it is replied: This is no fault; for we observe the metaphorical attribution of "possessing umbrellas" to many people based on the presence of even a single person with an umbrella, as in the expression, "The umbrella-bearers are going."
In this way, even when one person is drinking, two are said to be drinking;
or rather, while the individual soul (jīva) drinks,
the Lord (īśvara) causes it to drink.

Even one who causes another to drink is said to "drink," since we observe that the status of being the agent is conventionally attributed even to the one who causes cooking. Furthermore, it is also possible to understand this as referring to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Because the status of an agent is metaphorically attributed to the instrument,
as seen in the usage "the fuel cooks";
and within this context concerning the internal self (adhyātma), no other two [beings] who drink the covered [fluid] are possible.
Therefore, there arises the doubt: are these two the intellect (buddhi) and the individual soul (jīva), or the individual soul and the supreme self (paramātman)?
What, then, is the initial position? That they are the intellect and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
Why? Because of the qualification "entered into the cave. Whether the body is the cave, or whether the heart is the cave, [the two have entered it].
In either case, it is logical that both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) have entered the cave.
Furthermore, since this is possible, it is not reasonable to assume that the all-pervading Brahman occupies a specific location.
Moreover, the phrase "in the world of good deeds" shows that [the soul] does not transcend the sphere of karma.
But the Supreme Self does not abide within the sphere of either good or evil action, according to the Vedic scripture: "He increases not by action, nor does He become less.
Furthermore, the designation of the two as "shadow and light" is appropriate as a description of the conscious and the unconscious.
Because they are mutually distinct, like shadow and light;

therefore, when it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) are what are spoken of here, we reply: it is the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) that are spoken of here.
Why? Because both of them are conscious and possess an identical nature.
Furthermore, when a number is heard, it is observed in common worldly usage that the understanding applies only to things of the same nature;
for instance, when it is said, "A second for this cow must be sought," only a second cow is sought,
not a horse or a human being.

Thus, since the individual self (vijñānātman) has been determined by the mark of drinking the *ṛta*, when searching for a second [entity], it is understood that the Supreme Self alone is perceived, as it possesses a nature similar to it—namely, consciousness.
Now, was it not said that the Supreme Self should not be understood because of the observation of its being "hidden in the cave"?
We reply that it is precisely because of the observation of its being hidden in the cave that the Supreme Self is to be understood.

Furthermore, the state of being "placed in the cave" (guhāhita) is repeatedly seen in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as belonging to the Supreme Self alone, in such passages as: "The ancient one, placed in the cave, dwelling in the deep recess" (Kaṭha 1.2.12);
"He who knows Him hidden in the cave, in the supreme ether" (Taittirīya 2.1); and "Seek the Self that has entered the cave" (Mahābhārata), and others like them.
It has already been stated that even for Brahman, who is all-pervading, the instruction regarding a specific location is not contradictory for the purpose of its apprehension.

Furthermore, the state of residing in the world of meritorious deeds is not contradictory for both [Brahman and the individual soul], even though it resides in only one, just as the possession of an umbrella [is attributed to both the king and his retinue].
Likewise, the mention of "shadow and sunlight" is also not contradictory.
Because transmigratoriness and non-transmigratoriness are mutually distinct like shadow and sunlight,
because transmigratoriness is produced by ignorance,
and because non-transmigratoriness is ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) that are understood as having entered the cave. // 11 //
And for what reason are the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) understood [here]?—

[they are so understood] because they are "drinking" (*pibantau*), that is, experiencing the fruit of action (*ṛtam* = *satyam*), while abiding in the body which is the effect of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of well-performed deeds in this world; and because they are the two who constitute the "half" (*ardham*) of the Supreme Brahman.
That which is worthy of being the place is the "other shore" (parārdha), the heart; having entered that cave within the supreme and most excellent [heart],
they abide there— like shade and sunlight, which are mutually opposed— and of these two, the knowers of Brahman and the performers of ritual action speak.
Those who have built the fire-altar thrice with the Nāciketa rite also say this:
regarding a human being when he has passed away and died, there is this doubt or uncertainty;
some say that there is an enjoyer in the next world, while others say there is not.
The meaning is: "Instructed by you, I wish to know this reality.
"Elsewhere than dharma and adharma" means apart from these two; "apart from what has been done and not done" means untouched by dharma and adharma.
That which is distinct from cause and effect—whether produced or unproduced—is Brahman.
Or rather: agency is characterized by sovereignty, and since that [sovereignty] exists for the one who causes another to drink just as it does for the one who drinks, he too is an agent.
Therefore they say: "He who causes another to act is also a doer.
[The Self] is hidden in the cave, situated in the intellect; it resides in the body, which is a deep abyss crowded with manifold misfortunes;
it is the ancient, primordial Person.
"In the highest heaven"—that is, in the most excellent space of the heart; "there," in the cave of the intellect (*buddhi*), seek—that is, investigate—on account of this qualification. (BBs 1.2.12)
Furthermore, this qualification applies only to the individual self (*vijñānātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).

By means of the subsequent passage beginning with "Know the self as the rider, and the body as the chariot" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.3), the text employs the metaphor of the rider and the chariot to represent the individual self as the rider— the one who travels through both saṃsāra and liberation.
"And thus he reaches the end of the journey, that highest step of Viṣṇu" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.3.9); thus, the Supreme Self is the goal to be reached.
Likewise: "Him, difficult to see, hidden, entered into [all things], ancient... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.7).

In the preceding passage as well—"Having known the God through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow" (Kā. 1.2.12)—these two alone are specified as the knower and the object of knowledge;
moreover, this context concerns the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, the specific mention of the speakers as "the knowers of Brahman" (*brahmavidaḥ*) is appropriate only if the Supreme Self is being accepted;
therefore, in this context, both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) must be spoken of.
This same reasoning applies to the verse: "Two birds, inseparable companions... (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 3.1.1).
The same applies to such passages as these.
For there too, because the context concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), two ordinary birds are not being spoken of.
From the indicative mark of eating—“one of them eats the sweet fruit”—it follows that [the eater] is the individual self (*vijñānātman*).
"The one who eats does not perceive the other"—by these two [terms], eating and non-eating, the Supreme Self is indicated.

And in the immediately following mantra, He distinguishes those very two as the seer and the object of sight: "On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by his lack of lordship; but when he perceives the other, the Lord who is enjoyed, and His glory, he becomes free from sorrow" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.2).

Another says: "The verse 'Two birds... does not conform to the final conclusion (siddhānta) of this section, because it is explained otherwise in the Paiṅgi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa: 'Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit—this is the *sattva*; the other, not eating, looks on—thus the wise one, not eating, beholds. These two are the *sattva* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)."
As for what is said— that one who does not eat transcends the word "sattva" and perceives another—
that is not so,
because the words *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* are well known to refer respectively to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the body.

And because it has been explained in that very same [passage]: "That is the *sattva* by which one sees a dream; now, he who is the embodied witness is the *kṣetrajña*; these two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*.
Nor does this [argument] support the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) of this section.
For here, the embodied *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is not intended as one endowed with the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as agency and enjoyership.

How then? It is intended as that which transcends all attributes of transmigratory existence, whose nature is the state of Brahman and pure consciousness, according to the scriptural declarations: "The other, not eating, looks on," and "The other, not eating, looks on—the Knower."
This is also established by such scriptural and traditional texts as "That thou art" and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" (Gītā 13.2);
for it is only on this basis that the observation of the conclusion of knowledge (*vidyopasaṃhāra*) is appropriately understood.
"These two are the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*; indeed, nothing whatsoever clings to one who knows thus," and so forth.
But how, on this view, can it be said that "one of them eats the sweet fruit"—that is, that the *sattva* is the enjoyer—given that the *sattva* is insentient?
It is replied: this scripture did not set out with the intention of declaring that the insentient *sattva* is the enjoyer.
Rather, [the author] intends to state that the conscious *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is not an enjoyer and is of the nature of Brahman;
for that purpose, he superimposes the status of being an enjoyer upon the *sattva*, which is subject to modifications such as pleasure and so forth.
For this agency and enjoyment are imagined to belong to both *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* through the non-discrimination between their respective natures.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not possible for either of them, because the sentient being is insentient and the Knower of the Field is changeless.
Furthermore, because the nature of a sentient being is established by ignorance (*avidyā*), agency and the like are even more impossible.

Thus says the Śruti: "Where there is, as it were, another, there one might see another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15), and so forth; this shows that just like the conventional usage of elephants and other things seen in a dream, the conventional usage of agency and so on exists only within the domain of ignorance.
"But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
By such passages as these, he demonstrates the absence of conventional designations such as "agency" for the discerning one. (12) [Note:
"He" refers to the *jīva*, the referent of the pronoun;
"of the path" means of the path of *saṃsāra*.]
Difficult to perceive, it is difficult to know;

for that very reason, the Lord has entered into what is hidden and has attained a state of profundity. "Internal practice" (*adhyātma-prayoga*) means the concentration of the mind upon the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*); by that, there is "attainment," meaning the mental modification (*vṛtti*) born from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*). Having known [the Lord] through that—meaning they are joined together as the governed and the governor—they are "united" (*sayujau*).
"By lack of mastery" means by the non-perception of one's own lordship.

"Served" means attended to through meditation and so forth; when, at the stage of the maturation of meditation, one perceives the Lord as other—that is, distinct from one's own specific form—"sattva" refers to the intellect (buddhi).
By that much, through the mere explanation of the mantra,
*rajas*— which is ignorance—
is destroyed.
It clings;

otherwise, a diversity appearing as something else would be seen there through the connection with ignorance, intellect, and so forth, such that, having become one thing, one might see another with another eye.
In that regard, it is within ignorance.
But regarding the state of knowledge (*vidyāvasthā*):
Section 4, "The Internal [Self]"; Sūtra 13–17:
"The internal [self is meant], because it is logical. (BBs 1.2.13)
"That person who is seen in the eye, he is the Self," he said, "this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.
Even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the eyelashes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.1), and so forth, is heard in the Śruti.

In this regard, there arises a doubt: is this being who is perceived as having the reflection for his self designated here; or is it the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānātman*); or the self that is a deity (*devatātman*) presiding over the sense organ; or the Lord (*īśvara*)? What, then, is the initial position?
That it is the self consisting of a shadow, the counterpart of the person.
Why? Because it is well known that he is seen;
for there is an instruction based on what is commonly recognized in the passage, "This person who is seen in the eye.
Or rather, it is logical that this is a reference to the self consisting of consciousness (vijñānātman).
For he, while seeing a form with the eye, is present within the eye;
moreover, the word "self" (ātman) is consistent with this position.
Or rather, the person in the sun is understood to be the one who favors the eye.
"By means of rays, this one is established in this [sun]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.2), according to this scriptural statement;
and because immortality and other such qualities can somehow be possible even for a deity.
Thus, when it is argued that this is not the Lord because of the mention of a specific location, we reply:
It is the Supreme Lord alone who is taught here as the Person within the eye.
Why? Because of the logical consistency (*upapatti*).
For the entire collection of attributes being taught here is indeed consistent with the Supreme Lord.
First of all, the status of being the Self (ātmatva) applies to the Supreme Lord in its primary sense, according to the Vedic revelation:
"That is the Self; thou art That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Furthermore, immortality and fearlessness are repeatedly heard in scripture as belonging to Him.
Likewise, this location in the eye is suitable for the Supreme Lord;
for the Supreme Lord is untainted by all defects, as is heard from scriptural passages such as "He whose sins are destroyed."

Likewise, the location of the eye is taught as being free from all attachment, according to the Vedic scripture: "Therefore, even if one pours clarified butter or water upon it, it flows away along the eyelids.
Furthermore, the teaching of its qualities, such as being the "conductor of blessings" (*saṃyadvāma*), is appropriate only with respect to that [eye].
"They call this the 'Abode of All Gatherings' (saṃyaddhāma), for all blessings (vāmāni) gather toward it.
He indeed is the 'Bringer of Blessings' (vāmanī), for he leads all blessings [to the soul].
He indeed is the 'Shining One' (bhāmānī), for he shines in all worlds" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.15.2–4). Thus it is said.
Therefore, on account of this logical reasoning, the Supreme Lord is the one within [the eye].
[Note: "On the path" means in the place of the eyelashes;
the teaching is like a well-known fact, namely the statement that He is the "eye."]
The word "here" (iha) refers to the person in the eye. Regarding the term "the abode where all things unite" (saṃyaddhāma):
it is by depending on this person in the eye as their cause that desirable fruits of action (vāmāni karmaphalāni) come together, that is, they arise.
The term *vāmanī* means that it leads the world toward beautiful things;
*bhāmanī* means that it leads [beings] everywhere toward splendors and lights.
This is also because of the designation of its abodes and so forth. (BBs 1.2.14)
But how can it be possible for Brahman, which is all-pervading like space, to have its location within the cavity of the eye?
To this it is said: this objection would be valid only if this were the sole location specified for it.
For other abodes as well, such as the earth and so forth, have been designated for this [Self] in passages such as, "He who dwells in the earth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.3).
Indeed, the eye is also designated among them in the passage, "He who dwells in the eye.

By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" in the sūtra phrase "Because of the designation of abode and so forth," he shows that it is not only an unsuitable abode that is seen being designated for Brahman.

What then? Even such things as "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) are seen being designated for Brahman, which is itself devoid of name-and-form—for instance, "His name is 'Ut'"; "He has a golden beard," and so forth (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.6.7, 6).

It has already been stated that although Brahman is indeed without qualities (*nirguṇa*), it is taught in various places as possessing qualities (*saguṇa*) through the qualities pertaining to name-and-form, for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*).
It has already been stated that even for Brahman, who is omnipresent, a specific location is not contradictory for the purpose of perception, just as Viṣṇu is perceived at Śālagrāma. Furthermore,

it has been said that because of the designation of various names and forms— such as "from place" and so forth— which are the modes of name and form, the restriction of the omnipresent [Brahman] to a single location is not tenable.
And precisely because it is designated as distinguished by bliss;
furthermore, one should not dispute here whether Brahman is denoted in this passage or not.
The state of being Brahman is established as the very designation of that which is distinguished by bliss.
For it is precisely that Brahman distinguished by bliss which was introduced at the beginning of the passage in the words, "Prāṇa is Brahman, Ka is Brahman, Kha is Brahman," that is here designated;
for it is logical to accept what has been previously introduced.
And because of the promise to declare only the goal in the words, "But the teacher will tell you the way" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.1).
But how, then, is Brahman characterized by bliss understood at the very beginning of the passage?
It is said: Having heard these words of the fires, "Breath is Brahman; Ka is Brahman; Kha is Brahman," Upakosala said, "I understand that breath is Brahman, but I do not understand Ka and Kha.
To this, the reply was: "That which is indeed Ka is the same as Kha; that which is Kha is the same as Ka" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.10.5).
Thus [it is said].
In this context, the word *kha* is conventionally established in common usage to denote the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).
If the word *kaṃ*, denoting happiness, were not employed as its qualifier, [the meaning would be lost].

That being the case, there would arise the impression that the word "Brahman" is applied to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone with the intention of treating it as a mere symbol (*pratīka*), just as it is used for names and so forth. Likewise, since the word "kaṃ" is well-known to denote the conventional pleasure produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects,
if the word "khaṃ" were not employed as its qualifier, [the meaning would be misunderstood].

There might be the notion that worldly happiness is Brahman; however, when the two words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* function as mutual qualifiers, they lead one to understand Brahman as having happiness as its essence. In that case, if the second word *brahman* were not employed and it were merely said "Brahman is *kaṃ-khaṃ*," then because the word *kaṃ* would be used solely as a qualifier, happiness would become a mere quality to be meditated upon.
Lest this be so, both words *kaṃ* and *khaṃ* have the word *brahman* as their head, as in "Kaṃ is Brahman, Khaṃ is Brahman.
For it is indeed accepted that even a quality, such as bliss, may be meditated upon as possessing that quality.
Thus, at the beginning of the passage, Brahman qualified by bliss has been taught.

Furthermore, each of the fires— the Gārhapatya and the others— having taught its own respective greatness, concludes by saying, "This, my dear, is your knowledge of us and the knowledge of the Self," thereby making it known that Brahman was indicated previously.
Moreover, the promise, "But the teacher will tell you the way," precludes the intention to speak of anything other than the path.
And by stating that "just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows thus" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.14.3),
the text shows that the Person residing in the eye— who is free from affliction by evil for one who knows Him— is Brahman. Therefore,
having described the very Brahman under discussion as residing in the eye and possessing qualities such as being the "center of blessings," [the text teaches] the path beginning with light...

5. The Section on the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 18–20: The Inner Ruler is [the Lord] with respect to the deities, the worlds, and so forth, because of the designation of His attributes. (BBs 1.2.18)

Beginning with, "He who controls this world and the other world, and all beings, from within," the scripture is heard: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within— he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.1, 2), and so forth.

In this context, it is heard in scripture that there is a certain inner controller, the Antaryāmin, who presides over the divine (adhidaivata), the worlds (adhiloka), the Vedas (adhiveda), the sacrifice (adhiyajña), the elements (adhibhūta), and the self (adhyātma).

Regarding this being, a doubt arises because of the appearance of an unfamiliar designation: Is he some deity-soul possessing identification with the divine and so forth? Or is he some yogi who has attained powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest? Or is he the Supreme Self? Or is he something else entirely?
What, first of all, appears to us?
Because the name is not well-known, one might think that the named object must also be unestablished and must therefore be some other entity;
or rather, it is impossible to admit the existence of another entity whose form has not been defined.
Furthermore, the word "Antaryāmin" (Inner Controller) is applied by virtue of its connection with the act of controlling from within, and is not entirely unknown.
Therefore, some deity presiding over earth and the other elements must be the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmī*).
Thus it is heard in scripture: "He whose abode is earth, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind," and so forth (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.10).

And since he possesses both effects and causes, it is logical that the self of the deity, dwelling within earth and the others, should be their ruler; for such lordship over them is appropriate for a divine being.

Or, [one might argue] that some perfected yogin, through entering into all things, would possess the power of controlling them, but the Supreme Self would not be recognized as such because He lacks a body and organs; this being the position reached, the following is stated: That which is heard of as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) with respect to the divine beings and so forth must be the Supreme Self alone, and none other.
Why? Because of the designation of its attributes (*taddharmavyapadeśāt*). For the attributes of that Supreme Self (*paramātman*) are seen to be indicated here.

To begin with, it is appropriate for the quality of being the controller to belong to the Supreme Self, since He stands within and governs the entire aggregate of modifications—earth and so forth—which is divided into categories such as the deities (*adhidaivata*) and others.
Because all powers are possible when there is the causality of all modifications;

and because the attributes of being the Self and being immortal, stated in the passage "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," are applicable to the Supreme Self in their primary sense.

Furthermore, by stating that the inner controller is unknown even to the earth in the words "whom the earth does not know," the text shows the inner controller to be distinct from the deity who is the self of the earth.
"For I am indeed the deity Earth; one should know oneself as 'I am Earth,'" [it says].
Likewise, designations such as "unseen" and "unheard" are appropriate for the Supreme Self because it is devoid of form and other such qualities.
As for the objection that the status of being a controller is not possible for the Supreme Self, which lacks both body and organs—that is addressed as follows:
This is not a fault;
for he restrains them by means of those very instruments of action, since it is logically consistent that he possesses such instruments of action.
Nor does the fault of infinite regress arise from the claim that there must be another controller for that [controller] as well,
because there is no difference [between them];
for it is only when a difference exists that the fault of infinite regress can occur.
Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is the Inner Controller. (18) [FN:
The "abode" is the body;
the "eye of the world" is that by which the world is perceived.]
The mind consists of light;
nor is it of the nature described in the Smṛtis, because there is no mention of its possessing those attributes.

Attributes such as being unperceived and so forth are applicable even to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhya tradition, because that [pradhāna] is accepted by them as being devoid of form and other such qualities;
as it is said: "It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and as if entirely asleep" (Manu 1.5).

Although the Pradhāna was already refuted in the sūtra "Because [the Lord] is seen [as the inner ruler], that which is not based on scripture [is not the cause]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5), it is raised again here on the grounds that designations such as "not being seen" and so forth could possibly apply to it.

If the Pradhāna is not accepted as the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin) because qualities such as being a self and being a seer are impossible for it, then let the embodied soul (śārīra) be the Inner Ruler;
for the embodied soul, being conscious, is indeed a seer, a hearer, a thinker, and a knower.
And the self is [the agent] because of its inwardness;
and it is immortal, because the experience of the fruits of merit and demerit is logically possible for it.

Furthermore, qualities such as being unseen (adṛṣṭatva) and so forth are established by the opponent in the embodied self, since there is a contradiction in the activity of actions such as seeing occurring in the agent itself.

Furthermore, its nature is to inwardly govern the aggregate of the body and the instruments of perception.
Because [the embodied soul] is an enjoyer;
therefore, [if it is argued] that the embodied soul is the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), the author reads the following reply:
"And because he is immortal"—the meaning being that for one who is perishable, enjoyment in another body would be impossible.

Since it is contradictory for a single entity to possess both subordinacy and primacy within a single action, the meaning is that the agent cannot simultaneously function as the object.
For both [the Upanishads] study this embodied one as distinct [from the inner ruler].

Moreover, both schools of reciters—the Kāṇvas and the Mādhyandinas—indeed record this embodied self as distinct from the Inner Controller, as its substrate and its object of governance, just like the earth and other elements.
The Kāṇvas read: "He who dwells in cognition" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22), while the Mādhyandinas read: "He who dwells in the self."

In the reading "He who dwells in the self" (ya ātmani tiṣṭhan), the word "self" (ātman) denotes the embodied soul (śārīra). Even in the reading "He who dwells in consciousness" (yo vijñāne tiṣṭhan), the embodied soul is expressed by the word "consciousness" (vijñāna);
for the embodied soul consists of consciousness (vijñānamaya).
Therefore, it is established that the Lord who is the inner controller (antaryāmī) is distinct from the embodied one (śārīra).
But how can two seers be possible within a single body— one who is this Lord, the inner controller, and the other who is this different embodied one?
What, then, is the impossibility here?
It would contradict scriptural statements such as, "There is no seer other than this," for in this context,
[the scripture] refers to a seer other than the Antaryāmin under discussion.
It negates the self as one who hears, one who thinks, and one who cognizes.
If it is argued that this statement is for the purpose of negating another controller, we say no; for there is no possibility of another controller, and because the scripture declares no distinction.
To this, it is replied:

This designation of a distinction between the embodied self (śārīra) and the inner ruler (antaryāmin) is caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the body and organs presented by ignorance (avidyā); it is not ultimate (pāramārthika).
For there is indeed only one inner self (pratyagātman); two inner selves cannot possibly exist.

However, the conventional usage of distinctions regarding that which is in fact one is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as [one speaks of] "the space in a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) or "the great space" (*mahākāśa*).

Consequently, the scriptural texts concerning the distinction between the knower and the known and so forth, the means of valid cognition such as perception, the experience of transmigratory existence, and the scripture of injunctions and prohibitions—all of this is rendered intelligible.
Thus, the Śruti says: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another"; this shows that all conventional usage pertains to the sphere of ignorance (*avidyā*).
"But where for him everything has become the Self alone—by what and whom should he see? Thus, with respect to the domain of knowledge, it precludes all worldly transaction. // 20 //
The Section on the Invisible (Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa), Sūtras 21–23:
"That which possesses the qualities of invisibility and so forth [is Brahman], because of the mention of its attributes.
(BBs 1.2.21) "Now, the higher [knowledge] by which that Imperishable is attained..."

"It is heard [in scripture] thus: 'That which is invisible, ungraspable, without lineage, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and imperishable— that source of all beings which the wise perceive'" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.5–6).

In this regard, there arises a doubt: Is this source of beings (bhūtayoni), characterized by qualities such as invisibility and so forth, the non-intelligent Pradhāna, or the embodied soul (śārīra), or rather the Supreme Lord?
In this matter, it is logical that the non-intelligent Pradhāna is the source of beings, because only non-intelligent things are presented as its illustrative examples.
"Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its web], just as herbs arise from the earth,
and just as hair and body-hair grow from a living person, so does this entire universe arise here from the Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.7).
Now, it may be objected that the spider and the person cited here as examples are conscious beings.
We say: no;
for the conscious principle alone does not possess the status of being the source of the thread or the source of hair and body-hair.
Rather, it is the insentient body of the spider, presided over by consciousness, that is the source of the thread.
Furthermore, it is well known that the human body consists of hair and body hair.
Moreover, although the desire for invisibility and so forth was possible in the previous [passage], the Pradhāna was not accepted because the desire for being a seer and so forth was impossible;
here, however, the attributes of invisibility and the rest are possible in the Pradhāna.
Nor is any contradictory attribute predicated here.
Indeed, this supplementary statement, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9), is not possible in the case of the insentient *pradhāna*.
How is it that the Pradhāna is asserted to be the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*)?

To this it is replied: Having taught that the source of beings possesses qualities such as invisibility by means of the word "syllable" (*akṣara*) in the passages, "By which that Imperishable is attained" and "That which is invisible," the text will later declare at the end: "Higher than the high Imperishable" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 2.1.2).
In that context, that which is heard as beyond the Imperishable (akṣara) will be the omniscient and all-knowing one;
however, it is Primordial Matter (pradhāna) alone that is designated by the word "Imperishable" as the source of beings (bhūtayoni).
But when the word "source" (yoni) denotes a cause, then even the embodied self (śārīra) could be the source of beings.
"Because [the world] is acquired by means of dharma and adharma by that which is born from the elements.
This being the position reached, it is replied: That source of the elements, characterized by such qualities as invisibility and so forth, must be the Supreme Lord alone and nothing else.
How is this understood?
Because of the teaching of Dharma;
for here the Dharma of the Supreme Lord is seen being taught: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving.
Indeed, neither the insentient Pradhāna nor the embodied soul (śārīra), whose vision is limited by adjuncts (upādhi), can possibly possess omniscience or all-perceiving nature.

But has it not been stated that omniscience belongs only to that which is higher than the source of beings (bhūtayoni), which is designated by the word "Imperishable" (akṣara), and does not pertain to the source of beings itself? To this it is replied: this is not possible, because the source of beings under discussion here—in the phrase "from the Imperishable everything here arises"—is presented as the material cause (prakṛti) of that which is being born.

Immediately after pointing this out, the text designates the Omniscient One precisely as the source-nature (prakṛti) that is being produced: "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food.

Therefore, since it is recognized through the identity of its description, it is understood that the attributes of omniscience and all-perceiving nature are predicated of the very same Akṣara, the source of beings, which was under discussion.
Even in the passage, "Higher than the Imperishable is the High," no one other than the Imperishable, which is the source of beings under discussion here, is designated as being higher.
How is this understood?
From the statement: "He who knows the true Person, the Imperishable—he [the teacher] truly taught that knowledge of Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.13).
For it has been thus introduced that it is precisely this syllable, the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, that is proposed as the subject to be explained.
How then is it designated as "higher than the high" (akṣarātparataḥ paraḥ)? We shall explain that in the subsequent sūtra.
Moreover, two types of knowledge (vidyā) are stated here as being to be known: "the higher (parā) and the lower (aparā).

Having there described the lower knowledge, characterized by the Ṛgveda and so forth, [the text] says: "Now, the higher [knowledge] is that by which that Imperishable (akṣara) is attained," and so on.
In that context, the Imperishable is heard of as the object of the higher knowledge.
If, however, the Imperishable (akṣara) possessing qualities such as invisibility were imagined to be something other than the Supreme Lord, this would not be the higher knowledge (parā vidyā).
For this distinction between higher and lower knowledge is established on the basis of their respective fruits of worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) and the supreme good (niḥśreyasa);
and it is not accepted by anyone that the knowledge of primordial matter (pradhāna) results in the supreme good.
Furthermore, three sciences would have to be admitted on your view, because the supreme Self, which is higher than the source of beings— the Imperishable— is being set forth [as a third]; however,
only two sciences to be known are specified here.

And the expectation of knowing everything through the knowledge of one thing, expressed in the passage, "But by what being known, O Venerable One, does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka 1.1.3), is consistent only if Brahman, whose self is the whole, is intended; it is not consistent with the Pradhāna, which has as its sole abode only the non-intelligent.

Or [it refers] to an enjoyer distinct from the objects of enjoyment. Furthermore, having commenced with the knowledge of Brahman as the primary subject in the passage, "He taught the knowledge of Brahman, the foundation of all knowledge, to Atharvan, his eldest son" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1), and then showing the higher knowledge— which leads to the attainment of the Imperishable— by means of the division into higher and lower, it demonstrates that this [knowledge] possesses the nature of the knowledge of Brahman.
Furthermore, that designation as "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā) would be contradicted if the Imperishable (akṣara), which is to be attained through it, were not Brahman.
Ritual knowledge, characterized by the Ṛgveda and so forth, is introduced at the beginning of the section on the knowledge of Brahman for the purpose of praising the knowledge of Brahman:
"For these boats, consisting of sacrifice, are unstable; in them, eighteen inferior acts have been declared."
This is because of deprecatory statements such as: "Those fools who rejoice in this [worldly life] enter again and again into old age and death" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7).

Having thus deprecated the lower knowledge, the text shows that only one who has become detached from it is qualified for the higher knowledge: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, let the Brāhmaṇa attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created."
"For the sake of knowing that, one should approach a teacher alone, with fuel in hand— a learned man of noble lineage who is firmly established in Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12).
As for the argument that because insentient things such as earth and so forth are employed as examples, the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) which is the subject of the example must also be insentient—
that is incorrect.
There is no rule that an absolute similarity must exist between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Furthermore, since gross elements such as earth are employed as the examples, it is not accepted that the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), which is the subject of the illustration, is itself gross.
Therefore, the source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, is indeed the Supreme Lord. 21. @----------------------

it is not possible for the embodied soul, whose majesty is limited to his own body.
Nor is this presentation of form possible for the Pradhāna,
because it is impossible for it to be the inner self of all beings;
therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone is the source of beings, and not the other two.
How, then, is it understood that this presentation of form refers to the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*)?
It is understood from the context and from the fact that the word "this" (*eṣaḥ*) draws back upon what has been previously introduced.

For, with reference to the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), the statements "From this is born the vital breath (*prāṇa*)" and "This is the inner self of all beings" relate exclusively to the source of beings;
just as, when referring to a teacher, the statement "Study from him; he has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas" relates to the teacher, so it is here.
But how can a source of beings, characterized by qualities such as invisibility, possess a corporeal form?
There is no fault here, for this is stated with the intention of expressing its nature as the Self of all, and not with the intention of asserting that it possesses a corporeal body;
it is like [the statement], "I am food, I am the eater of food" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.6).
Others, however, think: "This presentation of forms is not [intended] as the source of the elements (bhūtayoni), because they are presented as being born; for it says:
'From this [source] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses.'"

For in the preceding passage, "Space, air, light, water, and earth, the supporter of all," he pointed out the entire collection of principles from Prāṇa down to Earth as being born; and in the subsequent passage as well, beginning with "From that [arose] fire, its fuel, and the sun," and ending with "And from this [arose] all herbs and juices," he will likewise point them out precisely as being born.
How could one introduce the form of the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*) here in the middle of this [text] so abruptly?
Furthermore, the fact that it is the self of all will be taught after the completion of the creation, through such passages as: "The Person alone is this universe, action... (Muṇḍaka 2.1.10).

Moreover, we observe that the birth and other states of Prajāpati, whose body is the three worlds, are pointed out in both Śruti and Smṛti: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists" (RV 10.121.1).
"He supported this earth and this heaven; to what god shall we offer worship with oblation? (Ṛgveda 10.121.1).
"He evolved" means he was born.
Likewise, "He is called Puruṣa."
And [it says]: "He, the first creator of beings, Brahmā, existed in the beginning.
Even for the *vikāra-puruṣa* (the person as a transformation), it is possible to be the inner self of all beings, because he abides within all beings as the self of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In this view, the presentation of all forms in passages such as "The Person alone is all this, [consisting of] action" (PU 2.11) is to be explained as a means for the realization of the Supreme Lord. 23 // [Note:
Agni is the heavenly world; the Vedas are speech; the feet are the two feet.]
Of small majesty and limited power,
he who is the illuminator of the sun— the fire of the celestial realm— as if it were its fuel,
Hiranyagarbha came into being in the beginning.
Having been born, he became the sole lord of the multitude of beings—this is the ellipsis.
For which Prajāpati? We shall worship him; we shall serve him.
The Section on Vaiśvānara (Sūtras 24–32). Sūtra 24:
"Vaiśvānara [is the Self], because of the distinction of common terms. [The text begins]:
"Who is our Self? What is Brahman? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.11.1).

Having begun with, "You are indeed studying this very Self, Vaiśvānara; tell us that," and having taught—by associating heaven, sun, air, ether, water, and earth with qualities such as "excellent splendor" (sutejas), while censuring the worship of each individually—that these [elements] constitute the head and other parts of Vaiśvānara, the scripture declares:
"But he who worships this Vaiśvānara Self, which is of the measure of a span and all-pervading, he [eats] in all worlds..."
"He eats food in all beings as in his own self. Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head indeed is *sutejas* (the well-luminous), the eye is *viśvarūpa* (multiform),

the breath is *pṛthagvartmātmā* (the self of diverse paths), the trunk is *bahula* (abundant), the bladder is *rayi* (wealth), the feet are the earth itself, the chest is the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), the body hair is the sacred grass (*barhis*), the heart is the *gārhapatya* fire, the mind is the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and so forth.

In this regard, there is a doubt: Is the term *vaiśvānara* taught here as the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), or as the elemental fire (*bhūtāgni*), or as the deity presiding over it, or as the embodied soul (*śārīra*), or as the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*)?
What, then, is the cause of this doubt?
It is because the word *vaiśvānara* is used commonly for the digestive fire, the elemental fire, and the deity, while the word *ātman* is used for both the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord.
In this regard, a doubt arises as to which [meaning] it is proper to adopt and which to reject.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
That it is the digestive fire (jāṭharo 'gniḥ).
Why?

Because in that context, the use of a qualification is observed in certain instances, such as: "This is Vaiśvānara Agni, who is within the person, by whom this food is cooked, which is eaten" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.9);
or it might refer to fire in general.
Because the term is seen used in a general sense even in such passages as, "The gods made Agni Vaiśvānara the banner of the days for the sake of the entire world" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.88.12),
[the deity] may be the deity whose body is Agni;
for its usage is also observed in that sense, as in, "May we abide in the good favor of Vaiśvānara, for he is the king, the glory of all beings" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.18.1).
Since such scriptural passages as these are possible with reference to a deity endowed with sovereignty and other attributes;

and since, on the grounds of grammatical coordination with the word "Self" (ātman) and because of the use of the word "Self" alone in the opening statement, "What is our Self? What is Brahman?", the word "Vaiśvānara" must be interpreted in accordance with the word "Self"—even so, [the Self] might be the embodied self (śārīra ātmā).
Because he is the enjoyer, due to his proximity to Vaiśvānara;
and because the qualification "measured by a span" is possible in him when he is delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Therefore, when it has been thus established that Vaiśvānara is not the Lord (Īśvara), this is said in reply: Vaiśvānara must be the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Why? Because of the distinction between two common terms.
"Distinction between two common terms" means a specific difference between two words that are both common.
Although both these words—*ātman* and *vaiśvānara*—are indeed common terms, [there is a distinction].
Although the word *vaiśvānara* is common to all three [fire, the digestive heat,

and the Supreme Lord], and the word *ātman* is likewise common to two [the individual self and the Supreme Lord], nevertheless a distinction is observed by which it is accepted that those two refer to the Supreme Lord.
"Of this very Vaiśvānara Self, the head indeed is Sutejas," and so forth. For here,
it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone— characterized by having heaven as his head and so on— is presented as the inner self (pratyagātman) in another state for the purpose of meditation,
because he is the cause.
For it is logical that the Cause possesses the nature of having the heavenly world and other regions as its constituent parts, since it is endowed with all the states belonging to its effects.

Furthermore, the fruit described in scripture as having all worlds and so forth as its locus—expressed in the passage, "He eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves"—is possible only if the Supreme Cause is accepted.
As it is said: "In this way, all his evils are burned away" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.24.3).
Furthermore, there is the hearing of the burning away of all evil for one who knows this;

and there is the introduction by means of the words "Self" and "Brahman" in the passage, "Who is our Self? What is Brahman? Thus, these indicative marks lead to the understanding that the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara.
Therefore, the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara. 24.
FN: "Who is he?
Prācīnaśāla, Satyayajña, Indradyumna, Jana, and Buḍila, having come together, deliberated thus and went to the King of Kekaya [to inquire]: "Do you know? Do you remember?"
He is called *abhivimāna* because he measures—that is, knows—the universe directly and without mediation.
*Saṃdeha* is the middle part of the body. *Rayi* means wealth.

The gods made Vaiśvānara Agni—the banner and sign of the days, the sun—for the sake of the entire world; for it is at his rising that the business of the day proceeds. May we abide in the benevolent thought, the auspicious wisdom, of the god Vaiśvānara.

The meaning is: "May his excellent mind be within our domain. An "alternative state" (*avasthāntara*) is of such a nature as being either *adhyātma* (pertaining to the self) or *adhidaiva* (pertaining to the divine).
Just as a tuft of reed-fiber thrown into fire is consumed, even so it is for this knower.
"Inference would be based on what is being remembered.

(BBs 1.2.25) For this reason as well, the Supreme Lord alone is Vaiśvānara, because such a form consisting of the three worlds is recorded in scripture as belonging to the Supreme Lord alone: "He whose mouth is fire, whose head is heaven, whose navel is the sky, and whose feet are the earth. (RV 10.81.3)
The sun is his eye, the quarters of space are his hearing; homage to him, the self of the worlds!

The meaning is as follows: this form, being thus remembered, serves as an inferential mark (liṅga)—that is, an indicator—by implying the existence of a foundational Vedic text (śruti), thereby establishing that the word *vaiśvānara* refers to the Supreme Lord.
The particle *iti* here signifies a reason.
Since this is an indicator, the meaning is that Vaiśvānara must therefore be the Supreme Self alone.
Although this is a hymn of praise— “Homage to Him, the Self of the worlds”—
even such praise is not possible in this form unless there exists an underlying Vedic statement as its foundation.
Know that he whose head the wise declare to be heaven, whose navel is indeed the sky, whose two eyes are the moon and the sun,
whose ears are the quarters, and whose feet are the earth— he is the inconceivable Self, the leader of all beings.
And a traditional text (smṛti) of this kind should be cited here as well. // 25 //

"If it be argued that [Vaiśvānara] is not [the Supreme Lord] because of the words [used] and because he is established within, we say no; for there is instruction regarding such a vision, because [otherwise] it would be impossible, and they also study him as the Puruṣa.
(BBs 1.2.26) On this point, an objection is raised: Vaiśvānara cannot be the Supreme Lord.
Why? Because of the words [used] and because he is established within.
To begin with, the word *vaiśvānara* cannot apply to the Supreme Lord,
because it is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in another sense;
likewise for the word *agni* in the passage, "This is that Agni Vaiśvānara."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the conceptualization of the three sacrificial fires, such as: "The heart is the Gārhapatya fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.2), and:
"Therefore, whatever food one eats first, that is the oblation" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
And by such passages as these, there is the mention of [Vaiśvānara] being the locus for the offering of the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*).
For these reasons, Vaiśvānara should be understood as the digestive fire within the stomach (*jāṭhara*).
Likewise, his abiding within is also heard in scripture: "He knows him as abiding within the person."
And that [fire] exists within the stomach.
As for what was said—that Vaiśvānara is the Supreme Self because of specific designations such as "the head itself is Sutejas" (of great splendor)—to this we reply:
from what source indeed does this conclusion arise?
Since a distinction is evident in both cases, one must resort to the distinction that pertains specifically to the Supreme Lord, and not to the gastric fire.
Alternatively, this description may refer to the elemental fire which abides both within and without;

for its connection with the heavenly world and so forth is understood from the wording of a mantra: "He who by his radiance overspread this earth and heaven, and the two worlds and the intermediate space" (Ṛgveda 10.88.3), and so on.
Alternatively, by virtue of the power of the deity whose body that [fire-altar] is, it may possess limbs such as the heavenly world and so forth;
therefore, Vaiśvānara is not the Supreme Lord.
To this, it is replied: "Not so, because of the teaching of [Him] as being seen thus."
It is not reasonable to reject the Supreme Lord on account of reasons such as sound and so forth.
Why? Because the instruction regarding the vision [of Him] is given without abandoning the gastric fire;
for here, the vision of the Supreme Lord is taught in relation to the gastric Vaiśvānara.

It is like [the passage] "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.1), and so forth; or else, the Supreme Lord is taught here as the object to be seen through the limiting adjuncts of the digestive fire (jāṭhara-vaiśvānara),
as in "Consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2), and so forth.

If the Supreme Lord were not intended here, and only the digestive fire within the body were intended, then such specific attributes as "the head itself is the brilliant [Sutejas]" would be impossible. Furthermore, we shall explain in the subsequent sūtra how these specific attributes cannot be established even by resorting to the deity who is the elemental fire. And if only the digestive fire were intended, [the following would be untenable].
The state of being established within the person would belong to Him alone, but not His being the Person.

Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins study this very one as the Person: "This Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the Person; he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara thus—as the Person-shaped, established within the person" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.1.11).
But since the Supreme Lord is the Self of all, both his being a person (*puruṣatva*) and his being established within the person (*puruṣe 'ntaḥpratiṣ�ṭhitatva*) are appropriate.

As for those who read the portion of the Sūtra as "and they also study him as being in the form of a person" (*puruṣavidham api cainam adhīyate*), their meaning is this: if one were to accept only the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), there would be only the state of being established within the person, but not the state of having the form of a person.
Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins study this [Self] as being "in the form of a person," according to the text: "He who knows it as being in the form of a person, established within the person.

And its "form of a person" is understood here by taking up that which pertains to the divine (adhidaivata), beginning with having heaven as its head and ending with being established on the earth, as well as that which is well-known in the individual self (adhyātma), beginning with having the head as its head and ending with being established in the chin. 26.

FN: "Food" (*bhakta*) means rice or grain; "sacrificial" (*homīya*) means that which serves as the instrument for the oblation (*homa*); the meaning is that one should perform the *prāṇāgnihotra* with that.

He who has spread across this earth and also the sky—that is, across both heaven and earth, the two worlds (*rodasī*)—in the form of light, and has also spread across the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) between them: that deity, whose limbs consist of the heavenly world and so forth, is the object of meditation; such is the meaning.
Whoever—
that person who is full—
who knows, he enjoys [the fruits] everywhere.
For this very reason, [the fire] is neither a deity nor an elemental being.

As for what was further stated— that because even the elemental fire is seen in the wording of the mantras to have a connection with the heavenly world and so forth, the attribution of limbs such as "the head itself is the brilliant one" must belong to that very [elemental fire],
on account of its association with sovereignty (vaiśvarya) like that of a deity possessing a body— [that is not so].
That must be refuted.
To this it is said: for these very reasons already stated, Vaiśvānara is not the deity;
likewise, even fire in its elemental form is not Vaiśvānara.
For it is not possible to conceive of the elemental fire— which consists merely of heat and light— as having heaven for its head and so forth,
because one modification cannot possibly have the nature of another modification.
Likewise, even though a deity possesses lordly power, it is not possible to conceive of such attributes as having heaven for its head.

Because it lacks causality and because its sovereignty is dependent upon the Supreme Lord, the impossibility of applying the term "Self" (ātman) remains established in all these alternative positions. // 27 //
Jaimini [maintains] that there is no contradiction even in the case of the direct [worship of the Supreme Lord].

(BBs 1.2.28) Previously, it was stated—on account of the mention of being "established within" and so forth—that the Supreme Lord is to be worshipped either with the gastric fire as His symbol (*pratīka*) or with the gastric fire as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Now, however, the teacher Jaimini considers that there is no contradiction whatsoever even in adopting the worship of the Supreme Lord directly, without the conceptualization of either a symbol or a limiting adjunct.

[Objection: But surely, if the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is not accepted [as the subject], then the statement regarding its being "established within" and other reasons such as the word [“fire”] would be contradicted.
To this it is replied: First, the statement regarding its being "established within" is not contradicted;
for here, in the passage, “He who knows him as person-shaped, established within the person,” this is not said with reference to the digestive fire.
Because that [Self] is neither the subject under discussion nor has been explicitly mentioned,
how then is it said— referring to the human form imagined in the parts of the person from the head down to the chin— that "one knows the one who is human-shaped and established within the person"?

It is just as one sees a branch established upon a tree; or rather, with reference to that which is the subject under discussion— the Supreme Self characterized by the limiting adjuncts of being the Person (puruṣavidhi) both with respect to the internal self (adhyātma) and the divine (adhidaivata)— it is said, "He knows it as established within the person," intending its aspect as the pure witness (sākṣin).

And once the Supreme Self has been determined through the consideration of what precedes and follows, the word *vaiśvānara* will apply to that very object by means of some etymological derivation (*yoga*):
namely, "He is both the universe (*viśva*) and the person (*nara*)," or "He is the person of all (*viśveṣām naraḥ*)."
He is called Viśvānara because all men (viśve naraḥ) belong to him;
he is the Supreme Self (paramātman),
since he is the self of all.
Viśvānara himself is indeed Vaiśvānara; here the secondary derivative suffix has no other meaning,
as in the case of words such as *rākṣasa* and *vāyasa*.

The word "Agni" (Fire) as well will refer exclusively to the Supreme Self by virtue of its association with qualities such as being the foremost; and the conceptualization of it as the Gārhapatya fire and so forth, as well as its being the locus for the oblation of breath, is appropriate for the Supreme Self too because of its nature as the Self of all. // 28 //
But how, then, is the scriptural mention of [the Self] as being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) consistent with its being the Supreme Lord? He begins to explain that:
[The meaning is: "Being established within" means being situated in the middle, that is, being the witness (*sākṣitva*).
Here, the lengthening of the first member of the compound is according to the rule *nare saṃjñāyām*.
"Having no other purpose" means being devoid of any meaning beyond that of the primary sense.
"On account of manifestation," says Āśmarathya (BBs 1.2.29):
even for the Supreme Lord, who is immeasurable, there may be a state of being "measured by a span" due to the cause of manifestation.
"It is said that the Supreme Lord, though limited to the measure of a span (*prādeśamātra*), is manifested for the sake of His worshippers;
or rather, He is manifested through specific attributes in particular locations such as the heart, which are the sites of perception.
Therefore, Master Āśmarathya maintains that the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "the measure of a span" is justified on account of this manifestation. (29)
FN: That is to say, it is that whose measure (*mātrā*) or dimension has been transcended.

Alternatively, it is "measured in a specific location" (*pradeśeṣu mīyate*), hence "measuring a span" (*prādeśamātra*). Bādari [holds] that [the soul's size] is according to its recollection (*anusmṛti*). (BBs 1.2.30)
Or rather, because he is remembered by means of the mind established within the heart—which is the size of a span—he is called "span-sized" (*prādeśamātra*).

It is just as barley grains measured by a *prastha* are called "a *prastha*. And although the measurement inherent in the barley grains themselves is merely manifested through its connection with the *prastha*, [the same logic applies here].
In this case, there is no dimension pertaining to the Supreme Lord that could be manifested through its connection with the heart.
Nevertheless, it is said that some form of recollection may serve as a support for the scriptural mention of "measuring a span" (*prādeśamātra*), however that may be.

Or else, even though He is not actually measuring a span, He is to be recollected as measuring a span, so that the meaning of the scriptural statement regarding His being "measuring a span" may remain purposeful.

Thus, the teacher Bādari maintains that the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "measured by a span" (prādeśamātra) is based on the sign of mindfulness (anusmṛti-nimitta); that is, it refers to the Lord who is measured by the mind (prādeśena manasā mīyate), or to the word [“prādeśa”] which,
when employed in its primary sense, functions to denote Him.
"Jaimini [holds that it refers] to attainment; for thus [the scripture] shows.
Or rather, the scriptural mention of 'measuring a span' may be based on attainment.
Why? Because..."

For instance, the *Vājasaneyi-brāhmaṇa*, in a corresponding section, shows that the Supreme Lord is to be realized as being of the measure of a span (*prādeśamātra*), by correlating the limbs of Vaiśvānara— who consists of the three worlds from heaven down to earth— with the limbs of the body from the head down to the chin: "The gods, having well understood him, attained him as one who is indeed of the measure of a span."
"Now I shall tell you these things so that I will bring them together into a mere span's length.
Pointing to the head, he said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Summit.
Pointing to the eyes, he said, "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as Fine Brilliance."
Pointing to the two nostrils, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the manifold-pathed Self. Pointing to the principal space within the mouth, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the abundant.
Pointing to the principal waters [within the mouth], he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as wealth."
Pointing to the chin, he said, "This indeed is the foundation.
By "chin" (cubuka) is meant the lower part of the face.
Although in the Vājasaneyaka the sky is recorded as having the quality of being the "support" (atiṣṭhā), and the sun as having the quality of being "well-luminous" (sutejas).
Furthermore, in the Chāndogya, the sun is recorded as having the quality of "splendid light" (sutejas), while [the person within the sun] has the quality of "multiformity" (viśvarūpa).
Nevertheless, nothing is lost by this distinction,
because the scriptural statement regarding the "span-long" (prādeśamātra) size remains without distinction in both cases.
And because it is supported by all the branches of the Veda,
the teacher Jaimini considers the scriptural statement that [the heart] is "measured by a span" to be more appropriate as a figurative description of its excellence.
And they declare him to be here;
the Jābālas declare this Supreme Lord to be here, in the space between the head and the chin: "That Self which is within, unmanifest, is established in the Unliberated (Avimukta).
"In what is that Unliberated one established?"
"It is established between the Varaṇā and the Nāsī.
"What indeed is the Varaṇā and what is the Nāsī?
In this regard, having explained that this very nose is the Varaṇā and the Nāsī: that which wards off all evils committed by the senses is the Varaṇā.
It is called *nāsī* because it destroys all sins committed through the sense organs.
Furthermore, they declare: "What is its location?
That which is the junction of the two eyebrows is the junction of this world and the world beyond" (Jābāla Upaniṣad 1).

Therefore, the scriptural mention of the Supreme Lord as being "the size of a span" is justified. The mention of Him as "immeasurable" (*abhivimāna*) is intended to convey His nature as the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
He is called "immeasurable" (*abhimāna*) because He is measured by all living beings through their own inner selfhood.

Or, because he has reached the innermost self (*pratyagātman*), he is "immeasurable" (*vimāna*); and because he is free from all human limitations (*māna*), he is "supremely immeasurable" (*abhivimāna*).
Alternatively, because he measures out the entire world as its cause, he is "supremely immeasurable" (*abhivimāna*).
Therefore, it is established that Vaiśvānara is indeed the Supreme Lord. // 32 //
Thus ends the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. [Note:

In *Avimukta*, which is delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), [the Lord] is established as the object of meditation through the conceptualization of the distinction between the individual self (*jīvātman*) [and the Supreme Self].
*Varaṇā* is the eyebrow.
It is measured (*vimīyate*) and known (*jñāyate*);
it is fashioned forth (*abhivimīmīte*) and created (*nirmimīte*). __________________________________________________________________________________________ First Chapter, Third Section.

[In this section, there is an investigation primarily of those passages where the marks of Brahman are not explicit, but which concern Brahman as the object of knowledge. Thus, the investigation of scriptural passages is carried out through three quarters. 1. The Section on Heaven, Earth, and so forth (Dyubhvādyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–7.
"The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word.

This is heard in scripture: "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven, along with the mind and all vital breaths—know Him alone as the one Self; cast off other words; He is the bridge to immortality" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
In this context, since heaven and the others are described as being "woven," some substratum (*āyatana*) is understood;
regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether that substratum might be the Supreme Brahman or something else entirely.
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the substratum must be some other entity.
Why? Because of the scriptural statement, "This is the bridge to immortality.
For in the world, a bridge is well known to have a further shore;
and it is impossible to admit that the supreme Brahman has a further shore.
Because of the scriptural statement, "endless and shoreless" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12);
and if any other entity were accepted as the abode, the Pradhāna well-known from Smṛti would have to be accepted.
Because it is logical for that [wind] to be the cause and the basis;
or else, wind may be what is well-known from scripture, as in:
"Wind, O Gautama, is indeed that thread; by wind, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world and all beings are held together" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.2).
