Since it is heard that even the wind possesses the quality of being a support, [it might be argued that] the embodied self (śārīra) could be the referent; for since that too is an enjoyer, it is possible for it to be the abode with respect to the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is the object of enjoyment. Having reached this preliminary conclusion, the Sūtra says: "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth."
"Heaven and earth" means heaven and earth; that which has heaven and earth as its beginning is "dyubhv-ādi.

That which is indicated in this sentence as heaven, earth, the intermediate space, mind, and vital breaths—thus described by us as the pervader of the world—that must be the Supreme Brahman, the abode.
Why? Because...
"From its own word" means from the word "Self" (ātman).
For the word "Self" occurs here in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self.
And the word "Self" is properly applicable when the Supreme Self is accepted, not when any other object is accepted.

In some places, Brahman is heard of as the abode by its own name: "O dear one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.4).

Moreover, in this very passage, Brahman is celebrated by its own name both before and after [the mention of the abode]: "The Person alone is all this—the work, the austerity, Brahman, the supreme immortality";
and also: "Brahman alone is this immortal in front; Brahman behind, Brahman to the south and to the north" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).
In this regard, because one hears of the existence of both "abodes" (āyatana) and "non-abodes" (anāyatana),

and because of the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All is Brahman," a doubt may arise that the Self is manifold— just as a tree consists of branches, trunk, and root— and thus the Self is of various flavors and diverse in nature.
To turn [the mind] away from that [worldly diversity], he says with emphasis: "Know him alone as the one Self.
This is what is meant: the Self is not to be known as something manifold, characterized by the phenomenal expansion of effects;
rather, dissolving the phenomenal expansion of effects created by ignorance through knowledge, know that very one Self, which is the sole substratum, as being of a single essence.

Just as when it is said, "Devadatta is not here; bring him," one brings only the seat and not Devadatta, in the same way, it is taught that the Self—which is of a single flavor and is the very locus—is what is to be known. Furthermore, a censure is heard regarding one who identifies with the unreal modifications [of the Self]: "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Katha Upaniṣad 2.4.11).

The grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All is Brahman" is for the purpose of dissolving the phenomenal world (prapañca), not for the purpose of establishing a manifold nature [of Brahman];

for we hear of its being of a single essence in the passage: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).
Therefore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the supreme Brahman.

As for what was stated—that because of the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (setu), and because it is logical that a bridge must have a further shore, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth must be something other than Brahman—it is replied here:
by the scriptural mention of a "bridge," only the quality of being a support (vidhāraṇatva) is intended, not the state of having a further shore and so on.
For although no bridge made of earth or wood is seen in the world, even here a bridge made of earth and wood is accepted [as the meaning].

Furthermore, the meaning of the word *setu* (bridge) is merely the state of holding together (*vidhāraṇatva*), and not having two banks and so forth, because the word *setu* is etymologically derived from the root *ṣiñ*, which means "to bind.
Another says: as for this knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) which has been proclaimed in the passage, "Know that alone as the one Self,"...

And as for this "releasing of speech" expressed in the words, "Release other words," that is celebrated here by the scriptural mention of it as a "bridge" in the phrase, "This is the bridge to immortality," because it is a means to attaining immortality; it is not, however, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.

In this regard, what was stated—that because of the scriptural mention of a "bridge" (setu), Brahman must be something other than the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth—is incorrect. [The commentary] explains the phrase "because of the scriptural mention of a bridge" by stating: "For it has a further shore," since there is the hearing of the word "immortality" (amṛtasya). This is the construction of the argument.
"Interwoven" means closely knit together.

Due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the connection is "the manifold self. One whose "intention" (*abhisaṃdhi*)—that is, one's conceit (*abhimāna*)—is fixed upon that which is a modification, unreal, and imagined.
It is called a *setu* (bridge) because it binds (*sinoti*) or holds fast (*badhnāti*);
the meaning is that it is a part of the object that performs the function of supporting.
Furthermore, it is so designated because it is described as that which is to be approached by the liberated (*muktopasṛpya*). (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.2)
For this reason as well, the Supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth,
because its state of being approachable by the liberated is observed to be designated; "approachable by the liberated" (muktopasṛpyam) means that which is to be approached by those who are liberated.
The notion of "I am" regarding the body and other non-self entities is ignorance (*avidyā*).

From that arises attachment to their worship and the like, aversion toward their humiliation and the like, fear from the perception of their destruction, and delusion; thus, this mass of endless misfortunes is continuously manifest to all of us.

In contrast to that, there is the designation concerning the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, stating that this [Brahman] is to be approached and reached by those who are free from the defects of ignorance, attachment, aversion, and the rest.
Having stated, "The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder, and his karmas are exhausted when He, who is both high and low, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8),
the text further declares: "Thus the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.7).

Furthermore, the fact that Brahman is to be approached by the liberated is well-established in the scripture, as in such passages as: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7).
However, it is nowhere well-known that the Pradhāna and other such principles are "to be approached by the liberated.

Furthermore, here, the state of being that which is to be known—preceded by the relinquishing of speech—is predicated of the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, in the passage: "Know Him alone as the one Self; abandon other words; He indeed is the bridge to immortality.
And this [quality of being known] is seen in another Śruti in reference to Brahman: "The wise Brāhmaṇa, having known Him alone, practices wisdom."
"One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21).
For this reason as well, the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Brahman. [Note:
*Prajñā* refers to the cognition of the meaning of the scriptural statement.]
The term "brāhmaṇa" is an indicator for any twice-born person not explicitly mentioned. [The opponent objects:
"Inference is not [the means of knowledge] because it lacks that specific word. [The author replies:
He says this because, whereas a specific reason (*vaiśeṣika-hetu*) was stated to establish the [existence of] Brahman, there is no such specific reason to establish another object.
The *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṃkhya tradition and based on inference is not to be understood here as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
Why? Because there is no word for it (*atacchabdāt*). A "word for it" (*tacchabda*) is a term that expresses that non-intelligent *pradhāna*.
That word is not a word for that;
for there is no word here whatsoever that denotes the insentient *pradhāna*, by which the insentient *pradhāna* could be understood as either the cause or the basis (*āyatana*).
There exists a word here that establishes a conscious being opposite to that [non-intelligent entity], namely: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.9), and so forth.
For this very reason, even Vāyu is not accepted here as the support of heaven, earth, and so on. // 3 //
"And [the term refers to] a living being.

(BBs 1.3.4) Even though it is possible for a living being— the individual self consisting of consciousness— to possess selfhood and sentience, nevertheless, since knowledge limited by adjuncts cannot possibly possess omniscience and other such qualities, a living being must not be understood as the substratum of the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, precisely because of this word "That" (*atat*).
Furthermore, it is not at all possible for a limited, non-omnipresent living being, as defined by its adjuncts, to be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
The separate formulation of this sūtra is for the sake of what follows. // 4 //
Furthermore, for what reason should the individual living being (*prāṇabhṛt*) not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth?

Because of the designation of difference (*bhedavyapadeśāt*). And here, a designation of difference occurs in the passage: "Know him alone as the one Self," by way of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower.

In that context, because the individual living being (prāṇabhṛt) desires liberation, it is the knower; by the method of elimination, it is understood that Brahman, denoted by the word "Self," is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and not the individual living being. // 5 //
Furthermore, why should the individual living being not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth?
Because of the context (prakaraṇa). And this context pertains to the Supreme Self.
"O Venerable One, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.3).

Because of this expectation of knowing everything through the knowledge of one thing, it must be the Supreme Self—the self of all—that, when known, makes all this known, and not merely the individual living being. // 6 //
Furthermore, for what reason should the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*) not be accepted as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth?
Because of its "dwelling" and "eating.
With reference to that which is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, [the scripture says]: "Two birds, inseparable companions and friends... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1).
In this passage, abiding and eating are indicated:
"One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit" refers to the consumption of the fruits of action, while "the other looks on without eating" refers to abiding in a state of indifference.
And by those two, abiding and eating, the Lord (Īśvara) and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) are understood therein.
If the Lord is intended as the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, then the separate mention of that aforementioned Lord from the Knower of the Field is appropriate;
otherwise, a mention of what is not the subject under discussion would be accidental and disconnected.
[Objection: But would it not follow that for you as well, the separate mention of the *kṣetrajña* from the Lord (*īśvara*) would be equally arbitrary? [Reply:
No, because that [distinction] is not intended to be expressed.

For the two *kṣetrajñas*—as agents and enjoyers, connected in each body with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—are already well-known through worldly experience alone; they are not what is intended to be expressed by the Śruti with its primary purport.
Since the Lord (Īśvara) is not well-known from worldly experience, He is intended to be expressed by the Śruti with its full purport; therefore, it is not reasonable for His mention to be accidental.

This has also been shown in the passage "the two selves have entered the cave," where it is demonstrated that in the verse "two birds... (dvā suparṇā), the Lord and the individual soul (kṣetrajña) are spoken of.
Even when, according to the interpretation provided by the Paiṅgi Upaniṣad, this verse is said to refer to the intellect (sattva) and the individual soul, there is still no contradiction whatsoever.
How so?

Here, the individual soul (*prāṇabhṛt*), which is perceived in each body through its identification with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the quality of existence (*sattva*)—much like the apertures in a jar—is negated on the grounds that it cannot be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
However, that which is characterized as being free from all limiting adjuncts in all bodies is not negated.
That which is perceived in all bodies as distinct from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Just as the apertures of jars and the like, when perceived apart from their limiting adjuncts such as the jars, become nothing other than the Great Space (*mahākāśa*), so too, since it is impossible for the living being (*prāṇabhṛt*) to be other than the Supreme, the denial [of its identity] is not tenable.
Therefore, the negation of being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth applies only to those who identify with limiting adjuncts such as the sentient being (sattva) and the rest.
Consequently, the Supreme Brahman alone is the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth.
This very point is established by the sūtra itself: "Because of the mention of attributes, [the one possessing] qualities such as invisibility [is Brahman]."
For this passage, "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space [are woven]," is recited in the midst of that very text concerning the source of beings (*bhūtayoni*);
it is introduced again for the purpose of detailed exposition.
2. The Section on the Plurality (Bhūmādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 8–9:
"The Plurality [is Brahman], because it is taught as being superior to the state of perfect serenity.
(BBs 1.3.8) They recite this: "But the Plurality indeed is what one must desire to understand; 'Venerable Sir, I desire to understand the Plurality.'"

"Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else—that is the finite (alpa)" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23.24), and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
first of all, the word "bhūman" denotes abundance.
This is because the rule *bahor lopo bhū ca bahoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.158) recalls that the word *bhūman* ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*).

Furthermore, when there arises a desire for a specific qualification as to what the nature of that "abundance" (*bahutva*) is, [the text states]: "Breath, indeed, is greater than hope" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1).
Thus, because of the proximity [of the word "Brahman"], it appears that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the "Fullness" (*bhūman*).

Likewise, because of the introduction of the context—"For I have heard from those like your reverence that one who knows the Self overcomes grief; I, O Venerable One, am grieving; may your reverence carry me across to the further shore of grief" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3)—it also appears that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the "Fullness."
In this regard, a doubt arises as to which [of the two] it is proper to adopt and which to reject.
What, then, is the prima facie position?
That "breath" (prāṇa) is the "fullness" (bhūman).
Why?
Because we observe a succession of further questions and answers, as for instance:
"Venerable sir, is there anything greater than name?"

"Speech, indeed, is greater than name"; likewise, "Is there, venerable sir, anything greater than name? and "Mind, indeed, is greater than speech"—thus a stream of questions and answers concerning what is greater than name and so forth, up to the vital breath (prāṇa), has proceeded.

No such question and answer regarding anything greater than the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is seen, such as "Is there, O Venerable One, anything greater than the vital breath? or "Indeed, there is something greater than the vital breath. On the contrary, after having explained in detail—starting with "The vital breath is indeed greater than name and the rest, up to hope"—that the vital breath is greater than everything from name to hope, and having authorized the status of one who perceives the vital breath as being an "exceeding speaker" by saying, "You are an exceeding speaker; you should say, 'I am an exceeding speaker,' and not deny it," [the text proceeds].

"But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth"—having thus drawn forward the state of "speaking transcendentally" as the vow of Prāṇa, and without abandoning Prāṇa, [the text] introduces the Bhūman through a succession beginning with Truth; from this it is understood that they consider Prāṇa itself to be the Bhūman.
But how, when the Bhūman is being explained as Prāṇa, can the statement "where one sees nothing else," which is intended as the definition of the Bhūman, be explained?

It is said: Since the cessation of activities such as seeing is observed when the organs have been swallowed by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), this definition—"where one sees nothing else"—is applicable to the *prāṇa* as well.

And so the Śruti, having described the state of deep sleep as the subsidence of the functions of all the organs through the passage beginning with "he does not hear, he does not see" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.2.1), states: "In this city, the fires of the vital breaths alone remain awake" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.2.3).

Thus, by stating that the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains awake in that very state, [the text] shows that the state of deep sleep has the *prāṇa* as its predominant factor. Furthermore, the scriptural teaching regarding the blissfulness of the Infinite— that "what is the Infinite, that is bliss" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.23)— is also not contradicted.
For it is heard that in the state of deep sleep alone there is bliss, as stated: "In this state, this deity does not see dreams; then, whatever happiness arises in this body" (Praśna Upaniṣad 4.6);
and also: "That which is the Infinite (bhūman), that is the Immortal" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1).
Thus, even that [immortality] is not inconsistent with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), according to the scriptural text: "The vital breath, indeed, is immortality" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.2).

But how, then, is the introduction of this section—beginning with "He who knows the Self overcomes sorrow"—justified for one who considers the vital breath to be the *bhūman*, given the desire to know the Self?

We maintain that it is indeed *prāṇa* (the vital breath) that is intended here as the Self (*ātman*). For instance, [the text] makes *prāṇa* itself the Self of all: "Prāṇa is the father, prāṇa is the mother, prāṇa is the brother, prāṇa is the sister, prāṇa is the teacher, and prāṇa is the Brahmin" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.15.1).
Thus, it identifies *prāṇa* as the universal Self.

Furthermore, by the two illustrations of being the self of all and of the spokes and the nave— namely, "Just as the spokes are fastened to the nave, so everything is fastened to this Prāṇa"— the quality of being *bhūman* (the Infinite), which consists in vastness, is possible for Prāṇa. Therefore,
it follows that Prāṇa is indeed *bhūman*.
Therefore, this is said: here, the Supreme Self alone must be the "Fullness" (bhūman), not the vital breath (prāṇa).
Why?
Because of the teaching that it is superior to the state of serene confidence (saṃprasāda).

"Tranquility" (*saṃprasāda*) refers to the state of deep sleep, according to its etymological derivation as "that in which one becomes completely serene. Furthermore, because it is mentioned alongside the states of dreaming and waking in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, and because it is said that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains awake in that state of tranquility," it is the vital breath that is intended here by the term "tranquility."
The meaning is that [the Bhūman] is taught as being superior to Prāṇa.
If the Bhūman were indeed Prāṇa itself, then it would be entirely inconsistent for that very same thing to be taught as being superior to itself;
for "Name" is not taught as being superior to Name by saying "Name is more than Name."
Rather, something other than name, namely that which is called speech, is taught as being greater than name: "Speech, indeed, is greater than name.
Likewise, in each successive stage, something distinct from speech and the others is taught up to breath.
Similarly, the "Full" (bhūman) which is taught after breath must be an entity distinct from breath.
But surely, in this case, there is no question such as "Is there, O Blessed One, anything greater than breath?
nor is there a reply such as "There is indeed something greater than breath.
How, then, is the "Fullness" (bhūman) taught as being superior to breath?

Furthermore, we observe that the status of being an "ativādin" (one who speaks beyond) regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is what is being drawn forward in the subsequent passage: "But he indeed is an ativādin who speaks beyond by means of the Truth (*satya*).
Therefore, there is no instruction concerning the Supreme [Self].
To this, it is replied: First of all, it cannot be said that this is a drawing forward of the status of being an ativādin specifically regarding the vital breath.
This is because of the specific statement, "He who speaks surpassingly by means of truth.
But surely this specific statement must also refer to the vital breath (prāṇa) alone.
How so?
Just as when it is said, "This is an *agnihotrī* who speaks the truth," one does not become an *agnihotrī* by speaking the truth; rather, one becomes so by the *agnihotra* sacrifice itself.
However, speaking the truth is stated to be a specific qualification for one who maintains the *agnihotra* sacrifice.
Thus, when it is said, "But he indeed speaks surpassingly who speaks surpassingly by means of truth," it is not through the mere act of speaking the truth that one becomes a superior speaker;
by what, then?
[The opponent says: "It is by means of the very knowledge of the vital breath under discussion;
however, what is intended to be expressed is that speaking the truth is a specific attribute of the knower of the vital breath.
[We reply: No, we say.
Because it would entail the abandonment of the literal meaning of the scripture.
For by the scriptural text itself, speaking the truth is understood here as "speaking beyond" (ativāda) in the passage: "He who speaks beyond by means of truth, he truly speaks beyond.
There is no mention here of the knowledge of the vital breaths (prāṇas).
However, on account of the context, the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa) would be connected [with the preceding].
In that case, the direct scriptural statement (śruti) would have to be set aside in deference to the context.
Furthermore, the word "but" (tu) in the phrase "But he indeed speaks more than this" would not be appropriate for the purpose of excluding what has been previously introduced.
And the statement, "But truth indeed must be sought to be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.16), indicates an intention to speak of a different subject by requiring a further effort.

Therefore, this should be viewed as analogous to how, when the praise of a single Veda is the topic at hand, one praises a person who has studied four Vedas— saying, "But he is a great Brāhmaṇa who has studied the four Vedas"— thereby praising the four Vedas as something distinct from the single Veda.

Nor is there a rule that a shift to another subject must necessarily take the form of a question and answer; for such a shift is caused by the impossibility of maintaining a connection with the topic at hand. In this case, having heard the instruction up to the point of "the end of life," Nārada remained silent, and Sanatkumāra himself proceeds to instruct him further.

That which constitutes "speaking beyond" (ativāditva) by means of knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇa), whose object is modification and unreality, is in fact not speaking beyond at all; for it is said: "But he indeed speaks beyond who speaks beyond by means of the Truth. In that context, "Truth" refers to the Supreme Brahman, because it is of the nature of ultimate reality (paramārtha).
And from another scriptural passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1); thus,

for Nārada who had been so instructed and who proceeded with the words, "Venerable Sir, may I speak beyond [the truth] by means of truth," the Teacher points out the Infinite (bhūman) through a succession of means such as discernment (vijñāna).
In this context, it is understood that what was promised as truth to be spoken beyond the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is precisely what is here called "the full" (*bhūman*).
Therefore, since there is an instruction regarding the "full" beyond the vital breath, the "full" must be the Supreme Self, distinct from the vital breath.
In this way, the commencement of this section with the desire to know the Self becomes logically consistent.
The claim that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is intended here as the Self (*ātman*) is also untenable; for the vital breath does not possess the nature of the Self in its primary sense,
nor is there the cessation of sorrow apart from the knowledge of the Supreme Self.

"Nor is there any other path for going [to that goal]," according to another Vedic text (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15); and, "May the Blessed One carry me across to the further shore of grief," according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (7.1.3).
And having thus begun, he concludes: "To him, whose impurities had been wiped away, the blessed Sanatkumāra showed the shore beyond darkness" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
Here, "darkness" refers to ignorance, which is the cause of sorrow and so forth.
Furthermore, if the instruction were to end with the vital breath (prāṇa), it would not state that the vital breath is dependent on anything else.
And there is the Brāhmaṇa passage: "From the Self comes the vital breath" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.26.2).
The intention to speak of the Supreme Self will occur at the conclusion of the section.
If it be argued that "the Bhūman is indeed Prāṇa," we say no;
for from the passage, "In what, O Venerable Sir, is he established? In his own majesty" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.24.1), the Bhūman alone is carried forward until the conclusion of the section.

Furthermore, the nature of being *bhūman* (the Infinite), which consists of vastness (*vaipulya*), is most appropriately established for the Supreme Self because it is the cause of all things. [This *bhūman* is a full reality beyond conventional usage.
It is for those like you who possess the vision of the Blessed One.
The "deity" (deva) is the individual soul (jīva) characterized by limiting adjuncts such as the intellect;
however, due to the context, it should be connected as the reason for being an "exceeding speaker" (ativādin)—this is the remainder [of the sense]. A further effort is required for investigation.
In this context, "consciousness" refers to meditative reflection (*nididhyāsana*) and so forth;
furthermore, because the attributes [of Brahman] are logically consistent.
Moreover, those attributes which are heard in relation to the "Great" (*bhūman*) are applicable to the Supreme Self.

The passage, "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā)," makes known that the Infinite is characterized by the absence of such activities as seeing and so forth. And this absence of activities like seeing is understood to belong to the Supreme Self, as in: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
This is because of other scriptural passages such as these.

Furthermore, that absence of activities such as seeing which was mentioned regarding the state of deep sleep is stated with the intention of expressing the non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*) of the Self itself, and not with the intention of describing the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because this occurs within the context of the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, even that which was described as happiness in that state was stated with the intention of expressing that the Self itself is of the nature of happiness;
for it is said: "This is his supreme bliss; other beings live on only a fraction of this very bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).

Here too, by rejecting conventional happiness with the words, "That which is the Plenum (bhūman) is bliss; there is no bliss in the limited (alpa); the Plenum alone is bliss," [the text] shows that Brahman alone is the Plenum which is bliss.
Furthermore, the immortality heard here in the passage, "That which is the Plenum is indeed immortal," points toward the Supreme Cause, because the immortality of modified effects is merely relative.

And from another scriptural passage, "Everything else is afflicted" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4.2). Thus, these attributes— truthfulness, being established in one's own glory, omnipresence, and being the self of all— which are heard in the texts, are logically possible only in the Supreme Self and not elsewhere.
Therefore, it is established that [this is] "the stage" (*bhūmi*).
[The term *sāmayika*] has been explained by the passage beginning with "he does not hear.
That which is accompanied by *āmaya*, i.e., suffering (*duḥkha*), is *sāmayika*.
To one in distress, it is transitory.
Section 3: The Topic of the Imperishable (Akṣarādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 10–12:
"The Imperishable [is Brahman], because of its supporting everything up to the ether" (BBs 1.3.10).
"In what, indeed, is space woven to and fro?

He replied: "O Gārgī, the Brahmins describe that as this very Imperishable (akṣara), which is neither gross nor subtle," and so forth, as it is heard in the scripture (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7, 8).
In this regard, there is a doubt: does the word "akṣara" denote a phoneme (varṇa), or rather the Supreme Lord?

On this point, since the word "akṣara" is well-known in such expressions as "the traditional collection of akṣaras" (akṣarasamāmnāya) to mean a phoneme, and because it is improper to override common usage; and furthermore, since in other scriptural passages such as "The syllable Om alone is all this" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 2.23.3), even a phoneme is determined to be the self of all as an object of meditation.
If it is argued that the word "akṣara" refers only to the phoneme (varṇa), this being the position reached, it is said in reply: the Supreme Self alone is what is denoted by the word "akṣara.
Why?
"Because of the support of the ends of space"—that is, because of the sustaining of the entire collection of effects, from earth up to space.

For there, after stating that the entire collection of effects, from earth on, distributed across the three periods of time, is supported in space in the words, "In space alone is that woven lengthwise and crosswise," [the text asks]: "In what, then, is space woven lengthwise and crosswise?"
By this question, this syllable (akṣara) is introduced; and likewise it is concluded: "In this very syllable, O Gārgī, the ether is woven like warp and woof.
And this support of everything up to the sky is not possible for anything other than Brahman.
As for the statement, "The syllable Om is indeed all this," that too should be understood as being for the purpose of praise, because it is a means for attaining Brahman.
Therefore, because it neither perishes (akṣarati) nor pervades (aśnute), the Imperishable (akṣara) is the supreme Brahman itself by virtue of its eternity and omnipresence. // 10 //

It might be argued: "If the support of everything up to the sky is accepted on the grounds that an effect is dependent upon a cause, then this is also consistent for the proponent of Pradhāna as the cause.
How, then, can the support of everything up to the sky lead to the realization that Brahman is the cause?"
To this he replies:
[He says] "by way of common usage" (*prasiddhi*), according to the maxim that "common usage sets aside etymological derivation.
And that [usage] is due to the command (*praśāsanāt*). (Brahma Sūtra 1.3.11)
And that support of the ends of space is the work of the Supreme Lord alone.
Why?
Because of His command.

For a governing command is heard here in scripture: "O Gārgī, by the governing command of this Imperishable, indeed, the sun and the moon stand held apart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.9), and so forth. And governing command is the function of the Supreme Lord;
a non-conscious Pradhāna cannot possess a governing command.
For there is no directing of non-conscious causes such as clay and the like toward objects such as jars. // 11 //
And because of the exclusion of other entities (anyabhāvavyāvṛtti).
Because of the exclusion of other entities, Brahman alone is denoted by the word "akṣara";
the supporting of everything up to the ether is its function, and not that of anything else whatsoever.
What is this "exclusion of the existence of another"? The existence of another is "other-existence" (*anyabhāva*); the exclusion of that is "exclusion of other-existence" (*anyabhāvavyāvṛtti*).
This is what is meant:

The Śruti excludes from this context any other Brahman denoted by the word "akṣara" that might be suspected here, stating: "Now, O Gārgī, this very akṣara is unseen yet seeing, unheard yet hearing, unthought yet thinking, unknown yet knowing" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
In that context, designations such as "unseen" and so forth are possible even for the Pradhāna;
however, designations such as "seer" and so forth are not possible for it because it is insentient.

Likewise, because of the negation of a plurality of selves in the passage, "There is no other seer than this, there is no other hearer than this, there is no other thinker than this, there is no other knower than this," [the term] does not refer even to the embodied self (śārīra) when it is possessed of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
It is because it is denoted by the word "the Perishable" (*kṣara*),
and because its possession of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is denied in the passage, "Without eyes, without ears, without voice, without mind" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8).
For there is no such thing as a "bodily" [self] that is free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
therefore, it is certain that the Imperishable (akṣara) is indeed the Supreme Brahman. // 12 //
Section 4: The Topic of the Designation of the Object of Beholding. Sūtra 13:
"He [is Brahman], because of the designation of Him as the object of the act of beholding.
(BBs 1.3.13) "O Satyakāma, this *oṃkāra* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman; therefore, the wise man, by means of this very support, attains one or the other."
Having introduced the subject thus, it is heard: "But he who meditates upon that supreme Person by means of this very syllable *oṃ* consisting of three measures" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.2, 5).
Is it the supreme Brahman that is intended as the object of meditation in this passage, or rather the non-supreme?
A doubt arises because of the context: "By means of this very abode, one follows either the supreme or the non-supreme."
In this regard, it follows that this [Brahman] is something else.
Why?

Because of the statements, "He becomes united with the heat in the sun" and "He is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāmans," which describe for the knower of that [Brahman] a fruit delimited by space.
For it is not logical that one who knows the supreme Brahman should obtain a fruit limited by space, since the supreme Brahman is all-pervading.
But [one might object]: if the lower Brahman is accepted, then the qualification "the supreme Person" would not be appropriate.
This is not a fault, because the superiority of the vital breath (prāṇa) is established in relation to the body (piṇḍa).
This being the position reached, it is replied: it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is taught here as the object of meditation.
Why?
Because of the designation of it as the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*).
"Seeing" (*īkṣati*) means perception.
That which is pervaded by seeing is the object of the act of beholding (*īkṣati*).

There is a designation in the remainder of the passage for this person who is to be meditated upon as the object of beholding: "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond this mass of living beings.
In that context, even an entity that does not actually exist can become the object of the verb "to meditate" (*abhidhyāti*).
Since even that which is merely imagined by the mind is the object of the act of desiring (*abhidhyāti*),

whereas in the world the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*) is observed to be only such a thing as actually exists, it is understood that this Supreme Self alone, being the object of perfect vision, is designated here as the object of the act of seeing. Furthermore, it is recognized here through the two words "the other" (*para*) and "Person" (*puruṣa*) as being the very same entity that is to be desired.

But surely, in the case of meditation, the Supreme Person was mentioned, whereas in the case of seeing, that which is "higher than the high" was mentioned; how then can one be recognized as the other in the other context?

To this it is replied: First of all, the words "supreme person" (*parapuruṣa*) and "person" (*puruṣa*) are common to both [contexts]. Moreover, in this passage, the "supreme person" under discussion is not referred to by the term "the one who consists of life" (*jīvanaghana*), such that this person to be seen would have to be something other than that supreme one.
What, then, is the "mass of life" (*jīvaghana*)? It is said: *ghana* means form (*mūrti*).
A mass characterized by life is the "mass of life."

The state of being a fragment (*khilya*) of the Supreme Self in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is distinct from the objects and the senses, is what is meant here by "the mass of living beings" (*jīvaghana*).

Another [teacher] says: that which was designated in the immediately preceding passage, "He is led up to the world of Brahman by the Sāman chants"—that world of Brahman, which is superior to other worlds, is here called the "mass of living beings.

For, since all individual souls (*jīvas*) accompanied by their instruments (the senses) are gathered together within Hiraṇyagarbha—the self of all instruments who dwells in the world of Brahman—that world of Brahman constitutes a "mass of living beings."

Therefore, it is understood that he who is the Supreme Self (paramātman), who is the object of seeing in the preceding [verse], is the very same one who is the object of meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*).
Furthermore, the qualification "the Supreme Person" (*paraṃ puruṣam*) is appropriate only if the Supreme Self is accepted;
for the Supreme Person is indeed the Supreme Self, since there exists nothing else whatsoever beyond him.
This is because of another scriptural passage: "There is nothing higher than the Person; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal.

Furthermore, the text—"The syllable Om is both the higher and the lower Brahman"—having thus distinguished them, subsequently teaches that the higher Person is to be meditated upon by means of the syllable Om; this leads one to understand that the higher Person is indeed the Supreme Brahman.

Moreover, the statement regarding the fruit of liberation from evil—"Just as a snake is freed from its skin, so indeed he is freed from evil"—indicates that the object of meditation here must be the Supreme Self.

Now, as for what was said—that for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self, a fruit limited by space is not appropriate—it is replied here: for one who meditates upon the Supreme Self with the three-measured *oṃkāra* as a support, the fruit is the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) and, through that, the gradual arising of perfect realization; thus, this will be intended as "gradual liberation" (*kramamukti*), and so there is no fault.
(FN: "Supreme" means devoid of distinctions.)
Furthermore, it follows— that is, it attains— the other task by means of the sense base (*āyatana*), which is the instrument of attainment.
The "higher Brahman" is Hiraṇyagarbha;
the "body" (piṇḍa) is the gross Virāṭ. The meaning of the samādhi is that the Sūtra is superior in relation to that [Virāṭ].
That which is pervaded is the object.
A lump of salt from Sindh is a *khilya*;
the state of being a *khilya* means smallness.
A *pādodara* is a snake.
5. The Section Concerning the Small One (Daharādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 14–21 / Sūtra 14: "The small one [is Brahman] because of the subsequent [statements].
Now, that which is within this city of Brahman, the small lotus-palace, the small space within it—that which is inside that, one should seek to find; that is what one should desire to understand."
The passage beginning with *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 8.1.1 is thus recited.

Regarding that, a doubt arises as to whether this "small ether" (*dahara ākāśa*) heard within the small lotus of the heart is the elemental ether, or the individual self (*vijñānātman*), or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Why does this doubt arise?
By means of the two words "ether" (ākāśa) and "city of Brahman" (brahmapura).
For this word "ether" is seen to be used both for the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa) and for the Supreme [Brahman].
In that regard, there arises the doubt: could the small [ether] be the elemental ether itself, or could it be the Supreme?

Likewise, regarding the phrase "the city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*), is it that the individual soul (*jīva*)—who bears the name "Brahman"—has this body as its city, and thus it is the "city of Brahman," or rather, is it the city of the supreme Brahman itself that is the "city of Brahman"?
In this regard, there arises a doubt as to whether the owner of the city is either the individual soul or the supreme [Brahman], and which of these two is the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*).

On this point, since the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), the initial position (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the term "small" (*dahara*) refers to the elemental ether alone.
And its smallness is relative to its small abode;

furthermore, the relationship of comparison and thing compared—expressed in the passage, "As large as this external space is, so large is this space within the heart"—is based on the distinction between the internal and the external. Moreover, heaven, earth, and so forth are contained within it, because space is one in its nature as the principle of vacuity.
Alternatively, it follows that the individual soul (jīva) is the "small" one, because of the term "city of Brahman" (brahmapura).
For this city of the body belongs to the individual soul; thus, it is called the "city of Brahman."
Because it is acquired through its own karma,
and because of devotion, it is designated by the word "Brahman";
for the Supreme Brahman has no relationship with the body in the form of a master and its possession.
In that regard, it is observed that the lord of a city resides in a specific part of the city, as is the case with a king.

Furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) has the mind as its limiting adjunct, and the mind is generally established in the heart; therefore, this residence within the heart must belong to the soul alone.
Its smallness is also possible because it is compared to the point of a needle;

and its comparison to space and so forth will be intended to express its non-difference from Brahman. Furthermore, it is not heard here that the small space itself is to be sought after or to be desired to be known.
Because it is mentioned as a qualification of the "other" in the phrase, "That which is within it.
To this we reply: here, the small ether (daharākāśa) must be the Supreme Lord alone, and not the elemental ether or the individual soul (jīva).
Why?
[This is known] from the reasons found in the subsequent supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣa).

For instance, regarding the small ether (dahara ākāśa) which has been enjoined as that which is to be sought after, there occurs a statement of resolution preceded by an objection, beginning with "If they should say to him... and continuing, "What is there in it that is to be sought after, that one should desire to understand? and so forth.
"He should say: 'As large as this external space is, so large is this space within the heart; both heaven and earth are contained within it alone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.3).

In this passage, by removing the smallness of the space—which had been attributed to it because of the smallness of the lotus—through a comparison with the well-known [external] space, it is understood that the teacher negates the identity of the "small" space with the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).

Although the word "ether" (ākāśa) is conventionally established as referring to the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), nevertheless, it is not tenable for it to be compared with itself; thus, the suspicion that it refers to the elemental ether is dispelled.

[Objection: But was it not stated that even for a single ether, the relationship of object of comparison and subject of comparison is possible through an imagined distinction between its external and internal aspects?
[Reply: This is not possible.
Indeed, this recourse to imagined distinctions is a desperate resort.

Furthermore, even if one were to describe the relationship between the object of comparison and the comparison by assuming such a distinction, it would not be logically tenable for the internal space to possess the same magnitude as external space, because the internal space is limited.

But surely, since there is another scriptural passage stating that "the Supreme Lord is greater than space" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.6.6.2), it is not tenable for Him to have the same dimension as space.
This is not a fault.
Since the sentence is intended to remove the smallness resulting from being enclosed within the lotus, it does not have the purpose of establishing [the actual] equality of size.
For if it were to establish both [smallness and equality], the sentence would be split.
Furthermore, even if a distinction were imagined, it is not possible for heaven, earth, and so forth to be contained within a single portion of space enclosed by a lotus.

"This Self is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"— thus, both the nature of being the Self and qualities such as freedom from evil are not possible in the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa).
Although the word "Self" (ātman) can apply to the individual soul (jīva), nevertheless, by virtue of the other reasons, even the suspicion that it refers to the jīva is set aside.
For it is not possible to remove the smallness of the individual soul (jīva)—which is delimited by adjuncts (upādhi) and compared to the tip of an awl—caused by its being enclosed within the lotus.

If it is argued that the all-pervasiveness and other attributes of the soul are intended to be expressed with the desire to convey its non-difference from Brahman, then it is more logical that those very attributes, such as all-pervasiveness, be directly attributed to Brahman itself, whose nature the soul possesses. Thus, it is appropriate that Brahman alone be intended as the subject of the description of all-pervasiveness and so forth.

As for what was also said— that because it is designated as the "city of Brahman" (brahmapura) by means of the individual soul (jīva), this city must belong to the individual soul alone as its master, just as a king's city belongs to the king—
we reply: this body, which is the city of the supreme Brahman, is called the "city of Brahman," because the word "Brahman" has its primary meaning when applied to that [Supreme Being].
This [Self] also has a connection with this city, because it is the locus of perception; for it is said:
"He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest mass of life" (Praśna Upaniṣad 5.5).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Verily, this person is the dweller in the city within all cities" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.18), and so forth;
or else, Brahman is perceived here as being present within the city of the individual soul itself.

Just as Viṣṇu is present in the Śālagrāma stone, so it is here. And having stated that the fruits of actions are finite—“Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so there the world acquired by merit perishes” (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6)—it continues: “But those who depart from here having realized the Self and these true desires, for them...”

By stating that "one has freedom of movement in all worlds" as the infinite fruit of the knowledge of the small ether (daharākāśa) under discussion, the text indicates its nature as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
Furthermore, it was argued that it is not heard [in the scripture] that the small ether is to be sought or to be known.

Regarding the statement, "Because it is mentioned as a qualification of another," we reply: if space (*ākāśa*) were not intended as that which is to be sought after, then the demonstration of the nature of space in such passages as, "As large as this external space is, so large is this space within the heart," would be of no use.
[Objection: But even this is demonstrated solely for the purpose of showing the existence of a reality residing within.

If they should object, "In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; within it is a small space (ākāśa). What is there that should be sought after, what is there that one should desire to understand?"—having raised this objection, on the occasion of its refutation, [the text] demonstrates that the heaven, earth, and so forth are contained within it by beginning with the analogy of the ākāśa.
This is not so;
for if this were the case, then that which is contained within, such as heaven and earth and so forth, would have been stated as what is to be sought after and what is to be desired to be known.
In that case, the remainder of the passage would be inconsistent.

For, having drawn forth from the context the ether— which is the substratum for the resting of heaven, earth, and so on, as indicated by the passages "In this all desires are contained" and "This Self is free from evil"—

the remainder of the sentence shows, by means of the word "and" (ca) signifying conjunction, that both the Self and the desires resting upon that substratum of desires are to be known, in the words: "But those who depart here, having discovered the Self and these true desires."

Therefore, it is understood that even at the beginning of the passage, the small ether (*dahara-ākāśa*) itself—situated within the lotus of the heart, together with the earth and other elements contained within it, as well as the true desires—is what is stated to be the object of knowledge;
and by the reasons already mentioned, that [ether] is the Supreme Lord.
(Note: *Brahmapura* refers to the body.)
The "small" and "subtle" refers to the heart itself, which is the subject under discussion because it has the shape of a lotus;
the word "abode" is used there because of the proximity of the Supreme Being.
"By devotion" means through the application of the qualities of pure consciousness (*caitanya*).
"Whose hunger has departed" means whose desire to eat has vanished; the sense is that he is free from the urge to consume food.
"Daharatva" means smallness.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including [qualities] such as being the substratum of all. "In the cities" means in bodies.

He is called *puruṣa* because he dwells (*śete*) in the city (*puri*) or in the heart (*hṛdaye*). Having understood and experienced this, those who are concentrated and firmly established [should meditate].
On account of the movement and the word, as well as the characteristic mark; for thus it has been seen.
It was stated that the "small one" is the Supreme Lord because of subsequent reasons;
those very subsequent reasons are now being elaborated.
For this reason as well, the "small one" (dahara) is indeed the Supreme Lord,

because in the supplementary portion of the passage concerning the small one, there occur the terms "going" and "word," which establish the Supreme Lord alone: "All these creatures go day after day into this world of Brahman, yet they do not find it" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2).

In this context, having designated the small [space] under discussion by the term "Brahma-world," the movement toward that [world] belonging to the living beings denoted by the word "prajā" (progeny), as it is being described, leads to the understanding that the small [space] is Brahman.

For thus, the daily movement of living beings toward Brahman during the state of deep sleep is observed in another scriptural passage: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with the True" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.1), and so forth.
In common worldly usage as well, they say of one who is in deep sleep that he has "become Brahman" (brahmībhūta) or "attained the state of Brahman" (brahmatāṃ gata).

Likewise, the term "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka), when applied here to the small [space] within the heart, removes the suspicion that it refers to the individual soul (jīva) or the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), and leads one to understand its nature as Brahman.
But could the term "Brahma-world" not also refer to the world of the Lotus-seated One (Viṣṇu)?
If it were explained by means of a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) as "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo loka*), [it would mean something else].

But when explained by means of a coordinate construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that "Brahman itself is the world" (*brahmaiva lokaḥ*) and thus "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*), it will lead one to the Supreme Brahman itself.
And this very fact—that there is a journey to the world of Brahman every day—is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) supporting the adoption of the coordinate construction for the word "Brahman."
For it is not possible to assume that these creatures go day after day to the world of the effected Brahman known as Satyaloka.
And because its greatness, consisting in support, is perceived in this [small ether].
For the reason of support as well, this small ether is the Supreme Lord alone.
How so?

For, having introduced the subject with "In this [space] within, there is a small ether," and having first used the analogy of the ether, described the dissolution of everything within it, applied the word "Self" (*ātman*) to that very same thing, and taught its connection with qualities such as being free from sin, the text points back to that very same topic without departing from the context:
"Now, that which is the Self is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.4.1).
In this context, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self" (*ātman*), *vidhṛti* refers to the sustainer;
for it is recorded that the suffix *ktic* denotes the agent.
Just as in the world a dam (*setu*) is the sustainer of a flow of water so that the excellence of the fields may not be confounded, [so too is the Self].

Thus, this Self is the supporter of these worlds—distinguished by internal and other divisions—as well as of the castes, stages of life, and so forth, serving as a dam for the sake of non-confusion and non-intermixture.
In this way, the text demonstrates the greatness characterized by such support within the small [space] under discussion here.
And this greatness belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, as is known from another scriptural passage: "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart," and so on.

Likewise, in another passage where the word of the Supreme Lord is ascertained, it is heard: "He is the Lord of all, He is the sovereign of beings, He is the protector of beings, He is the bridge, the support, so that these worlds may not be confounded.
For this reason of being the sustainer (*dhṛti*), this *dahara* (the small one) is indeed the Supreme Lord. [Note: The bridge is the cause of non-confusion.]
And because of its well-known usage.
For this reason as well, the Supreme Lord alone is referred to by the words "the small ether within this";
for the word "ether" (ākāśa) is well known to denote the Supreme Lord.

This is because we observe such usages as: "That which is called space is indeed the bringer-forth of name and form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.4), and "All these beings, verily, arise from space alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
However, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is never observed to be applied to the individual soul (*jīva*).

As for the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), although the conventional usage of the word "ether" is well-established for it, it must not be accepted [as the referent here], because the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison is impossible; this has already been stated. (17) [Note:
*Ākāśa* is so called because it shines or manifests itself on all sides (*ā samantāt kāśate*); it is the Self-luminous Lord.]

If it be argued that he [the Supreme Lord] is meant because of a reference to the other, we say no, because of impossibility. (BBs 1.3.18) If, on the strength of the supplementary passage, the "small one" were understood to be the Supreme Lord, there is likewise a reference to the other—the individual soul—in the supplementary passage: "Now, this serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light..."
"He emerges in his own form; this is the Self," so he said (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4).

For here, the word *saṃprasāda*—being seen in another scriptural passage to refer to the state of deep sleep—is capable of bringing to mind the individual soul (*jīva*) who possesses that state, and not any other entity.
Likewise, the "emergence from the body" is possible only for the individual soul which has its support in the body.

Just as wind and other elements, which depend upon space, arise from space, so it is here. Furthermore, just as the word "space" (ākāśa), although its primary worldly referent is not the Supreme Lord, is nevertheless accepted as referring to the Supreme Lord in such passages as "Space, indeed, is the bringer-forth of name and form," because of its association with the attributes of the Supreme Lord, so too [is it here].
It might also refer to the individual soul (jīva).
Therefore, if you argue that because of the reference to "the other," the very same individual soul is being spoken of here in the passage, "In this small space within," this cannot be so.
Why? Because it is impossible.
For the individual soul (*jīva*), while identifying with the limitations imposed by adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*), cannot be compared to space.
Furthermore, qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth are not possible for one who does not identify with the attributes of the adjuncts.
This has already been explained in detail in the first Sūtra;

however, it is presented here again to dispel the suspicion that there might be something additional. Furthermore, the author will state later on: "And the reference is for another purpose" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.20).

FN: *Saṃprasāda* (perfect serenity) is a particular state of the individual soul (*jīva*) in which it becomes perfectly serene, abandoning the turbidity produced by the contact between the sense objects and the senses; this is deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
Another scriptural passage from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* states: "Having rejoiced and moved about in perfect serenity...
The attributes of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are evil and so forth.
"But if [it is argued] from the subsequent [passage], his true nature is indeed manifested" (BBs 1.3.19).
The doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) that arose from the reference to the "other" has been refuted on the grounds of impossibility;
now, however, a renewed doubt concerning the *jīva* is raised based on the subsequent statement of Prajāpati, like the rising again of one who was dead through the sprinkling of nectar.

For there, having first proposed that the Self—characterized by attributes such as being "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*)—is that which is to be sought and understood, [the text] says, "This person who is seen in the eye, this is [he]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.4), thereby pointing out the individual soul (*jīva*), the seer residing in the eye, as the Self.
Then it continues: "I shall explain this very same one to you further" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3).

Thus, repeatedly referring back to that very same [subject], the text explains the individual soul (jīva) as it exists in different states: "This is the Self which moves about in the dream state, being honored" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.10.1), and "When he is thus asleep, composed, serene, and knows no dream—this is the Self.
It further shows that this very [Self] possesses qualities such as freedom from sin: "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman."

And having perceived the defect in the state of deep sleep through the passage, "Indeed, he does not know himself at that time thus: 'I am this,' nor indeed these beings" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.1, 2), and having begun with the words, "This very Self I shall explain further to you, and nothing other than this," [the text proceeds] by first censuring the connection with the body: "This serene being, having risen up from this body... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).

"Having attained the highest light, he appears in his own true form; he is the supreme person"—this passage shows that it is the individual soul (jīva) itself, having emerged from the body, that is the supreme person.
Therefore, there is the possibility of the attributes of the supreme Lord existing in the individual soul.

If someone should say, "Therefore, because of the statement 'In this, there is a small inner space,' it is the individual soul (jīva) alone that is spoken of," one should say to him: "But [it is] the one whose true nature has become manifest.
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of setting aside the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa).
The meaning is that even from the subsequent passage, no doubt regarding the individual soul (jīva) arises here.
Why?
Because even there, the individual soul is intended to be described as having its true nature manifested.
"Āvirbhūtasvarūpaḥ" means one whose true nature has become manifest.
The term "jīva" (the living self) is used here by way of referring to what was previously so.
This is what is intended: having pointed out the seer characterized by the eye in the passage "He who is in the eye," [the text] [describes him] by means of the Udaśarāva Brāhmaṇa.

Having set aside the notion that the body is the self, and having repeatedly drawn back that very self as the subject to be explained with the words "But him alone, indeed, to you," the text proceeds through the presentation of the states of dreaming and deep sleep to declare, "Having reached the highest light, he manifests in his own true form. Thus,
it explains this individual soul (jīva) as being of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, which is its ultimate reality, and not in its state as an individual soul.
That supreme light which is to be attained, as heard in scripture, is the Supreme Brahman;
and that [Brahman] possesses attributes such as being free from evil (apahatapāpmatva),
and that alone is the ultimate essential nature of the individual soul (jīva), according to scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (tattvam asi).
The other [self] is not that which is imagined through limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

For as long as one does not realize the Self— which is of the nature of immutable, eternal consciousness— as "I am Brahman," by thereby subverting the ignorance characterized by duality (such as the notion of a person in what is actually a post), so long does the state of being a *jīva* persist for the *jīva*.
But when one is awakened by the Śruti, having been raised up from the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect, [it is said]:
"You are not this aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect; you are not a transmigrating being."

What then is that? That which is Truth is the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness; "That thou art. Then, awakening to the Self whose nature is the immutable, eternal Seer, and rising above this identification with the body and so forth, one becomes that very Self whose nature is the immutable, eternal Seer. As it is said: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9).
This is according to such scriptural passages as these.
And that very [nature] is its ultimate (pāramārthika) form, by which, having risen out of the body, it manifests in its own true form.
But how is it possible for that which is immutably eternal (kūṭasthanitya) to manifest in its own form by itself, as is the case with gold and other such substances?

However, for substances whose own nature is suppressed due to contact with other substances, and whose specific uncommon characteristics are unmanifest, there may be the manifestation of their own nature when they are purified by the application of alkaline solutions and other means.
Likewise, for stars and the like, whose light is suppressed during the day, there may be the manifestation of their own nature at night upon separation from the obscuring agent.
But it is not possible for the eternal light of the self's consciousness to be obscured by anything, because of its non-contacting nature like that of space,
and because that would contradict what is perceived;
for seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing constitute the very nature of the individual soul (jīva).
Moreover, that [knowledge] is seen to be eternally perfected even for the individual soul (*jīva*) prior to its emergence from the body;
for every living being conducts worldly affairs by seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing—otherwise, such conduct would be impossible.
If that knowledge were only to be accomplished after the soul had emerged from the body, then the observed conduct prior to that emergence would be contradicted.
Therefore, what is the nature of this emergence from the body, or what is the nature of its manifestation in its own form?

To this it is replied: prior to the arising of discriminative knowledge, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the light of vision and so forth, becomes as if non-discriminated from the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations.

Just as the transparency and whiteness—which are the essential nature of a pure crystal—appear as if non-different from it prior to the apprehension of their distinction due to limiting adjuncts such as red or blue;

yet, subsequent to the apprehension of their distinction produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the crystal is said to "manifest" in its own nature through its transparency and whiteness, even though it was already exactly so before.

Likewise, for the individual soul (*jīva*), which exists as non-different from limiting adjuncts such as the body, there is the discriminative knowledge produced by scripture; this "rising up from the body" is the fruit of that discriminative knowledge, namely the manifestation in one's own true nature, which is the realization of the absolute nature of the Self.
Thus, it is solely through discrimination or non-discrimination that the Self possesses bodilessness or embodiedness, as stated in the mantra-text: "Bodiless among bodies" (*Katha Upaniṣad* 1.2.22).

Thus, because of the traditional teaching that there is no distinction between being embodied and being disembodied— as stated in "Though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, he neither acts nor is tainted" (Gītā 13.31)—
it is said that one whose true nature is unmanifest due to the absence of discriminative knowledge becomes one whose true nature is manifest through discriminative knowledge.

Having bowed, [it is said that] manifestation and non-manifestation of another kind are not possible for the true nature (svarūpa), precisely because it is the true nature itself. Thus, the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Lord (parameśvara) is caused solely by false knowledge (mithyājñāna) and is not caused by the reality of things (vastu),
since there is no distinction in their being unattached (asaṅga), like space (vyoma).
This must be understood from the following:
after teaching, "This person who is seen in the eye," the text teaches, "This is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman.

If the well-known seer in the eye, who is perceived as a seer, were other than Brahman—characterized by immortality and fearlessness—then there could be no grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with Brahman, which is defined by immortality and fearlessness.
Nor is this "Self in the reflection" indicated as the one observed in the eye,
for that would entail the consequence of Prajāpati being a speaker of falsehood.
Likewise, in the second section as well, in the statement, "This one who moves about being honored in a dream," no seer other than the person-in-the-eye specified in the first section is indicated.
This is because the instruction begins with the words, "I shall explain this very matter to you further.
Furthermore, upon waking, one rejects what was seen, saying, "Today in a dream I saw an elephant; I do not see it now.
Yet, one recognizes that very same seer, thinking, "I who saw the dream am the very same I who now see the waking state."

Likewise, in the third passage as well—"For indeed, in this state, he does not know himself thus: 'I am this,' nor does he know these beings"—it shows only the absence of specific cognition during the state of deep sleep, but it does not deny the cognizer.
As for the statement there that "he has gone to utter destruction," that too is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognition, not the destruction of the cognizer.
For another scriptural passage states: "There is no loss of consciousness for the knower, because of its imperishability" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30).
Likewise, in the fourth section as well, it says: "I shall explain this very same thing to you further, and nothing other than this."

Having begun thus, with the detailed exposition starting from "O Maghavan, this body is indeed mortal," [the text] shows— by rejecting the connection with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) relative to the body—

that the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the term "serenity" (saṃprasāda), "attains its own true form" (svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate); thereby it demonstrates that the soul has attained the nature of Brahman, and does not show the soul to be other than the supreme Brahman, whose nature is immortal and fearless.

However, some, considering it improper to refer back to the individual soul (jīva) when the intention is to speak of the Supreme Self (paramātman), imagine that the text means: "I shall explain further to you this very Self—endowed with qualities such as freedom from sin—which was indicated at the beginning of the passage by the words 'But him alone to you...
For them, the use of the pronoun *etam* ("this one"), which refers to what is proximate, would be set aside.
Furthermore, the repeated hearing [of the same teaching] would be contradicted, because that which was expressed in one turn of discourse is not expressed in another turn of discourse.

Moreover, having made the promise "But this very one I shall explain to you," Prajāpati would incur the charge of being a deceiver if he were to explain something other than that until the fourth turn of discourse.

Therefore, by means of knowledge (*vidyā*), that supreme nature of the Lord— which is the opposite of the individual form presented by ignorance (*avidyā*), which is defiled by defects such as agency, enjoyership, passion, and hatred, and which is joined with manifold evils— is established through the dissolution of that [individual form],
just as the rope and so forth are [established] through the dissolution of the snake and so forth.
However, there are other disputants, including some among our own [followers], who believe that the individual form (*jaiva-rūpa*) is indeed ultimately real.
This *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtra] has been commenced for the sake of awakening all of them—those who stand as opponents to the correct vision of the oneness of the Self (*ātma-ekatva-samyag-darśana*).

There is only one Supreme Lord, the eternally immutable essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), who, through ignorance (*avidyā*) or illusion (*māyā*), is manifested in manifold ways like a magician; there is no other essence of consciousness.

As for the fact that the author of the Sūtras, having raised the doubt regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) within the discourse on the Supreme Lord, refutes it with the words "Not so, because of impossibility" (Brahmasūtra 1.3.18) and so forth—the intention there is this: since the one, immutable, eternal, and unattached Supreme Self is by nature eternally pure, conscious, and free, whereas the state of being an individual soul is its opposite—like the imagined dust and stains upon the sky—he intends to remove that [false] state of the soul by means of passages whose purpose is to establish the identity of the Self and by reasoned refutations of dualism; thus, he confirms the distinctness of the Supreme Self from the individual soul.

However, [the scripture] does not intend to establish that the individual soul (*jīva*) is different from the Supreme; rather, it merely restates the distinction between souls as it is well-known in the world and imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*).
For he considers that in this way, the injunctions for ritual action (*karma-vidhi*), which proceed by restating the innate status of being an agent and an enjoyer, are not contradicted.

But as for the actual meaning of the scripture to be established, he shows it to be the oneness of the Self alone: "But the teaching is based on the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.30).

By these and other such statements, we have described the resolution of the contradiction regarding the injunctions for ritual action through the distinction between the learned (*vidvat*) and others.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the section concerning dreaming (*svapna-paryāya*), where [the text says] "being honored" (*mahīyamānaḥ*)—meaning being worshipped by objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmayair viṣayaiḥ*)—and in the section concerning deep sleep (*suṣupti-paryāya*), where [it says] "in that place" (*tad yatra*), Prajāpati explains that it is the individual soul (*jīva*) itself.
The particle *aha* expresses dejection.
"Other than this self under discussion" means another.
"In a water-filled bowl" (*udaśarāve*) refers to the reflection-self, the body; the meaning of the Śruti is that he was told, "That which is unknown to yourself must be told to me."
The connection is as follows: having emerged and having reflected, "he accomplishes"—this is what is meant here.
It is the solar light that overcomes [the darkness] upon its separation from that [light].
Feelings consist of joy, sorrow, and so forth;
discriminative knowledge, however, is the purification of the referent of the term "thou.
These two truths are of different kinds.
The state of being devoid of parts and so forth is non-attachment (*asaṅgatva*).
This one is in deep sleep; at present, in deep sleep.

"I do not know myself" means that one does not know the self, which is the locus of the conceit "I. The word "not" (na) signifies that there is no alteration of the consciousness that constitutes the very nature of the self, because it is inherently capable [of such knowledge]. This occurs through dissolution (*vilayana*), that is, through purification (*śodhana*).

"By knowledge" means by the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), such as "That art thou" (*tat tvam asi*) and others. Since there is no distinction between the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, it is logical that no difference exists between them, whether in their own form or in any other form.
The prohibitions against dualism consist of statements such as "not here, not this" (*neha nānāsti kiṃcana*).
And the reference has another purpose. (BBs 1.3.20) Now,

as for the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) shown in the supplementary passage of the "small" (*dahara*) section— beginning with "Now, he who is this serene one" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.4)— if that [small ether] is explained as the Supreme Lord, it follows that the passage would have the sense of neither being an instruction for the meditation on the individual soul nor an instruction regarding the specific subject under discussion.

Therefore, he says: this reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) has another purpose; it does not culminate in the essential nature of the *jīva*, but rather culminates in the essential nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
How so?

The *jīva*, designated by the term "perfect tranquility" (*saṃprasāda*), having become the presiding overseer of the cage of the body and senses during the activity of the waking state, [perceives] those things constructed from the impressions (*vāsanā*) thereof...

Having experienced [objects] while moving through the channels during dreams, the one who has become weary and seeks refuge rises from the identification with the body— which consists of both [the gross and subtle forms]— and, in the state of deep sleep, attains the supreme light designated by the word "ether," which is the Supreme Brahman; having abandoned the possession of specific cognitions, it manifests in its own true nature.

That supreme light which is to be attained by him, and by means of which he manifests in his own true form—that very Self, characterized by qualities such as freedom from sin and so forth, is the object of meditation;
thus, this reference to the individual soul (jīva) is also logically consistent for one who maintains that the Supreme Lord is the subject. 20.
If it is argued that this is because of the smallness of its hearing, that has already been answered.
As for what was also said—
