that the smallness of the ether heard in the passage, "The ether within this is small," is not tenable in the case of the Supreme Lord— [that objection has been refuted].
However, since the smallness of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is limited by the tip of an awl, is logically consistent, an answer to that objection must be stated.

Indeed, the answer to this has already been stated in the passage: "If it be said that [the Lord is not the Self] because of His having a small abode and because of the designation of Him as such, we say no, because He is to be perceived in this way, and like space" (Brahma-sūtra 1.2.7), wherein the relative smallness of the Supreme Lord is logically established.
He indicates that this very same solution should be applied here as well.

This smallness has already been refuted by the Scripture itself, which compares it with the well-known space [of the sky] in the passage: "As large as this space is, so large is this space within the heart. (21)

6. The Section on Imitation (Anukṛtyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 22–23: "On account of imitation, and of that [Brahman] as well. (BBs 1.3.22) "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10)
"They declare: 'Everything shines after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined' (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.10).

Regarding the doubt as to whether that one whom everything follows as He shines, and by whose light all this is illumined, is some element of fire (*tejodhātu*) or the conscious Self (*prājña ātmā*), the initial position reached is that it is an element of fire.
Why? Because it is precisely the luminous bodies such as the sun that are negated as being manifest.
For it is well known that while the sun—which is of the nature of light—shines during the day, the moon, stars, and so forth, which are also of the nature of light, do not shine.
Likewise, it is understood that that in which all this—the moon, stars, and so forth—together with the sun, does not shine must itself be something of the nature of light.
Resonance (anubhāna) also is logically possible as having the nature of light,
because imitation is observed among things of a similar nature,
just as it is said, "he follows one who is walking."
Therefore, when it might be concluded that "the fire element is something [else]," we say: the Self must indeed be the conscious one (prājña).
Why?
Because of imitation (anukṛti).
Imitation means emulation.
This "shining after" that which is mentioned in the passage, "Everything shines only after Him who shines," is intelligible only if the wise one (the Prājña) is accepted as the subject.
For they declare the conscious Self to be "of the nature of light, whose resolve is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.2);
it is not, however, well known that the sun and other luminaries shine after some element of fire.
Furthermore, because the fire-elements of the sun and so forth are equal, there is no dependence on another fire-element that they might illuminate by following its radiance;
for one lamp does not illuminate another lamp. As for what was said—that imitation is observed among things of a similar nature—[that too is incorrect].
This is not an absolute rule;
for even among things of different intrinsic natures, imitation is observed.
For example, a red-hot iron ball, which imitates fire, burns along with the fire that it burns.
"Or the dust of the earth follows the wind as it blows"— by this,
he indicated the "following" (*anubhāna*) through the word "in imitation" (*anukṛteḥ*).
And by the words "of that" (*tasya ca*), he indicates the fourth quarter of this verse.
The statement, "By its light all this shines," which declares that the shining of the sun and other luminaries is caused by it, leads one to understand the Self as the Prājña.
For they declare the Prājña Self in the passage: "The gods worship Him as the life, the immortal light of lights" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).
It is both unestablished and contradictory that the light of the sun and so forth shines by means of another light,
because one light obstructs another light.
Alternatively, it is not only the light of the sun and others mentioned in the verse that is said to shine due to that [other] cause.

Rather, because of the unrestricted scriptural statement "all this," the manifestation of this entire collection of names, forms, actions, agents, and results is caused by the existence of the light of Brahman.
Just as the manifestation of the entire range of forms is caused by the existence of the light of the sun and so forth, so it is here.
Furthermore, by employing the word "there" in the passage "the sun does not shine there," the text indicates that what is under discussion [in the preceding context] is being referred to.
And Brahman is the subject under discussion in such passages as, "In whom heaven, earth, and the intermediate space are woven" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5).
Immediately thereafter, it is said: "In the supreme golden sheath is the stainless, fruitless Brahman;
that is the pure light of lights, which those who know the Self know."
How is it that [the Self] is "the light of lights"? To this, the following has arisen: "The sun does not shine there.

As for what was also said—that the negation of the shining of luminous bodies such as the sun is only possible if there is another luminous element, just as the others are compared to the sun—that too has been demonstrated to be untenable, since no other such luminous element is possible.
Furthermore, the negation of their manifestation even with respect to Brahman is logically consistent;
for whatever they perceive is perceived solely by means of the light that is Brahman,
whereas Brahman itself is not perceived by any other light, because its very nature is self-luminosity.
By which [light] the sun and other luminaries shine—that is the light in him.
For Brahman manifests other things, but Brahman is not manifested by anything else; as it is said: "By his own light he sits" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.6).
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "It cannot be grasped, for it is not grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4).
[In that state], other stars and the moon do not shine; that is to say, they do not illuminate it.
Wisdom (*prājñatva*) is its self-luminosity, stated for the purpose of its illuminating nature. *Anukāra* means subsequent shining. *Viraja* means free from adventitious impurities.
It is pure and naturally free from impurity.
Furthermore, it is recorded in the Smṛti:
Moreover, this very nature of the wise Self is recorded in the Bhagavad Gītā: "Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines That."
"That supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return" (15.6),
and "That light residing in the sun which illumines the entire world,
and that which is in the moon and in fire— know that light to be Mine" (15.12). // 23 //
7. The Section on the Measured (Pramitādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 24–25:
"He is known from scripture alone. (BBs 1.3.24) It is heard in the Śruti: "The Person, the size of a thumb, stands in the middle of the self."

Likewise, [it is said]: "The person the size of a thumb, smokeless like a light, the lord of what has been and what is to be; he alone is today, he is tomorrow—this indeed is that" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.4.13).
Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether this person who is heard of as being the size of a thumb is the individual self (vijñānātman) or the supreme self (paramātman).
In this regard, because of the instruction concerning its size, it follows at first that it is the conscious self (*vijñānātman*).
For a measurement of one thumb is not possible for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is infinite in length and breadth;
however, since the conscious self possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), its being the size of a thumb is possible through a certain figurative conception.
And from the Smṛti: "Then, from the body of Satyavat, Yama forcibly drew out a person the size of a thumb, bound by a noose and brought under his control."
(Mahābhārata 3.297.17). For the Supreme Lord cannot be extracted by force; therefore, in that context, it is determined that the transmigrating soul is the size of a thumb.
This being the position reached—that it must be that very [individual soul] even here—we reply: this person measured as the size of a thumb must indeed be the Supreme Self.
Why? Because of the word:
"The Lord of what has been and what is to be."
For there is no one other than the Supreme Lord who possesses unimpeded sovereignty over the past and the future;
and the phrase "This indeed is That" connects what was previously introduced here with what was asked.
The meaning is: "This indeed is that which was asked about as Brahman."

The meaning is that because Brahman is asked here in the words, "Tell me that which you see as other than dharma and other than adharma, other than this cause and effect, and other than the past and the future" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14), and because of the scriptural statement of its designation, "by the word itself," it is understood that this is the Supreme Lord, the Ruler (Īśāna). // 24 //
But how can there be a teaching regarding the size of the omnipresent Supreme Self? To this we reply:
[The phrase] "in the self" means in the middle of the body, specifically in the heart.
The mention of "the past and the future" is intended as an illustration for the present as well; the meaning is that He is the controller of the three periods of time.

"By some [measure]" means by the measure of the thumb, referring to the sheath of the heart-lotus, which is the locus for the perception of the individual soul (*jīva*). However, this is said with reference to the heart, because the treatise is intended for human beings.
Even though the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is omnipresent, this "thumb-sized" nature is stated with reference to its abiding within the heart.
Just as space possesses the measure of a cubit in relation to the joints of a bamboo,
so too the measure of a thumb is not possible for the Supreme Self in its direct sense;
nor is it appropriate to understand anyone other than the Supreme Self here, on account of terms such as "Lord" (Īśāna) and others, as has already been stated.

Now, an objection is raised: since the hearts vary according to the differences among individual living beings, even the thumb-sized dimension is untenable as a universal requirement; to this, the following answer is given: "Because the qualification belongs to human beings.

For although the scripture is promulgated without distinction, it qualifies only human beings, because they possess the capacity [for understanding], have the desire [to know], are not excluded [from the rites], and because of the scriptural injunctions regarding initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth; this has been explained in the section on the definition of qualification (*adhikāra-lakṣaṇa*, Jaimini Sūtra 6.1).
Furthermore, the body of human beings has a fixed size;
and by proportion, their heart is likewise of a fixed size, measuring only the breadth of a thumb.
Therefore, since this scripture concerns human beings, it is appropriate that the Supreme Self is described as being the size of a thumb, with reference to its abiding within the human heart.

As for what was said—that on account of the teaching regarding its size and because of traditional Smṛti, this one who is the size of a thumb must be understood as being only a transmigrating soul—that is answered as follows:
just as in such passages as "That is the Self; That thou art," this teaching points out that the very same transmigrating being who is the size of a thumb is in fact Brahman.
For the operation of Vedāntic statements is twofold.

In some places it is devoted to defining the nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and in others it is devoted to teaching the identity of the individual self (*vijñānātman*) with the Supreme Self.
Therefore, what is taught here is the identity of the individual self with the Supreme Self, not that anyone possesses the size of a thumb.
This very point will be made clear later: "The Person the size of a thumb, the inner self, is always seated in the hearts of men."
"One should draw that out from one's own body with fortitude, like a stalk from a reed;
one should know that as the bright, immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.17). [FN:
An *aratni* is a hand together with the little finger.]
In this context, the word "human" (manuṣya) refers to those belonging to the three higher castes (traivarṇika),
because of the exclusion [of others] in the statement, "A Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice," and because [only they] are initiated (upanīyate).
"One should teach him"—
this is the exclusion of the Śūdra from eligibility.
One should extract that individual soul (jīva) from both the gross and the subtle body, separating it [from them].
"By means of fortitude, tranquility, and so forth"—this is the meaning.
8. The Section on the Deities (Devatādhikaraṇa). Sūtra 26–33:
"Above that [the world of Brahman] as well, Bādarāyaṇa [maintains this], because it is possible. (BBs 1.3.26)
It has been stated that the scriptural mention of [the self] being "the size of a thumb" is with reference to the human heart, because the scripture has humans as its intended audience;
in connection with that, this is now said:
it is certainly true that the scripture has humans as its intended audience.
However, there is no restriction here in the knowledge of Brahman that it applies to humans alone.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the scripture qualifies those who are above those humans—namely, the gods and others as well.
Why?
Because it is possible;
for even in their case, the causes for qualification—such as desire and so forth—are indeed possible.

Among these, first of all, desire directed toward liberation is possible even for gods and others, arising from such causes as the contemplation of the impermanence of the splendors belonging to the realm of transformation.

Likewise, their capacity is also possible, because their possession of form and other attributes is understood from mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), histories (itihāsas), purāṇas, and common worldly usage;
nor is there any prohibition against them.
Nor would their eligibility be precluded by the injunction regarding initiation (*upanayana*),
because initiation is for the purpose of Vedic study,
and they possess the Vedas through their own innate intuition.

Moreover, it shows that for the sake of acquiring this knowledge, they practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and other disciplines: "For one hundred and ten years, indeed, Maghavan lived as a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.11.3);
and "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa, approached his father Varuṇa."
"Teach me, O Blessed One, the Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1), and so forth.
Furthermore, as for the reason stated for their lack of eligibility for ritual acts: "Not [for] the gods, because of the absence of another deity;
not [for] the sages, because of the absence of another ancestral lineage" (Jaiminīya Sūtra 6.1.6, 7).

There is no purpose served by those [rites] in the case of the *vidyās*; for when the *vidyās* of Indra and others are being performed, there is no task to be accomplished directed toward Indra and the rest,
nor is there any for Bhṛgu and others by virtue of their belonging to the same lineage as Bhṛgu and the rest.
Therefore, by whom can the eligibility of even the gods and others for the Vidyās be denied?
Even if the gods and others are eligible, the scriptural statement regarding being "the size of a thumb" is not contradicted, as it refers to their own thumbs. (26) [FN:
The gods have no eligibility for ritual acts.]
The meaning of the first sūtra is that [the Veda cannot be eternal] because there would be an absence of other deities to whom it could be addressed.

The meaning of the second sūtra is that it is not [eternal] even for the sages, because there is an absence of other sages and because one would lack the capacity to perform a ritual act associated with a sage [if he himself were the author].
That [inability] is the reason for their lack of capacity.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction regarding ritual action, we say no, because we observe multiple ways of participating.

It might be thought: if the eligibility of gods and others for the sciences were described by accepting that they possess bodies, then, because they possess bodies, priests and others such as Indra would also have to be physical participants in the ritual as constituent parts through the presence of their own forms.
If that were accepted,
there would be a contradiction regarding the ritual action;
for the status of Indra and the others as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) in the sacrifice is not observed by virtue of their presence in their own essential form (*svarūpa*).
If it is argued that this is not possible because the simultaneous presence of a single Indra's essential form in many sacrifices is untenable, we reply:
there is no such contradiction.
Why?
Because of the assumption of multiple forms;
it is possible for even a single divine being to assume many forms simultaneously.
How is this understood? From scriptural observation. For instance, beginning with "How many gods are there? it says, "Three and three hundred, and three and three thousand."

Having thus explained [the term], when asked "Which are they?", the Śruti, answering with "These are indeed their powers; there are only these thirty-three gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.1–2), demonstrates that each individual divine self simultaneously possesses multiple forms.

Likewise, by showing that even the thirty-three gods are included within the sequence beginning with the six [classes of gods]—through the statement, "Which one is the single god? It is Prāṇa"—it demonstrates that the gods have the singular form of Prāṇa, and thereby shows that this one Prāṇa simultaneously possesses manifold forms.
Similarly, Smṛti also says: "O bull among the Bharatas, the Self indeed has many bodies."
Having attained strength, the yogi should act; and with all those [powers], he should traverse the earth.
One might obtain sense objects through some means, or one might perform severe austerity.
And he should withdraw them again, just as the sun withdraws its multitude of rays.

This kind of reasoning demonstrates that even for yogins who have attained powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest, the simultaneous occupation of multiple bodies is possible; how much more so, then, for gods who are perfected by birth (*ājānasiddha*)?
Furthermore, because of the possibility of assuming multiple forms, a single deity, having divided itself into many forms, simultaneously becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*) in many sacrifices.
And it is logical that he is not seen by others due to his employment of such activities as invisibility.

There is another explanation for the statement "because multiple modes of participation are observed": even among those possessing physical bodies, multiple modes of participation as auxiliary members (*aṅga*) are seen in injunctions regarding ritual acts.
In some cases, even a single embodied being cannot simultaneously serve as an auxiliary member in multiple places;
just as when many people are feeding [guests], a single Brahmin is not fed by all of them at once.
And in some cases, even a single embodied being can simultaneously become a constituent part in many places,

just as a single Brahmin is saluted at once by many people who are bowing down. Similarly here, since sacrifice consists of both the dedication [of an object] and its relinquishment, many [persons] may perform it while dedicating it to a single embodied deity.

Since each deity will simultaneously relinquish its own respective substance, there is no contradiction whatsoever in the performance of the ritual, even though the deities possess corporeal forms. (27) [FN:

Because of observation and because of the authority of the Śruti; for in the *Nivid* of the *Vaiśvadeva-śāstra*, having begun with "How many gods are there?", Yājñavalkya gave the answer to Śākalya: "Three."]
The *nivid*s are mantra-words that express the number of deities being praised.
*Bala* refers to the perfection of yoga:
"atomicity (*aṇimā*), magnificence (*mahimā*), heaviness (*garimā*), reach (*prāpti*), and mastery (*īśitā*)."

"Prākamya, vaśitva, and kāmāvasāyitā therein"—these are [the powers] beginning with aṇimā. [The objection is raised: "If [you say they are] 'inborn' (ājānasiddha), [we reply] no, because they originate from this [scripture], as established by both perception and inference. (BBs 1.3.28)
Granted that no contradiction regarding karma might arise if one were to admit that gods and others possess physical bodies;
however, a contradiction would indeed arise in the case of sound.
How so?

For it was established that the authority of the Veda rests upon the innate connection between word and meaning, on the grounds of its "independence. Now, however, if a deity possessing a physical body is admitted—even if, through the possession of sovereign power, she were to consume sacrificial offerings related to multiple rites simultaneously—nevertheless, by virtue of having a physical body, she would be subject to birth and death like ourselves; thus, for an eternal word...
If it is argued that there would be a contradiction with the established authority of Vedic words when an eternal meaning and an eternal relationship are perceived,
this contradiction does not exist either.
Why?
Because it originates from that;
for it is precisely from this Vedic word that the world, beginning with the gods, originates.
An objection is raised: since it was established in the sūtra "From which [Brahman] the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]" (BrSū 1.1.2) that the world originates from Brahman,
how can it be stated here that it originates from the Word?

Furthermore, even if it is admitted that this [Veda] originates from Vedic words, how is the contradiction regarding the word itself thereby avoided? For the referents—namely the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, and Maruts—are indeed non-eternal, because they possess an origin. And since these [referents] are non-eternal, who can prevent the non-eternality of the Vedic words "Vasu" and so forth that denote them?
If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction regarding words, because it is well-known in the world that when Devadatta’s son is born, the name Yajñadatta is given to him, we say: no,
for we observe the eternity of the relationship between the word and its meaning in the case of words such as "cow" (go).
For even if individual instances such as cows were subject to origination, it would not follow that their generic forms (ākṛti) are also subject to origination.
Indeed, it is only the individual instances of substances, qualities, and actions that originate, not their generic forms.
Furthermore, the relationship of words is with generic forms, not with individual instances.
Because individuals are infinite, it is impossible to grasp their relationship [with words];
furthermore, since universals (*ākṛti*) are eternal even as individuals arise, no contradiction is observed in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*).

Likewise, it should be understood that even if the arising of individual deities and others is admitted, there is no contradiction in the case of words such as "Vasu," because the universal is eternal.
The specific form of the gods and others, however, is to be understood from the mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and so forth, through the comprehension that they possess bodies.
Terms such as "Indra" and the like are based on connection with a particular station, just like terms such as "army commander.
Consequently, whoever occupies a particular station is designated by the term "Indra" and so forth; thus, no fault arises.
This "origination from speech" is not stated with the intention of referring to a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as is the case with [the world's] origination from Brahman.

How then? While the eternal word exists in its nature as the signifier (*vācaka*) and possesses an eternal connection with its objects, there occurs the manifestation of individual objects capable of being engaged with through verbal usage; therefore, it is said that [the world] originates from this. But how, again, is it understood that the world originates from the word?
By means of perception and inference.
Perception is sacred scripture (śruti), because it possesses authority independently of anything else.
Inference is memory,
because it is dependent [upon other means] regarding its validity;
for those two [scriptures] show creation to be preceded by the Word (śabda).

"These," so indeed Prajāpati created the gods; "the essence," [he created] human beings; "the drops," the ancestors; "through the filter," the cups; "the swift ones," the hymn of praise; "all," the recitation; "for the sake of prosperity," other creatures—so says the Śruti. Likewise elsewhere: "He, through the mind, entered into union with speech" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4).

In these and other passages, it is heard here and there that creation is preceded by sound. Smṛti also states: "The eternal speech, without beginning or end, was emitted by the Self-existent One at the beginning, consisting of the Veda and divine, from which all activities proceed."
Thus,
this "emission" (utsarga) of speech should be understood as consisting in the transmission of the tradition,
since no other kind of emission is possible for that which is without beginning or end.
"Likewise, in the beginning, that Great Lord fashioned from the very words of the Veda the names and forms of beings and the operation of their actions."
"But he, at the beginning, fashioned the names and the distinct actions of all beings, as well as their various conditions, from the words of the Veda alone."
And so it is.
Furthermore, it is evident to all of us that when one intends to perform a certain action, one first recollects the word expressive of that action and only afterwards performs that action.
In the same way, even for Prajāpati the creator, the Vedic words appeared in his mind prior to the act of creation.
It is understood that he subsequently creates the objects that follow from those [names];
and thus the Śruti says: "He uttered 'Bhūḥ'; he created the earth" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.4.2).
In this way, such passages show that he created the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ from the very words "Bhūḥ" and so forth, which had appeared in his mind.
Furthermore, with reference to what kind of "word" (śabda) is this "origination from the word" stated? He says: "The sphoṭa.

For, according to the position that the phonemes (varṇa) are the word, because they perish as soon as they arise, it would be untenable to say that the manifestations of gods and so forth originate from eternal words.
Furthermore, phonemes are subject to arising and destruction, because they are perceived differently with each utterance.

For instance, even when a particular person is not visible, he is specifically identified simply by hearing the sound of his recitation, such that one discerns: "This is Devadatta who is studying; this is Yajñadatta who is studying."
Furthermore, this cognition of alteration regarding the phonemes is not a false cognition,
because there is no sublating cognition [to contradict it]. Moreover, it is not logical that the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes.
For indeed, each individual phoneme cannot convey the meaning,
because of the lack of invariable concomitance;
nor is there a cognition of a collection of phonemes.
If it were argued that because phonemes occur sequentially,
the final phoneme— accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme— will cause the meaning to be understood,
that is not so.

For a word, depending upon the apprehension of its relationship [to its meaning], would cause the object to be understood when it is itself perceived, just like smoke and other such signs. However, there is no perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each preceding phoneme, because those impressions are not themselves perceptible.
If it is argued that the final phoneme, accompanied by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the preceding phonemes, will cause the meaning to be understood, this is not so;
for even the recollection, which is the effect of those impressions, occurs sequentially.
Therefore, the *sphoṭa* alone is the word.

And that [cognition] manifests instantaneously as the object of a single cognition within the cognizer, whose seed of latent impression has been deposited by the cognitions of each preceding phoneme and whose maturation has been produced by the cognition of the final phoneme.
Nor is this single cognition a memory whose objects are the phonemes;
for since the phonemes are many, it is impossible for them to be the object of a single cognition.
Furthermore, because it is recognized as the same in every utterance, it is eternal;
for the cognition of difference pertains only to the phonemes (*varṇa*).
Therefore, from this eternal word in the form of *sphoṭa*, which is the signifier, the world—which consists of actions, factors of action, and results—arises as the signified.
But the venerable Upavarṣa maintains that it is the phonemes themselves that constitute the word, not something else.
Now, it was argued that phonemes are subject to arising and perishing; that is not so, because there is recognition of them as being "those very same [phonemes]."
If it is argued that recognition occurs due to similarity, as in the case of [re-growing] hair and so forth, we say no;
for it is impossible for recognition to be sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that recognition has the generic form (*ākṛti*) as its cause, we say no.
Because there is recognition of the individual [phoneme].
For if, at each utterance, distinct individual phonemes were perceived—just as distinct individuals such as cows are perceived—then that recognition would be based on their generic form (*ākṛti*).
But this is not the case.
For it is indeed the individual phonemes (*varṇavyakti*) themselves that are recognized in each utterance;
for the cognition is "the word *go* has been uttered twice," and not "two *go*-words [have been uttered].

But was it not said that even phonemes are perceived as distinct due to differences in utterance, since a distinction is perceived merely from hearing the sounds of the recitation of Devadatta and Yajñadatta?

To this it is replied: Since there exists a certain recognition regarding the phonemes (*varṇa*), and because phonemes are manifested by conjunctions and disjunctions [of the articulators], this diverse cognition concerning the phonemes is caused by the diversity of their manifestors, not by their own intrinsic nature. Furthermore, even by one who maintains that there is a difference between individual phoneme-manifestations, generic forms (*varṇākṛti*) must be postulated for the sake of establishing recognition.
And in those cases, one must admit that the cognition of difference is due to external adjuncts (*paropādhika*).

Therefore, it is simpler (the principle of parsimony) to assume that the cognition of difference resides precisely in the individual phonetic manifestations (*varṇavyakti*) as being caused by external adjuncts, while the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is based on their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
And this very recognition is the subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*) that overrides the cognition of difference regarding the phonemes.

For how could a single *saṅga*-sound, when uttered by many people at the same time, simultaneously possess multiple forms—namely, as acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), nasalized (*sānunāsika*), and non-nasalized (*niranunāsika*)?
Alternatively, this difference in cognition is caused by the sound (*dhvani*) and not by the phoneme (*varṇa*); thus there is no fault.
What, then, is this so-called *dhvani*? It is that which enters the path of the ear of one listening from a distance who does not perceive the distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*), and which,
as one draws closer, imposes distinctions such as clarity or indistinctness upon the phonemes.
The specific qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth are based on that [temporal duration], not on the intrinsic nature of the phonemes (*varṇa*),
because phonemes are recognized as being identical in every utterance.
This being the case, the cognitions of the acute accent and so forth will have a real objective basis (*sālambana*).

Otherwise, since the phonemes (*varṇa*) are recognized as being without distinction, the specific qualities such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth would have to be imagined as produced by conjunctions and disjunctions [of air].

Furthermore, because conjunctions and disjunctions are imperceptible, it would be impossible to determine that their dependent qualities reside in the phonemes; consequently, these cognitions of the acute accent and so forth would be entirely without a basis.
Moreover, one should not insist that the recognition of phonemes as identical implies that they must remain undifferentiated despite distinctions such as the acute accent.
For it is not possible for that which is undivided to possess division through the division of another;
indeed, people do not consider the universal (*jāti*) to be divided by the division of individuals (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, since the comprehension of meaning is possible from the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves, the postulation of *sphoṭa* is purposeless.

If it is argued: "I do not postulate a *sphoṭa*, for I perceive it directly; it appears instantaneously in the cognition that has been refined by the impressions deposited by the apprehension of each individual phoneme," [we reply]: No, because even this cognition has the phonemes as its object.
This single cognition "cow" (gaur), which occurs after the successive apprehension of each individual phoneme, has all the phonemes as its object and not some other entity.
How is this known?
Because even in this cognition, the phonemes *ga* and so forth persist, but the phonemes *da* and so forth do not.

For if the object of this cognition were the *sphoṭa*, which is a distinct entity from the letter *ga* and so forth, then the letters *ga* and so on would be excluded from this cognition just as the letters *da* and so on are;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, this single cognition is merely a memory whose object is the phonemes themselves.
Now, it was argued that because phonemes are manifold, it is not possible for them to be the object of a single cognition;
to this we reply: it is indeed possible for even a plurality to be the object of a single cognition, as is seen in cases such as "a row," "a forest," "an army," "ten," "a hundred," and "a thousand."

As for the cognition that "this word *gauḥ* (cow) is one," that is merely figurative, based on the delimitation of a single meaning among many phonemes, just like the cognitions of a "forest" or an "army. Here [the opponent] says: if the phonemes themselves, by occurring in their entirety as the object of a single cognition, were the word (*pada*), then there would be no apprehension of the distinction between words in cases such as *jārā*, *rājā*, *kapiḥ*, and *pikaḥ*.
"For those very same phonemes appear here and there [in different words].

To this we reply: even though there is a recollection of all the phonemes together, just as ants ascend to the cognition of a "row" only by following a specific order, so too will the phonemes ascend to the cognition of a "word" only by following a specific order.
In that regard, although there is no difference in the phonemes themselves, the comprehension of distinct words produced by a specific sequence is not contradictory.
Furthermore, in the linguistic usage of elders, these phonemes—being assisted by their sequence and having acquired a relationship with specific meanings—are likewise manifested in one's own usage;
following the apprehension of each individual phoneme, they appear in the intellect which reflects upon them as a whole, and thus [convey] that [meaning].

For those who maintain that the letters [themselves] convey that meaning without deviation, the assumption is simpler. For the proponents of *sphoṭa*, however, there is both the abandonment of what is observed and the assumption of what is unobserved.
The assumption would be more cumbersome: "These letters, being perceived in succession, manifest the *sphoṭa*; that *sphoṭa* then manifests the meaning."

Furthermore, even if it were the case that different phonemes (varṇa) arise with each utterance, nevertheless, because one must necessarily admit the existence of universals (sāmānya) of phonemes as the objective basis for recognition, the process by which meaning is communicated as established regarding individual phonemes must be transferred to those universals.
Consequently, there is no contradiction in the view that the manifestation of entities such as gods proceeds from eternal words.
FN: *Autpattika* means innate or inherent.

From a word denoting a genus such as "substantiality" (*vastutva*), one mentally delineates the individual instance of that genus which one intends to produce; its arising from that [word] is what constitutes "origination from it" (*tatprabhavatva*).
Of the forms and the classes [of words]:
"These swift drops have flowed across the filter toward all auspicious fortunes."
Having recollected by means of the words contained in this mantra, Brahmā created the gods and others.

Therein, the word *etad* (this), which denotes that which is proximate, serves to recall the gods who are present as the presiding deities (*anugrāhaka*) within the sense organs. The word *agra* (foremost) recalls humans, because blood (*asrk*) is their primary constituent and they delight in it.
The word *indu* is a reminder of the Pitṛs who abide in the moon;
the word *tiraḥpavitra* is a reminder of the Grahas who purify the Soma and spread it within themselves;
the word *āśu* is a reminder of the Stotras that pervade the *Ṛc*s; and the word *viśva* is a reminder of the Śastras that enter into performance immediately following the Stotras.

The meaning of the word "kim" (what) is as follows: *saṃpradāya* refers to the study transmitted through the succession of teacher and disciple; *saṃsthā* refers to its various states; and *varṇarūpa* refers to whether it has the form of phonemes or the form of a *sphoṭa* distinct from them.

It is called *sphoṭa* because it "bursts forth" (*sphuṭate*) by means of the phonemes (*varṇa*) and is manifested by them; that is, the word-sound such as "cow" (*gavādiśabda*), which is eternal and manifests the meaning that is itself manifested by the phonemes—referring to this, the aforementioned [statement] was made.

This connects with the preceding argument: because of deviation, since the comprehension of meaning is not seen from a single phoneme alone, and because the futility of other phonemes is not perceived.

Regarding the phrase "each one": just as the true nature of a jewel (*ratnatattva*) shines forth clearly through many visual cognitions (*cākṣuṣapratyaya*), so too does the *sphoṭa* of words such as "cow."

The meaning is as follows: in that consciousness wherein the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—produced by the individual cognitions of each letter beginning with *ga* and having the *sphoṭa* as their object—have been deposited, there arises a final impression (*antya-saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of the final letter; in that conscious mind, the final maturation (*paripāka*) results in the direct perception of the cognition "this is one word, *gauḥ*," which appears clearly as its object.
It is logical that the cognition "these very same hairs" immediately after shaving is an error,
because it contradicts the cognition of difference [between the previous and subsequent states].

The meaning is that the cognition of variety regarding the phonemes arises because they are manifested by the diverse conjunctions and disjunctions of the abdominal air with the locations such as the palate.
That which enters [the auditory organ] is "sound" (dhvani); this is the implied meaning.
The meaning is that sound is the word-element distinct from the phonemes (varṇa).
The distinction is that while the phonemes persist in every utterance, the sound (dhvani) varies.
The meaning is that "imperceptibility" refers to being inaudible;

just as the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is undifferentiated across various individual instances such as the spotted or hornless cow which are mutually distinct, so too are the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves undifferentiated across various sounds (*dhvani*).
The construction is: by means of the cause of the distinction between those [sounds], such as the acute accent (*udātta*) and others, there is [distinction] for the phonemes as well.
The determination of an object is the ascertainment of its meaning;
reflective awareness is memory;
and the stage of linguistic proficiency is the usage of elders.
By the word "successively" (*kramāt*) and so forth, "number" (*saṃkhyā*) is understood.

One's own conventional usage (*svasvavyavahāra*) is the state of activity of the middle-aged person who has learned the language. "Being of such a nature" (*tādṛśatva*) means being assisted by the sequence and other factors observed at the stage of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*).
The capacity of phonemes (varṇas) to convey meaning is observed,
whereas the sphoṭa is unobserved;
for this very reason, it possesses eternality.

Since the eternity of the Veda has been established through such arguments as the non-recollection of an independent author, one might suspect a contradiction with that eternity by admitting the production of individual beings such as gods. Having resolved this doubt with the sūtra "Because [the world] originates from that," he now further strengthens that very established eternity of the Veda with the words: "And for this very reason, there is eternity."
For this very reason, since the world—including gods and others of fixed form—originates from the words of the Veda, the eternity of the Vedic word must also be recognized.
And thus says a mantra: "By means of sacrifice, they found the path of speech; they discovered her who had entered among the seers" (Ṛgveda 10.71.3).
This shows that speech was already established when it was discovered.

And Vedavyāsa likewise records this: "At the end of the age, the great seers, authorized by the Self-born One, recovered through austerity the Vedas along with the Itihāsas that had been lost. (29) [Note:
By means of sacrifice, or by their previously performed deeds, they attained the path of speech—that is, the fitness for receiving and the capacity for grasping the Veda.

Then, the ritualists (yājñikas)—meaning those who had not previously found it—discovered (anvavindan), that is, they obtained, that speech which existed having entered into the sages; "anuvinām" means that which was discovered.
This occurred formerly at the beginning of the intermediate kalpa.

"And because name and form are the same, there is no contradiction even in the case of recurrence, as seen from scripture and tradition. (BBs 1.3.30) Now, it might be argued: if the individual manifestations of gods and so forth were to arise and cease in a continuous stream—just like the individual manifestations of cattle and other animals—then, because the linguistic usage of signifier, signified, and signifier would remain uninterrupted, the relationship [between word and meaning] would be eternal.
The contradiction regarding the word might be resolved [in other cases];

but when the declarations of the Śruti and Smṛti state that the entire triple world, having abandoned name and form, dissolves without residue and emerges anew, how then can there be no contradiction?
In this regard, it is stated: "Because names and forms are the same. Therefore, even then, the beginninglessness of saṃsāra must first be accepted.
And the Teacher will establish the beginninglessness of saṃsāra in the passage: "It is both logical and observed" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.36).

Furthermore, in a beginningless saṃsāra, just as there is no contradiction regarding worldly activity in a subsequent awakening—despite the scriptural accounts of dissolution and origination—just as in a previous awakening, so too here.

In this same way, it should be understood that [the process applies] to the emergence and dissolution of other kalpas. Furthermore, the dissolution and emergence are heard of in relation to sleep and waking: "When one is asleep and sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this prāṇa alone; then speech, along with all names, merges into him; the eye, along with all forms, merges into him..."

"The ear merges with all sounds; the mind merges with all meditations. When he awakens, just as sparks fly out in all directions from a blazing fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths (*prāṇa*) emerge according to their respective natures; from the vital breaths, the gods; and from the gods, the worlds" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.3).
It might be argued as follows:

[The case of] deep sleep is not contradictory because the linguistic activity of other persons continues uninterrupted, and because for one who has himself awakened from sleep, it is possible to reconnect with the linguistic activity of the previous waking state.

However, in the case of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), there is a disparity because all linguistic activity is annihilated; thus, just as it is impossible to reconnect with the linguistic activity of another birth, it is impossible to reconnect with the linguistic activity of another cosmic age (*kalpa*).
This is not a fault;

for even though the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) brings about the cessation of all worldly transactions, it is possible for lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others to reconnect with the transactions of a previous kalpa through the grace of the Supreme Lord.
Although ordinary living beings are not seen to reconnect with the transactions of a previous birth, [the case of the lords is different].
Nevertheless, the Lords (Īśvaras) must not be regarded as being like ordinary beings.

For instance, although there is no difference in their status as living beings, it is observed that among those ranging from humans down to plants, the obstruction of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, becomes increasingly greater at each successive lower level;

likewise, among those ranging from humans up to Hiraṇyagarbha, the manifestation of knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, also becomes increasingly greater at each successive higher level—a fact repeatedly heard in the declarations of the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
It cannot be said [that there is no such continuity]; therefore,

it is possible for lords such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others— who have performed preeminent deeds of knowledge in past kalpas, who appear at the beginning of the present kalpa, and who are favored by the Supreme Lord— to reconnect with the conventional practices of other kalpas, just like one waking from sleep.

And so says the Śruti: "I, seeking liberation, take refuge in that God who illumines the self through the intellect, who ordained Brahman in the beginning and who indeed bestowed the Vedas upon him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18).
And Śaunaka and others record: "The [Vedas] were seen as they were revealed by the seers, beginning with Madhucchandas."
In the same way, for each Veda, the *kāṇḍarṣis* and others are recorded in the traditional texts (*smṛti*).

Furthermore, Śruti itself shows that the performance of a rite must be preceded by knowledge of the seer (*ṛṣi*): "He who, indeed, sacrifices or teaches with a mantra whose seer (*ārṣeya*), metre (*chandas*), deity (*daivata*), and explanatory formula (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown, either strikes against a pillar or falls into a pit" (*Sarvānukramaṇī-pariśiṣṭa*).
Having begun thus, [the text] concludes: "Therefore, one should recognize these [qualities] in every mantra.
Furthermore, dharma is prescribed for the attainment of happiness by living beings, and adharma is prohibited for the avoidance of suffering.

Furthermore, since attachment and aversion arise toward objects of seen and traditionally heard pleasure and pain, and not toward objects of a different nature, the subsequent creation, being produced as the fruit of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), is produced as something similar to the previous creation.
And there is a traditional scripture (*smṛti*): "Whatever actions those [beings] performed in the previous creation..."
Being created again and again, they enter into those very same [conditions].

Violent and non-violent, mild and cruel, righteous and unrighteous, truthful and false—conditioned by these, beings enter into them; therefore, each finds pleasure in that which corresponds to its own nature.
Thus,
even as this world dissolves, it dissolves entirely along with its powers;
and it arises only from the root of power.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of their being causeless;
nor is it possible to postulate multiple forms of causal powers.
Consequently, regarding the streams of worlds such as the earth, which arise intermittently, [there must be a single, uniform cause].

Furthermore, in this beginningless saṃsāra, the fixed nature of the streams of living beings characterized as gods, animals, and humans, as well as the established order of the fruits of the duties of the castes and stages of life, must be understood to be as constant as the fixed relationship between the sense organs and their objects.

Indeed, it is impossible to imagine that the worldly conventions, such as the relationship between the senses and their objects, would undergo any alteration at each dissolution (pratisarga), as if there were a sixth sense-organ and its corresponding object.

And for this reason—since all world-ages (*kalpa*) possess identical linguistic conventions and since the Lords (*īśvara*) are capable of reconnecting with the linguistic conventions of the end of a previous age—the particularities (*viśeṣa*) manifest at each new creation (*pratisarga*) have exactly the same names and forms.

And because they have identical names and forms, even when the recurrence of the world characterized by great creation and great dissolution is admitted, there is no contradiction whatsoever with the authority of the Word (*śabda-prāmāṇya*) and other means of knowledge.
Scripture and tradition both demonstrate this identity of names and forms: "The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon just as before."
"Both heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and then the sky" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.190.3).
The meaning is that just as the world, beginning with the sun and moon, was fashioned in the previous *kalpa*, so too did the Supreme Lord fashion it in this *kalpa*.
Likewise: "Agni indeed desired, 'May I be the eater of food among the gods.'"
"He offered this cake on eight potsherds to Agni and the Kṛttikās" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.1.4.1).

In this injunction for a sacrifice to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatreṣṭi*), such scriptural passages should be cited here, which demonstrate the identity of name and form between the Agni who performed the offering and the Agni to whom the offering was made.
There is also a Smṛti passage: "The names of the sages and the visions found in the Vedas..."
At the end of the night, the Unborn One gives those very same things back to those who have been born.
Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle,
so too do those very same things reappear at the beginnings of the ages.
Just as those who possessed conceit in the past were equal to those here at present,
so too are the gods equal to the gods of the past, both in their forms and indeed in their names.
Expressions of this kind are to be understood in this way.
[Note: By the term "designator" (abhidhātṛ), both the teacher and the student are meant;
even so, this applies even when the great dissolution and the great creation are accepted. // 30 //
The word "atha" (then) has the sense of "tadā" (at that time), following the commencement [of the process].
Prāṇa is the Supreme Self; therein the individual soul (jīva) becomes one. The ellipsis is: "he [the individual soul] goes to this prāṇa. Therefore, from that prāṇa-self...
The term "āyatana" means a sphere (golaka).
The word "iti" is connected with the phrase "yadyapi" (even though).
There are scriptural declarations such as, "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being," and so forth.

The Smṛti declarations beginning with "He whose knowledge is incomparable" and so forth [are the source]. It discards [ignorance] and causes [the truth] to go [to the disciple]; it brings about the manifestation of realization in his intellect.
The Ṛgveda consists of ten maṇḍalas; because there are exactly ten maṇḍalas, the ṛks found therein are called *dāśatayyaḥ*.
The *ārṣeya* is the lineage of the seers (*ṛṣi-yoga*);
the *chandas* is the meter, such as *gāyatrī* and others;
the *daivata* is the deity, such as Agni and others.
The application [of this rule] is to the Brāhmaṇa: in whichever mantra these [elements] are unknown,
one falls into a "sthāṇu," meaning an immovable object, or a "garta," meaning hell.
Among those living beings,
they are of that very same kind;
the sixth faculty is the mind (manas), according to the traditional teaching that "the faculties have the mind as the sixth."
The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of stars. He offered the oblation to be cooked on eight potsherds to Agni, the deity of the Kṛttikās.
In the word "deveṣu" (among the gods), the locative case is used in the sense of a sphere or domain.
"At the end of the night" means at the end of the dissolution;
"the signs of the season" refers to fresh sprouts and so forth;
"in the cycle" means in the recurrence, like a waterwheel.
"Bhāvas" refers to entities.
"Jaimini [holds that there is] no eligibility because of the impossibility [of it] in the case of honey and so forth.
(BS 1.3.31) This overturns the previously asserted position that even gods and others possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman.
The teacher Jaimini maintains that gods and others lack the qualification [for Vedic study].
Why?
Because of the impossibility [of such qualification] in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and other [meditations].

For if one were to admit the eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), then, because there is no distinction in its being "knowledge," one would have to admit eligibility for the *madhu* and other such meditations as well;
yet this is not possible. How so?
In the passage, "That sun, indeed, is the honey of the gods" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1.1), human beings should approach the sun by meditating upon it as honey.
For if gods and others were admitted to be the meditators, what other sun would the sun itself meditate upon?

Furthermore, having introduced the five nectars beginning with the red [light], which depend upon the sun, and having taught that the five groups of deities— the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Maruts, and Sādhyas— subsist respectively upon those respective nectars, [the text continues] with the passage: "He who thus knows this nectar becomes one of the Vasus themselves and, with Agni as his mouth, being satisfied by beholding this very nectar," and so forth, [referring to] the nectars subsisted upon by the Vasus and others.
This shows that for those who possess knowledge, there is the attainment of the greatness of the Vasus and others.
But who else could the Vasus and others know as other Vasus and others living upon the nectar?
Or what other greatness of the Vasus and others would they desire to attain?
"Likewise, fire is one foot, wind is one foot, the sun is one foot, and the quarters are one foot" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.18.2);
"Wind, indeed, is the absorber" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.3.1);
"The sun is Brahman—this is the instruction" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.11.1).

In meditations on the self of the deities, such as these, it is not possible for those very deities themselves to have the qualification [for practice]. Likewise, in meditations associated with sages, such as "These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja; I am Gotama, this one is Bharadvāja" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4), it is not possible for those very sages themselves to have the qualification. // 31 //
And for what reason do the gods and others have no qualification?—[as it is said:

"The five" refers to the rites prescribed in the four Vedas and the *praṇava*, making five; from these, substances such as *soma* and clarified butter are offered. The [blood] beginning with *lohita* refers to the red, the white, and so forth.
Black,
supremely black,
as if agitated in its center.

The meaning is as follows: these five nectars, beginning with *rohit*, have been described. By means of the solar-ray channels (*nāḍīs*) situated in the five directions from east to upward—each corresponding to a specific portion of the mantras, appearing as apertures present within the honey-bees—and brought from the solar orb, they are transformed into the nature of fame, splendor, sensory power, vigor, and food. One attains the status of the Vasus and others by meditating that these [nectars] are the sustenance for the Vasus and other deities residing in the five directions. This is what has been stated.

And because of [the application of] designations to luminaries (jyotis). BBs 1.3.32: That is to say, regarding this orb of light situated in the sky which revolves through day and night and illuminates the world, words denoting deities such as "Āditya" and so forth are employed for it, both due to worldly convention and due to its establishment in the context of scriptural passages (*vākyaśeṣa*).

Furthermore, it is not possible to understand that the sphere of light possesses a body consisting of a heart and so forth, nor that it possesses consciousness, desire, and the like; for it is understood to be insentient, just like a corpse or similar objects.
By this, fire and the other elements are also explained.
This might be argued:

[The opponent argues: "This fault does not arise, because we understand that deities and others possess physical forms (vigraha) from the perspective of mantra-exegesis, arthavādas, itihāsas, purāṇas, and common worldly usage.
[The author replies: No;
for there is no such thing as "worldly usage" that exists as an independent means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For it is said that an object established from means of valid cognition such as perception—provided their specific qualifications have not been investigated—is established according to worldly convention.
Yet, in this case, none of the means of valid cognition, such as perception and the rest, exists;
even Itihāsa and Purāṇa, being of human origin, require another basis for their authority.

Even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), being part of a single syntactical unit with the injunctions and serving the purpose of praise, do not independently function as a cause for establishing the existence of bodies and other attributes in gods and so forth.

Furthermore, the mantras, which are employed according to direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and the like and are integrated into the ritual performance for the purpose of denotation, are said not to be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for any factual matter.
Therefore, there is no eligibility (*adhikāra*) for gods and others [to perform Vedic rites]. 32.

Mantras such as "Vajrahastaḥ purandaraḥ" (Indra with the thunderbolt in hand); explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as "He wept" (*so 'rodīt*); historical and mythological narratives (*itihāsa-purāṇa*) such as "O gods, [give] the enjoyments you desire" (*iṣṭān bhogān hi vo devā*); and even in the world, [the depiction of] Yama with a staff in his hand.

The meaning is that because the five factors—beginning with *vigraha* (embodiment)—exist in the phrase "they depict Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt," there is no fault of lack of qualification (*anadhikāra-doṣa*). [These five are:
embodiment, the enjoyment of oblations, sovereignty, and graciousness.
"The fivefold [process] beginning with the assumption of a body consists of this: the bestowing of the fruit.
But Bādarāyaṇa holds that there is indeed [a body]; for [the sūtra states]: "But Bādarāyaṇa [says] there is, for it exists" (BS 3.1.33). The word "but" (tu) sets aside the prima facie view.
The teacher Bādarāyaṇa, however, maintains that gods and others also possess the capacity for qualification.

Even though there may be an impossibility of qualification in the case of the Madhu-vidyā and other such meditations that involve a mixture of deities and so forth, nevertheless, there is indeed the possibility of it in the pure knowledge of Brahman;
for qualification depends upon factors such as desire, capability, and the absence of prohibitions.
Nor should the eligibility for those cases where it is possible be set aside merely because it is impossible in some instances.
For even among humans, it is not the case that all Brahmins and others are eligible for all sacrifices such as the Rājasūya;
the same principle that applies there shall apply here as well.

And with reference to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there is a scriptural vision (*darśana*) indicating the eligibility of the gods and others: "Of the gods, whoever awakened to That, he indeed became That; likewise of the seers (*ṛṣis*), and likewise of men" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
Also: "They said, 'Come, let us search for that Self, by searching for which one obtains all worlds and all desires'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3).
And there are such passages as, "Indra, indeed, went forth from among the gods, and Virocana from among the Asuras" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.2),
as well as the dialogue between the Gandharva and Yājñavalkya recorded in the Smṛti.
As for what was also stated, "because of its existence in light," [that too has been addressed].

To this we reply: even those words denoting deities such as Āditya, which refer to objects like light and so forth, designate specific divine selves endowed with consciousness and possessed of sovereignty and other attributes, because they are treated as such in the mantras, arthavādas, and other texts.
For, by virtue of their sovereign power, the deities possess the capacity to abide in the form of light and other such elements and to assume various bodies at will.
For it is heard in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the *subrahmaṇyā* formula: "The ram of Medhātithi.
[It says: "Indra, having become a ram, carried off Medhātithi, the descendant of Kaṇva" (*Ṣaḍviṃśa-brāhmaṇa* 1.1).
And it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The Sun, having become a man, approached Kuntī."
Even in the case of clay and other such materials, conscious presiding agents are admitted, as seen in such passages as "The clay spoke" and "The waters spoke.
However, regarding the elemental constituents such as light, their lack of consciousness in the sun and so forth is admitted;
yet it has been stated that conscious presiding agents exist in the form of deities, based on the usage found in mantras, explanatory passages (arthavādas), and the like.
As for what was also stated— that because mantras and arthavādas have other purposes, they lack the capacity to reveal the embodied form of the deities and so forth—
we reply: it is indeed belief and non-belief that are the causes for the existence or non-existence [of a thing],
not whether [the statement] has another purpose or no other purpose.
For instance, even one who has set out for another purpose perceives that grass, leaves, and so forth, which have fallen on the path, exist simply because they are there.
To this, he replies: "The analogy is flawed;
for in that case, there is indeed a perceptual cognition directed toward the object—the grass, leaves, and so forth—by means of which their existence is apprehended."

Furthermore, in this case, because it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction (*vidhi*), the application of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the purpose of praise can be determined as having a distinct subject matter regarding a past event.

For in the sentence "One should not drink liquor" (*na surāṃ pibet*), which contains the negative particle *nañ*, only the prohibition of drinking liquor is understood as the sole meaning due to the connection of all three words; one does not likewise understand an injunction to drink liquor from the connection of the two words "one should drink liquor" (*surāṃ pibet*).
To this it is replied: the analogy is unequal.

It is appropriate that in the prohibition of drinking liquor (*surāpāna-pratiṣedha*), because there is a single syntactical connection (*padānvaya*), no intermediate sentence-meaning (*avāntaravākyārtha*) is apprehended.

However, in the case of an injunction (*vidhi*) and its explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the words situated within the *arthavāda* first undergo a process of separate syntactical connection regarding their own respective subjects; subsequently, by virtue of the requirement for purpose (*kaimarthyavaśena*), they may indeed function as eulogies (*stāvaka*) of the injunction.

For instance, in the injunction "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," the words such as "to Vāyu" occurring within the injunctive statement are connected with the injunction itself;

however, this is not the case for words occurring in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest deity; he approaches Vāyu with his own share; he [Vāyu] leads him to prosperity.
For it does not follow that "Vāyu should sacrifice" or "the swiftest deity should sacrifice," and so forth.
By proclaiming the nature of Vāyu, however, they establish an intermediate connection and thus praise the injunction, [stating] that "this ritual has such-and-such a deity.

In cases where that intermediate sentence-meaning falls within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) proceeds as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of it.
Where it is contradicted by another means of valid cognition, it proceeds by way of figurative speech (*guṇavāda*).

But where neither of those two [conditions] exists, should one resort to a figurative description (guṇavāda) due to the absence of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), or should one resort to a statement of what actually exists (vidyamānavāda) because it does not contradict other means of valid cognition? Those who rely on direct perception must adopt the latter, not the figurative description. By this, the case of mantras is also explained.
Moreover, the very injunctions that enjoin the oblations for deities such as Indra presuppose the essential nature (svarūpa) of Indra and the others;
for it is impossible to conceive of Indra and the rest in the mind if they are devoid of an essential nature,
and it is impossible to offer an oblation to a particular deity unless that deity has been mentally conceived.
And it is declared: "One should meditate upon that deity for whom the oblation has been taken up, when about to utter the vaṣaṭ-call" (Ai.
Brā. 3.8.1). Furthermore, it is not possible for the mere word to be the very nature of the object, because of the difference between the word and its meaning.
In this regard, it is not proper to reject the nature of Indra and other deities as it is understood from the mantras and arthavādas by means of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—being possible on the basis of the path already explained and being rooted in mantras and arthavādas—are capable of establishing the embodied form of the deities and so forth;
they may also be rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge.
For even that which is not perceptible to us was perceptible to those of ancient times;
likewise, it is recorded in tradition that Vyāsa and others interacted directly with gods and other beings.
He who would say that former beings lacked the capacity to interact with gods and others—just as people today do—would be denying the manifold diversity of the world.
One might as well say that there is no other universal sovereign kṣatriya now as there was then,
and thereby obstruct the injunctions for the Rājasūya and other sacrifices;
or one might assert that the duties of the castes and stages of life were as unsettled in other times as they are now.
Consequently, the scripture that establishes the rules [for perception] would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, it follows that by virtue of the excellence of their merit (*dharma*), the ancients perceived the gods and other beings directly.
Furthermore, they record in their tradition: "From the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), there arises union with the desired deity" (Yogasūtra 2.44), and so forth.
Furthermore, yoga—which is recorded in tradition as having the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* as its fruit—cannot be rejected on the basis of mere audacity alone.

Moreover, scripture proclaims the greatness of yoga: "When the fivefold quality of yoga, consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether, has arisen and is set in motion, for him who has attained the body made of the fire of yoga, there is no disease, no old age, and no death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.12).
The capacity of even the sages who perceived the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is not fit to be compared with our own capacity;
therefore, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are rooted in reality.
Furthermore, worldly renown, when possible, should not be determined as being without a basis.
Therefore, the understanding that gods and others possess embodied forms (vigrahavattva) is established on the basis of the mantras and other such sources.

Consequently, since the presence of desire for liberation (arthitva) and other necessary qualifications is possible, the eligibility (adhikāra) of gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is likewise established.
Furthermore, the scriptural accounts regarding gradual liberation (kramamukti) are also consistent with this very view.
FN: Since it is not possible for everyone to have authority in all respects, the logical connection is that [the qualification] is therefore not to be set aside.
That Brahman which one realizes as the inner self (*pratyak*) among the gods;
by the inclusion of the word "etc.," the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras are understood.
The injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) is the sentence that prescribes an action; by virtue of being a single syntactical unit with it,
the narrative (*vṛttānta*), which has the nature of an accomplished fact (*bhūtārtha*),
is "joined" (*śliṣyate*), that is, rendered coherent.
The meaning of the sūtra is that through the recitation of mantras, there is the presence of the deity and conversation with them.
This concludes the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (apaśūdrādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 34–38:
"Because his grief [is mentioned], because of hearing that [grief] and because of his running toward him, it is indeed indicated. (BBs 1.3.34)

Just as the restriction that the qualification for knowledge belongs only to humans was set aside and the qualification of gods and others for the sciences was stated, so too, one might raise the doubt that the qualification of a Śūdra could likewise exist by setting aside the restriction that it belongs only to the twice-born; it is to dispel this doubt that this section (adhikaraṇa) is commenced.
In this regard, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there should indeed be qualification for a Śūdra as well.
Because both the desire [to know] and the capacity [to understand] are possible;
and because, unlike the prohibition "therefore a Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 8.1.1.6), no such prohibition as "a Śūdra is not entitled to knowledge" is heard.

Furthermore, the fact that the Śūdra lacks the sacred fires (*anagnitva*), which is the reason for his lack of entitlement to ritual acts (*karma*), is not an indicative mark (*liṅga*) that precludes his entitlement to knowledge (*vidyā*).
For it is not impossible for one devoid of the *āhavanīya* and other such fires to know the Vidyā.
Moreover, there exists an indicative mark that supports the Śūdra’s entitlement.

For in the Saṃvarga-vidyā, the text refers to Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa, who was desirous of hearing, by means of the word "Śūdra": "O Śūdra, let this horse, together with the cows, remain yours indeed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.2.3).
Furthermore, Vidura and others, though born from a Śūdra womb, are recorded in tradition as being endowed with distinguished knowledge.
Therefore, a Śūdra is qualified for the [study of] vidyās.
This being the case, we reply: there is no entitlement for a Śūdra, because of the absence of Vedic study.
For only one who has studied the Veda and understood its meaning is entitled to engage with the contents of the Veda.
Furthermore, there is no Vedic study for a Śūdra,
because Vedic study is preceded by initiation (upanayana),
and initiation pertains only to the three [upper] castes.
However, mere desire for the goal does not constitute a cause for entitlement in the absence of capacity;
nor does worldly capacity alone constitute a cause for entitlement,
because in the case of a scriptural matter, scriptural capacity is required.
Furthermore, since scriptural competence has already been refuted by the rejection of the study [of the Vedas],
the statement "a Śūdra is not entitled to sacrifice" indicates that he is likewise not entitled to knowledge, because that principle applies equally to both.
This is due to the commonality of the underlying logic.

Furthermore, as for the fact that you consider the hearing of the word "śūdra" in the Saṃvarga-vidyā to be an indicative mark (liṅga), that is not an indicative mark because it lacks logical justification;
for the observation of an indicative mark becomes illuminative only when it is supported by reasoning.
Nor is there any logical principle for this;
at most, this word "Śūdra" might authorize only a Śūdra in the Saṃvarga-vidyā alone,
because that [passage] is its specific subject matter.
This does not apply to all branches of knowledge;
for, since it occurs within an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is not capable of authorizing a *śūdra* in any instance whatsoever.
Moreover, this word "śūdra" can be applied to refer to those who are authorized [to study].
How so? It is said: "O, how can you speak thus of him who is such [a person], like Raikva with the cart? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 4.1.3).
From these words of the swan, grief arose in Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa upon hearing his own lack of respect;
it is understood that the seer Raikva indicated that grief by means of this word "śūdra" in order to manifest his own knowledge of the hidden truth.
Because a Śūdra by birth lacks the qualification [for Vedic study].
