The incidental discussion regarding the scope of the subject matter is concluded. We shall now proceed with the investigation of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) that is relevant to the present topic.
"Whatever there is in this entire world, it quivers, having issued forth from the vital breath (*prāṇa*);
a great terror, a raised thunderbolt—those who know this become immortal" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.2).
This statement is characterized by its conformity with the meaning of the verbal root *ejṛ*, "to tremble."

In this passage, it is heard that this entire world vibrates resting upon the Prāṇa, that some great cause of fear designated by the word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is raised, and that through the knowledge of that [Prāṇa], the attainment of immortality occurs.

In this regard, when an inquiry is undertaken because of the lack of understanding as to what that *prāṇa* is and what that terrifying *vajra* is, it is first reached—on account of common usage—that the *prāṇa* is the wind with its fivefold functions (*pañcavṛtti-vāyu*).
And on account of common usage alone, the *vajra* would be the thunderbolt (*aśani*).
For it is the greatness of the wind that is being celebrated here.
How so?
This entire world moves for the sake of being established upon the fivefold wind designated as *prāṇa*;
and it is solely due to the wind that the great, terrifying thunderbolt is raised up.
For they declare that when the wind transforms itself into the state of Parjanya (the rain-god), lightning, thunder, rain, and thunderbolts transform accordingly.
And this immortality results precisely from the knowledge of the wind.
Thus, another scriptural passage states: "The wind is indeed the individual manifestation, the wind is the collective totality; he who knows this conquers recurrent death."
"Therefore, this wind is what must be understood here.
This being the position reached, we reply: Brahman alone is what must be understood here.
Why?
Because of the consideration of what precedes and follows;
for in the preceding and following portions of the text, we perceive that Brahman alone is being pointed out.
How then could we understand Vāyu as being pointed out here in the middle, quite unexpectedly?

In the preceding passage, Brahman was indeed indicated: "That alone is the bright, that is Brahman, that alone is called the immortal; in it all worlds are supported, and no one transcends it" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 2.6.1).

Therefore, it is understood that here too, by virtue of proximity and because of the recognition of its being the support of the worlds— as seen in the statement "the entire world trembles in the Prāṇa"—
it is indicated [as the Self]. Furthermore, this word "Prāṇa" is employed [in this sense], as in "the breath of the breath" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18).
From this observation, it follows that this quality of being the impeller also belongs only to the Supreme Self and not to air alone.
And so it has been said: "No mortal lives by means of the out-breath (prāṇa) or the in-breath (apāna)."
"But by the other they live, upon which these two depend" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.5.5).
And later also: "Out of fear of Him the fire burns, out of fear the sun shines;
out of fear Indra and Vāyu, and Death as the fifth, run on" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.6.3).
Thus, it is Brahman alone that is being pointed out here, not Vāyu;
for it has been stated that [Brahman] is the cause of fear for the entire world, including Vāyu.
Therefore, by virtue of proximity, it is that very same [Brahman] which is the "great fear" here as well.
And it is understood that the phrase "the raised thunderbolt" is indicated because it is recognized as a cause of fear;
this word "thunderbolt" (vajra) is also employed here due to its commonality as a cause of fear,
just as one thinks, "May the raised thunderbolt fall upon my very head if I do not carry out his command."

Just as people engage in their duties out of fear and kings and others out of obedience to commands, so too this world—consisting of fire, wind, the sun, and so forth—proceeds in its respective functions out of fear of this very Brahman. Thus, Brahman is terrifying and is compared to a thunderbolt.
And likewise, there is another scriptural passage concerning Brahman: "Out of fear of Him the wind blows..."
"Out of fear of Him the sun rises; out of fear of Him both fire and Indra,
and Death as the fifth, run away" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.8.1).
Furthermore, because the fruit of immortality is heard [in the scriptures], it is understood that this [Self] is indeed Brahman;
for the attainment of immortality results from the knowledge of Brahman, as stated:
"Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15).
This is from the wording of the mantra.
As for the immortality mentioned in some places as resulting from the knowledge of Vāyu, that is relative;
for in that very context, after introducing the Supreme Self by means of a different section, it says: "The end [of everything else] is other than the Immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.4).
Thus, because air and the other elements are stated to be subject to suffering,
the determination that the Supreme Self is the subject here follows from the context as well:
"That which is other than dharma, other than adharma, other than what is done or not done by us..."
Because the Supreme Self is what is being asked about in the passage: "Tell me that which you see as other than the past and the future" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.14).
[FN: *Bhīṣā* means through fear.]
"From this Brahman" means for the purpose of [attaining] this Brahman.
The mention of "five" is intended as an illustration for all moving and non-moving beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

For, by the scriptural statement "he conquers death no more," the conquest of *apamṛtyu* (premature or accidental death) is declared, but not the conquest of *paramamṛtyu* (the ultimate death); thus, [the former] is relative.
11. The Section on Light (Jyotir-adhikaraṇa). Sūtra 40: "Light, because it is seen.
Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form."
Thus it is heard in scripture.
Regarding this, a doubt arises:
does the word "light" refer to that physical light which is the object of the eye and dispels darkness, or rather to the supreme Brahman?
What, then, is the prima facie position? That the word *jyotis* (light) refers to fire (*tejas*) is well-established.
Why?
In that context, because the word "light" (*jyotis*) is used in its conventional sense, [it is said]:
"Because of the mention of the feet of light" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.24).
For in that passage, by virtue of the context, the word "light" sets aside its own primary meaning and refers to Brahman.
And here, no such reason for abandoning its own primary meaning is observed.

Thus, in the section on the channels, it is stated: "Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5), whereby the attainment of the sun is declared for the seeker of liberation.
Therefore, it is well established that the word "light" (jyotis) refers to physical fire.
This being the position reached, we reply: the word "light" refers to the Supreme Brahman itself.
Why?
Because it is seen [in the text];
for its continuation as the subject to be explained is observed here in this context in the passage: "That Self which is free from evil" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).

This is because, at the beginning of the section, the Self—characterized by qualities such as being free from evil—is declared to be that which is to be sought after and that which is to be desired to be known;
and because of the subsequent connection [made] with the statement: "But this very one I shall explain further to you" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.9.3).

Furthermore, because this attainment of light is stated for the sake of bodilessness in the passage, "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who dwells in the bodiless" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1),
and since bodilessness is impossible except through the state of Brahman, [the text speaks of] "the highest light" and "that supreme Person" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).
And because of this qualification;
as for what was said— that the attainment of the sun is declared for one desiring liberation—
that is not ultimate liberation, because it is connected with going and departing.

For we shall explain that in absolute liberation there is neither going nor departure [from the body]. (40) [Note: Regarding the section on the channels beginning with "Now, these channels of the heart," the connection is that the attainment of that [world of the sun] by one desiring liberation was described in accordance with the solar eclipse.
12. The Section on the Designation of Being a Different Entity. Sūtra 41:
"Ether [is Brahman], because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth.
(BBs 1.3.41) "That which is called ether is indeed the bringer-forth of name and form; that within which they are is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14.1).
Thus it is heard.
In the inquiry as to whether the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the Supreme Brahman or to the well-known elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), the acceptance of the elemental ether is appropriate,
because the word "ether" is conventionally established (rūḍha) in that sense.

Furthermore, because it is possible to connect [the passage] with that [Brahman] by way of providing space for the manifestation of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and because no clear mark of Brahman—such as being the creator—is heard here;
such being the position reached, this is said in reply: the Supreme Brahman alone must be what is denoted here by the word "ether" (ākāśa).
Why?

Because it is designated as being a different entity and so forth. For, in the passage "That which is between those two is Brahman," the text designates the ether (ākāśa) as an entity distinct from name and form.
Furthermore, no entity other than Brahman can exist apart from name and form, because the entire aggregate of modifications is differentiated solely by means of name and form.
Moreover, the unrestricted manifestation of name and form is not possible anywhere other than in Brahman, as stated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.3.2):
"Entering with this living self, let me manifest name and form."
This is because of scriptural declarations such as these regarding Brahman’s agency in creation.
Now, one might object: "But even the individual soul (jīva) possesses, through direct perception, the capacity to bring about names and forms.
Certainly, it does.
But here, non-difference is intended to be expressed.
Furthermore, by the very mention of the carrying out of names and forms, the characteristic marks of Brahman, such as its being the creator and so forth, are thereby stated.
"That is Brahman, that is the Immortal, that is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.14).
And these are the marks of the discourse on Brahman;
this is an elaboration of the very sūtra, "The ether [is Brahman], because of its marks" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.22). // 41 //
FN: The meaning is that it is illogical for names and forms—which fall within [the scope of] sound and its referents—to be distinct from them or to be their agents.
13. The Section on Deep Sleep and Departure. Sūtra 42–43:
"Because of the difference [of the Self] in deep sleep and departure. (BBs 1.3.42)
The phrase "on account of designation" (*vyapadeśāt*) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra].

In the sixth chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, beginning with "Which is the Self? He who consists of cognition among the vital breaths, the person who is the light within the heart" (*BṛU* 4.3.7), an extensive elaboration concerning the Self is presented.
Thus, the doubt arises: does this sentence merely aim at describing the nature of the transmigrating soul (saṃsārin), or does it aim at establishing the nature of the non-transmigrating [Self]?
What, then, is the initial position?
That it concerns only the nature of the transmigrating soul.
Why?
Because of the introduction and the conclusion;
for in the introduction, the phrase "this which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" contains a characteristic mark of the embodied self.
And because at the conclusion [of the section] it says, "This indeed is that great unborn Self, which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22),
that [Self] is not abandoned; and because even in the middle [of the section], by the presentation of states such as waking and dreaming, it is that very same [Self] which is being elaborated upon.
This being the case, we reply: this passage has as its primary purport the instruction regarding the Supreme Lord, and does not merely aim at describing the embodied soul (śārīra).
Why?
Because during deep sleep and at the time of departure, the Supreme Lord is designated as distinct from the body.
First, regarding deep sleep, the text states: "This person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing external nor internal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21).
Here, it designates the Supreme Lord as distinct from the embodied self;
for in this context, the "person" must be the embodied self, since it is that which possesses the capacity for cognition.
Because it is possible to negate that [duality] when there is the occurrence of external and internal sensations,
he is the wise Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*),
owing to his eternal non-separation from wisdom (*prajñā*) characterized by omniscience.

Likewise, even in the context of the departure [from the body], the text designates the Supreme Lord as distinct from the individual soul: "This embodied self, mounted by the conscious self, goes forth uttering [the sound]" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.35).
In that passage as well, the "embodied self" would be the individual soul, because it is the master of the body.
But that very one is the wise Supreme Lord.
Therefore, because of the designation by way of distinction in the states of deep sleep and departure, it is understood that the Supreme Lord alone is intended here.
As for what was said—that this passage refers to the embodied soul because of the marks of the embodied soul at its beginning, middle, and end—[that is refuted].

To this we reply: at the outset, in the passage "this one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths," it is not the nature of the transmigrating soul that is intended to be described; rather, having referred to the nature of the transmigrating soul, the text intends to teach its identity with the Supreme Brahman.
For the subsequent portion of the text beginning with "it meditates as it were, it moves as it were" is observed to be devoted to the refutation of the attributes of the transmigrating soul.
Likewise, in the conclusion as well, he concludes exactly as he began: "That indeed is this great unborn Self (ātman), which consists of consciousness among the vital breaths.

The meaning is that this very transmigrating being who is perceived among the vital breaths as consisting of consciousness—that indeed is this great unborn Self, the Supreme Lord himself, as has been established by us.

As for those who, because of the presentation of states such as waking and dreaming in the middle [of the passage], believe that the intention was to describe the nature of the transmigrating being, [they are mistaken].
Even if one were sent toward the eastern direction, one would not set out toward the western direction;

for [the author] does not intend to assert that [the Self] possesses states or is subject to transmigratory existence by introducing states such as waking and dreaming, but rather intends to show its freedom from states and its non-transmigratory nature.
How is this understood?
Because [Nārada] asks at every step, "Speak further for the sake of liberation," and because [the text states],
"He becomes untouched by that, for this person is unattached" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.14, 15).
Thus it replies at every step;
and also: "He is untouched by merit, untouched by evil, for he has then crossed beyond all sorrows of the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.22).
Therefore, it must be understood that this passage is solely intent upon establishing the nature of the non-transmigrating Self.
Note: "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) means intelligence (*buddhi*); "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) means being predominantly composed of that.
The locative case in "among the vital breaths" (*prāṇeṣu*) has the sense of distinction;
the meaning is that [the Self] is distinct from both the vital breaths and the intellect.
The end of the Buddhas is the waking state;
"mounted" means presided over;
"emitting" means uttering terrible sounds.

The construction is as follows: since the Self (ātman) replies, "I am," when the intellect (buddhi) meditates, it is as if the Self meditates; and when the intellect moves, it is as if the Self moves; therefore, it is understood [that the Self is distinct from the intellect].
Therefore, by virtue of that state-dharma, one is unaccompanied and untouched [by it] due to its non-existence.
Hereafter, immediately following the seclusion from desire and so forth, [the suffixes occur] after words such as *pati* (husband) and others. (BBs 1.3.43)
For this reason as well, it should be understood that this passage is intended solely to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self;

for in this passage, words such as "Lord" (pati) and so forth serve both to establish the nature of the non-transmigrating Self and to negate the nature of the transmigrating Self. Expressions such as "the controller of all, the ruler of all, the sovereign of all" are of the nature of establishing the character of the non-transmigrating Self.
"By good action he does not become greater, nor indeed by evil action smaller"—passages of this kind negate the nature of one who is subject to transmigratory existence.
Therefore, it is understood that the Supreme Lord, who is not subject to transmigratory existence, is the one spoken of here. // 43 //
Thus ends the third quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.

The Fourth Pāda of the First Adhyāya.
[In this section, there is an investigation of terms such as *avyakta* and *aja*, which are employed with reference to the Pradhāna.
1. The Section Concerning that Which is Based on Inference (Ānumānikādhikaraṇa). Sūtras 1–7.

If it be argued that for some [schools] there is also an inferential [pradhāna], we say no; because [the Sūtra] shows that [the pradhāna] is grasped as being set forth through the metaphor of the body, and because it further demonstrates this.
Having proposed the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), the definition of Brahman was stated: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2).

Fearing that this definition might apply equally to the Pradhāna, it was refuted on the grounds of its lack of scriptural authority: "Because of [Brahman's] seeing, that which is not based on scripture [is not Brahman]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5).

It has already been explained at length in the preceding section that the Vedānta texts have a uniform tendency toward the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, and not toward the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause.

Now, however, this remaining objection is raised: that which was stated regarding the lack of scriptural authority for the Pradhāna is unproven, because in certain Śāstras there are heard words that appear to present the Pradhāna.
Consequently, it would follow that the causality of *pradhāna*—which is established by the Veda itself—is accepted by the great supreme seers such as Kapila and others.
Therefore, until it is demonstrated that those words have another referent, the teaching that the omniscient Brahman is the cause of the world, even if already established, would become confused.
Thus, the subsequent section proceeds to demonstrate that they have another referent.
Even that which is inferential—that is, the *pradhāna* as determined by inference—is found to be mentioned in the words of certain Vedic schools.
For it is recited in the *Kaṭhaka*: "Greater than the Great is the Unmanifest; greater than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa" (1.3.11).
There, those very entities named Mahat, Avyakta, and Puruṣa, and in that same sequence, which are well-known from the Smṛti, are here recognized.
In this context, because it is well-known from the Smṛti as "the Unmanifest" (avyakta),
and because the etymological derivation is possible— namely, that it is "unmanifest" (avyakta) due to being devoid of sound and other qualities—
the term refers to the Pradhāna as established in the Smṛti.
If it is argued that because it possesses sound, its being devoid of sound is untenable,
and that this very [Brahman] is the cause of the world on account of its establishment through Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning—
this is not so.
This passage from the *Kaṭhaka* does not aim to establish the existence of the "Great" (*mahat*) and the "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) as they are well-known in the Smṛti and through logical reasoning.

For here, that which is recognized is merely the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*); it is not the independent cause, the Pradhāna consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), which is well-known from the Smṛti, that is being identified.

Furthermore, that word "unmanifest" (avyakta) is used not only in its etymological sense of "that which is not manifest," but also in reference to other things that are subtle and difficult to perceive;
nor is it conventionally established (rūḍha) in reference to anything [specific].

As for the conventional usage among those who propound Pradhāna, since that is merely their own technical terminology (pāribhāṣikī), it does not serve as a basis for determining the meaning of the Veda.
Nor does the cognition of an identical object arise from the mere similarity of sequence when there is no recognition of its specific form;
for one who sees a cow in the place of a horse does not, being undeluded, determine "this is a horse.
Furthermore, upon examining the context here, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined by others is not perceived.
Because of the apprehension [of the body] through its presentation as a metaphorical chariot;
for here, the body presented as a metaphorical chariot is what is grasped by the term "the unmanifest" (avyakta).
Why?
This is evident from both the context and the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

For instance, the immediately preceding passage shows the metaphorical construction of the chariot and its parts according to those who maintain the existence of the self and the body: "Know the Self as the rider, and the body indeed as the chariot;
know the intellect (*buddhi*) as the charioteer, and the mind (*manas*) as the reins."
The wise say that the senses are the horses and their objects are the paths;
they say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer.
By means of those [faculties] such as the senses when they are unrestrained, one enters into saṃsāra;
but by means of them when they are restrained, one attains the further shore of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—having shown it.

In response to the inquiry, "What is that further shore of the path, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu?", the text shows the Supreme Self as the further shore of the path and the supreme abode of Viṣṇu by way of its transcendence over those very things previously mentioned—the senses and so forth: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind."
"But higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self;

higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the culmination, that is the supreme goal" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.10–11).

In this context, those very same things—the senses and so forth—which were previously presented in the metaphor of the chariot as being the horses and other parts, are here also adopted in order to avoid abandoning what was introduced and introducing what was not.
Among these, the senses, mind, and intellect have identical names in both the preceding and the present passages.
As for the objects—namely, sound and the other sense-objects—which were described as the domain of the horses that are the senses, their superiority over the senses is established.
This is because it is well-known from scripture, such as Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2: "The senses are the seizers, and the objects are the over-seizers";
and because the mind is superior to the objects.
Since the functioning of objects and the senses is rooted in the mind,
the intellect (buddhi) is higher than the mind;
for it is by ascending to the intellect that the collection of objects to be enjoyed approaches the enjoyer.
The Great Self, which is higher than the intellect, is that which was introduced as the charioteer in the passage, "Know the Self as the rider in the chariot.
Why? Because:
Because of the word "self" (ātman),
and because it is logical for the enjoyer to be distinct from the instruments of enjoyment;
furthermore, its greatness is established by virtue of its lordship.
Alternatively, it is recited thus: "Mind, the Great One, Intellect, Brahmā, Forethought, Consciousness, the Lord, Wisdom, Perception, Cognition, and Memory."

According to the Smṛti, and according to the Śruti, "He who in the beginning created Brahmā and who indeed delivered the Vedas to him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18), that intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha, the first-born, is the supreme foundation of all intellects;
it is this which is here called the "Great Self" (mahān ātmā).
And that [intellect], having already been grasped previously by the very mention of "intellect" (buddhi), is here taught separately;
for it is possible for it, too, to be superior to our own intellects.

However, according to this view, the mention of the "Person" (puruṣa) as the "highest" should be understood as referring to the Self who is the charioteer, by means of that same highest [Self] which has the Supreme Self as its object.

Since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no difference between the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), only the body remains as such. Thus, while sequentially enumerating the other factors under discussion— beginning with the senses— in order to demonstrate the supreme state (*paramapada*), [the text] shows that the body, which is the subject under discussion and the one remaining here, is indicated by the final term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*).
It is understood as follows:

for the sake of the ignorant enjoyer who is conjoined with the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations, the intended meaning here is the realization of the inner self as Brahman, achieved by defining the course of transmigration and liberation through the metaphorical conception of the body and other factors as a chariot and so forth.
And thus: "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth;
but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect."

Having thus stated the difficulty of perceiving the supreme state of Viṣṇu, he shows the yoga for the sake of its realization: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the self consisting of knowledge; he should restrain knowledge in the great self; and he should restrain that [great self] in the peaceful self. (Kā. 1.3.12)
(Kārikā 1.3.13).
This is what is meant: one should restrain speech within the mind; having abandoned the activity of the external senses such as speech and so forth, one should abide in the mind alone.

Furthermore, the mind—which is directed toward the conceptualization of objects—one should fix within the intellect (*buddhi*), which is designated by the word "knowledge" and has the nature of ascertainment, by perceiving the defects of conceptualization.

One should restrain even that intellect by bringing it to a state of subtlety within the Great Self—the experiencer—or within the supreme intellect. Furthermore, one should establish the Great Self within the Peaceful Self, which possesses the context of the Supreme Person, in the highest pinnacle.
Thus, upon considering the preceding and following passages, there is no room here for the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) imagined by others. // 1 //
Note: Because the *pradhāna* is devoid of any Vedic words [denoting it], the remainder [of the argument] is neither suspected nor refuted.
The term "semblance" (*ābhāsa*) is used to state that although [the word "unmanifest"] conveys the *pradhāna* through conventional understanding, it does not do so in reality.

By the use of the words "api" (also) and "eka" (one), it is indicated that this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and this investigation occur only occasionally, as they accept [the existence of] Brahman.
On account of both the Smṛti and the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the word *avyakta* refers to the Pradhāna.
The scriptural passage beginning with "ajāmekām" (the one unborn female) is the Śruti.

The Smṛti states, "The cause is called Prakṛti," and so forth; the logical principle (nyāya) holds that "whatever is limited is of an insentient nature. Therefore, the implication is that this [position] would undermine the doctrine that Brahman alone is the cause of the universe.
The fashioning of forms is the conceptualization of resemblance;
the rein is the horse's bridle;
[this refers] to those horses.
The "spheres" (gocara) are the paths;
the "self" (ātman) is the body.
They are called "graspers" (graha) because they seize—that is, bind—the human beast; these are the sense-faculties (indriya).
Superior to those are the objects of perception, which are the "seizers" (atigrahas).
The sense is that their superiority refers to being more excellent (*śraiṣṭhya*), not to being internal.
The ellipsis is: "He is recognized as superior to the intellect."
"Hiruk" means separately (*pṛthak*).
"Vedanā" is the experience of pleasure and so forth.
In the word "vāk," the elision of the accusative case-ending is Vedic (*chāndasa*), as is the lengthening of the vowel in "manasī."
The foremost [knowledge] is born from the maturation of meditative concentration;
however, it is subtle because of its state of arhatship.
Thus, by means of this section and the remaining analysis, it has been stated that the body is what is denoted by the term "the unmanifest" (avyakta), and not the Pradhāna.

Now this objection is raised: How can the body be fit for the designation "unmanifest" (avyakta), since, being gross, this body is more clearly perceived and thus fits the designation "manifest" (vyakta), whereas the word "unmanifest" refers to that which is indistinct?
To this, the following reply is given: Here, however, the body is intended in its subtle causal form, because the subtle is fit for the designation "unmanifest."
Although this gross body does not itself deserve to be designated by the term "unmanifest" (avyakta), nevertheless, its constituent subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma) do deserve that designation.
Furthermore, the word "nature" (prakṛti) is seen to be applied to a modification (vikāra).

And as the Śruti says, "Mix the intoxicating drink with milk" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 9.46.4), so too the text, "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7), shows that this very world— differentiated by name and form— is, in its prior state, devoid of differentiated name and form, existing in the state of a seed-potency, and thus connected with the term "unmanifest" (avyakta). // 2 //

FN: Because the modifications (*vikāra*) are non-different from their primal nature (*prakṛti*), the unmanifest state of the *prakṛti* is figuratively attributed to the modification. "With cows"—meaning with the products of cows, namely milk—one should "mix" (*śrīṇīta*), that is, make the *matsara* (Soma) blended.
Indeed, at that time, in its prior state, this world was "unmanifested," that is, unevolved and unmanifest.
"Because it is dependent on that, it is meaningful.

(BBs 1.4.3) Here [the opponent] says: If this world, in its prior state, were admitted to be in the form of a seed with name and form unmanifested, and thus worthy of being called "unmanifested," and if, by virtue of that nature, the body were also asserted to be worthy of being called "unmanifested," [then the objection would stand].
"In that case, this would result in the very doctrine of the Primal Cause (pradhāna-kāraṇavāda), because you are accepting the prior state of this very world as being the Primal Cause.
To this it is replied: "If we were to accept some independent prior state of the world as its cause,"
In that case, we would be falling into the doctrine of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause.
However, we accept this prior state of the world as being dependent upon the Supreme Lord, not independent;
and it must necessarily be accepted as such.
For she is not devoid of power;
indeed, without her, the Supreme Lord’s status as creator cannot be established,
because activity is impossible for one who is devoid of power.
Furthermore, for those who are liberated, there is no further rebirth.
Why?
Because through knowledge, the seed-potency of that [ignorance] has been burnt away.

For the seed-potency consisting of ignorance—designated by the term "the unmanifest" (*avyakta*), resting upon the Supreme Lord, composed of *māyā*, and being a great sleep—in which the transmigrating individual souls lie, devoid of awakening to their true nature;

this very unmanifest is in some places designated by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*), according to the scriptural text: "In this Imperishable, O Gārgī, indeed, the ether is woven like warp and woof" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
In some places it is expressed by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable), according to the Śruti: "Higher than the high Imperishable" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.1.2).
In other places it is indicated as "māyā" (illusion), from the wording of the mantra: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10).
For that *māyā* is indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*),
because it is impossible to define it as being either identical to or different from the principles (*tattva*).
Thus, it has been stated that "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great" (*mahat*), because the Great arises from the Unmanifest.

When the intellect belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha is meant by "the Great," and when the individual soul (jīva) is meant by "the Great," then too, because the state of being an individual soul is dependent upon the Unmanifest, it is said that "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great.
For the Unmanifest is indeed ignorance (avidyā).
The entire continuous worldly activity of the individual soul (jīva) proceeds solely on the basis of its possession of ignorance (avidyā).
The state of being "higher than the Great One" (mahat) is figuratively attributed to the body, which is a modification of that [Mahat], by means of a metaphorical identification (abhedopacāra).

Although the senses and other organs are no different from the body in being modifications of that same [Mahat], it is the body alone that is grasped by the term "the Unmanifest" (avyakta) through such figurative identification.
Since the sense faculties and so forth are already included by their own specific terms, and since the body remains as that which is left over, others explain it thus:
for the body is of two kinds, gross and subtle;
the gross is that which is perceived here.

That which is subtle will be explained later: "In the interval between [deaths], he goes enveloped [by the elements], according to the question and the exposition" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1). Both of these bodies, without distinction, were previously mentioned as the chariot; however, here it is the subtle body that is grasped by the word "unmanifest."
Because the subtle possesses the fitness for the designation "unmanifest" (avyakta),
and because the conventional usage of bondage and liberation depends upon it, it is superior to the individual soul (jīva).
Just as objects are superior to the senses because the functioning of the senses depends upon them, so too is that [subtle principle] superior to the soul.
However, they must say this:

since both bodies have been mentioned without distinction as being like chariots previously, and since both are equally the subject under discussion and remain as possibilities, how can it be that only the subtle body is understood here and not the gross one as well?
We are capable of understanding the meaning of what has been taught, but we cannot challenge what has not been taught.

If it is argued that the word *avyakta* (the unmanifest) mentioned in the scripture is capable of denoting only the subtle [Prakṛti] and nothing else because the latter is manifest (*vyakta*), we say no;
for the comprehension of meaning depends upon the unity of the sentence.
Indeed, these two scriptural passages, the preceding and the following, do not convey any meaning unless they attain the status of a single syntactical unit.
Because this would entail the abandonment of what was composed by another and the introduction of what was not composed;
furthermore, there is no comprehension of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) in the absence of mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).

In that case, while there remains an expectancy for the two bodies to be grasped as objects, if a connection is not admitted according to that expectancy, the very status of being a single sentence is subverted; how then could there be comprehension of the meaning of what has been revealed in scripture?

Nor should it be thought that only the subtle body is mentioned here because it is difficult to purify, while the gross body is not mentioned because it is easily purified due to its visibly loathsome nature;
for no purification of anything whatsoever is intended here.
For there is nothing stated here that prescribes a process of purification;
rather, because it has been mentioned immediately prior, this is what is intended here: "What is that supreme abode of Viṣṇu?
For, having said, "This is superior to that, this is superior to that," he concludes, "There is nothing whatsoever superior to the Puruṣa."
In any case, since the refutation of the inferential [view] is established, let it be so named;
nothing of ours is thereby undermined. // 3 // [FN:
"Then" (tarhi) means "at that time" (tadā).]
It consists of illusion (*māyāmaya*), being compared to well-known illusion (*prasiddhamāyā*).
Due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, there is the plural expression "living beings" (*jīvāḥ*).
Because it is unconditioned (*anavacchinna*), it is the nature of space (*ākāśatva*).
The distinction is that it possesses imperishability because there is no cessation without the knowledge of reality, and it possesses the nature of *māyā* because its effects are manifold;
that is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
This should be understood as being like the expression "cow and bull" (*gobalīvarda*).
*Ekavākyatā* (syntactic unity) is the state of words that convey a single meaning being mutually expectant and integrated into a single cognition.
The expectancy for what is to be apprehended is *ekavākyatā*.
The meaning is: "by that state" (*tattayā*) refers to that in which loathsomeness and disgust are perceived;
that is to say, even when either the gross or the subtle [aspect] is grasped in every way.
Furthermore, it is because there is no mention of [the self] being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).
Furthermore, the Sāṃkhyas maintain that *pradhāna* is an object of knowledge, as they say: "Liberation results from the knowledge of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*.
For it is impossible to know the distinction of the *puruṣa* from the *guṇas* without first knowing the nature of the *guṇas*.
Moreover, in some instances, they maintain that *pradhāna* is to be known for the sake of attaining specific supernatural powers (*vibhūti*).
If this unmanifest were not stated here as an object of knowledge,
then the word "unmanifest" would be merely a [grammatical] term;
for there is no sentence here stating that "the unmanifest is to be known and to be meditated upon."
Furthermore, it cannot be maintained that knowledge of an entity not taught [in scripture] constitutes a human goal;
therefore, for this reason as well, the Pradhāna is not denoted by the word "Unmanifest.
For us, however, this presentation is faultless, as it aims to reveal the supreme abode of Viṣṇu alone by following the metaphorical framework of the chariot, the body, and so forth. 4.
"If you say [it is] so, no; for the wise one [is meant], according to the context.
Here the Sāṃkhya says: "Because of the non-statement of being an object of knowledge" is unestablished.
How so?

For it is heard further on that there is a statement regarding the knowability of the Pradhāna, which is denoted by the word "unmanifest": "Having perceived that which is without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying, likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell; which is without beginning or end, beyond the Great (Mahat), and constant—one is liberated from the jaws of death."
For here, that very same Pradhāna which is described in Smṛti as being beyond the Mahat and devoid of sound and other qualities is indicated as the object to be perceived;
therefore, this is indeed the Pradhāna.
And that very [Self] is what is designated by the word "unmanifest.
To this we reply: here the *pradhāna* is not designated as the object of contemplation;
rather, it is understood that the wise Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is designated here as the object of contemplation.
Why?
Because of the context;
for the context of a wise person extends far and wide.

Because of such scriptural indications as, "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the limit, that is the supreme goal," and because of the statement regarding its difficulty of knowing—namely, "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth"—there arises a desire to know that very Puruṣa as the object of knowledge.
Furthermore, because the restraint of speech and other faculties is prescribed for the sake of attaining that knowledge alone, in the passage, "The wise man should restrain speech and mind."
And because it has as its fruit liberation from the jaws of death;
for the Sāṃkhyas do not maintain that one is liberated from the jaws of death merely by perceiving the Pradhāna alone.
For their accepted position is that one is liberated from the jaws of death through the knowledge of the conscious Self.
In all the Vedānta texts, it is the conscious Self alone that is described as having the attributes of being "without sound" and so forth.
Therefore, it is not the Pradhāna that is the object of knowledge here, nor is it that which is designated by the word "unmanifest. (5) [FN:
In the phrases beginning with "without sound," the word "eternal" (nitya) is to be connected with each term individually.]
Furthermore, there is an introduction and a question regarding these three alone.
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna cannot be denoted by the word "Unmanifest" (avyakta), nor can it be the object of knowledge (jñeya).

Because in this text, the Kaṭhavallī Upaniṣad, we observe that only three categories—the fire, the individual soul (jīva), and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—are introduced as subjects to be explained due to the power of the granted boons.
And the question indeed concerns that very subject;
there is no question or presentation of anything else.
In this regard, it says: "O Death, you know that fire which leads to heaven; explain it to me, for I am full of faith" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 1.1.13).
Thus ends the question concerning fire.

"Regarding this doubt that exists concerning a man who has died—some say he exists, others say he does not exist—I wish to be instructed by you in this knowledge; this is my third boon among the boons."
Thus ends the question concerning the individual soul (*jīva*). [The next question is:

"Tell me that which you perceive as other than merit (*dharma*) and other than demerit (*adharma*), other than what has been done and what has not been done by us, and other than what has been and what is yet to be."
The statement, "Thus [he spoke] concerning the Supreme Self" (Kā. 1.2.14), refers to the Supreme Self;
whereas the reply, "He spoke to him concerning that Agni, the beginning of the worlds—what bricks he had, or how many, or how [they were placed]" (Kā. 1.1.15), refers to Agni.
"Come now, I shall declare to you this secret, eternal Brahman,
and how the self becomes [after] reaching death, O Gautama. Some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of acquiring a body."
"Others follow the post, according to their karma and according to their learning" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.5.6–7).
This refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) which was previously mentioned:
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.18).
Thus, there is an extensive elaboration concerning the Supreme Self;
however, there is no such question regarding the Pradhāna.
And because it was not asked, it need not be introduced.

Here [the opponent] asks: Is this very question concerning the self— "There is this doubt regarding a person after death"— being drawn back again as "Other than dharma, other than adharma," or is a different, previously unarisen question being raised?
What follows from this?

If it were argued that "this very same question is being brought forward again," then because two questions concerning the Self would result in becoming one— the question concerning fire and the question concerning the Self— therefore it should not be said that there is a presentation of three questions.

If it were argued that "this is another unprecedented question being raised," then just as there would be no fault in postulating a question apart from the granting of the boons, so too there would be no fault in postulating the introduction of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) apart from a question.
To this we reply: We do not at all postulate any such question here apart from the granting of the boons, because of the force of the opening of the passage.

Indeed, the progression of the discourse in the Kaṭha Upaniṣads, from its beginning with the granting of boons down to its conclusion, is observed to take the form of a dialogue between Mṛtyu and Naciketas.
It is said that Mṛtyu granted three boons to Naciketas, who had been sent by his father; and it is said that with the first of those boons, Naciketas chose benevolence.
By the second [question] he asks about the knowledge of fire, and by the third, the knowledge of the Self,
according to the indicative mark [of the text]: "That which [arises] when one has died" and "This third is indeed the best of boons" (KaU 1.1.20).

In that regard, if this new question—"Is he other than dharma?"—were raised as something distinct, then the statement would be contradicted by the assumption of a question even apart from the granting of the boon.
[Objection: But surely this must be a new question because of the difference in what is to be asked;
for the previous question had the individual soul (jīva) as its subject matter.

This doubt regarding the deceased—that there is or is not [a self] in a human being—is expressed by the term "doubt. Furthermore, the *jīva* (living soul) deserves the question "Is it other than dharma and so forth? because it is the object of inquiry concerning dharma and the like; however, the wise one, having transcended dharma and the like, deserves the question "Is it other than dharma and so forth? because he is beyond dharma and the rest.
Furthermore, the shadow of the questions is not seen to be identical;
for the former has as its object existence and non-existence, whereas the latter has as its object things that have passed away, such as the *dharmas*.
Therefore, due to the absence of recognition [between them], there is a difference between the questions.
If it is argued that there is no carrying forward of the preceding [subject] into the subsequent [question], we say no;

for the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme conscious one (prājña) is accepted. There would be a distinction between the questions due to a distinction in what is to be asked only if the individual soul were different from the supreme conscious one.
However, there is no difference [between them],
based on other scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (Tattvamasi).

Furthermore, in this context, the answer to the question "Is it other than dharma?"— namely, "The wise one is neither born nor dies"— establishes the non-difference between the embodied soul and the Supreme Lord by means of the negation of birth and death.
He shows this:
for a negation is meaningful only when there is a possibility [of its application].
And the possibility of birth and death through contact with a body belongs to the embodied soul (śārīra), not to the Supreme Lord (parameśvara).
Likewise: "The wise person does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self by which one perceives both the state of dreaming and the state of waking."

(Kārikā 2.4.4) Thus, by demonstrating that the cessation of sorrow occurs through the contemplation of the *jīva* itself—characterized by greatness and omnipresence—as the seer of both dream and waking states, [the author] shows that the *jīva* is not other than the *prājña*.
For it is the established doctrine of Vedānta that the cessation of sorrow results from the realization of the *prājña*.
Likewise, later on: "What is here, that is there; what is there, that is also here."

"He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.4.10); thus [the text] refutes the perception of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the conscious Lord (prājña).

Likewise, immediately following the question regarding the existence or non-existence of the individual soul, Naciketas—though being tempted by Death with various desires beginning with the words "Choose another boon, Naciketas"—[remains steadfast].

When he did not waver, Death approached him by demonstrating the distinction between the higher and lower good (*naiḥśreyasa*), and by demonstrating the distinction between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*): "I consider Naciketas to be one who desires knowledge; many desires did not distract you" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4).

Having thus praised [the questioner] and commending his very question, he said: "The wise man, having realized through the attainment of the yoga of the supreme self that ancient God—who is difficult to see, who has entered into the hidden, who is seated in the cave, who dwells in the abyss—casts off both joy and sorrow."

(Kā. 1.2.12). By this also, it is understood that the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) and the wise one (prājña) alone is intended here. Furthermore, since Naciketas received great praise from Death for the reason of his question, if he were to set that aside and propose another question immediately after the praise, that entire praise would have been extended out of place.
Therefore, the phrase "other than dharma" is a restatement of that very question, "that which [is] after death.
As for the objection raised regarding the difference in the form of the questions, that is not a valid criticism;
for it is precisely that same specific point which is being asked again.
For in the former [section], the existence of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth was questioned, whereas in the latter, its state of being beyond saṃsāra is questioned.
As long as ignorance is not removed, the individual soul's (jīva) status as a transmigrating being and its domain of dharma and the like do not cease;
but upon the cessation of that [ignorance], it is realized through the scriptural text "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) that it is indeed the Omniscient One (prājña).
Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever in the nature of an object between its state when it is accompanied by ignorance and its state when that ignorance has been removed.
It is just as when someone, seeing a rope lying in deep darkness, mistakes it for a snake; terrified and trembling, he flees.
Then another person says to him, "Do not be afraid! This is not a snake, it is merely a rope."
Upon hearing that, he would abandon the fear, trembling, and flight caused by the snake;
yet there would be no difference whatsoever in the object itself between the time when it was perceived as a snake and the time when that [perception] has vanished.
This case should be understood in exactly the same way.
Consequently, even such passages as "It is neither born nor does it die" serve as a response to the question regarding existence.
However, the Sūtra should be interpreted with reference to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the wise Self (prājña), which is imagined through ignorance.

For, although the subject of the question concerns the unity of the Self, in the state prior to death there remains a doubt regarding the mere existence of something distinct from the body, and because the nature of transmigratory existence—such as agency and so forth—has not yet been dispelled, the first section [of the Upaniṣad] is addressed.

The state of having the individual soul (jīva) as its object is inferred for the former [passage], whereas the latter has the conscious self (prājña) as its object because it mentions the transcendence of dharma and so forth;
and thus, the conceptualization of fire, the individual soul, and the supreme self is appropriate.
But in the case of the postulation of Pradhāna, there would be a discrepancy: there would be neither the granting of boons, nor the question, nor the answer. [FN:
Since Mṛtyu told Naciketas, "Choose three boons," Naciketas asked questions regarding only those three, and Mṛtyu provided the corresponding explanations.]
"O Death, you who have granted me boons, do you remember the fire that was for the sake of heaven?
When one has departed, having died, there is a doubt as to whether there exists something other than the body. Therefore, the meaning is: 'May I know this true nature of the self without doubt.'"
She whose introduction is heard,
whose commencement consists of the granting of a boon—
that [speech] was sent forth, dispatched toward the realm of Yama.
Because it is the object of experience and because it is the basis,
it is logically connected as a constituent part; "end" refers to a state.
The connection is that by means of which witness the knower sees—that is the Self.

Whatever consciousness exists here in this body is the very same as that in the sun and so forth over there. The meaning is: setting aside that which is the subject of the question, or that [question] itself.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the *viśeṣokti* (specific statement).

And it is like the word "mahat": just as the word *mahat*, though employed by the Sāṃkhyas for the first-born [evolute] which is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), does not denote that same thing even when used in Vedic application.
"The Great Self is superior to the intellect" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.3.10); "the great, all-pervading Self" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 1.2.22);
"I know this great Puruṣa" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).

For these reasons, such as the employment of the word "Self" (*ātman*) in passages beginning with those cited above, the term "Unmanifest" (*avyakta*) likewise cannot denote the *pradhāna* in Vedic usage. Consequently, this [Pradhāna] inferred by means of logic lacks the quality of being supported by scripture (*śabdavat*). // 7 //
2. The Section on the Chamasas. Sūtra 8–10:
"Like the cups, because there is no distinction.
(BBs 1.4.8) Furthermore, the proponent of Pradhāna states that the scriptural non-mention of Pradhāna remains unestablished.
Why?

Because of the wording of the mantra: "The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form—the one unborn male lies beside her, enjoying her; another unborn male abandons her once her enjoyment has been experienced" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5).
For in this mantra, the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas are denoted by the words "red," "white," and "black" respectively:
red is rajas because its nature is to color or stain;
white is sattva because its nature is luminosity.
It is "black" (kṛṣṇa) because it is dark due to its quality of obscuration (āvaraṇa).
It is designated by the qualities of its constituent parts in their state of equilibrium as "red, white, and black.
Furthermore, it may be called "unborn" (ajā) because it is not born.

Because of the accepted principle that "the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not an evolute. Now, one might object: "The word *ajā* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) as meaning a she-goat. Certainly so.
But that conventional usage cannot be adopted here, because the context concerns knowledge;
and she (Māyā) gives birth to many creatures endowed with the three qualities.
The one unborn Puruṣa, delighting in—that is, being pleased with or serving—that Prakṛti, lies along with it;
having accepted that very Prakṛti as his self through ignorance, he wanders in saṃsāra due to a lack of discrimination, thinking "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded.

But another unborn Puruṣa, having developed discriminative knowledge and becoming dispassionate, abandons this Prakṛti—having enjoyed her and accomplished both experience and liberation—and leaves her behind.
The meaning is that [the soul] is released.
Therefore, the conceptualization of the Pradhāna and so forth is indeed rooted in scripture.
This being the position reached, we reply: it is not possible to rely on this mantra as a scriptural basis for the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
For this mantra is not capable of supporting any particular doctrine independently;
for in every case, it is possible to establish [terms] such as "unborn" through some conceptual construction or other.
Since there is no reason for determining a specific distinction, the Sāṃkhya doctrine alone is intended here.
It is like the case of the *camasa* cup.

For instance, in the mantra, "This cup has its mouth below and its bottom above" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.2.3), it is impossible to determine independently that this specific cup is intended by the name [in question].
Since it is possible to conceive of "having a mouth facing downward" and so forth in any way whatsoever in all cases, there is likewise no distinction here regarding this mantra, "the one unborn.
It cannot be determined that the *pradhāna* alone is intended by the term "unborn" in this mantra. (8)

In that case, however, the understanding of a specific cup arises from the supplementary passage: "This is that head; for this cup has its opening below and its bottom above. But here, on the other hand, what is this "ajā" (goat/she-goat) to be understood as?
To this we reply:

FN: "The one unborn" (*ajāmekām*): she is called "unborn" (*ajā*) because she is not born; she is the Root Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), characterized by red, white, and black—that is, the qualities of *rajas*, *sattva*, and *tamas*.

Producing offspring that possess the same nature as herself and consist of the three *guṇas*, the one unborn individual soul (*jīva*), while enjoying her as she assumes the form of objects such as sound and so forth, lies close to her and remains perpetually deluded.

The *bhoga* (enjoyment) is that which is enjoyed by the individual soul (*jīva*), or rather, that which is being enjoyed by the *jīva*; another—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—abandons it, meaning He does not form an attachment to it.

The "parts" (*avayava*) are the qualities of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), such as *rajas* and the others; their "attributes" (*dharma*) are qualities such as being colored or stimulating, and so on.
They are called "progeny" (*prajā*) because they are born; these are the principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*).
The three qualities (traiguṇya) are pleasure, pain, and delusion.
Here, "selfhood" (ātmatva) means identity with those qualities.
Experience (bhoga) is the perception of sound and the other sense objects.
Apavarga (liberation) is that by which one is released through the knowledge of the distinction between the qualities (*guṇa*) and the Person (*puruṣa*).
But [the unborn] begins with light, for so it is taught by some:

this *ajā* (unborn), consisting of fire, water, and food, and serving as the material cause of the fourfold aggregate of beings, is to be understood as having originated from the Supreme Lord, beginning with light.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of emphasis.
This *ajā* (the Unborn) is to be understood as characterized by the three elements (*bhūta*) alone, not as characterized by the three qualities (*guṇa*).
Why?

For thus some followers of a Vedic school, having recorded the origin of fire, water, and food from the Supreme Lord, declare that these very elements possess the nature of redness and so forth: "That which was its red form was the nature of fire, that which was white was the nature of water, and that which was black was the nature of food.
These same three—fire, water, and food—are recognized here [in the present context] because of the commonality of the terms "red" and so forth.

Furthermore, since words such as *rohit* and others primarily denote specific forms while only secondarily referring to qualities, it is considered logical to determine the doubtful by means of the non-doubtful. The same applies here as well: "The exponents of Brahman say..."

For, beginning with "What is the cause, O Brahman? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1), the text states, "Those who have attained the path of yoga beheld the power of the Divine Self, concealed by its own qualities" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3);
thus, at the very outset of the passage, the supreme power of the Lord, which ordains the entire universe, is understood.

Even from the remainder of the passage, namely, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), and "He who alone presides over each and every womb" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.11), it is understood that it is this very [Māyā] which is meant; therefore, it cannot be said that some independent Prakṛti called Pradhāna is what is taught by the *ajā* mantra.

Rather, on account of the context, it is said that this same divine power (*daivī śakti*), whose name and form are unevolved (*avyākṛta-nāmarūpa*), is what is taught by the mantra as the prior state of name and form.
And its three-fold nature has been explained by means of the three-fold nature of its own transformation-object. // 9 //
But how can the goat (*ajā*) be understood as having a threefold nature consisting of fire, water, and food? For, on the one hand, the form of a goat does not exist within fire, water, and food;
and on the other hand, since there is no mention of a genus (*jāti*) for fire, water, and food, it is impossible for the word "goat" (*ajā*) to be based on a genus.
To this, he recites the following:—
The followers of the *Śākha*, namely the *Chandogas*,
being exponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*), having deliberated in this manner and having followed through the yoga of the two worlds (*dyānayoga*), entered into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
It has been stated that the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*) is the womb (*yoni*) and that it is manifold for each individual soul; therefore, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is appropriate.
Furthermore, because it is taught as a figurative designation (*kalpanopadeśa*), there is no contradiction, as in the case of the honey [in the *Madhuvidyā*] and other such examples.
This word "goat" (*ajā*) is not caused by the form of a goat.
Nor is it etymological;
rather, this is a figurative instruction.
The fabrication of the form of a she-goat is taught as a metaphor for the source of all moving and non-moving beings, characterized by fire, water, and earth.

For just as in the world there might be some she-goat by chance red, white, and black in color, having many kids and kids of similar appearance, and a certain goat, being fond of her, might lie with her, while another might abandon her once he has enjoyed her; even so this primordial nature of the elements, characterized by fire, water, and earth, possessing the three colors, produces a manifold collection of modifications consisting of moving and non-moving beings of similar form, which is enjoyed by the ignorant knower of the field (kṣetrajña), but not by the wise one.
"One should abandon that.

Nor should it be suspected that because one *kṣetrajña* lies down while another abandons [the body], a real (*pāramārthika*) plurality of *kṣetrajñas* follows as the position desired by our opponents;
for this is not an intention to establish a plurality of *kṣetrajñas*, but rather an intention to establish the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation.
Having merely restated the well-known distinction [between souls], the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation is established.
However, this distinction is caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and is constructed by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*); it is not ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
This is known from such scriptural passages as: "The one God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings."
It is like honey and so forth;
as in "the honey-nature of the sun which is not honey" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.1),
and "the cow-nature of speech which is not a cow" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.8).

The meaning is that just as in such passages as "the non-fire nature of the heavenly world and so forth" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sheṣad 8.2.9), fire-nature is attributed [to what is not fire], so too this non-birth-nature of the unborn is attributed.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in applying the word *ajā* to fire, water, and earth.
[FN: "Having many kids" means having many young ones; *barkara* refers to a young animal.]
3. The section concerning the inclusion of the Sāṃkhya [doctrine], Sūtras 11–13:

"Not even from the inclusion of the number [of principles], because of their manifoldness and because of the excess. (BBs 1.4.11) Even though the *ajā* mantra has been thus interpreted, the Sāṃkhya again objects on the basis of another mantra.
"In that in which the five groups of five and the ether are established—

him alone, I consider, the wise one, knowing him as the immortal Brahman, [becomes] immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.17). In this mantra, because of the observation of the word "five" twice, another number five is heard within the context of the number five in the phrase "the five groups of five."
These five pentads thus amount to twenty-five.

Accordingly, by the number twenty-five, as many numerable entities as are desired are enumerated as principles (tattvas) by the Sāṃkhyas: "Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is unevolved; the seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are both nature and evolute."
"And the sixteenfold is a modification; the Puruṣa is neither nature nor modification" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3).

Because those twenty-five principles established in Smṛti are subsumed under that number of twenty-five well-known from Śruti, it follows that Pradhāna and the others indeed possess scriptural authority.
To this we reply: one should not entertain the hope that Pradhāna and the others possess scriptural authority even on the basis of the inclusion of their number.
Why?
Because of their diversity;
for these twenty-five principles are indeed diverse.
There is no common property among these taken five by five, by virtue of which another five-fold number could be applied within the interval of twenty-five;
for numbers such as "two" and so forth do not apply to diverse things in the absence of a single unifying basis.

Now, it might be argued that this very number twenty-five is indicated by way of its constituent parts, just as when one says, "Indra did not rain for five and seven years," people speak of a twelve-year drought;
but even that is not tenable.
In this view, the very same defect remains: that one would have to resort to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
Furthermore, in this case, the word *pañca* is compounded with the word *jana* as *pañcajanāḥ*, because its status as a single word is determined by its technical accentuation.
Furthermore, in another application [of the mantra], namely "pañcānāṃ tvā pañcajanānām" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.6.2.2),
because it is understood as a single word with a single accent and a single case-ending,
there is no distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) of the compound such as "five five."
Nor is there a grasping of two fives as "five, five";
nor is there a qualification of a single number five by another number five as "five fives," because a subordinate term cannot be connected with a qualifier.

[Objection: Surely, people who have already attained the number five, when further qualified by the number five, will be understood as twenty-five—just as in the expression "five five-bundles," twenty-five bundles are understood; it is exactly like that. [Reply: We say, "No."

It is appropriate that, because the word *pañcapūlī* intends a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), when there is a desire for distinction as to "how many?", the qualification "five" is used, as in "five five-bunches. But here, in the case of "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) and so forth, since the distinction is already established from the outset, there is no desire for further distinction as to "how many?"; therefore, the qualification "five" would not apply to "five-people. Even if this qualification were to apply, it would apply only to the number five itself.
And the fault in that case has already been stated.
Therefore, the expression "five five-people" does not intend to refer to twenty-five principles;
furthermore, because there is an excess [of elements], it does not intend to refer to twenty-five principles.
Furthermore, because there is an excess, it does not intend to refer to twenty-five principles;
for there is an excess over the number twenty-five due to the self and space.
First, the self is indicated here as the foundational support.

Because that which is indicated by the locative case in the phrase "in which" (*yasmin*) is drawn back as being the Self (*ātman*) in the statement "I consider that very [Self] to be the Self," and because the Self is the conscious person (*puruṣa*),
and since that [person] is already included within the group of twenty-five principles, it is not logical for it to be both the substratum and the contained.
Furthermore, if another entity were admitted, there would result an excess in the enumeration of the principles (*tattva*), which would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

Likewise, since space is included within the twenty-five [principles] as expressed in the statement "and space is established," it is not logical to mention it separately. Moreover, if another entity were admitted, the aforementioned refutation would apply.
And how, upon hearing a mere number, can the inclusion of the twenty-five principles (tattvas) not explicitly mentioned be understood?
For the word *jana* is not conventionally established (*arūḍha*) in the sense of "principles," and the number remains possible even if it refers to something else entirely.
How then is the expression "five five-people" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*) to be explained?

It is said: because of the specific grammatical rule *diksaṃkhye saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 2.1.50), which prescribes that a qualifier is compounded with a noun when it forms a proper name (*saṃjñā*), the word *pañca* is compounded with the word *jana* only in the sense of a proper name. Consequently, by intending this as a conventional term (*rūḍha*), certain "five-people" are intended to be expressed, and not with reference to the principles (*tattva*) of the Sāṃkhya school.
When there arises the expectation "How many are they?", the word "five" is employed again.
The meaning is that those who are called the "five peoples" (pañcajanāḥ) are exactly five, just as in the expression "the seven seers are seven. (11)
Who, then, are these so-called "five people"? This is explained as follows:
primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification (*avikṛti*), meaning it is not a transformation of anything else.
The seven—namely, the Great One (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—are both natures and modifications (*prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ*).
The Great Principle (mahat) is the nature (prakṛti) of ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra) and a modification (vikṛti) of the primal nature (mūlaprakṛti).

Ego-consciousness, when characterized by darkness (tāmasa), is the nature of the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi); when characterized by goodness (sāttvika), it is the nature of the eleven organs. The subtle elements are the natures of the gross elements, such as space and the rest.
The group of sixteen—consisting of the five elements and the eleven faculties—is exclusively a modification (*vikāra*).

Although earth and the other elements serve as the material causes (*prakṛti*) for jars and the like, they are indeed modifications because they do not serve as the material cause for any further principles (*tattva*).
The meaning is that the *puruṣa*, however, being immutable (*kauṭasthya*), is devoid of being either a material cause or a modification.
Difference (*bheda*) means qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
Excess (*atireka*) means redundancy (*ādhikya*).
The aforementioned fault is the excess of number (*saṃkhyādhikya*).
"Prāṇa and the others [are the five], because of the supplementary statement.

(BBs 1.4.12) In the mantra following "In whom the five groups of five persons [dwell]," five things beginning with prāṇa are specified for the purpose of defining the nature of Brahman: "The breath of breath, and the sight of sight, and the hearing of hearing, and the food of food... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18).
"Those who know the mind of the mind"—
these [beings], occurring as a supplementary part of the sentence, are intended here by the term "five people" (pañcajana) due to their proximity.
But how, then, can the word "people" (jana) be applied to the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth?

Or how could the word "people" (jana) be applied to the [subtle] principles (tattva)? Since the departure from conventional usage is equal in both cases, the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth must be understood by virtue of the remainder of the sentence. Furthermore, because of their connection with people, the vital breaths and so forth come to be designated by the word "people."
Furthermore, the word *puruṣa* is used in the sense of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*s), as in the passage, "These indeed are the five Brahman-puruṣas" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.6),
and in the Brāhmaṇa text, "The vital breath is indeed the father; the vital breath is indeed the mother," and so forth.

Furthermore, due to the power of the compound, it is not contradictory for the whole to possess conventional meaning (*rūḍhatva*). But how can conventional meaning be resorted to when there has been no prior usage?
He says: "It is possible, as in the case of *udbhid* and other such terms."

For when a word of unknown meaning is used in proximity to a word of well-known meaning, its referent is restricted by that co-occurrence (samabhivyāhāra), as in the cases: "One should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," "He cuts the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)," and "He prepares the altar (*vedī*).

Likewise, this term *pañcajana*, having its status as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) understood from the grammatical analysis of the compound and thus requiring a named object (*saṃjñin*), will apply to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth mentioned in the remainder of the sentence.

By some, however, the five *pañcajanāḥ* are explained as the gods, the ancestors, the *gandharvas*, the *asuras*, and the *rakṣases*; by others, they are taken to be the four social classes (*varṇas*) with the *niṣādas* as the fifth; and in some places, as in the verse "by the people of the five tribes" (*yatpāñcajanyayā viśā*, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.53.7).
Thus, the application of the word *pañcajana* is seen as referring to the creatures (*prajā*). Even if that interpretation were accepted here, there would be no contradiction whatsoever.

However, the Teacher [Śaṅkara] stated, "The breath and so forth [are the five], because of the supplementary passage," with the intent that there is no comprehension here of the twenty-five principles.
The five "people" (*pañcajana*) might indeed be the breath and so forth among the Mādhyandinas, who mention food (*anna*) among the breath and the rest;
but how can the breath and so forth be the "five people" for the Kāṇvas, who do not mention food among the breath and the rest? To this, he reads the following reply:
Note: The word *uta* has the sense of "also.
The meaning is that those who know the Self, which is the witness of that [universe] and the impeller of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, are the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*).
The word *jana* refers to people; that is to say, the term *pañcajana*.
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother is a Niṣāda.
According to some, [the number is completed] by means of light when food is absent;
even when food is absent for the Kāṇvas, their number five is fulfilled by means of light.

For in the mantra preceding "In whom the five classes of beings [dwell]," light (*jyotis*) is indeed studied for the very purpose of defining the nature of Brahman: "That is the light of lights, which the gods worship.
But how is it that this light, being mentioned equally by both groups, is accepted by some as included within the number five found in the same mantra, yet not by others?
He says: "Because of a difference in perspective."

For the Mādhyandinas, since they obtain the five classes of beings (pañcajana), such as prāṇa and the rest, which are recited in the same mantra, there is no need for them to look to the light (jyotis) recited in this other mantra;
however, because they do not obtain it, the Kāṇvas do have such a need.
And due to this difference in need, there is the inclusion or non-inclusion of the light, even though the mantra is the same.
Just as, even though the *atirātra* sacrifice is the same, there is the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup due to a difference in scriptural injunctions, so it is here.
Thus, in this way, there is no established authority from direct revelation (*śruti*) regarding the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*).
As for the establishment through tradition (*smṛti*) and logic (*nyāya*), those will be refuted later. // 13 //
FN: Here, as in the case of the taking or not taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup, there is an option regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* due to the split of the sentence.
4. The Section on Being the Cause. Sūtras 14–15:
"And because it is declared as the cause in the cases of ether and so forth, exactly as described. (BBs 1.4.14)
The definition of Brahman has been established;
