the uniformity of the purport of the Vedānta texts regarding Brahman as their object has been established;
and the fact that the Pradhāna is not based on the scriptures has been established.

In this regard, another objection is raised: it is not possible to establish that Brahman is the cause of birth and so forth, nor that there is a uniformity of purport (*gatisāmānya*) among the Vedānta texts concerning Brahman.
Why?
Because contradictions are observed.
For in each Vedānta text, a different account of creation is found due to the diversity of sequences and other details.
To illustrate: in some places, a creation beginning with space is recorded, as in "From the Self, space was produced" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).
In some places, the creation begins with fire and so forth, as in: "That [Being] created fire" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

In other places, it begins with the vital breath and so forth, as in: "He created the vital breath; from the vital breath, faith" (Praśna Upaniṣad 6.4). In yet other places, the origin of the worlds is recorded without any specific order: "He created these worlds."
"Water, the rays, death, and water" (AiU 4.2.1).

Likewise, in some places, creation preceded by non-existence is taught: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, existence was born" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), and "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; it became existent; it developed" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1).

In some places, a process preceded by "Being" (sat) is asserted by means of refuting the doctrine of non-existence (asat), beginning with: "Regarding this, some say that in the beginning this was indeed non-existent," and continuing: "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? He said: 'How could Being be born from non-being? In the beginning, my dear, this was only Being'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1–2).
In some places, the evolution of the world is said to have itself as its agent: "In the beginning, this was indeed unevolved; it was evolved by name and form alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).

Thus, because there are such diverse contradictions and because conceptual alternatives regarding a real entity are untenable, it is not logical that the Vedānta texts aim to determine the cause of the world.
Rather, it is more logical to accept another cause that is well-established through Smṛti and reasoning.

This being the case, we reply: although there is a discrepancy regarding the order and other details concerning the ether and the rest that are created in each Vedānta text, there is no discrepancy whatsoever regarding the Creator.
Why?
Because He is described as being exactly as stated [in all texts].

For just as that which is truly one—the omniscient, the Lord of all, the Self of all, the single without a second—is designated as the cause in one Vedānta text, so too is it designated in other Vedānta texts as well.
For example: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1).

Here, by the word "Knowledge" and by the subsequent statement regarding its being the subject of desire, the text characterizes Brahman as conscious; and by its independence from any other motive, it declares the Lord to be the cause.

By means of the supreme word "Self" (ātman) referring precisely to that [Brahman], and by way of entering inward through the successive layers of the sheaths beginning with the body, [the scripture] determined the innermost Self within all.

Furthermore, by the declaration of the desire for multiplicity— "May I become many, may I be born"— which refers to the Self, it declared the non-difference of the created modifications from their Creator.

Likewise, by the instruction regarding the creation of the entire world in the passage, "He created all this, whatever there is" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), [the text] declares the Creator to be without a second prior to creation.

Therefore, that very Brahman characterized as the cause which is known here is understood to have the same characteristics elsewhere as well: "In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only, without a second"; "It thought, 'May I be many... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1–3).
"May I be, may I procreate"—thus it emitted heat (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1, 3).
Likewise: "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking."

And [it says], "He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds'" (AiU 4.1.1, 2). Since such a collection of passages, which aims at defining the nature of the cause, is consistent in its meaning across every Vedānta text, whereas a discrepancy regarding the effect is observed—such as creation beginning with ether in some places and with fire in others—it follows that [the cause is one].

Nor can it be said that because there is disagreement regarding the subject of the effect, Brahman—the cause—which is understood without disagreement across all Vedānta texts, should be considered unintended; for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
And the Teacher will resolve even the disagreement concerning the subject of the effect in the sūtra: "The ether [is not produced], because it is not so heard" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.1).
Starting from this point, even if there were a contradiction regarding the effect, it would not be a subject to be established;
for this manifold expansion of creation and so forth is not intended to be established.
Indeed, no human goal (puruṣārtha) dependent upon that [expansion] is seen or heard of anywhere.

Nor can it be so imagined, because in various places it is understood that [these passages] form a single syntactical whole together with sentences concerning Brahman, as evidenced by their opening and concluding sections.
Furthermore, it shows that the detailed account of creation and so forth is for the purpose of realizing Brahman: "By means of food, my dear, as a sprout, [the waters...]"
"O gentle one, seeking the root through the sprout, seek the root through fire; O gentle one, seeking the root through fire, seek the root that is Being" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.4).

It is understood from this, as well as from the analogies of clay and so forth, that the detailed account of creation and so on is taught in order to declare the non-difference of the effect from its cause.
And thus those who know the tradition say: "The creation which has been described otherwise by means of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth..."
That is the means for entry; there is no difference whatsoever.
(Māṇḍūkya 3.15).
However, the fruit connected with the realization of Brahman is heard in scripture: "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (Taittirīya 2.1);
"The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya 7.1.3).
"Only by knowing That does one go beyond death" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8).

And this fruit is directly perceived when the realization of the Self as non-transmigrating occurs through the instruction "That thou art," because the transmigrating nature of the Self is thereby sublated. // 14 //

Furthermore, as for the contradiction regarding the cause that was shown in the passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*), that must be refuted.
To this, it is said:
[The word] "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes the lack of sequence as well.
The meaning of the word *ambhaḥ* is the heavenly world (*svargaloka*), which abounds in bodies consisting of water.
The intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*), pervaded by the rays of the sun, is *marīcayaḥ*.
*Maraḥ* refers to one subject to death, that is, a mortal (*martya*).
The meaning of the Vedic text is that water abounds in the world of Pātāla;
"prakriyā" means creation;
"tat" refers to that cause.
Some [hold that] the outsiders [are meant]; "by that object" means by the object which is Brahman;
"miṣat" means active.
Because they have non-contradictory meanings;
"by means of the sprout" refers to the effect;
the repetition "in this way and in that way" (anyathānyathā) is to be understood as an intensive distributive.
For the purpose of descent and for the birth of the knowledge of Brahman;
therefore, even if there is a difference in that [knowledge], there is no division in Brahman. There is no disagreement regarding the object of knowledge.
Because of the context of "drawing together" (*samākarṣāt*):
in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadvā idamagra āsīt*, Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7), it is not taught that a non-existent, soulless entity is the cause.
For it is said: "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent;
but if he knows that Brahman exists..."

Having determined that Brahman, characterized by existence, as the inner self through the series of sheaths beginning with the "food-sheath" (annamaya) by means of the refutation of the doctrine of non-existence in the passage, "The wise know him to be existing," and having drawn back to that same subject under discussion with the words, "He desired," and having caused the creation of the phenomenal world to be heard from Him,
and having concluded with, "That they call the Truth," [the text continues]: "Regarding this, there is also this verse."
To this effect, he cites this verse regarding that very subject of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*): "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*).

If, however, "non-existent" (*asat*) were intended here as being devoid of self-nature (*nirātmaka*), then by citing one thing while drawing in another, the statement would become incoherent. Therefore, since the word "existent" (*sat*) is generally well-known to refer to an entity differentiated by name and form (*nāmarūpa-vyākṛta-vastu*), Brahman—which was already existent—is figuratively described as having been "as if non-existent" prior to its manifestation, with reference to the absence of such differentiation.
This same interpretation applies here as well to the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1),
because of the subsequent attraction [of the term] by the words, "That was existent" (tat sad āsīt).

For if absolute non-existence were accepted, how could it be drawn back [into the fold] by the statement, "That indeed existed"? Furthermore, even in the passage, "On this point some say: in the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1), this presentation of the opinion of certain individuals is not intended to represent the view of another Śruti.
Since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible regarding an existing entity (*vastu*) in the same way it is impossible regarding an action (*kriyā*),

it should be understood that this [discussion] is intended solely to strengthen the correct position (*satpakṣa*) embraced by the sacred scripture (*śruti*), by means of setting forth and then refuting the false position (*asatpakṣa*) imagined by those of dull intellect.
"At that time, this was indeed unmanifest" (*taddhedaṃ tarhyavyākṛtamāsīt*, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7).
In this passage as well, the evolution of a world without a presiding director is not being described;
for by the phrase "He entered here unto the very tips of the nails," there is a pull toward the presiding director, since he is drawn in as having entered into the effects that have been evolved.

For if one were to accept an evolution without a presiding director, then by what [subject] would the pronoun "He" (saḥ)—which relies on the immediately preceding context—be drawn in as having entered into the effects?
Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that this conscious Self enters into the body;
for once it has entered, its consciousness is heard of in the passage: "seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, thinking with the mind.

Moreover, just as this world today, being differentiated by name and form, is differentiated under the supervision of a presiding agent, so too was it at the beginning of creation; this is understood.
Because it is impossible to conceive of a construction that contradicts what is perceived;
furthermore, another scriptural passage, "Entering with this living self, let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2),
shows that the manifestation of the world occurs precisely under the supervision of a conscious agent.

The verbal suffix in "vyākriyata" (it was manifested) is to be understood as a reflexive-passive form (*karmakartari*), even while the Supreme Lord exists as the agent, with reference to ease of action;
just as in the expression "the field is harvested by itself," even though the reaper exists.
Alternatively, this suffix is to be understood as being in the passive sense (*karmani*) with reference to an agent implied by the sense of the word.
Just as it is understood that "one goes to the village.
[In this context, *tat* refers to that Brahman;
*śloka* means a verse.]
The supervisor is the agent;
the eye is the seer,
the ear is the hearer.
The mind is called "thought" (*manas*).
At present, now.
Section on Bālāki, Sūtras 16–18.
Because of the mention of the world.
In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, it is heard: "O Bālāki, he who is the maker of these, whose work this is—he indeed is to be known" (Kauṣ. Brā. 4.19).
In this regard, there is a doubt as to whether the individual soul (jīva) is taught as the one to be known, or the chief vital breath (mukhya prāṇa), or the supreme self (paramātman).
What, then, is the prima facie position? That it is the vital breath (prāṇa).
Why?
Because of the scriptural statement, "Of whom this is the work," and because action characterized by motion has the vital breath (prāṇa) as its substratum,
and because the word "prāṇa" is seen in the supplementary passage, "Then it becomes onefold in this very prāṇa."

Furthermore, because the word "prāṇa" is well-known in its primary sense as the vital breath, Prāṇa is also the agent of those persons previously mentioned by Bālāki—such as "the person in the sun," "the person in the moon," and so forth—for these deities are specific states of Prāṇa.
As it is said: "Which one is the single deity? Prāṇa. He is Brahman; they call him 'Tyat'. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.9).
This is because it is well-known from another scriptural passage;
furthermore, it is the individual soul (jīva) that is taught here as the object to be known.
Of that soul also, action characterized by merit and demerit can be made known through the statement, "He whose this is the action."
He, moreover, as the enjoyer, is logically established as the agent of these persons who constitute the instruments of enjoyment;
furthermore, a characteristic mark of the individual soul (jīva) is perceived in the remainder of the passage.
For this reason, Ajātaśatru, desiring to awaken Bālāki—who had approached him for the sake of knowledge—intends to make known the agent of the persons who was introduced as the object to be known.

By addressing a sleeping man and observing that he does not hear the sounds of being addressed, it is demonstrated that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are not the experiencer; then, by his rising at the stroke of a staff, it is demonstrated that the living self (*jīva*), distinct from the vital breaths and so forth, is the experiencer.
Likewise, further on, the characteristic mark of the living self is understood: "Just as a lord enjoys [the wealth] with his own people, or as his own people [enjoy]..."
"Just as people eat from a merchant, even so this conscious self (prajñātman) eats by means of these selves; even so these selves eat this self" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣad 4.20).
Furthermore, because it is the sustainer of the vital breaths (prāṇabhṛt), it is appropriate for the individual soul (jīva) to be designated by the term "prāṇa."
Therefore, either the individual soul (jīva) or the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) must be understood here, and not the Supreme Lord, because no characteristic mark of Him is perceived.
This being the position reached, we reply: this creator of these persons must indeed be the Supreme Lord.
Why?
Because of the force of the context.
For here, Bālāki began a conversation with Ajātaśatru, saying, "I shall tell you about Brahman."
Having described several persons—such as those presiding over the sun and other deities—who possessed the view of the non-primary Brahman, he became silent.

Ajātaśatru, refuting him on the grounds that he had spoken of a non-primary Brahman, said, "Indeed, you have been speaking falsely to me; let me tell you of the Brahman," and introduced another person as the agent of those [deities] who was to be known.
If that [other person] were also one who possessed the view of a non-primary Brahman, the initial premise would be contradicted.
Therefore, this [Self] must necessarily be the Supreme Lord.
Furthermore, the agency of these persons cannot be conceived as independent of the Supreme Lord.
Moreover, the phrase "he whose work this is" does not refer to action characterized by physical movement or action characterized by merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*).
Because neither of those two is the subject under discussion,
and because they have not been mentioned;
nor is this a designation of the persons.
This is because they are designated as "the agent of these persons"; furthermore,
due to the discrepancy in gender and number, this is not a designation of the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to act) as having the person as its object, nor of the fruit of the action,
since both of those are already included by the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) itself.
By process of elimination, the entire world, being present before the eyes, is indicated by the pronoun *etac-chabda* (this).
And at that very moment, the world is the object (*karman*) because it is "being made.
But surely, the world is neither under discussion (*aprakṛta*) nor has it been previously mentioned (*asaṃśabdita*)?
This is true;

nevertheless, since no specific qualification is mentioned, it is understood that this designation refers to any object present by virtue of its common presence, rather than to any particular [object],
because there is an absence of the presence of any specific [qualification].

And since, in the preceding [passage], the world itself—without being qualified by the specific mention of those persons who constitute a single part of that world—is understood to be what is referred to here;
this is what is meant: "He who is the creator of these persons who constitute a single part of the world"—what is the purpose of this qualification?

The phrase "for whom the entire world without exception is the object of action" uses the word "or" (*vā*) to exclude the notion of agency limited to only a single part [of the world]. The specific qualification is employed to demonstrate that those persons whom Bālāki identified as Brahman are, in fact, not Brahman.

Thus, according to the method of the Brahmin and the wandering ascetic, the creator of the world is taught as something to be known through both general and specific characteristics. Furthermore, the Supreme Lord is determined in all the Vedāntas to be the creator of the entire world. (16) [FN:
This world is whose work.]
By the etymological derivation "that which is being done," the meaning is "the effect" (kārya);
that is the vital breath (prāṇa).
"Tyat" means the remote (parokṣa).
The construction is as follows: because it awakens the individual soul (jīva), therefore there exists the waking up of one who was asleep, which is a characteristic mark of the jīva.
This is like the statement, "Brāhmaṇas are to be fed, and the wandering mendicant [is also to be fed]," where, through both the general and the particular, all nearby Brāhmaṇas are included.
If it is argued that this is not so on account of the characteristics of the jīva and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), that has already been explained. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17)

Therefore, that which was stated—that because of the marks of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the marks of the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) found in the supplementary passage, it is logical to grasp one of those two here and not the Supreme Lord—must be refuted. To this it is replied:

this has already been refuted in [Brahma-sūtra] 1.1.31: "Not so, because of the threefoldness of meditation; because [the other two] are resorted to elsewhere; and because of the connection with that [Supreme Lord] here."
For if this were the case, three kinds of meditation would result here: meditation on the individual soul (jīva), meditation on the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa), and meditation on Brahman.
And this is not logical;
for it is understood from both the opening and the conclusion that this passage has Brahman as its subject matter.
In that regard, it has already been shown that the opening statement has Brahman as its object;

likewise, the concluding statement is seen to have Brahman as its object because of the mention of an unsurpassed fruit: "Having cast off all evils, he who knows this attains the preeminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings."
But if this is so, then this passage too would be determined by the very determination of the Pratardana passage;
it is not so determined,
because the statement "and whose work this is" was not established there as having Brahman for its object.
Therefore, the doubt here concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) is again dispelled.
Furthermore, the word *prāṇa* is seen to refer to Brahman in the passage: "For the mind, my dear, is fastened to the *prāṇa*" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.2).
Even the characteristic marks of the individual soul must be interpreted as intending non-difference, since the opening and concluding sections of the text concern Brahman. // 17 //

The distinction is as follows: *śraiṣṭhya* is the excellence of qualities; *ādhipatya* is the state of being a ruler or controller; and *svārājya* is the state of being independent or not subject to another's control.
But Jaimini [holds that the reference to the individual soul] is for another purpose, on account of both the question and the explanation; and thus some [teachers] also [maintain].
Furthermore, one should not dispute here whether this scriptural statement has the individual soul as its primary subject or Brahman as its primary subject;
for the teacher Jaimini considers that the reference to the individual soul in this passage is for the sake of understanding Brahman, being intended for another purpose.
Why?
Because of the question and the explanation.

First, the question—by means of awakening the person in deep sleep—having awakened the individual soul (jīva) as distinct from the vital breaths and so forth, further concerns a subject distinct from that individual soul.

It is seen [in scripture]: "O Bālāki, where was this person sleeping? Where did he become [this]? Whence did he come? (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 4.19). The reply as well begins: "When, being asleep, he sees no dream at all, then he becomes one with this very prāṇa," and so on, up to: "From this self, the vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge according to their respective locations; from the vital breaths, the gods; from the gods..."
And as it is said: "The worlds" (Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa 4.20).
Furthermore, at the time of deep sleep, the individual soul attains oneness with the supreme Brahman;
and from the supreme Brahman, the world consisting of the vital breaths and so forth is born—this is the established doctrine of the Vedānta.

Therefore, it is understood that where this individual soul (jīva) has its state of sleep— characterized by non-cognition and transparency, which is its own nature devoid of specific cognitions produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)— and from which its departure consists in the loss of that [state], it is that Supreme Self (paramātman) who is proclaimed here as the object to be known.

Moreover, in this very dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, certain followers of the Vājasaneya branch clearly designate the individual soul by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) and then teach the Supreme Self as distinct from that, in response to the question: "Where was this person consisting of consciousness then? Whence did he come? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.16).
Even in the reply, it says: "He rests in that space which is within the heart.
Furthermore, the word *ākāśa* is used for the Supreme Self in the passage, "In this, there is a small inner space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.1).

And since the text declares that "all these selves issue forth from the Self," thereby teaching the emergence of the conditioned selves from something else, it is understood that they teach the Supreme Self alone as the cause.

The teaching that [the Self] is distinct from the vital breaths and so forth is further reinforced by the awakening of the person in deep sleep, even though the vital breaths were not previously created [as separate entities]. [Notes:
"Lack of consciousness" (*niḥsaṃbodhatā*) means being devoid of specific cognition. "Transparency" (*svacchatā*) means being devoid of the impurity of distraction (*vikṣepa*).
6. The Section on the Connection of the Sentence (Vākyānvayādhikaraṇa) / Sūtras 19–22:
On account of the connection of the sentence.
(BBs 1.4.19) In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, it is recited—beginning with "Verily, not for the sake of the husband" and so forth—[ending with] "not..."

"Verily, it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear; it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear. Verily, the Self, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
Verily, by seeing, hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing the Self, all this is known."

(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upani�sad 4.5.6). Regarding this, a doubt arises: is it the individual self (*vijñānātman*) alone that is taught here in the form of being "that which is to be seen," "that which is to be heard," and so forth, or rather the supreme self (*paramātman*)?
But whence does this doubt arise?
It arises because the teaching appears to concern the individual self, since the passage begins with the experiencer indicated by what is dear.
What, then, is the established position?
That it is an instruction concerning the self as consciousness.
Why?
Because of the force of the context:
for the husband, wife, children, wealth, and so forth—the entire world which is an object of enjoyment—become dear only because they exist for the sake of the Self.
Thus, having first introduced the Self as the enjoyer indicated by what is dear, this [text] subsequently teaches the seeing and other attributes of that very Self.

To what other self could this belong? Even in the middle [of the text], it is said: "This great being, infinite and boundless, consisting of nothing but a mass of consciousness, arises from these elements and perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death"—referring precisely to that very great being which is to be perceived as the subject.
By stating that [the Self] arises from the elements in the form of the conscious self (*vijñānātman*), the text shows that this very conscious self is what is to be seen.
Likewise, by concluding with the word "knower" in the phrase, "But by what, my dear, should one know the knower? it shows that it is indeed the conscious self that is taught here.
Therefore, the claim that through the knowledge of the Self all is known must be understood as figurative, since the entire range of objects of experience exists for the sake of the enjoyer.
This being the case, we reply: this is indeed an instruction regarding the Supreme Self.
Why?
Because of the connection of the sentence.
Indeed, when this statement is examined in its proper sequence from beginning to end, its constituent parts are seen to be connected with reference to the Supreme Self.

How so? That is now demonstrated: having heard from Yājñavalkya that "there is no hope for immortality through wealth," she, desiring immortality, said, "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which the Blessed One knows. Thus, for her who was seeking immortality—
Yājñavalkya teaches this knowledge of the Self to Maitreyī;
and the declarations of Śruti and Smṛti state that there is no immortality apart from the knowledge of the Supreme Self.
Likewise, the statement that through the knowledge of the Self all is known cannot be understood in its primary sense unless it refers to the knowledge of the Supreme Cause.
Nor can this [statement] be regarded as figurative, because,

having asserted that "by the knowledge of the Self, all is known," the text immediately thereafter establishes that very point with the passage beginning, "Brahman would desert him who sees Brahman elsewhere than in the Self," and so forth;
for [the text speaks of] him who perceives the world— consisting of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and so on— as existing independently, apart from the Self.

By negating the perception of difference—on the grounds that it is precisely this world of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, when viewed through false vision, that one rejects—the text introduces the non-difference of the entire aggregate of things from the Self, stating: "All this is what this Self is.
This is further supported by the analogies of the drum and other instruments (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.8).
He confirms that very non-difference [of the individual self from Brahman] by means of such passages as,
"This Rigveda is the breath of this great Being" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.11).
By explaining how the Self under discussion is the cause of the manifold expansion of names, forms, and actions, he leads us to understand this very Supreme Self.

In the very same way, even in the section concerning the "single path" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.12), the text leads one to understand this very Supreme Self by explaining that the single path of the phenomenal world—along with its objects, senses, and internal organs—is without interior or exterior, entirely a mass of consciousness.
Therefore, it is understood that this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers exclusively to the Supreme Self. // 19 //
As for what was further stated— that because the opening is indicated by something dear, this instruction regarding seeing and so forth refers only to the *vijñānātman*— to this we reply:
[this is] "this" (the direct object).
Great and undivided;
real and true;
infinite and eternal.
If it is shoreless, all-pervading, and of a single essence—
the knower and the agent of cognition—
it cannot be attained by wealth, that is, by ritual action accomplished through it.
"There is no other path," "Not by action," and so forth are the declarations of the Śruti;
"Liberation comes from knowledge alone," and so forth are the declarations of the Smṛti.
It rejects [them] and causes one to fall away from the path to the highest good.
"Name" refers to the Ṛgveda and so forth; "sacrifice" (iṣṭa) and "oblation" (huta) refer to ritual action.
"And this world" refers to form (*rūpa*). "Process" (*prakriyā*) means context (*prakaraṇa*).
Āśmarathya holds that it is a mark (*liṅga*) for the establishment of the proposition (*pratijñā*). (BBs 1.4.20)
There is a declaration here: "When the Self is known, all this becomes known," and "All this is what this Self is.
This indicative mark—the mention of the Self, who is indicated by what is dear, as being that which is to be seen and so forth—points toward the fulfillment of that declaration.

For if the individual self (vijñānātman) were different from the Supreme Self (paramātman), then even upon the knowledge of the Supreme Self, the individual self would not be known; thus, the declaration that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be contradicted.

Therefore, the teacher Āśmarathya maintains that the introductory statement is made by way of the non-difference between the individual self (vijñānātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) for the purpose of establishing the thesis.
"Auḍulomi [holds that] this is because [the self] will depart from its state of being thus.

Master Auḍulomi considers that this introduction by way of non-difference is possible for the individual self (vijñānātman) itself— which has become turbid through contact with the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and intellect, and which has not yet attained clarity through the practice of means such as knowledge and meditation— as it departs from the aggregate of the body and so forth, and attains identity with the Supreme Self (paramātman).
And scripture says thus: "This serene being, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3).

And in another place, it makes known that name and form, though residing in the individual soul, are cast off by means of the illustration of rivers: "As rivers flowing along disappear into the ocean, losing their names and forms;
so the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine Person, who is higher than the high" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).

Just as in the world rivers, having abandoned their own names and forms which constitute their very basis, enter the ocean, so too the individual soul (jīva), having abandoned its own names and forms which constitute its very basis, approaches the Supreme Person; for this is the meaning understood there in order to maintain the correspondence between the illustration and the thing illustrated. 21.
[FN: "Arising" (samutthāna) means departing (utkrānti).]
"Because of the abiding [of the Self]," says Kāśakṛtsna.

The teacher Kāśakṛtsna considers this introductory statement regarding non-difference to be appropriate because this very Supreme Self abides even in the form of the individual cognizing self (*vijñānātman*).
And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Entering with this living self (*jīva*), let me manifest names and forms" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2).
Thus, this kind of passage shows that the Supreme Self alone exists in the state of the individual soul (*jīva*);
and there are also Vedic verses of this kind, such as: "The Wise One, having fashioned all forms and made their names, sits calling them by those names" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7).
Furthermore, in the accounts of the creation of fire and the other elements, no separate creation of the individual soul (jīva) is heard of,
such that the soul could be something other than the supreme Self and merely a modification (vikāra) thereof.

The view of the teacher Kāśakṛtsna is that the individual soul (jīva) is the unmodified Supreme Lord and not something other than Him. As for Āśmarathya, although he intends the non-difference of the individual soul from the Supreme, it is understood from his statement regarding the "fulfillment of the initial proposition" (*pratijñāsiddhi*)— which implies a state of dependence— that he accepts some degree of the relationship between cause and effect.

In the view of Auḍulomi, however, difference and non-difference are clearly understood as being dependent upon different states; therein, the doctrine of Kāśakṛtsna is understood to be in accordance with the Śruti, because it conforms to the meaning intended to be established by such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (Tat tvam asi). This being the case, immortality is logically possible through the knowledge of that [identity].

For if the individual soul (jīva) were admitted to be of the nature of a modification (vikāra), then since a modification would necessarily dissolve into its primal source (prakṛti) at the time of cosmic dissolution, immortality could not be attained through knowledge of that [Self].
Furthermore, since name and form cannot reside in the soul itself, name and form are attributed to the soul only by way of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

For this very reason, even the birth of the soul which is sometimes heard of in scripture through the illustration of sparks from a fire must be understood as being dependent solely on the limiting adjuncts.

As for what was also said— that by showing the emergence of the very great being under discussion from the elements in the form of the cognitional self (*vijñānātman*), the text demonstrates that this very cognitional self is the object to be seen— in that case as well, these same three sūtras are to be applied:
"Āśmarathya [holds that it is] a sign for the fulfillment of the initial proposition."
This was the proposition made here: "When the Self is known, everything becomes known," and "All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6).

And this has been established, because the entire manifold of names, forms, and actions originates from one and dissolves into one, and because the non-difference between cause and effect has been demonstrated through the analogies of the drum and so forth.

The teacher Āśmarathya maintains that this sign— namely, the statement that the Great Being, who is to be seen, arises from the elements in the form of the conscious self (vijñānātman)— indicates the fulfillment of that very proposition;
for only when there is non-difference can the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one be logically established as the stated proposition.
"Auḍulomi holds that [the identity] is due to the future departure from this state;

for when the conscious self (vijñānātman), having become serene through the power of knowledge, meditation, and so forth, departs [from the body], its unification with the supreme Self becomes possible, and thus this declaration of non-difference is made.
"Kāśakṛtsna holds that it is because of the abiding [of the individual soul within the Supreme]."
The teacher Kāśakṛtsna maintains that this declaration of non-difference is appropriate, because this very Supreme Self exists even in the form of the individual cognizing self (*vijñānātman*).

But [an objection is raised]: "This is a statement of annihilation, for it says, 'Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12). How, then, can this be a statement of non-difference?"
This is not a fault;

this statement regarding destruction is intended to mean the destruction of specific cognition (viśeṣavijñāna), not the annihilation of the self (ātman). For, having been questioned by the words, "Right here, O Blessed One, you have bewildered me; there is no consciousness after death," the Śruti itself [provides] another meaning.
Because it has been shown: "Verily, I say nothing bewildering; this Self, indeed, is imperishable and of an indestructible nature, but its association with the elements (mātrās) occurs.
What is meant by this is that this Self, a mass of consciousness, is indeed eternally immutable, and there is no possibility of its annihilation.
However, through knowledge, there comes about a non-association with the "measures" (mātrās) characterized by the elements and the senses, which are produced by ignorance.
And because of the absence of association, there is an absence of the specific cognition under discussion; thus it was said, "After departing, there is no consciousness.

As for what was also stated—that because the conclusion is made using a word denoting an agent, namely "vijñātāram" ("the knower"), this must be understood as referring to the cognizing self alone—this is not so.
That too must be refuted by the very view of Kāśakṛtsna.

Furthermore, beginning with the passage, "For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.13), the scripture elaborates upon that very same specific cognition—characterized by seeing and so forth—which pertains to the sphere of ignorance; then, [continuing] with "But where for him... [it proceeds].

By the passage beginning with "When everything has become the Self alone, through what and whom should one see?", [the text] declares the absence of that specific cognition characterized by seeing and so forth within the sphere of knowledge.
Furthermore, having raised the doubt that one might still cognize the Self even in the absence of objects, it says: "O, by what should one cognize the cognizer?"

Furthermore, since the sentence is intended to establish the absence of specific cognition, it is understood that the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) alone is indicated by the agentive suffix *tṛc* (the suffix *-tṛ*), based on its prior state of being an agent.
It has already been shown previously that the position of Kāśakṛtsna is supported by scripture.

Therefore, this meaning must be accepted by all proponents of Vedānta: the distinction between the individual consciousness and the Supreme Self is not ultimate, but is caused by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body, which are fashioned from name and form presented by ignorance (*avidyā*).
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1);
"All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2);
"All this is indeed Brahman" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.11).

"All this is what this Self is" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.6); "There is no other seer than He" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.23); "There is nothing else besides Him that sees" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.11).
From such scriptural passages as these,
and from the Smṛtis such as "Vāsudeva is all" (Gītā 7.19) and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O Bhārata" (Gītā 13.2).

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The Supreme Lord abides equally in all beings" (Gītā 13.27), and because of the censure of the perception of difference: "He who thinks 'He is one and I am another' does not know; he is like an animal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).
From such passages as, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19),
and "Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25).
Thus, because all modifications are denied in the Self,
otherwise it would be impossible for those seeking liberation to possess an uncontradicted realization, and it would also be impossible for that realization to be well-ascertained in its meaning.
For it is held that consciousness which has the Self as its object is free from contradiction and removes all desires,
according to the Śruti: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the knowledge of the Vedānta" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6).
And as it is said: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśā Upaniṣad 7).
Furthermore, this is supported by the traditional definition of the one whose wisdom is steady (Gītā 2.54).

And when the perfect vision (samyagdarśana) regarding the oneness of the individual self (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) is established, [the distinction between them] is merely a difference in names, such that the individual self is called the supreme self.

The insistence on the subject of the distinction between selves—such as "this knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is different from the Supreme Self" and "this Supreme Self is different from the knower of the field"—is useless.
For this Self is one; it is designated in many ways merely through differences in name.
Indeed, [the scripture declares]: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."
Regarding the statement, "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1), this was said with reference to a certain single cave;
and there is nothing other than Brahman that is hidden in the cave.

Because it is heard in scripture that "having created that, he entered into that very thing" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6), the creator himself enters; those who insist otherwise, by contradicting the meaning of the Vedānta, obstruct right vision itself, which is the gateway to the highest good.
They imagine that liberation is something produced and impermanent, and this does not accord with reason. // 22 // [Note:
*dhīra* means the Omniscient One.]

Having discerned— that is, having fashioned— forms, both moving and stationary, which are bodies, and having assigned names to them, he enters into them, addressing them and performing such acts as speaking;
"delusion" refers to speech that causes delusion.

"Non-perishing" (*anucchitti*) means non-destruction; that which possesses this quality is "of a non-perishing nature" (*anucchittidharman*). [The text says] "other than some state of the living being" (*jīvasthānāt*);
however, there are those such as Āśmarathya and others.
The Section on Primordial Matter (Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa). Sūtras 23–27.
"And [Brahman is] the material cause, because there is no contradiction with the initial proposition and the illustrative examples.

(BS 1.4.23) It was stated that just as Dharma is to be investigated because it is the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), so too Brahman is to be investigated because it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
And Brahman has been defined by the sūtra, "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2).

Since that definition applies equally to being both the material cause— as clay is to jars and gold ornaments, or as gold is to golden vessels— and the efficient cause— as the potter is to the jar or the goldsmith to the ornament, a doubt arises.
Furthermore, what is the nature of Brahman’s causality?
In this regard, it first appears that it must be solely an efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa).
Why?
Because the scripture declares that [Brahman's] agency is preceded by reflection;
for Brahman's agency is understood to be preceded by reflection, as in: "He reflected" (Praśna 6.3) and "He created the vital breath" (Praśna 6.4).
This is known from such scriptural passages as these.
Furthermore, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in efficient causes such as potters and the like.
Moreover, in the world, the accomplishment of the fruit of an action is seen to be preceded by multiple causal factors.
And that same principle is applicable even to the Primordial Creator;
for his status as a Lord is well-established.

Indeed, in the case of lords such as kings and Vaivasvata, it is understood that they possess only the status of an efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*); likewise, it is appropriate to understand that the Supreme Lord also possesses only the status of an efficient cause.
Moreover, this world, which is the effect, is observed to possess parts, to be insentient, and to be impure; therefore,
its cause must also be of a similar nature, because we observe a correspondence between cause and effect.

Furthermore, Brahman is not understood to possess such characteristics, on account of scriptural passages such as, "It is partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19). By the method of elimination, one must accept that the material cause other than Brahman is something characterized by impurity and other such qualities, as established in the Smṛtis.
Because the scriptural statement regarding Brahman as the cause culminates in its being merely the efficient cause (*nimittatva*).
This being the position reached, we reply: Brahman must be accepted as both the material cause (*prakṛti*) and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*);
it is not merely the efficient cause alone.
Why?
Because there is no contradiction between the thesis and the example;
thus, the thesis and the example are not contradicted by what is heard from the scriptures.
The proposition is as follows: "Have you ever asked for that instruction by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.2).
In this context, it is understood that when one thing is known, everything—even that which was previously unknown—becomes known.
And this universal knowledge is possible only through the knowledge of the material cause, because the effect is not distinct from its material cause.
However, there is no non-distinction of the effect from its efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), because in the world we observe the carpenter to be distinct from the palace [he builds].

Furthermore, the illustrative example—"O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth"—refers to the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
Thus it is handed down in tradition:
"By means of a single iron gem, all that is made of iron would be known"; and "By means of a single nail-cutter, all that is made of black metal would be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4–6).
Likewise elsewhere: "Venerable sir, when what is known does all this become known? (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.1.2).
This is the proposition (*pratijñā*);
"Just as herbs arise from the earth" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.7) is the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Likewise, there is the proposition: "When the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known.

And there is the illustration: "Just as when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp the external sounds, but by grasping the drum or the beating of the drum, the sound is grasped" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6–7).

Thus, according to the possibility in each Vedānta text, the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should be understood as establishing [Brahman] as the material cause (*prakṛti*).

As for this ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the phrase "from which indeed these beings are born" (*yato vā imāni bhūtāni jāyante*), it should be seen as denoting the *apādāna* specifically characterized as a material cause, because of the specific grammatical rule: "The source of the agent of birth is the material cause" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*, Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.30).
Its status as the efficient cause (nimittatva) must be understood from the absence of any other presiding agent.

For just as in the world, material causes such as clay or gold proceed to act depending upon presiding agents such as potters or goldsmiths, it is not so with Brahman; since Brahman exists as the material cause, no other presiding agent is required, because of the restrictive declaration that "prior to creation, there was only one, without a second."
The absence of another controller should also be understood as having been established precisely through the non-contradiction of the proposition and the example.

For if one were to admit a controller distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*), there would again be a contradiction of both the proposition and the example, because it is impossible for all cognitions to arise from a single cognition.

Therefore, due to the absence of another controller, the Self possesses the status of an agent (*kartṛtva*); and due to the absence of another material cause, it possesses the status of primordial nature (*prakṛtitva*). // 23 //
And from what [source] could there be agency and material causality for the Self?
[Note: *vimarśaḥ* means doubt;
*niṣkalam* means partless.]
It is devoid of activity and immovable, peaceful and unchanging, faultless, and with all defects cast away.
"Loha" means gold.

"Nakhanikṛntana" refers either to a nail-cutter made of black iron or to a lump of iron. Alternatively, it means a specific sound related by way of being produced from that which produces the beating of a drum; this is the meaning of "viśeṣaśabda" (specific sound).
And because of the teaching of desire (*abhidhyā*).

The teaching of desire—namely, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'"—indicates that the Self is both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the material cause (*prakṛti*).
In this context, it is understood that [the Self] is the agent because its activity is preceded by volition and proceeds with independence.

Furthermore, because the meditation on becoming many—expressed as "May I be many"—has the inner self (pratyagātman) as its object, it is understood that [the Self] is the material cause (prakṛti). Moreover, this is directly stated in both [scriptural] traditions. (BBs 1.4.25) *Note: Abhidhyā means the volition for creation.*
This is a further argument for [Brahman] being the material cause:

for this reason as well, Brahman is the material cause, because both the origin and the dissolution of all things are recorded in scripture as having Brahman itself as their direct cause: "All these beings, indeed, arise from Ākāśa alone."
"They merge back into space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.9.1).
For it is well known that whatever originates from something and into which it dissolves, that is its material cause;
just as the earth is the material cause of rice, barley, and so forth.
By stating "directly from [it]" and "directly," [the text] shows the non-appropriation of any other material cause, as expressed in the phrase "from space alone.
Furthermore, the dissolution of an effect is never observed to occur elsewhere than in its material cause. (25) [FN:
*Abhyuccaya* means an additional reason.]
Because of its own self-creation through transformation.
For this reason as well, Brahman is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*); because in the exposition of Brahman, it is said: "It made itself by itself" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).
Thus he demonstrates the self's state of being an object and its state of being an agent:
"the self" indicates the state of being an object, and "he made himself" indicates the state of being an agent.
But how can it be possible for that which already exists as an established entity and is fixed in its status as an agent to be something that is being produced?
We reply: "Because of transformation.
For although the Self is already established, it transforms itself into a specific nature of modification.
Furthermore, transformation in the form of modification is observed in primal materials such as clay;
and by the qualification "itself," the independence from any other instrumental cause is also understood.
Alternatively, "pariṇāmāt" may be treated as a separate aphorism.

The meaning of this [passage] is as follows: for this reason also, the source-material is Brahman, because the transformation of Brahman itself into the form of its modifications is recorded in grammatical coordination [with it]:
"It became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).
"By [the words] beginning with 'ityādinā' (26). [Note:
*Sat* refers to the three manifest elements (*pratyakṣa*), while *tyat* refers to the two unmanifest elements (*parokṣa*).]
That which can be defined is exemplified by a jar and the like; that which cannot be defined is exemplified by the form of a pigeon and the like.
For it is also described as having a source (yoni). BBs_1,4.27.

For this reason as well, Brahman is recited in the Vedāntas as the source (*yoni*) which is *prakṛti*: "The agent, the Lord, the Person, the Brahman-source" (Muṇḍaka 3.1.3), and "that source of beings which the wise perceive" (Muṇḍaka 1.1.6).
Furthermore, the word *yoni* is understood in common worldly usage to denote *prakṛti*, as in: "The earth is the source of herbs and trees."
Even in the case of the female womb, there exists the status of being the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) with respect to the embryo by way of the aperture of the [male] organ.
Furthermore, the word *yoni* is seen in some instances to denote "place," as in: "O Indra, a place has been prepared for you to sit" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.104.1).
However, in this context, based on the remainder of the passage, it is understood to denote "material cause," as in: "Just as a spider emits and withdraws [its thread]" (*Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad* 1.1.7).
From such passages as these,
Brahman’s status as the material cause is established.

As for the further objection that was raised— that in the world, agency preceded by deliberation is observed only in efficient causes such as potters and the like, and not in material causes, and so forth— [this is now addressed].
To that it is replied: one must not proceed here as one does in the world. For this matter is not accessible through inference;
rather, because this matter is accessible through scripture, it must be understood here exactly according to the scripture.
We have already stated that the word [Īśvara] indicates that the Lord is the primordial material cause (prakṛti);
furthermore, we shall address all of this in detail later. // 27 // [FN:
The agent, who possesses the power of action.]
The Lord as the controller,
the Person who is inward-facing,
and Brahman as the plenum.
"Yoni" means the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
O Indra, this "yoni"—that is, a place or seat—has been prepared by me for your "niṣada," meaning for your sitting down.
8. Section on the Exposition of All [Mantras]. Sūtra 28.
By this, all [theories] have been explained, have been explained.

Starting from the sūtra "Because of seeing, [Brahman is] not that which is not based on scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.5), the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause has been repeatedly raised as an objection and refuted by the sūtras themselves.
For certain fallacious marks that appear to support that position flash before the eyes of those of dull intellect upon a superficial reading of the Vedānta texts.
Furthermore, because it accepts the non-difference of cause and effect, this view is closely related to the doctrine of the Vedānta;
it has also been adopted by certain authors of Dharma-sūtras, such as Devala and others, in their own works.
Therefore, he has exerted great effort in refuting that [theory], but not so much in refuting the theories of atoms and other such causes;
for those too must be refuted because they stand as counter-positions to the doctrine of Brahman as the cause.
Furthermore, some Vedic indicative mark might appear, at first glance, to support even those [other theories] for those of dull intellect.

Therefore, according to the maxim of "defeating the chief wrestler," he extends [the argument] by stating: "By this collection of logical arguments for refuting the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause, all doctrines of atoms and other causes are also to be understood as explained by way of being refuted;
for like Pradhāna, they too lack scriptural authority and are contradicted by scripture."
The repetition of the word "explained" (vyākhyātā) by means of these two words indicates the completion of the chapter. // 28 //
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the first chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, the worshipful Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda.
Thus ends the first chapter, named "Samanvaya," in the Śrīmad-Brahmasūtra-Śāṅkarabhāṣya. // 1 //
